case_title: Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Ltd. vs. Kalvakolanu Murali Krishna Prasad RP for Vaksh Steels Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: IA No. 361/2021 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 177/2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Ltd. (Applicant/Appellant/Operational Creditor); Kalvakolanu Murali Krishna Prasad (Resolution Professional for Vaksh Steels Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor); Committee of Creditors of Vaksh Steels Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent 2); SVSS Commercial Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant/Respondent 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Electricity supply by the appellant utility to the Corporate Debtor Vaksh Steels Pvt. Ltd. resulting in outstanding electricity dues claimed during CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of electricity consumption charges leading to operational debt claims collated in CIRP; the CoC with 100% voting share approved a revised Resolution Plan by SVSS Commercial Pvt. Ltd. on 04.01.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Hyderabad) approved the Resolution Plan on 31.01.2020 in IA No. 69/2020 in CP(IB)/499/7/HDB/2018. The 30-day statutory limitation under Section 61(2) expired on 01.03.2020, and the condonable 15-day period expired on 16.03.2020. The appeal was filed on 28.05.2021 without a condonation application, and IA No. 361/2021 was subsequently filed on 04.08.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email correspondences of 18.06.2019 and 02.01.2020 from the Appellant's email address proving active participation and knowledge of CIRP; application for certified copy made only on 30.04.2021; Certified copy received on 30.04.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved the Resolution Plan on 31.01.2020. The Appellant filed the appeal before NCLAT Chennai on 28.05.2021 after a delay of approximately 451 days, seeking benefit of the Supreme Court's Suo Motu COVID-19 limitation extension orders.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appellant seeking to challenge an order approving a Resolution Plan under Section 61 of the IBC is entitled to the benefit of the Supreme Court's Suo Motu COVID-19 limitation extension where the principal statutory limitation period of 30 days expired prior to 15.03.2020 and no application for a certified copy was made within that period. 2. Whether an attendee or member of the CoC with email notice of proceedings can claim exemption from limitation as a 'person aggrieved' who was allegedly not a formal party to the petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant under Section 61 of the IBC who fails to apply for a certified copy of the impugned order within the initial statutory limitation period of 30 days cannot claim the benefit of limitation exclusion or extension under judicial COVID-19 relief directives if the primary limitation period expired prior to the effective date of the COVID-19 moratorium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'person aggrieved' in Section 61(1) of the IBC is wider than 'party to the proceedings' and encompasses any person whose legal interests are affected; such persons remain strictly bound by the mandatory timeline in Section 61(2) and cannot plead absence of formal party status to bypass the obligation to apply for a certified copy within 30 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Section 114 of the Evidence Act, undisputed email communications originating from and sent to the appellant establish deemed knowledge of CIRP proceedings, creating an estoppel by conduct against subsequent pleas of lack of knowledge. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The principal 30-day limitation period expired on 01.03.2020, well before the Supreme Court's COVID-19 limitation cutoff on 15.03.2020; since the appellant did not apply for a certified copy until 30.04.2021, the appeal is barred by limitation and cannot be condoned.
operative_order: IA No. 361/2021 for condonation of delay is dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 177/2021 is dismissed as time-barred. Connected pending Interlocutory Applications stand closed.
summary: Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Ltd. appealed an order dated 31.01.2020 of NCLT Hyderabad approving the Resolution Plan of Vaksh Steels Pvt. Ltd., filing the appeal on 28.05.2021 along with a delay condonation application (IA No. 361/2021) citing Supreme Court Suo Motu COVID-19 extension orders and lack of party status. NCLAT Chennai held that as a 'person aggrieved' with deemed knowledge via email correspondences, the appellant was required to apply for a certified copy within the statutory 30 days. Since that 30-day period expired on 01.03.2020 (before the 15.03.2020 COVID cutoff) and the certified copy was applied for only on 30.04.2021, the appeal was time-barred. The delay condonation application and the appeal were dismissed.

case_title: Major Atul Dev (Retd.) & Ors. vs. Union of India, MCA Through Regional Director (North Region) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Major Atul Dev (Retd.) and 6 other permanent members of Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited; Respondent 1 is the Union of India, MCA; Respondent 2 is Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited; Respondents 3 to 17 are former General Committee members; Respondent 18 is Col. Ashish Khanna (Retd.), ex-Secretary. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Delhi Gymkhana Club Ltd., incorporated on 14.07.1913 under Section 26 of the 1913 Act (Section 8 company), holds 27.03 acres of prime government land at 2 Safdarjung Road, New Delhi on perpetual lease dated 20.02.1928 at a nominal rent for promoting sports and pastimes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory and managerial default involving collection of hundreds of crores in unauthorized non-AoA registration fees, additional fees, and penalties from waiting-list applicants while expending merely 2.77% of total revenue on sports, and using deposits to enrich the club and existing members. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MCA ordered inspection under Section 206(4) on 16.03.2016; Inspection Report dated 31.07.2019 submitted; Supplementary Inspection Report submitted on 03.03.2020; Regional Director recommendation sent on 04.03.2020; Competent Authority sanctioned prosecution and petition on 18.03.2020; CP No. 71/241-242/PB/2020 filed on 22.04.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease deed dated 20.02.1928, statutory inspection report of July 2019 and 4,000-page supplementary inspection report of March 2020 proving only 2.77% expenditure on sports, massive catering and liquor expenditure, unauthorized creation of Green Card and UCP categories (up to 5,333 holders) fostering 'parivaar-vaad' hereditary access, 36-year waiting lists for non-dependent applicants, and forensic audit reports. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union of India filed CP No. 71/241-242/PB/2020 under Sections 241(2) and 242. On 01.04.2022, NCLT Principal Bench allowed the petition, superseding the General Committee and permitting the Central Government to nominate 15 Directors to restructure the Club. Appellants challenged this final order before NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Central Government satisfied the statutory prerequisites under Section 241(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 regarding formation of opinion and demonstration of affairs being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest. 2. Whether the affairs of a private Section 8 members' club operating on leased public land touch upon 'public interest'. 3. Whether the NCLT's order superseding the General Committee and nominating 15 Directors constituted an impermissible perpetual delegation of judicial power.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 8 non-profit company established for charitable/utility objectives that occupies public land on concessional terms owes a fiduciary duty to align its conduct with its charter; diverting resources away from primary statutory objects and maintaining exclusive hereditary privileges at public expense constitutes conduct prejudicial to public interest, justifying government intervention under Section 241(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 241(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, the formation of opinion is a subjective administrative satisfaction that is legally valid if supported by demonstrable material circumstances; 'public interest' is wide and embraces the operation and management of Section 8 companies functioning on public trust resources. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comprehensive statutory inspection reports detailing financial irregularities, collection of deposits ultra vires the Articles of Association, and systemic departure from core objects establish prima facie and conclusive grounds of mismanagement and prejudice to public interest. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Central Government had sufficient grounds and validly formed an opinion under Section 241(2); while NCLT's appointment of a government-nominated committee was lawful under Section 242, such supersession cannot continue indefinitely, necessitating a definite timeframe for remedial restructuring and holding fresh democratic elections.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 01.04.2022 passed by NCLT Principal Bench is upheld. The Central Government-nominated Committee is directed to complete all remedial measures on or before 31.03.2025, and conduct elections for President and Members of the General Committee under Clause 20 of the Articles of Association within three months thereafter (by 30.06.2025) to hand over management to a newly elected General Council. Appeals are disposed of; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: Seven club members appealed against NCLT Principal Bench's order dated 01.04.2022 in CP No. 71/241-242/PB/2020, which allowed the Union of India's petition under Section 241(2) and replaced the General Committee of Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited with a 15-member Central Government-nominated committee. The appellants contended that the club is private, no public interest was affected, and the government lacked a valid opinion. Upholding NCLT's decision, NCLAT held that the club, as a Section 8 company enjoying 27 acres of prime public land, acted prejudicially to public interest by neglecting sports (spending only 2.77%), collecting unauthorized fees, and creating arbitrary hereditary membership schemes ('parivaar-vaad'). However, holding that supersession cannot be indefinite, NCLAT directed the nominated committee to conclude remedial work by 31.03.2025 and conduct fresh elections within three months thereafter.

case_title: Rajeev Sabharwal vs. Union of India, MCA Through Regional Director (Northern Region) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rajeev Sabharwal, a permanent member of Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited; Respondent 1 is the Union of India, MCA; Respondent 2 is Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited; Respondents 3 to 17 are erstwhile General Committee members; Respondent 18 is Col. Ashish Khanna (Retd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Leased premises of 27.03 acres granted by the Ministry of Urban Affairs under perpetual lease dated 20.02.1928 at nominal consideration to Delhi Gymkhana Club Ltd., an association not-for-profit registered under Section 26 of the 1913 Act (corresponding to Section 8 of the 2013 Act) primarily for promoting sports and recreation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Systemic financial and statutory defaults including collecting unauthorized deposits/registration fees of hundreds of crores against Section 58A of the 1956 Act / Acceptance of Deposit Rules, while incurring less than 3% (2.77%) of total expenditure on sports activities and spending the majority on consumables, liquor, and catering. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Inquiry ordered under Section 206(4) on 16.03.2016; supplementary inspection directed on 12.09.2019; supplementary report dated 03.03.2020 forwarded on 04.03.2020; Central Government sanction issued on 18.03.2020; Petition filed on 22.04.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Comprehensive findings in Inspection Reports indicating 4,000 to 5,333 Green Card and UCP holders inducted contrary to Articles of Association, arbitrarily collected multi-lakh registration charges treated as revenue, investments of deposits into mutual funds to enrich club finances, and blatant non-adherence to primary corporate objects. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union of India filed CP No. 71/241-242/PB/2020 alleging mismanagement and prejudice to public interest. NCLT Principal Bench allowed the petition on 01.04.2022, permitting the Central Government to nominate 15 Directors to take over management. Appellant filed this appeal praying in the alternative for a direction to hold elections and reinstate an elected board under appropriate oversight.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the management of a Section 8 company superseded under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 can be continued indefinitely by a government-nominated committee without fixing a time frame for democratic elections. 2. Whether the NCLT's final order dated 01.04.2022 properly exercised power 'with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained of'.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Remedial orders under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 are designed to bring to an end the matters complained of and cannot result in perpetual state supersession of a company's democratic self-governance; the Adjudicating Authority must establish an enforceable timeline to achieve restorative targets and restore elected administration. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(1) ordains that any order made for prevention of oppression or mismanagement must be directed toward 'bringing to an end the matters complained of', meaning corrective state management is transitory and must conclude once the foundational anomalies are cured. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a government-appointed committee has functioned for over two and a half years and filed eight periodic status reports demonstrating stabilizing progress in compliance and accounting, maintaining indefinite supersession without an exit roadmap exceeds the remedial purpose of Section 242. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The findings of mismanagement and prejudice to public interest justify the appointment of the 15-member committee, but ends of justice require fixing an absolute deadline of 31.03.2025 to conclude restructuring and mandate elections within three months thereafter.
operative_order: The order dated 01.04.2022 passed by NCLT Principal Bench is affirmed. The Central Government-nominated Committee is directed to complete all remedial measures by 31.03.2025 and conduct elections for President and General Committee members in accordance with Clause 20 of the Articles of Association within three months after 31.03.2025, handing over management to the elected General Council. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Appellant Rajeev Sabharwal, a member of Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited, appealed the order dated 01.04.2022 passed by NCLT Principal Bench under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013, which superseded the club's General Committee with 15 Central Government nominees due to severe mismanagement, ultra vires membership levies, and failure to pursue its primary sports objectives. Appellant sought in the alternative that an elected board be restored within defined timelines. NCLAT upheld the NCLT's findings on public interest and mismanagement but held that state supersession cannot continue indefinitely. NCLAT directed the nominated committee to conclude all remedial steps by 31.03.2025 and conduct fresh elections under Clause 20 of the Articles of Association within three months thereafter.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. vs. Raj Kumar Sahani & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Ashish Singh (Resolution Professional/Appellant in CA 253-254/2024); Committee of Creditors of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant in CA 442-443/2024); Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant/Appellant in CA 256-257/2024); Raj Kumar Sahani (Suspended Director/Shareholder/Respondent 1); Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed financial credit from Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd.; upon default, insolvency proceedings were initiated under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayments leading to CIRP; Raj Kumar Sahani alleged the Corporate Debtor's account became an NPA on 14.06.2020 after a 90-day default period, remaining unpaid for over one year prior to CIRP initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 22.02.2022; RP published Form-G on 05.05.2022; Corporate Debtor obtained MSME registration certificate on 24.05.2022; Bishwanath Traders submitted its Resolution Plan on 11.07.2022; CoC approved the plan with 100% voting share on 29.08.2022; RP filed IA No. 5458/2022 for plan approval on 29.10.2022; Raj Kumar Sahani filed IA No. 4173/2023 challenging SRA eligibility on 04.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MSME Udyam Registration Certificate dated 24.05.2022; due diligence report by DGA IB Resolution LLP confirming eligibility; CoC voting records demonstrating 100% approval; Resolution Plan stipulating adjustment of Rs. 12 Crores owed by Financial Creditor to SRA. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Raj Kumar Sahani filed IA No. 4173/2023 alleging SRA ineligibility under Section 29A(c) due to common management/promoter Birendra Kumar Pasari. On 24.01.2024, NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV allowed IA No. 4173/2023, declared SRA ineligible, rejected the plan approval application (IA No. 5458/2022), and ordered liquidation under Section 33(1)(b).
legal_issues: 1. Whether an SRA is disqualified under Section 29A(c) of the IBC when the Corporate Debtor obtained MSME registration after the commencement of CIRP but prior to the submission of the Resolution Plan. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting a Resolution Plan approved with 100% CoC voting share by assessing Section 29A(c) without applying the exemption under Section 240A.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 240A of the IBC, the disqualifications under clauses (c) and (h) of Section 29A do not apply to resolution applicants bidding for MSME entities if the Corporate Debtor secures valid MSME registration prior to the date of submission of the resolution plan, irrespective of whether the registration was obtained post-CIRP commencement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A opens with a non-obstante clause overrides Section 29A(c) and (h) for micro, small, and medium enterprises; the crucial cut-off date to determine eligibility under Section 29A(c) is the date of submission of the resolution plan, not the insolvency commencement date. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of a valid MSME registration certificate obtained prior to the date of submitting the resolution plan conclusively entitles the applicant to Section 240A protection against Section 29A(c) disqualification. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was duly registered as an MSME on 24.05.2022, prior to the submission of the Resolution Plan on 11.07.2022; hence, Section 240A applied, erasing any ineligibility under Section 29A(c), and the CoC's unanimous commercial approval of the plan must be upheld.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 253-254 of 2024 are allowed; impugned order dated 24.01.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV is set aside; IA No. 4173 of 2023 is dismissed; IA No. 5458 of 2022 is allowed, approving the Resolution Plan submitted by Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd.; Adjudicating Authority directed to pass consequential approval orders within 60 days. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Appeals were filed challenging NCLT New Delhi's order dated 24.01.2024 which declared Successful Resolution Applicant Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd. ineligible under Section 29A(c) of the IBC, rejected its unanimously approved resolution plan, and directed liquidation of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. The respondent argued that SRA's promoter managed the Corporate Debtor whose account had become an NPA. Allowing the appeals, NCLAT held that pursuant to the Supreme Court's ruling in Hari Babu Thota, obtaining MSME registration after CIRP commencement but before plan submission attracts Section 240A exemption from Section 29A(c). NCLAT set aside the impugned order, dismissed the objections, and approved the Resolution Plan.

case_title: Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd. vs. Ashish Singh, RP of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondents are Ashish Singh (Resolution Professional of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd.), Raj Kumar Sahani (Suspended Director/Shareholder), and CoC. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP under Section 7 on 22.02.2022; RP issued Form-G and subsequently registered the Corporate Debtor as an MSME on 24.05.2022 to attract resolution applicants. Appellant submitted its Resolution Plan on 11.07.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to CIRP; suspended management contended the loan account was an NPA since 14.06.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-G issued on 05.05.2022; MSME registration secured on 24.05.2022; Resolution Plan submitted on 11.07.2022; CoC approval with 100% votes on 29.08.2022; Plan approval application IA No. 5458/2022 filed on 29.10.2022; Objections in IA No. 4173/2023 filed on 04.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Due diligence report of DGA IB Resolution LLP verifying SRA eligibility; MSME certificate dated 24.05.2022; Form-H compliance certificate; unanimous 100% CoC voting records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV on 24.01.2024 allowed IA No. 4173/2023 filed by Raj Kumar Sahani, holding Appellant ineligible under Section 29A(c) due to common promoter Birendra Kumar Pasari, rejected the resolution plan, and ordered liquidation. Appellant challenged this order.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Appellant SRA suffered disqualification under Section 29A(c) of the IBC despite the Corporate Debtor holding MSME status prior to plan submission. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority had jurisdiction to discard the unanimous commercial wisdom of the CoC approving the Resolution Plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution applicant cannot be declared ineligible under Section 29A(c) of the IBC where the Corporate Debtor is registered as an MSME prior to plan submission, as Section 240A provides an overriding statutory carve-out. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A expressly renders Section 29A(c) inapplicable to MSMEs; under the dictum of Hari Babu Thota, the decisive date for testing disqualification under Section 29A(c) read with Section 240A is the date of submission of the resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Timely procurement of MSME registration prior to bidding, corroborated by professional due diligence reports and absence of contemporaneous objections during CoC deliberations, establishes legal eligibility. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA submitted its plan on 11.07.2022, well after the Corporate Debtor received MSME status on 24.05.2022; Section 240A applied, nullifying Section 29A(c) disqualification, and making the rejection of the plan erroneous.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 256 & 257 of 2024 are allowed; impugned order dated 24.01.2024 is set aside; IA No. 4173 of 2023 is dismissed; IA No. 5458 of 2022 is allowed approving the Appellant's Resolution Plan; Adjudicating Authority to pass consequential orders within 60 days. Parties to bear their own costs.
summary: Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant for Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT New Delhi order dated 24.01.2024 which disqualified it under Section 29A(c) of the IBC, rejected its plan, and ordered liquidation on objections from a suspended director. NCLAT held that because the Corporate Debtor obtained MSME registration prior to the submission of the resolution plan, the SRA was entitled to the statutory exemption under Section 240A, which overrides Section 29A(c). Applying the Supreme Court's decision in Hari Babu Thota, NCLAT reversed the NCLT's order, dismissed the suspended director's objections, and approved the resolution plan.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. vs. Raj Kumar Sahani & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Committee of Creditors of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd.; Respondents are Raj Kumar Sahani (Suspended Director), Ashish Singh (RP), and Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd. (SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial credit facility provided by financial creditor Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd. to Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in servicing financial debt resulting in insolvency admission; suspended director asserted account was NPA from 14.06.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 22.02.2022; MSME registration granted on 24.05.2022; SRA submitted Resolution Plan on 11.07.2022; CoC approved plan with 100% voting share on 29.08.2022; RP filed approval application IA No. 5458/2022 on 29.10.2022; Suspended Director filed objections in IA No. 4173/2023 on 04.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deliberations of the 4th, 6th, 7th, and 8th CoC meetings; independent due diligence report by DGA IB Resolution LLP; MSME certificate dated 24.05.2022; 100% CoC voting records approving the SRA's plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi Court-IV) allowed IA No. 4173/2023 on 24.01.2024, holding the SRA disqualified under Section 29A(c), rejected the approval application IA No. 5458/2022, and directed liquidation. The CoC appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the CoC's unanimous commercial decision approving a Resolution Plan can be overturned by disqualifying the SRA under Section 29A(c) when the Corporate Debtor is an MSME. 2. Whether Section 240A shields the SRA from Section 29A(c) ineligibility when MSME registration was obtained during CIRP prior to plan submission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating and approving a compliant resolution plan is paramount, and judicial authorities cannot reject the plan on alleged grounds of promoter-related ineligibility where the statutory exemption under Section 240A for MSME entities applies. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A expressly excludes the operation of Section 29A(c) for MSMEs; the relevant date to assess eligibility under Section 29A(c) read with Section 240A is the date of submission of the resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Full consideration by institutional creditors based on due diligence reports and the presence of a valid MSME certificate prior to plan presentation leaves no room for judicial interference on Section 29A(c) grounds. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor was an MSME before plan submission; hence Section 240A applied, eliminating Section 29A(c) disqualification, and the CoC's 100% approval must be given effect.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 442 & 443 of 2024 are allowed; impugned order dated 24.01.2024 is set aside; IA No. 4173 of 2023 is dismissed; IA No. 5458 of 2022 is allowed approving the Resolution Plan; Adjudicating Authority to pass consequential orders within 60 days. Parties to bear their own costs.
summary: The Committee of Creditors of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 24.01.2024 which rejected the unanimously approved Resolution Plan submitted by Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd., disqualified the SRA under Section 29A(c), and ordered liquidation based on an application by a suspended director. NCLAT set aside the order and allowed the appeal, holding that pursuant to Hari Babu Thota, MSME registration obtained during CIRP prior to plan submission grants the benefit of Section 240A, exempting the SRA from Section 29A(c) disqualification. The CoC's commercial wisdom was reinstated, and the plan was approved.

case_title: Jindal Power Ltd. vs. Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi, RP of SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jindal Power Ltd. (Appellant/Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant); Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi (Resolution Professional/Respondent 1); Committee of Creditors consisting of Bank of Baroda and State Bank of India (Respondent 2); Sarda Energy and Minerals Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant/Respondent 3); SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of Baroda initiated CIRP under Section 7 against the Corporate Debtor; prospective resolution applicants submitted resolution plans under the RFRP and Process Note. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory financial default leading to CIRP admission on 29.04.2022. Final evaluated financial offers following inter-se bidding on 19.04.2023 were SEML (INR 1805 Crores), Torrent (INR 1810 Crores), and Vantage (INR 1815 Crores); JPL offered INR 2003 Crores plus an unquantified 10% equity upside with a buyback value of INR 27 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 29.04.2022; inter-se bidding held on 19.04.2023; revised plans submitted on 28.04.2023; clarifications sought via email on 08.05.2023; addendums submitted on 10.05.2023; CoC voted 100% in favor of SEML's plan between 28.05.2023 and 08.06.2023; Plan approval application IA No. 2794/2023 filed on 17.06.2023; Intervention Petition No. 40/2024 filed by JPL on 02.06.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses 2.6.2(d), 2.9.4, and 4.1.8 of RFRP; Process Note dated 13.04.2023; evaluation matrix showing scoring criteria for equity upside; return and acceptance of EMDs by JPL without contemporaneous objection; minutes of the 31st and 34th CoC meetings confirming factual correctness of plan evaluations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV on 13.08.2024 dismissed JPL's Intervention Petition No. 40/2024 and approved SEML's Resolution Plan in IA No. 2794/2023. JPL appealed, alleging material irregularity and improper evaluation of its 10% equity upside.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant who accepted the refund of its EMD without contemporaneous objection has locus standi to challenge the approval of another applicant's resolution plan. 2. Whether the non-addition of an uncommitted 10% equity upside into the upfront cash component of a financial proposal constitutes a material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsuccessful resolution applicant has no vested right to have its plan approved, and where it accepts the return of its earnest money deposit without objection, it cannot subsequently challenge the approval of the successful resolution plan or demand inclusion of conditional equity upside in upfront cash metrics. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(3)(ii) permits interference only on proof of a material defect in procedure; the evaluation of equity upside falls exclusively within the qualitative evaluation matrix governed by the CoC's non-justiciable commercial wisdom under Section 30(4). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Transparent scoring under pre-determined RFRP evaluation matrices, verified by CoC minutes affirming numerical accuracy across all plans, precludes allegations of material irregularity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC fully considered JPL's plan and properly scored its equity upside under the evaluation matrix; the refusal to treat equity upside as upfront cash did not constitute a material irregularity, and the CoC's commercial wisdom is inviolable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1696 & 1697 of 2024 are dismissed. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Jindal Power Ltd. (JPL), an unsuccessful resolution applicant for SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 13.08.2024 approving the resolution plan of Sarda Energy and Minerals Ltd. (SEML) and dismissing JPL's intervention petition. JPL contended that its offer of 10% equity upside (valued at INR 27 Crores) was erroneously excluded from its upfront financial offer, which would have made its bid higher than SEML's. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that JPL had accepted the refund of its EMD without protest and had no vested right to approval. Furthermore, equity upside was properly treated under the qualitative evaluation matrix rather than upfront cash. Finding no material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii), NCLAT upheld the CoC's commercial wisdom.

case_title: Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd. vs. Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi, RP of SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd. (Appellant/Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant); Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi (Resolution Professional/Respondent 1); Committee of Creditors (Bank of Baroda and SBI/Respondent 2); Sarda Energy and Minerals Ltd. (SRA/Respondent 3); SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP under Section 7 on 29.04.2022; RP issued RFRP and Process Note for resolution plans. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities of the Corporate Debtor; post-negotiation bidding metrics on 19.04.2023 showed Appellant's proposal at INR 1815.04 Crores (highest net present value) versus SEML at INR 1805 Crores. On 14.06.2023, Appellant sent an unsolicited email offering to enhance its bid by an additional INR 50 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Inter-se bidding concluded on 19.04.2023; revised plans submitted on 28.04.2023; clarifications sought by RP on 08.05.2023 and answered on 10.05.2023; CoC approved SEML's plan with 100% vote share on 08.06.2023; LoI issued on 08.06.2023 and accepted on 12.06.2023; Appellant's revision offered on 14.06.2023 and rejected by CoC on 17.06.2023; Plan approval application IA No. 2794/2023 filed on 17.06.2023; Appellant filed IA No. 3336/2023 on 01.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses 4.1.8 of RFRP and 9(e) of Process Note stipulating that CoC is not bound to accept the highest financial offer; minutes of the 31st and 32nd CoC meetings recording rejection of Appellant's post-voting unsolicited offer; Form-H compliance certificate. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following an earlier remand by NCLAT on 10.05.2024, NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV on 13.08.2024 dismissed IA No. 3336/2023 filed by Appellant and approved SEML's plan in IA No. 2794/2023. Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the CoC is legally obligated to approve the resolution plan offering the highest nominal financial value to maximize asset value under the IBC. 2. Whether the rejection of an unsolicited revision offer submitted after CoC voting and approval of a resolution plan constitutes a material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Maximization of value under the IBC does not mandate the automatic approval of the highest monetary bid; the Committee of Creditors is entitled in its non-justiciable commercial wisdom to evaluate feasibility, viability, and qualitative parameters, and is not required to entertain unsolicited bid enhancements submitted after e-voting has concluded. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(4) confers absolute discretion upon the CoC to approve a plan; RFRP terms stating that the CoC is under no obligation to approve the highest-value plan are legally binding, and the exclusion of post-vote revisions violates no statutory provision under Section 30(2) or Section 61(3). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented unconditional acceptance by bidders of Process Note terms disclaiming any entitlement based solely on H-1 ranking estops applicants from claiming unfairness when evaluated holistically by financial institutions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC acted within its jurisdiction in rejecting Appellant's unsolicited post-vote offer of INR 50 Crores and approving SEML's compliant plan; no material irregularity existed under Section 61(3)(ii).
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1619 & 1620 of 2024 are dismissed. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd., an unsuccessful resolution applicant for SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd., appealed NCLT Mumbai's order dated 13.08.2024 approving the resolution plan of Sarda Energy and Minerals Ltd. (SEML) and dismissing its application (IA No. 3336/2023). Vantage argued that as the highest bidder (INR 1815.04 Crores vs. SEML's INR 1805 Crores) with a further post-vote offer of INR 50 Crores, rejecting its plan violated the objective of asset value maximization. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the CoC is not legally bound to accept the highest financial offer under the RFRP and IBC. The CoC evaluated feasibility and viability holistically, and properly refused unsolicited revisions received after voting concluded.

case_title: Torrent Power Ltd. vs. Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi, RP of SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Torrent Power Ltd. (Appellant/Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant); Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi (Resolution Professional/Respondent 1); Sarda Energy and Minerals Ltd. (SRA/Respondent 2); Committee of Creditors comprising Bank of Baroda and SBI (Respondent 3); SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution of Corporate Debtor through CIRP initiated under Section 7 by Bank of Baroda. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP default on credit facilities; inter-se bidding concluded on 19.04.2023 where Appellant offered INR 1810 Crores (all upfront) and SEML offered INR 1805 Crores NPV (INR 1553 Crores upfront + INR 301.64 Crores deferred, having a discounted NPV of INR 240 Crores). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Inter-se bidding concluded on 19.04.2023; Resolution Plans submitted on 28.04.2023; RP sent clarification emails to all bidders on 08.05.2023; clarifications/addendums submitted on 10.05.2023; CoC voted 100% in favor of SEML's plan between 28.05.2023 and 08.06.2023; IA No. 3399/2023 filed by Torrent on 03.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 08.05.2023 from RP seeking clarifications from all applicants without commercial change; SEML's reply dated 10.05.2023 clarifying that INR 240 Crores was the discounted NPV of the deferred amount payable upfront if CoC opted, and confirming replacement of bank guarantees totaling INR 180.05 Crores; Appendix-1 showing original NPV calculations; minutes of the 31st and 34th CoC meetings confirming absence of commercial deviations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai originally remitted the plan to CoC on 06.10.2023; NCLAT set aside that order on 10.05.2024 and remanded the applications. On 13.08.2024, NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV rejected IA No. 3399/2023 filed by Torrent and approved SEML's Resolution Plan in IA No. 2794/2023. Torrent appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Resolution Professional and CoC permitted the SRA to impermissibly modify its commercial offer after the conclusion of bidding under the guise of seeking clarifications, thereby committing a material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii) of the IBC. 2. Whether seeking simultaneous clarifications from all resolution applicants regarding bank guarantee margin money and deferred discount options violates procedural fairness.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Seeking clarificatory addendums from all resolution applicants pursuant to express enabling clauses in the RFRP does not constitute an impermissible modification or material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii) of the IBC, provided the underlying net present value and core commercial offer remain unchanged. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(3)(ii) of the IBC requires proof of a material defect in procedure resulting in substantial prejudice; routine clarifications to resolve ambiguities regarding the exercise of pre-existing plan options (such as discounted NPV upfront settlement or treatment of bank guarantee margin money) do not amount to post-bid commercial modifications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where comparative financial matrices and Appendix-1 filings demonstrate that the SRA's evaluated net present value remained identical before and after clarifications, and identical query mechanisms were extended to all bidders, the process is non-discriminatory and fair. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Sarda's option to pay the discounted NPV of INR 240 Crores upfront and its commitment to replace INR 180.05 Crores in bank guarantees were already part of its 28.04.2023 plan; no modification took place, no material irregularity occurred, and the 100% CoC approval was lawful.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1621 & 1622 of 2024 are dismissed. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Torrent Power Ltd., an unsuccessful bidder for SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Ltd., challenged NCLT Mumbai's order dated 13.08.2024 approving the resolution plan of Sarda Energy and Minerals Ltd. (SEML) and dismissing Torrent's IA No. 3399/2023. Torrent alleged a material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii) of the IBC, arguing that SEML was allowed to alter its commercial bid post-auction via a clarification email dated 08.05.2023 by converting deferred amounts into INR 240 Crores upfront cash and increasing bank guarantee margin replacements. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the clarification email was issued to all applicants under valid RFRP terms, the discounted NPV of INR 240 Crores and full BG replacement were already embedded in SEML's original plan, and no financial modification occurred. The CoC's unanimous commercial wisdom was upheld.

case_title: Century Aluminium Company Limited vs. Religare Finvest Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Century Aluminium Company Limited (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Religare Finvest Limited (Respondent/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial assistance by way of a loan against property sanctioned on 26.08.2015 for an amount of Rs. 12,50,00,000/- secured by equitable mortgage and hypothecation over factory land (9.34 acres), building, and constructions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed financial debt default of Rs. 16,89,54,976.03/-; first default occurred on 01.05.2019, and the last part-payment was made on 10.02.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor unilaterally appointed an arbitrator on 26.07.2019; the sole arbitrator terminated the proceedings on 26.10.2021; Section 7 petition filed on 23.06.2023; Corporate Debtor filed its reply to Section 7 on 20.12.2023 (affidavit dated 28.12.2023); Corporate Debtor subsequently filed IA No. 542/2024 under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act on 12.03.2024 (motion notice dated 07.03.2024). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letter dated 26.08.2015; written OTS acknowledgement letters by the Corporate Debtor dated 22.08.2019 and 25.05.2022 (acknowledging debt of Rs. 8.09 Crores); arbitral termination order dated 26.10.2021 citing Perkins Eastman. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In pending Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 142(KB)/2023, Corporate Debtor filed IA (IBC) No. 542(KB)/2024 seeking reference of disputes to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration Act and dismissal/stay of Section 7 proceedings. NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-II rejected the application on 10.07.2024, holding that Section 7 must be decided first and prior arbitration proceedings do not bar IBC admission. Corporate Debtor appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the pendency or prior invocation of arbitration proceedings by a Financial Creditor bars the Adjudicating Authority from proceeding with and adjudicating an application under Section 7 of the IBC. 2. Whether an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is maintainable before the Adjudicating Authority after the Corporate Debtor has already filed its reply/substantive statement on the Section 7 petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act cannot derail or defer an insolvency petition under Section 7 of the IBC; the Adjudicating Authority is duty-bound to first determine whether there is debt and default, and any pending or prior arbitration proceedings do not create a legal bar to the exercise of insolvency jurisdiction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in Indus Biotech, Section 7 of the IBC is an overriding special summary remedy; when an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration Act is filed during the pendency of a Section 7 petition, the tribunal must first record its satisfaction regarding default, and upon satisfaction of default, the Section 8 application is rendered unmaintainable. Furthermore, under Section 8(1) of the Arbitration Act, the right to apply for arbitration is forfeited if not moved before or at the time of submitting the first statement on the substance of the dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unconditional admissions of debt and default in written settlement proposals (such as OTS letters) establish statutory default, rendering any reference to arbitration redundant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor forfeited its Section 8 right by filing its application months after filing its reply to the Section 7 petition; moreover, default was established through OTS acknowledgments, obliging the NCLT to reject the Section 8 application and proceed with Section 7.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1719 of 2024 and IA No. 6230 of 2024 are dismissed. The order dated 10.07.2024 passed by NCLT Kolkata rejecting IA No. 542(KB)/2024 is affirmed.
summary: Century Aluminium Company Limited appealed against NCLT Kolkata's order dated 10.07.2024 rejecting its application (IA No. 542/2024) filed under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 seeking reference to arbitration and stay/dismissal of Religare Finvest Limited's Section 7 IBC petition. The Corporate Debtor argued that the Financial Creditor had previously invoked arbitration in 2019 which was never lawfully terminated under Section 32. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under the Supreme Court's Indus Biotech judgment, the Adjudicating Authority must prioritize the Section 7 petition to ascertain debt and default, unaffected by pending arbitration. Furthermore, because the Corporate Debtor filed its Section 8 application months after submitting its reply to the Section 7 petition, its right to seek arbitration was forfeited.

case_title: Sunil Kumar Agarwal & Anr. vs. Anand Sonbhadra RP of Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sunil Kumar Agarwal & Anr. (Appellants/Successful Resolution Applicants); Anand Sonbhadra (Resolution Professional/Respondent 1); New Okhla Industrial Development Authority/NOIDA (Respondent 2); Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority/GNIDA (Respondent 3); Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Concord Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NOIDA executed a 90-year lease deed dated 30.07.2010 for Plot No. GH-05, Sector 137, Noida ('Shubhkamna Techhomes')[cite: 13]. GNIDA executed a 90-year lease deed dated 04.04.2011 for Plot No. GH-02, Sector 1, Greater Noida ('Shubhkamna City')[cite: 13]. The Corporate Debtor was developing residential projects on these leased lands[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of lease rents, land premium installments, and operational debt; NOIDA filed Form B on 22.02.2019 for Rs. 99,32,55,183/- (including future dues of Rs. 8,12,05,605/-), admitted by the RP[cite: 13]. GNIDA filed no timely claim; the IM recorded unclaimed GNIDA dues of Rs. 60,64,54,762/-[cite: 13]. Post-impugned order, NOIDA claimed Rs. 27,65,02,686/- and GNIDA claimed Rs. 1,00,95,82,526/- as CIRP costs[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 26.11.2018 under Section 9[cite: 13]. Public announcement on 29.11.2018[cite: 13]. CoC approved the Appellants' resolution plan with an 87.57% voting share on 09.10.2019 (concluded 17.10.2019)[cite: 13]. RP filed plan approval CA No. 485/ND/2019[cite: 13]. NCLT passed the impugned order on 12.09.2022 directing payment of lease rents/premiums during CIRP as CIRP costs[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan allocating Rs. 25 Crores to NOIDA and Rs. 18.50 Crores to GNIDA in six equal half-yearly installments, with Rs. 2.20 Crores budgeted as CIRP costs[cite: 13]; lease deeds dated 30.07.2010 and 04.04.2011[cite: 13]; Information Memorandum dated 26.11.2018[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CA No. 485/ND/2019, NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV approved the resolution plan on 12.09.2022 but simultaneously held in paragraph 11 that accrued lease rentals and premiums from CIRP commencement (26.11.2018) to plan approval (12.09.2022) constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31, directing their submission within 15 days[cite: 13]. SRA appealed against this modification[cite: 13].
legal_issues: 1. Whether accrued lease rentals and lease premium dues for leased land during the CIRP period constitute 'Insolvency Resolution Process Costs' under Section 5(13) of the IBC read with Regulation 31 of the CIRP Regulations and the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d)[cite: 13]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 31(1) of the IBC to modify an approved resolution plan by directing inclusion of substantial statutory lease dues as CIRP costs[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction only to approve or reject a resolution plan in terms of Section 31 and cannot alter, modify, or add financial obligations to an approved resolution plan; furthermore, lease premiums and lease rentals payable to statutory land authorities are not covered as essential supply costs or 'similar grants' under the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d) so as to automatically constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13)[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31 and the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d) applies strictly to licenses, permits, registrations, quotas, concessions, or clearances required to keep the debtor running, and cannot be expanded to include lease land premium amounts or general lease rentals[cite: 13]. Section 31 uses the mandatory word 'shall' to approve a compliant plan, without granting power to make alterations[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the CoC in its commercial wisdom has approved a financial allocation for operational/statutory creditors based on the Information Memorandum, subsequent post-approval claims cannot be grafted into CIRP costs to alter plan viability[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Following the precedent in Sunil Kumar Agrawal vs. NOIDA, the direction of the Adjudicating Authority treating lease rentals and premiums as CIRP costs was contrary to law and constituted an impermissible modification of the plan[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1351 of 2022 is allowed; the impugned direction in the order dated 12.09.2022 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV in CA No. 485/ND/2019 categorizing lease rentals and premiums as CIRP costs is set aside. No order as to costs[cite: 13].
summary: The Successful Resolution Applicant of Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV order dated 12.09.2022 which approved the resolution plan but directed that accrued lease rentals and premiums payable to NOIDA and GNIDA during the CIRP period (amounting to over Rs. 128 Crores) be included as CIRP costs under Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31 and the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d)[cite: 13]. Setting aside the direction, NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority cannot modify or alter an approved resolution plan[cite: 13]. Following its earlier decision in Sunil Kumar Agrawal vs. NOIDA, NCLAT held that land lease rentals and premiums do not fall within the scope of the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d) or Section 5(13)[cite: 13]. The appeal was allowed[cite: 13].

case_title: Visa Coke Limited vs. Mesco Kalinga Steel Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Visa Coke Limited (Appellant/Operational Creditor); Mesco Kalinga Steel Limited (Respondent/Corporate Debtor)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of operational goods/coke by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor against unpaid commercial invoices[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt default of Rs. 4,19,77,245.17/- inclusive of 15% penal interest per annum computed till 31.03.2021[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued in Form-3 dated 31.03.2021[cite: 14]. Section 9 petition subsequently filed before NCLT Cuttack Bench[cite: 14]. Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petition on 24.01.2023[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statutory demand notice dated 31.03.2021 in Form-3 addressed individually to three Key Managerial Personnel (Sameer Singh, Director; Bibhuti Bhushan Rath, CFO; and S. Subudhi, Manager Commercial) delivered via courier at the registered office address: 3915, Lewis Road, Mesco Tower, Kedar Gouri Square, Bhubaneswar - 751002[cite: 14]. Courier delivery receipts confirming receipt by the individuals[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 petition seeking CIRP[cite: 14]. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Cuttack Bench) on 24.01.2023 held that the demand notice was addressed only to individual managerial personnel and not to the Corporate Debtor (the juristic entity), rendering the notice invalid and the Section 9 petition unmaintainable[cite: 14]. Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 14].
legal_issues: 1. Whether delivery of a Section 8 statutory demand notice addressed individually to Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) of a company at its registered office satisfies the mandatory requirement of delivering a demand notice to the 'Corporate Debtor'[cite: 14]. 2. Whether failure to address the Section 8 demand notice to the Corporate Debtor is a fatal, non-curable defect rendering a Section 9 application unmaintainable[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Issuance and delivery of a statutory demand notice addressed specifically to the Corporate Debtor as a distinct juristic person is a non-negotiable condition precedent for maintaining a Section 9 insolvency application; addressing the notice merely to individual Key Managerial Personnel in their personal capacities, even if delivered at the registered office, does not constitute valid service upon the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8(1) and Section 9(1) of the IBC read with Rule 5 and Form-3 of the AAA Rules, 2016, the legislature has strictly used the expression 'corporate debtor' and not 'key managerial personnel'[cite: 14]. While Rule 5(2)(b) permits electronic service to KMP via email, physical delivery under Rule 5(2)(a) and Form-3 mandates that the demand notice must be addressed to the Corporate Debtor company by name at its registered office[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examining the facial address of Form-3: where the notice names only natural persons (directors/officers) rather than the corporate body corporate incorporated under Section 7 of the Companies Act, 2013, legal service upon the juristic entity is absent as a matter of law[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no statutory demand notice was addressed or delivered to the Corporate Debtor itself, the condition precedent under Section 8 was not fulfilled, rendering the Section 9 application rightly dismissed[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 247 of 2023 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 24.01.2023 passed by NCLT Cuttack Bench is affirmed. No costs[cite: 14].
summary: Visa Coke Limited appealed against NCLT Cuttack's order dated 24.01.2023 dismissing its Section 9 application against Mesco Kalinga Steel Limited for default of Rs. 4.19 Crores[cite: 14]. The dismissal was on the ground that the Section 8 demand notice was addressed personally to three Key Managerial Personnel (Director, CFO, Manager Commercial) rather than to the Corporate Debtor itself, despite being delivered at the registered office[cite: 14]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT affirmed that a company is an independent juristic entity distinct from its KMP[cite: 14]. Under Section 8 of the IBC and Rule 5, the demand notice must be addressed and delivered to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. The defect was incurable, making the Section 9 petition unmaintainable[cite: 14].

case_title: Ramesh Kumar Chugh vs. Assets Care & Construction Enterprises Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ramesh Kumar Chugh/RKC (Appellant/Personal Guarantor/Partner); Assets Care & Construction Enterprises Limited/ACRE (Respondent/Assignee Secured Creditor); White Line Enterprises (Operational Creditor); Sahil Home Loomtex Pvt. Ltd. (Principal Debtor); M/s Sheena Exports (Partnership Firm under dissolution); M/s Sheena Textile Ltd./STL (Borrower)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant stood as personal guarantor for operational debts owed by Sahil Home Loomtex Pvt. Ltd. to White Line Enterprises[cite: 15]. Separately, Appellant held a 25% share in partnership firm M/s Sheena Exports, which availed loan facilities from HSBC and Citi Bank[cite: 15]. Appellant was also a guarantor for loans availed by STL from PNB and IDBI[cite: 15]. All debts of Sheena Exports and STL and underlying mortgaged properties were assigned to Respondent ACRE[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of assigned loans exceeding Rs. 200 Crores, resulting in four DRT decrees and recovery certificates in favor of Respondent[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 95 petition filed against Appellant on 22.12.2023 by White Line Enterprises[cite: 15]. ACRE issued SARFAESI auction sale notices on 15.12.2023 for auctions on 22.01.2024 and second notice on 01.02.2024[cite: 15]. IRP appointed under Section 95 on 12.02.2024[cite: 15]. Appellant issued notice of dissolution of partnership firm to co-partners on 06.02.2024[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Partnership deed dated 01.04.2023; dissolution notice dated 06.02.2024; title records showing the subject mortgaged properties stood exclusively in the name of M/s Sheena Exports and not in the personal name of Appellant; DRT recovery certificates[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In pending Section 95 CP (IB) No. 10/ND/2024, Appellant filed IA No. 317/2024 seeking to stay and restrain Respondent's SARFAESI auction sales, arguing that the Section 96 interim moratorium barred actions against partnership properties[cite: 15]. NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI dismissed IA No. 317/2024 on 03.07.2024[cite: 15]. Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 15].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the statutory interim moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC triggered by a Section 95 petition against an individual personal guarantor operates to stay SARFAESI auction proceedings against mortgaged assets owned by a partnership firm in which the individual is a partner[cite: 15]. 2. Whether post-dissolution devolution of partnership liabilities under the Partnership Act extends the Section 96 interim moratorium to partnership assets[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The interim moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC operates strictly in rem with respect to the specific debt of the individual debtor and does not protect or encompass assets owned by an independent partnership firm or corporate entity, even if the debtor is a partner in that firm[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the Supreme Court doctrine in Dilip B. Jiwrajka, the interim moratorium under Section 96 is debt-specific ('in respect of any debt') rather than debtor-centric[cite: 15]. It protects the debtor only against personal debt enforcement, in contrast to Section 14 which stays proceedings against all assets[cite: 15]. Under partnership law, partners possess no individual right, title, or interest in specific assets of a firm until full discharge of debts upon dissolution[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verifying asset title: where SARFAESI mortgages stand in the name of the partnership firm securing firm-specific debts, a personal guarantee insolvency petition filed by an unrelated third-party creditor cannot stay enforcement against the mortgaged properties[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 95 petition was filed against the Appellant solely in his capacity as personal guarantor for Sahil Home Loomtex; hence Section 96 interim moratorium did not extend to properties owned by M/s Sheena Exports, and the refusal to stay the SARFAESI auction was valid[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1726 of 2024 is dismissed. The order dated 03.07.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI in IA No. 317/2024 is affirmed. No order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: Appellant Ramesh Kumar Chugh appealed against NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI's order dated 03.07.2024 dismissing IA No. 317/2024, wherein Appellant sought to restrain Assets Care & Construction Enterprises Ltd. (ACRE) from auctioning properties under the SARFAESI Act[cite: 15]. Appellant contended that an interim moratorium commenced under Section 96 on filing of a Section 95 petition against him as personal guarantor for Sahil Home Loomtex, which extended to assets of partnership firm M/s Sheena Exports (in dissolution) where he held a 25% share[cite: 15]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that under Dilip B. Jiwrajka, the Section 96 moratorium operates strictly against the personal debt of the debtor and does not attach to properties of a partnership firm, in which partners have no distinct proprietary title prior to debt liquidation[cite: 15].

case_title: Jatin Mehta vs. Rushabh Civil Contractors Pvt. Ltd. Through: Debi Prasanna Sarangi, IRP & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jatin Mehta (Appellant/Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor); Rushabh Civil Contractors Pvt. Ltd. through IRP Debi Prasanna Sarangi (Respondent 1/Financial Creditor); Point Developers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial Creditor disbursed an inter-corporate loan of Rs. 3.50 Crores to the Corporate Debtor on 16.12.2016, repayable on demand with interest at 18% per annum[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default amount of Rs. 9,56,83,836/- (Principal Rs. 3,50,00,000/- plus interest of Rs. 6,06,83,836/- computed till 31.12.2022)[cite: 16]. The IRP issued a demand notice on 29.11.2022 demanding payment within 7 days, fixing the date of default as 07.12.2022[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan disbursed on 16.12.2016[cite: 16]. Corporate Debtor executed a letter acknowledging debt and undertaking repayment on 20.08.2020 (repayment promised by 01.12.2020)[cite: 16]. Financial Creditor admitted to CIRP on 27.06.2022[cite: 16]. IRP issued demand notice on 29.11.2022[cite: 16]. Default materialized on 07.12.2022[cite: 16]. Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 244/2023 filed on 20.01.2023[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited ledgers and financial statements from 01.04.2016 to 15.12.2023 recording interest accruals and TDS deductions; closing balance of Rs. 4,78,69,260/- due as on 31.03.2020; letter dated 20.08.2020 promising repayment by 01.12.2020 or allotment of two residential flats[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent 1 filed Section 7 application[cite: 16]. Corporate Debtor resisted on grounds of Article 21 limitation expiry on 15.12.2019, bar under Section 10A (alleging default on 01.12.2020), and lack of financial debt[cite: 16]. NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I admitted the Section 7 petition on 26.07.2024[cite: 16]. Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the loan facility along with accrued interest and TDS entries in the audited ledgers constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 16]. 2. Whether a Section 7 petition filed in 2023 for a loan disbursed in 2016 is barred by limitation under Article 21 of the Limitation Act, or saved by a written promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872[cite: 16]. 3. Whether the Section 7 petition was barred by Section 10A of the IBC on the ground that the Corporate Debtor's letter undertook repayment by 01.12.2020[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Continuous recording of loan transactions with interest accruals and tax deductions at source (TDS) in the debtor's books of account establishes financial debt; moreover, a written promise to pay an existing or time-barred debt constitutes a valid, enforceable contract under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, creating a fresh period of limitation from the date of the promise[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25(3) of the Contract Act novates the obligation and forms an independent basis of enforcement within three years of the written promise[cite: 16]. A debtor cannot voluntarily manipulate repayment promises during the Section 10A moratorium window to manufacture an artificial date of default and claim statutory immunity, especially when default was formally triggered by a post-10A demand notice[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Audited ledger entries containing explicit entries of interest alongside a signed written letter acknowledging liability and promising repayment provide conclusive proof of financial debt and subsistence of limitation[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was established; limitation was saved by the 20.08.2020 acknowledgment/promise under Section 25(3); default occurred on 07.12.2022 upon expiry of the demand notice, falling outside Section 10A[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1515 of 2024 is dismissed. The order dated 26.07.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I admitting CP(IB) 244/2023 is affirmed[cite: 16].
summary: Suspended Director of Point Developers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 26.07.2024 admitting a Section 7 application filed by Rushabh Civil Contractors Pvt. Ltd. (through IRP) for default of Rs. 9.56 Crores arising from a 2016 loan[cite: 16]. Appellant argued that the loan was barred by Article 21 of the Limitation Act and that default occurred on 01.12.2020 pursuant to a letter dated 20.08.2020, attracting the Section 10A moratorium[cite: 16]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that ledger entries of interest and TDS established a financial debt[cite: 16]. The letter dated 20.08.2020 constituted a valid promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, renewing limitation[cite: 16]. Default arose on 07.12.2022 following the IRP's demand notice, placing the action outside Section 10A[cite: 16].

case_title: Amreesh Neon Private Limited & Anr. vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amreesh Neon Private Limited (Appellant 1/Opposite Party 5); Manish Thakkar, Managing Director (Appellant 2); Competition Commission of India (Respondent 1); SBI Infra Management Solutions Pvt. Ltd./SBIIMS (Respondent 2/Informant/Procuring Entity); other competing signage vendors/cartelists (Respondents 3-14)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tender floated on 08.02.2018 by SBIIMS for procurement and installation of branch signboards across 13 circles/regions in India via e-reverse auction[cite: 17]. Out of 44 applicants, 9 vendors were shortlisted to submit bids[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Anti-competitive bid rigging and market sharing; collusive emails dated 02.06.2018 and 04.06.2018 distributed price floors across four geographic tiers (ranging from Rs. 7850 to Rs. 8150 per sq. m.) to manipulate auction outcomes[cite: 17]. CCI imposed a 1% penalty on average turnover: Rs. 32,15,795/- on Appellant 1 and Rs. 31,200/- on Appellant 2[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tender floated on 08.02.2018[cite: 17]; collusive emails circulated on 02.06.2018 and 04.06.2018[cite: 17]; complaint received on 28.06.2018[cite: 17]; DG investigation report submitted on 22.06.2021[cite: 17]; CCI final order passed on 03.02.2022[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email threads dated 02.06.2018 and 04.06.2018 detailing agreed circle-wise price floors copied to Appellant 1[cite: 17]; mirror bid pricing submitted by vendors matching the cartel allocations[cite: 17]; DG Investigation Report[cite: 17]; financial statements showing average total turnover of Rs. 32,15,79,533/- versus claimed illuminated signage turnover of Rs. 19,77,73,440/-[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI initiated suo motu Case No. 02 of 2020 under Section 19(1)[cite: 17]. On 03.02.2022, CCI held Appellants guilty under Sections 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) and imposed a 1% penalty on relevant turnover[cite: 17]. Appellants challenged the penalty quantum before NCLAT[cite: 17].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the penalty imposed under Section 27 of the Competition Act, 2002 must be confined strictly to the turnover of 'illuminated signages' (claimed relevant product) rather than the enterprise's total signage-related turnover under the doctrine of proportionality in Excel Crop Care[cite: 17]. 2. Whether an artificial segmental distinction between illuminated and unilluminated products within the same signage industry is tenable for calculating relevant turnover[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The principle of 'relevant turnover' established in Excel Crop Care applies to multi-product companies to exclude distinct, unrelated product lines from penalty computation; it does not permit an enterprise to carve out artificial segmental sub-categories within the same line of business (such as different varieties of signage) to dilute penalties for collusive bid rigging[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27 of the Competition Act permits penalties up to 10% of average turnover[cite: 17]. In cartelization and bid rigging under Section 3(3), relevant turnover encompasses the entire business activity pertaining to the infringed product market, and different varieties or technical formats of the same product constitute a singular relevant product market[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where audited accounts reveal that an enterprise's core operations are centered in the signage business, attempts to segregate illuminated from unilluminated signages for penalty mitigation constitute an impermissible after-thought[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCI's penalty of 1% on average turnover of Rs. 32,15,79,533/- was already lenient and fully proportionate; no further reduction was warranted[cite: 17].
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 30 of 2022 is dismissed. The order dated 03.02.2022 passed by the Competition Commission of India in Suo Moto Case No. 02 of 2020 is affirmed. No order as to costs[cite: 17].
summary: Amreesh Neon Pvt. Ltd. and its Managing Director appealed against the CCI order dated 03.02.2022 in Suo Moto Case No. 02 of 2020, which found them guilty of bid-rigging and cartelization under Section 3(3) of the Competition Act in an SBIIMS signage tender and imposed a 1% penalty of Rs. 32,15,795/-[cite: 17]. In appeal, Appellants conceded guilt on merits and sought reduction of penalty, arguing that under Excel Crop Care, relevant turnover should be confined to illuminated signages (Rs. 19.77 Crores) rather than total turnover (Rs. 32.15 Crores)[cite: 17]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the Excel Crop Care multi-product doctrine does not permit artificial segmentation of different varieties within the same signage line of business[cite: 17]. The 1% penalty was already lenient, requiring no interference[cite: 17].

case_title: Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd. vs. Ashish Singh, RP of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd. (Appellant/Successful Resolution Applicant); Ashish Singh, RP of Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent 1); Raj Kumar Sahani, Suspended Director/Shareholder (Respondent 2); CoC of Corporate Debtor (Respondent 3)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP under Section 7 on 22.02.2022; RP issued Form-G and subsequently registered the Corporate Debtor as an MSME on 24.05.2022 to attract resolution applicants[cite: 18]. Appellant submitted its Resolution Plan on 11.07.2022[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to CIRP; suspended management contended the loan account was an NPA since 14.06.2020[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-G issued on 05.05.2022; MSME registration secured on 24.05.2022; Resolution Plan submitted on 11.07.2022; CoC approval with 100% votes on 29.08.2022; Plan approval application IA No. 5458/2022 filed on 29.10.2022; Objections in IA No. 4173/2023 filed on 04.08.2023[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Due diligence report of DGA IB Resolution LLP verifying SRA eligibility; MSME certificate dated 24.05.2022; Form-H compliance certificate; unanimous 100% CoC voting records[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV on 24.01.2024 allowed IA No. 4173/2023 filed by Raj Kumar Sahani, holding Appellant ineligible under Section 29A(c) due to common promoter Birendra Kumar Pasari, rejected the resolution plan, and ordered liquidation[cite: 18]. Appellant challenged this order[cite: 18].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Appellant SRA suffered disqualification under Section 29A(c) of the IBC despite the Corporate Debtor holding MSME status prior to plan submission[cite: 18]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority had jurisdiction to discard the unanimous commercial wisdom of the CoC approving the Resolution Plan[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution applicant cannot be declared ineligible under Section 29A(c) of the IBC where the Corporate Debtor is registered as an MSME prior to plan submission, as Section 240A provides an overriding statutory carve-out[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A expressly renders Section 29A(c) inapplicable to MSMEs; under the dictum of Hari Babu Thota, the decisive date for testing disqualification under Section 29A(c) read with Section 240A is the date of submission of the resolution plan[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Timely procurement of MSME registration prior to bidding, corroborated by professional due diligence reports and absence of contemporaneous objections during CoC deliberations, establishes legal eligibility[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA submitted its plan on 11.07.2022, well after the Corporate Debtor received MSME status on 24.05.2022; Section 240A applied, nullifying Section 29A(c) disqualification, and making the rejection of the plan erroneous[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 256 & 257 of 2024 are allowed; impugned order dated 24.01.2024 is set aside; IA No. 4173 of 2023 is dismissed; IA No. 5458 of 2022 is allowed approving the Appellant's Resolution Plan; Adjudicating Authority to pass consequential orders within 60 days. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 18].
summary: Bishwanath Traders & Investment Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant for Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT New Delhi order dated 24.01.2024 which disqualified it under Section 29A(c) of the IBC, rejected its plan, and ordered liquidation on objections from a suspended director[cite: 18]. NCLAT held that because the Corporate Debtor obtained MSME registration prior to the submission of the resolution plan, the SRA was entitled to the statutory exemption under Section 240A, which overrides Section 29A(c)[cite: 18]. Applying the Supreme Court's decision in Hari Babu Thota, NCLAT reversed the NCLT's order, dismissed the suspended director's objections, and approved the resolution plan[cite: 18].

case_title: Sunil Kumar Agarwal & Anr. vs. Anand Sonbhadra RP of Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sunil Kumar Agarwal & Anr. (Appellants/Successful Resolution Applicants); Anand Sonbhadra (Resolution Professional/Respondent 1); New Okhla Industrial Development Authority/NOIDA (Respondent 2); Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority/GNIDA (Respondent 3); Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Concord Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: NOIDA executed a 90-year lease deed dated 30.07.2010 for Plot No. GH-05, Sector 137, Noida ('Shubhkamna Techhomes'). GNIDA executed a 90-year lease deed dated 04.04.2011 for Plot No. GH-02, Sector 1, Greater Noida ('Shubhkamna City'). The Corporate Debtor was developing residential projects on these leased lands. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of lease rents, land premium installments, and operational debt; NOIDA filed Form B on 22.02.2019 for Rs. 99,32,55,183/- (including future dues of Rs. 8,12,05,605/-), admitted by the RP. GNIDA filed no timely claim; the IM recorded unclaimed GNIDA dues of Rs. 60,64,54,762/-. Post-impugned order, NOIDA claimed Rs. 27,65,02,686/- and GNIDA claimed Rs. 1,00,95,82,526/- as CIRP costs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 26.11.2018 under Section 9. Public announcement on 29.11.2018. CoC approved the Appellants' resolution plan with an 87.57% voting share on 09.10.2019 (concluded 17.10.2019). RP filed plan approval CA No. 485/ND/2019. NCLT passed the impugned order on 12.09.2022 directing payment of lease rents/premiums during CIRP as CIRP costs. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan allocating Rs. 25 Crores to NOIDA and Rs. 18.50 Crores to GNIDA in six equal half-yearly installments, with Rs. 2.20 Crores budgeted as CIRP costs; lease deeds dated 30.07.2010 and 04.04.2011; Information Memorandum dated 26.11.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CA No. 485/ND/2019, NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV approved the resolution plan on 12.09.2022 but simultaneously held in paragraph 11 that accrued lease rentals and premiums from CIRP commencement (26.11.2018) to plan approval (12.09.2022) constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31, directing their submission within 15 days. SRA appealed against this modification.
legal_issues: 1. Whether accrued lease rentals and lease premium dues for leased land during the CIRP period constitute 'Insolvency Resolution Process Costs' under Section 5(13) of the IBC read with Regulation 31 of the CIRP Regulations and the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d). 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 31(1) of the IBC to modify an approved resolution plan by directing inclusion of substantial statutory lease dues as CIRP costs.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction only to approve or reject a resolution plan in terms of Section 31 and cannot alter, modify, or add financial obligations to an approved resolution plan; furthermore, lease premiums and lease rentals payable to statutory land authorities are not covered as essential supply costs or 'similar grants' under the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d) so as to automatically constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13). 2.
