STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31 and the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d) applies strictly to licenses, permits, registrations, quotas, concessions, or clearances required to keep the debtor running, and cannot be expanded to include lease land premium amounts or general lease rentals. Section 31 uses the mandatory word 'shall' to approve a compliant plan, without granting power to make alterations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the CoC in its commercial wisdom has approved a financial allocation for operational/statutory creditors based on the Information Memorandum, subsequent post-approval claims cannot be grafted into CIRP costs to alter plan viability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Following the precedent in Sunil Kumar Agrawal vs. NOIDA, the direction of the Adjudicating Authority treating lease rentals and premiums as CIRP costs was contrary to law and constituted an impermissible modification of the plan.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1351 of 2022 is allowed; the impugned direction in the order dated 12.09.2022 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV in CA No. 485/ND/2019 categorizing lease rentals and premiums as CIRP costs is set aside. No order as to costs.
summary: The Successful Resolution Applicant of Shubhkamna Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV order dated 12.09.2022 which approved the resolution plan but directed that accrued lease rentals and premiums payable to NOIDA and GNIDA during the CIRP period (amounting to over Rs. 128 Crores) be included as CIRP costs under Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31 and the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d). Setting aside the direction, NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority cannot modify or alter an approved resolution plan. Following its earlier decision in Sunil Kumar Agrawal vs. NOIDA, NCLAT held that land lease rentals and premiums do not fall within the scope of the Explanation to Section 14(1)(d) or Section 5(13). The appeal was allowed.

case_title: Mr. Kailash Motilal Kakrania & Anr. vs. M/s Apurva Oil and Industries Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Kailash Motilal Kakrania and Mrs. Manju Kailash Kakrania (Appellants/Financial Creditors/Shareholders); M/s Apurva Oil and Industries Private Limited (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unsecured loans advanced by the Appellants (erstwhile Director and shareholder) to the Corporate Debtor to fund its business operations in oil seeds, oil products, and agro products. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed financial debt default of Rs. 1,22,42,927/- (Principal amount of Rs. 1,01,50,009/- plus interest at 9% p.a. of Rs. 20,92,918/- till 30.06.2021). Demand notice issued on 16.07.2021. Corporate Debtor claimed a counter-set-off of Rs. 10,85,850/- to argue the debt fell below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on 16.07.2021; Section 7 petition filed on 04.09.2021; NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the petition on 14.07.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's Financial Statements and Balance Sheet for FY 2020-21 and FY 2021-22 (Note No. 3(B)) acknowledging liability of Rs. 1,01,50,009/-; ledger entries dated 10.07.2021 showing 8 sequential vouchers created on a single day for Rs. 10,85,850/- as 'Other Current Assets' without any prior demand notice; vague police complaint dated 06.06.2021 without specifying transaction details. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP (IB) No. 986/NCLT/MB/C-IV/2021 under Section 7. NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the petition on 14.07.2023, holding that interest was not agreed upon, and deducting the Corporate Debtor's counter-claim of Rs. 10,85,850/- to arrive at an outstanding debt of Rs. 90,64,159/-, which was below the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore. Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction in summary proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC to adjudicate, entertain, and allow set-off, adjustments, or counter-claims raised by a Corporate Debtor against an admitted financial debt. 2. Whether unilateral entries of receivables in the balance sheet made after default can reduce an admitted financial debt below the Section 4 statutory threshold.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: There is no statutory provision or mechanism under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 for entertaining set-offs, adjustments, or unadjudicated counter-claims by a Corporate Debtor at the pre-admission stage of a Section 7 petition; once an admitted, legally enforceable financial debt exceeds the statutory threshold, the petition must be admitted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 read with Section 4 requires the Adjudicating Authority only to record satisfaction as to the existence of a 'default' in respect of a 'financial debt' exceeding the threshold of Rs. 1 Crore; the summary nature of Section 7 precludes conducting a trial on disputed cross-claims or damages asserted by the debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unbroken acknowledgment of a debt exceeding Rs. 1 Crore in audited balance sheets establishes debt and default; suspicious, uncommunicated ledger entries posted on a single date showing alleged receivables under 'Other Current Assets' cannot legally offset admitted long-term financial borrowings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The financial debt of Rs. 1,01,50,009/- was admitted, acknowledged in balance sheets, and within limitation; the NCLT erred in adjusting Rs. 10,85,850/-, and the threshold under Section 4 was fully satisfied.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1257 of 2023 is allowed; impugned order dated 14.07.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside; matter is remanded back to NCLT Mumbai Bench for passing necessary consequential orders admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP under Section 7 of the Code. Connected IAs stand disposed of. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellants Kailash Motilal Kakrania and his wife appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 14.07.2023 which dismissed their Section 7 IBC application against Apurva Oil and Industries Pvt. Ltd. Although the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets acknowledged a debt of Rs. 1,01,50,009/-, the NCLT adjusted an alleged counter-claim of Rs. 10,85,850/- (unilateral rent collection entries) to hold that the net debt was Rs. 90,64,159/-, thereby falling below the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 Crore. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT held that the IBC provides no mechanism for set-offs, adjustments, or counter-claims at the pre-admission stage. Because the acknowledged financial debt exceeded Rs. 1 Crore and was within limitation, NCLAT set aside the dismissal and remanded the matter for admission into CIRP.

case_title: Dr. Yarlagadda Krishna Mohan vs. Mr. Dantu Indu Sekhar RP of YKM Entertainment & Hotels Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Yarlagadda Krishna Mohan (Appellant/Promoter & Ex-Director of Corporate Debtor); Dantu Indu Sekhar (Respondent 1/Resolution Professional); State Bank of India (Respondent 2/Sole Financial Creditor & CoC); M/s Square Four Housing & Infrastructure Development Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent 3/Successful Resolution Applicant); YKM Entertainment & Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was constructing a 5-star hotel in Tirupati under an O&M agreement with Intercontinental Group (Holiday Inn); term loan facilities sanctioned by SBI under agreements dated 30.08.2011 and 27.10.2015 for Rs. 138.7 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account classified as NPA on 29.11.2016; SBI attempted SARFAESI public auction on 08.12.2021 with reserve price of Rs. 150 Crores; Corporate Debtor admitted to CIRP on 05.01.2022; CoC approved SRA's resolution plan with liquidation value benchmark of approx. Rs. 80 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 05.01.2022; second Form-G published on 22.08.2022; CoC approved SRA's plan in 12th meeting on 01.02.2023; Appellant's earlier challenge in IA No. 315/2023 dismissed by NCLT on 05.07.2023, by NCLAT on 30.11.2023, and by Supreme Court on 13.12.2023; NCLT approved Resolution Plan on 07.12.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 4th, 7th, 8th, and 12th CoC meetings; resolution of CIBIL card overdue and DIN reactivations qualifying SRA; forensic due diligence reports; dismissal orders of prior proceedings in IA No. 315/2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved Respondent 3's Resolution Plan in IA No. 192/2023 on 07.12.2023. Appellant, having previously failed in challenging the approval process up to the Supreme Court, filed this appeal challenging the plan on grounds of SRA ineligibility under Section 29A and asset undervaluation.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appeal challenging the approval of a resolution plan is barred by res judicata where the promoter/suspended director previously challenged the CoC's approval process in separate proceedings which were dismissed up to the Supreme Court. 2. Whether the approval of a resolution plan is vitiated under Section 29A and Section 30(2) when the SRA cured initial disqualifications during a re-issued Form-G process.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party who has unsuccessfully litigated the validity of a resolution plan's approval process up to the highest appellate forum is barred by the principles of res judicata from re-agitating challenges against the same plan under new grounds that were available but omitted in earlier rounds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: When the CoC exercises its power to re-issue Form-G, eligibility under Section 29A is assessed afresh based on the documentation submitted in the subsequent round; prior observations in earlier aborted rounds do not create a perpetual statutory disqualification once defects are cured. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where contemporaneous CoC minutes confirm that an applicant remedied previous documentation defects and expert valuation reports substantiate liquidation benchmarks, allegations of statutory non-compliance cannot survive. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was barred by res judicata, the Appellant waived objections by attending CoC meetings without raising them, and the SRA was fully eligible under Section 29A.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 9/2024 is dismissed as devoid of merits. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary: Suspended Director Dr. Yarlagadda Krishna Mohan appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 07.12.2023 approving the Resolution Plan of Square Four Housing & Infrastructure Development Pvt. Ltd. for YKM Entertainment & Hotels Pvt. Ltd. Appellant argued that the SRA was ineligible under Section 29A and that the CoC undervalued the asset. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the challenge was barred by res judicata because the Appellant had previously challenged the CoC's approval process up to the Supreme Court and failed. Furthermore, on the merits, the SRA had cured its earlier documentation defects in the second round of Form-G, and the approved plan complied fully with Sections 29A and 30(2).

case_title: Mr. A. Guhan & Anr. vs. Ms. Sunita Umesh, Liquidator, M/s Deltronix India Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. A. Guhan & A.G.S. Sumyuha (Appellants/Lessors); Ms. Sunita Umesh (Respondent/Liquidator of M/s Deltronix India Limited); Deltronix India Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Registered Lease Deed dated 04.04.2012 executed by Appellants' predecessor-in-title leasing an industrial shed and open space in Thiruvallur District to the Corporate Debtor for 7 years at a monthly lease rent of Rs. 21,83,000/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in lease rent payments commenced in December 2014; lease terminated on 01.05.2015; Arbitral Award dated 07.09.2016 granted arrears of Rs. 1,26,95,876/- and monthly damages of Rs. 21,83,000/- until possession was restored; Appellants filed Form-B claiming Rs. 12,18,30,000/-. Claim for lease rent/damages during CIRP (03.02.2021 to 18.10.2022) amounted to Rs. 21,83,000/- per month. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default began in December 2014; lease expired on 04.04.2019; CIRP commenced on 03.02.2021; Liquidation ordered on 18.10.2022; Liquidator communicated decision rejecting CIRP cost status on 03.01.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral Award dated 07.09.2016; pending Execution Petitions EP Nos. 40/2018 & 41/2018; Liquidator's email dated 03.01.2023 admitting claim as an Operational Debt rather than CIRP cost; Corporate Debtor's operations having ceased five years prior to CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In Company Appeal (IBC) No. 13/2023 under Section 42 of the IBC, NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II held on 09.05.2023 that rent/damages for the CIRP period (03.02.2021 to 18.10.2022) could not be treated as CIRP cost, directed handover of vacant possession by 09.05.2023, and permitted adjustment against the Rs. 2,18,30,000/- security deposit. Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether occupation charges/damages for leased premises during the CIRP period constitute 'Insolvency Resolution Process Costs' under Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31(b) of the CIRP Regulations when the lease had expired and rent had been defaulted years prior to CIRP commencement. 2. Whether the stay on execution proceedings under Section 14(1)(a) constitutes a prejudicial effect of moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) so as to convert operational rental claims into CIRP costs.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a lease has expired and default in rent occurred long before the commencement of CIRP, the continuation of possession by the Corporate Debtor does not cause prejudice on account of the moratorium under Section 14(1)(d), and occupation damages during CIRP cannot be classified as CIRP costs under Regulation 31(b) unless the premises are actively utilized to run the Corporate Debtor as a going concern. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 31(b) read with Section 5(13)(e) and Section 14(1)(d) applies only to situations where an ongoing, functioning contractual right to receive rent is disrupted by the moratorium; an inability to execute a pre-existing arbitral award falls under the moratorium in Section 14(1)(a), which does not convert execution debts into CIRP costs. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evidence showing non-payment of rent for over 6 years prior to CIRP and absence of active business operations confirms that the premises were not utilized as a going concern, precluding classification under Section 5(13)(c). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants' claim for occupation charges during CIRP was properly classified by the Liquidator as an Operational Debt to be distributed under Section 53, and could not be treated as CIRP cost.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1095 of 2023 is dismissed. The order dated 09.05.2023 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II is affirmed.
summary: Appellants/Lessors appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 09.05.2023 which affirmed the Liquidator's decision treating lease rent/occupation damages (Rs. 21.83 Lakhs per month) during the CIRP of Deltronix India Limited as an Operational Debt rather than CIRP cost under Regulation 31(b). The lease had expired in 2019 and rent had remained unpaid since December 2014, with Appellants holding an execution decree. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the stay on executing the arbitral award arose under Section 14(1)(a) and not Section 14(1)(d). Since the Corporate Debtor had ceased operations long before CIRP, the premises were not used to maintain it as a going concern, making the dues an operational debt payable under Section 53.

case_title: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II (Legal), EPFO vs. Vinod Balachandran, RP of M/s Albanna Engineering (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II (Legal), EPFO (Appellant); Vinod Balachandran, Resolution Professional/Liquidator of M/s Albanna Engineering (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent); Albanna Engineering (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory provident fund contributions, interest, and damages assessed against the Corporate Debtor as an employer under the Employees' Provident Funds & Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in remitting provident fund dues resulting in statutory assessment of interest under Section 7Q and penal damages under Section 14B totaling Rs. 3,00,972/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claim lodged by EPFO before the Liquidator; claim rejected/relegated to waterfall distribution; Company Appeal (IBC)/04/KOB/2023 filed under Section 42 before NCLT Kochi Bench; NCLT dismissed the appeal on 21.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statutory assessment orders under Section 7Q and Section 14B of the 1952 Act; proof of claim filed with the Liquidator; admission of default under statutory heads. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi Bench on 21.03.2024 dismissed the Appellant's appeal under Section 42 of the IBC, holding that amounts due under Sections 7Q and 14B were not covered under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) and were subject to distribution under the Section 53 waterfall mechanism. EPFO appealed to NCLAT Chennai.
legal_issues: 1. Whether statutory interest and penal damages assessed under Section 7Q and Section 14B of the Employees' Provident Funds & Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 are excluded from the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC or are subject to the waterfall distribution under Section 53. 2. Whether the priority of provident fund dues under Section 11 of the 1952 Act applies to interest and damages in insolvency and liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory dues payable by an employer under Section 7Q (interest) and Section 14B (damages) of the Employees' Provident Funds & Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 fall squarely within the meaning of 'any amount due from an employer' under Section 11 of that Act and must be kept outside the liquidation estate of the Corporate Debtor pursuant to Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC, requiring full payment rather than distribution under the Section 53 waterfall. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC explicitly excludes all sums due to any workman or employee from the provident fund, pension fund, or gratuity fund from the liquidation estate; as established in Maharashtra State Co-operative Bank and Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association, this protection extends to statutory damages under Section 14B and interest under Section 7Q. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Valid statutory assessment orders issued by the competent authority under Sections 7Q and 14B establish non-derogable claims that cannot be compromised or treated as ordinary operational debts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in subjecting the EPFO's claim of Rs. 3,00,972/- to Section 53; the amount must be kept out of the liquidation estate and paid in full.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 351/2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 21.03.2024 passed by NCLT Kochi Bench is quashed. The Liquidator is directed to pay the admitted claim of Rs. 3,00,972/- outside the Section 53 waterfall mechanism. No costs.
summary: The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner-II (EPFO) appealed against NCLT Kochi Bench's order dated 21.03.2024 in Company Appeal (IBC)/04/KOB/2023, which denied full payment of Rs. 3,00,972/- assessed as interest and damages under Sections 7Q and 14B of the EPF Act, 1952 against Albanna Engineering (India) Pvt. Ltd. and relegated the dues to the Section 53 waterfall. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT Chennai held that following the Supreme Court's ruling in Maharashtra State Co-operative Bank and NCLAT's decision in Jet Aircraft, all amounts due under the EPF Act (including Sections 7Q and 14B) fall within Section 36(4)(a)(iii) of the IBC and are excluded from the liquidation estate. NCLAT quashed the impugned order and directed full payment.

case_title: Getz Cables Private Limited vs. State Bank of India and Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Getz Cables Private Limited is the Corporate Applicant / Corporate Guarantor (Appellant). State Bank of India (Respondent No. 1) and Northern ARC Capital Limited (Respondent No. 2) are the Financial Creditors. M/s Shivpriya Cables Pvt. Ltd. is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Principal Borrower availed fund-based and non-fund-based credit facilities from SBI sanctioned up to Rs. 42,58,00,000/- and credit facilities of Rs. 1,64,59,163/- from Northern ARC Capital Limited, secured by Corporate Guarantees and equitable mortgages over industrial plot Plot No. E-448, RIICO Industrial Area, Chopanki, City Bhiwadi, Rajasthan executed by the Corporate Applicant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed by SBI was Rs. 52,94,32,352.10 and by Northern ARC Capital Ltd was Rs. 1,64,59,163/-; account was classified as NPA on 04.08.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Northern ARC issued guarantee invocation notice on 23.01.2023. SBI issued notice under Section 13(2) SARFAESI on 24.02.2023 (referenced also as 22.02.2023), followed by possession notice on 22.06.2023 and Section 14 SARFAESI order on 05.12.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 10 petition disclosed all liabilities of lenders, mortgage deeds, board resolution dated 30.09.2023, balance sheets for FY 2021-22 and 2022-23, and lack of ongoing business for five years. SBI filed Section 65 application asserting Section 10 was filed on the verge of completion of SARFAESI actions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Applicant filed Section 10 petition CP(IB) No. 749/ND/2023 on 02.11.2023 before NCLT New Delhi III. On 30.09.2024, NCLT dismissed the Section 10 petition and allowed SBI's IA No. 1955/2024 under Section 65, imposing a Rs. 1,00,000/- penalty on the ground of malicious and fraudulent intent to stall SARFAESI recovery.
legal_issues: Whether the initiation of an application under Section 10 of the IBC by a Corporate Applicant can be dismissed and penalized under Section 65 solely because it was filed during the pendency and advanced stages of SARFAESI proceedings initiated by a secured financial creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The initiation of insolvency proceedings under Section 10 of the IBC cannot be deemed fraudulent or malicious under Section 65 merely because recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act were initiated or imminent prior to the filing; an independent right exists upon occurrence of debt and default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 65 requires strict proof that proceedings were initiated fraudulently (with deceit resulting in injury) or with malicious intent (wrongful act intentionally done without just cause or excuse) for purposes other than resolution of insolvency; mere halting of creditor recovery caused by statutory moratorium does not per se fulfill Section 65. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete material and specific evidentiary foundation must establish malicious or fraudulent intent beyond the mere existence and timing of Section 13(2) or 13(4) SARFAESI notices. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of the Section 10 petition and imposition of penalty under Section 65 by the Adjudicating Authority was erroneous as no foundational evidence of fraudulent intent existed; Section 10 petition is restored for adjudication afresh.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed without costs. The impugned order dated 30.09.2024 is set aside, IA No. 1955 of 2024 filed by SBI under Section 65 is dismissed, the penalty of Rs. 1,00,000/- is nullified, and CP (IB)-749/ND/2023 under Section 10 is revived for fresh consideration on merits in accordance with law.
summary: Getz Cables Private Limited appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi Court-III which dismissed its Section 10 IBC application and imposed a Rs. 1,00,000 penalty under Section 65 on an application by State Bank of India. The NCLT had held that filing Section 10 while SARFAESI recovery against mortgaged properties was underway demonstrated malicious and fraudulent intent. NCLAT set aside the order, ruling that the pendency or advanced stage of SARFAESI proceedings does not debar a corporate debtor from seeking insolvency resolution or establish fraudulent intent under Section 65 without independent evidence. The appeal was allowed, and the Section 10 petition revived for determination on merits.

case_title: Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd. vs. Summit Binani, Resolution Professional of KSK Mahanadi Power Company Limited and Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd. (formerly PGCIL) is the Appellant / Operational Creditor. KSK Mahanadi Power Company Limited is the Corporate Debtor, represented by Resolution Professional Summit Binani (Respondent No. 1). Power Finance Corporation is Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor entered into a Bulk Power Transmission Agreement dated 24.02.2010 and Transmission Service Agreement (TSA) dated 05.12.2012 with CTUIL/PGCIL for transmission of power using the inter-state transmission system. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding pre-CIRP transmission claim was filed for Rs. 356.41 Crores (out of which Rs. 98.75 Crores was admitted by RP). A cash security deposit of Rs. 108.44 Crores had been deposited by the Corporate Debtor in February 2019 in lieu of a letter of credit following CERC orders. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 03.10.2019. CTUIL filed Form B claim on 03.01.2020. CTUIL encashed/adjusted the Rs. 108.44 Crores security deposit towards pre-CIRP dues on 28.03.2020. CTUIL issued power regulation notices on 03.06.2020. Corporate Debtor filed IA No. 487/2020 on 22.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 28.03.2020 showing unilateral encashment and adjustment of the cash security deposit by CTUIL towards pre-CIRP invoices while CIRP and moratorium were active. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 09.10.2020 in IA No. 487/2020 held that post-CIRP unilateral appropriation of the security deposit towards pre-CIRP dues was impermissible under Section 14 and ordered CTUIL to adjust the Rs. 108.44 Crores against post-CIRP transmission dues.
legal_issues: Whether a creditor is legally permitted to unilaterally encash and adjust a cash security deposit lying with it against pre-CIRP dues of the Corporate Debtor during the currency of the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Assets or cash security deposits furnished by a corporate debtor prior to CIRP remain the property of the corporate debtor until lawfully adjusted, and any post-commencement unilateral adjustment towards pre-CIRP dues violates the statutory moratorium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC strictly prohibits any action to foreclose, recover, or enforce any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property; Section 238 confers overriding supremacy to the Code over conflicting statutory regimes including the Electricity Act, 2003. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pre-CIRP claims must be submitted and adjudicated via the claim collation procedure before the RP to be settled strictly in accordance with an approved resolution plan, whereas during CIRP only current supplies under Section 14(2) and (2A) are entitled to contemporaneous discharge. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appropriation of the security deposit after the insolvency commencement date to satisfy pre-CIRP debts violates Section 14, and NCLT rightly directed adjustment towards post-CIRP operational dues.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs. The NCLT Hyderabad Bench order dated 09.10.2020 in IA No. 487/2020 is affirmed, directing CTUIL to adjust the Rs. 108.44 Crores only against post-CIRP dues. All connected Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary: Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Hyderabad which declared CTUIL's unilateral encashment and adjustment of a pre-CIRP cash security deposit of Rs. 108.44 Crores towards pre-CIRP transmission dues as illegal and violative of Section 14 of the IBC. CTUIL contended that under CERC Regulations and the TSA, the FIFO method permitted adjustment against older dues. NCLAT held that once moratorium triggers under Section 14, pre-CIRP dues are frozen and recoverable solely through claims in the resolution plan, while security deposits remain corporate debtor assets. The Tribunal affirmed that the deposit could only be adjusted against post-CIRP operational charges.

case_title: K.H. Khan & Anr. vs. Art Constructions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1116 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1117 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K.H. Khan & Anr. are land owners (Appellants). M/s Adel Landmarks Ltd. (formerly Era Landmarks (India) Ltd.) is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP represented by RP Udayraj Patwardhan. Art Constructions Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant. Parinda Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Collaboration Agreement dated 05.07.2008 and Addendum dated 28.10.2009 executed between land owners, Upkar Developers, and Corporate Debtor for development of 36 acres 04 Guntas in Kengeri Village, Bangalore. Corporate Debtor was to pay HUDCO loan and interest-free refundable deposit of Rs. 35 Crores (later Rs. 25 Crores), with revenue share ratio of 29.5:70.5. Assignment Agreement executed on 25.01.2010 assigning rights to Parinda Buildcon. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor infused over Rs. 64 Crores including clearing Rs. 17.19 Crores principal and Rs. 1.34 Crores interest to HUDCO. Appellants terminated agreements claiming default by notices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellants issued termination notices on 17.02.2012 and 22.02.2012. Arbitrator appointed on 20.04.2012 terminated arbitration proceedings on 15.07.2015. Section 7 CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 05.12.2018. Appellants filed IA No. 4648/2020 on 05.10.2020. CoC approved SRA plan on 06.12.2022 (82.66%). SRA filed IA No. 58/2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Collaboration Agreement, Addendum, Assignment Agreement, Sole Arbitrator termination order dated 15.07.2015 under Section 32(2)(c), Karnataka High Court dismissal dated 25.06.2019, and Public Notice dated 07.08.2020 by Brigade Enterprises. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III on 30.04.2024 allowed SRA's intervention IA No. 58/2023 and disposed of IA No. 4648/2020 holding complex title disputes must go to Civil Court.
legal_issues: 1. Whether NCLT has jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to decide if development rights in land form part of the Corporate Debtor's CIRP assets or if parties must be relegated to Civil Court. 2. Whether an arbitral order terminating proceedings under Section 32(2)(c) constitutes an arbitral award with res judicata effect. 3. Whether development rights constitute 'property' under Section 3(27) includible in the Information Memorandum under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 29.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Development rights acquired under a collaboration agreement constitute 'property' and 'assets' of a corporate debtor under Sections 3(27) and 18(1)(f) of the IBC; NCLT possesses full jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to determine the inclusion or exclusion of such assets in CIRP without relegating parties to a civil court. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 32(2)(c) orders terminating arbitral proceedings are distinct from final arbitral awards under Section 31/32(1) and do not determine substantive rights of parties or carry finality under Section 35. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where substantial investments have been made and contractual development rights vested, the Explanation to Section 18(1)(f) does not preclude inclusion of intangible development rights in the Information Memorandum even if third parties retain underlying fee title. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP correctly included development rights in the Information Memorandum, and NCLT did not err in refusing to delete the schedule property from CIRP, nor in allowing SRA intervention.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1116 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1117 of 2024 are dismissed with no order as to costs. The refusal to exclude development properties from CIRP and the allowance of SRA's intervention in IA No. 58 of 2023 are affirmed, with the clarification that NCLT has full jurisdiction to decide asset inclusion.
summary: Landowners appealed NCLT New Delhi orders refusing to exclude 36 acres of project land from the CIRP of Adel Landmarks Ltd. and allowing the intervention of the Successful Resolution Applicant. The Appellants argued that the Collaboration Agreement was terminated, an arbitral order had terminated developer claims, and third-party owned land could not be included under Section 18(1)(f). NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that development rights constitute 'property' under Section 3(27) and are properly includible in the Information Memorandum. It held that the arbitral termination order under Section 32(2)(c) was not an award determining substantive rights, and affirmed NCLT's jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to decide asset controversies.

case_title: K.H. Khan & Anr. vs. Udayraj Patwardhan, Resolution Professional of Adel Landmarks Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1117 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1116 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K.H. Khan & Anr. are land owners (Appellants). Adel Landmarks Ltd. (formerly Era Landmarks (India) Ltd.) is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP represented by RP Udayraj Patwardhan (Respondent No. 1). Art Constructions Pvt. Ltd. is SRA. Parinda Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. is subsidiary and assignee. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Collaboration Agreement dated 05.07.2008 and Addendum dated 28.10.2009 for joint real estate development of 36 acres 04 Guntas in Kengeri Hobli, Bangalore, wherein Corporate Debtor paid off Appellants' HUDCO bank liability and agreed to pay Rs. 25 Crores refundable security deposit with 70.5% developer revenue share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor made overall project investments of Rs. 64 Crores including Rs. 17.19 Crores principal and Rs. 1.34 Crores interest to HUDCO; Appellants alleged breach of project milestones. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellants issued termination notices on 17.02.2012 and 22.02.2012. Section 11(5) arbitration commenced 20.04.2012; Arbitrator terminated proceedings on 15.07.2015. CIRP initiated under Section 7 on 05.12.2018. Appellants filed IA No. 4648/2020 on 05.10.2020 after Brigade Enterprises published JDA notice on 07.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Collaboration Agreement, Supplementary Addendum, unstamped Assignment Agreement dated 25.01.2010, Section 32(2)(c) termination order of Arbitrator, and orders of Civil Court and Karnataka High Court dismissing Section 34/MFA challenges. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III on 30.04.2024 disposed of IA No. 4648/2020 declining to exclude the properties on the ground that complex disputes of title and contract validity must be decided by a Competent Civil Court.
legal_issues: 1. Whether NCLT has jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to adjudicate asset exclusion applications concerning development rights claimed by the Corporate Debtor. 2. Whether an arbitral tribunal order under Section 32(2)(c) constitutes an arbitral award terminating the Corporate Debtor's rights. 3. Whether development rights over third-party owned land can be included in the Information Memorandum under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 29.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Development rights acquired by a corporate debtor under collaboration agreements constitute proprietary 'assets' within the definition of property under Section 3(27) and are properly includible in the Information Memorandum; the NCLT retains exclusive jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to decide disputes on whether such rights belong to the corporate debtor's CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An administrative or procedural termination order passed under Section 32(2)(c) of the Arbitration Act does not determine parties' substantive contractual rights and cannot operate as an arbitral award under Section 31 or create res judicata under Section 35. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unilateral contractual termination via legal notice without return of agreed investments (Clause 6) or judicial decree does not extinguish development rights recognized in CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Professional was legally justified in maintaining the subject land's development rights in the Information Memorandum, and NCLT did not err in denying exclusion of the properties from CIRP.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1117 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs. The impugned order of NCLT New Delhi Court-III in IA No. 4648 of 2020 refusing to delete the schedule properties from CIRP is affirmed.
summary: Appellants/landowners appealed against the NCLT order disposing of IA No. 4648/2020 in the CIRP of Adel Landmarks Ltd., challenging the inclusion of their 36-acre property in the Information Memorandum. The Appellants contended that the underlying Collaboration Agreement was terminated in 2012, confirmed by an arbitral termination order, and that third-party property cannot form part of CIRP assets under Section 18(1)(f). NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that development rights constitute 'property' under Section 3(27) IBC, the arbitral termination under Section 32(2)(c) did not constitute a binding award on merits, and the RP acted properly in reflecting development rights in the CIRP to protect corporate assets.

case_title: Clarion Health Food LLP vs. Goli Vada Pav Pvt. Ltd. (through IRP Vinod Radhakrishna Nair) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Clarion Health Food LLP is the Appellant (majority shareholder holding 63.64% equity in the Corporate Debtor). Goli Vada Pav Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1). Vista Processed Foods Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor supplied food products and goods to the Corporate Debtor under a Manufacturing Agreement dated 06.12.2016 with an interest clause for overdue invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed was Rs. 3,56,04,233/- arising from invoices raised between 02.08.2018 and 30.06.2021. Balance confirmations acknowledging liability were executed on 18.08.2020 (Rs. 2,57,00,271/-), 12.07.2021 (Rs. 2,68,20,777/-), and 08.07.2022 (Rs. 2,68,20,867.11/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Operational Creditor issued Section 8 Demand Notice on 15.10.2022 and Corrigendum on 29.10.2022. Corporate Debtor replied on 04.11.2022. Appellant filed CP No. 28/2023 under Sections 241-242 on 05.01.2023. Section 9 petition CP (IB) 145(MB)/2023 was filed on 29.01.2023 and admitted on 05.09.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Ledger accounts (Annexure L), three signed balance confirmations, and invoices demonstrating supply and default. Corporate Debtor did not specifically deny the balance confirmations in its reply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-II admitted the Section 9 petition on 05.09.2023. The Appellant appealed the admission order under Section 61 asserting an inter-se shareholder dispute and lack of notice.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an equity shareholder of a Corporate Debtor has the locus standi as a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61 of the IBC to maintain an appeal against an order admitting a Section 9 application. 2. Whether an inter-se shareholder dispute or oppression/mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual or majority equity shareholder of a corporate debtor does not have locus standi as a 'person aggrieved' under Section 61 of the IBC to challenge an order admitting the corporate debtor into CIRP, nor can they maintain a derivative action on its behalf. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC is strictly confined to a dispute between the Corporate Debtor and the Operational Creditor; disputes among shareholders or oppression and mismanagement claims do not constitute a dispute qua the creditor. Section 238 overrides the Companies Act, 2013. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where operational debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold are established with unrefuted balance confirmations, admission under Section 9 is mandatory, and shareholder grievances cannot derail the proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant has no standing to maintain the appeal against the Section 9 admission order, and inter-se shareholder proceedings under Sections 241-242 do not vitiate a valid CIRP.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed as not maintainable for lack of locus standi, and on merits. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed. No order as to costs.
summary: Clarion Health Food LLP, holding 63.64% shares in Goli Vada Pav Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Mumbai Bench-II's order admitting an operational debt application of Rs. 3.56 Crores filed by Vista Processed Foods Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant claimed it had filed an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 prior to the Section 9 petition, alleging collusion and pre-existing dispute. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that equity shareholders have no locus standi under Section 61 as 'aggrieved persons' to challenge a CIRP admission order or pursue derivative actions. It further reaffirmed that Section 5(6) requires a dispute directly between the debtor and creditor, not inter-se shareholder conflicts.

case_title: Entegra Limited vs. Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Entegra Limited is the Promoter/Shareholder (Appellant). Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1). Power Finance Corporation Ltd. (PFC) is the Lead Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financing of a 400 MW hydroelectric project at Mandaleshwar, MP via multiple agreements: Rupee Term Loan/Foreign Currency Loan (04.12.1998), Amendatory & Restated Agreement (16.09.2005), Common Loan Agreement (29.09.2006), Subordinate Loan Agreement of Rs. 375 Cr (29.09.2006), Master Restructuring Agreement (22.06.2010), and Additional Loan Agreement of Rs. 600 Cr (27.04.2017) wherein Rs. 384.59 Cr was disbursed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under Section 7 was Rs. 2789.42 Crores as of 15.01.2018 (including principal, interest, DPG liability of Rs. 318.49 Cr, and ZCB liability of Rs. 103.87 Cr). Loan account classified as NPA on 31.03.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand letters issued on 06.07.2017, 01.10.2017, 05.01.2018. Loan recall notice issued on 17.01.2018. Section 7 petition CP (IB) 111/2018 filed on 16.02.2018. MoU executed on 22.07.2019 automatically terminated on 22.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Balance sheet acknowledgments for FY 2013-14 (signed 17.11.2014 by Promoter Mukul Kasliwal) and FY 2016-17 (signed 28.08.2017); BoD minutes dated 29.09.2015 and 02.03.2017 welcoming additional funding; Schedule II of Additional Loan Agreement acknowledging Rs. 1750.93 Cr debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Split verdict on 08.10.2021 by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench (Judicial Member admitted; Technical Member dismissed under Section 65). Third Member (Judicial), NCLT Kolkata on reference under Section 419(5) concurred on 27.09.2022 to admit Section 7.
legal_issues: 1. Whether financial creditors whose subordinate debt was converted to equity and who invoked pledged shares lose their status as financial creditors or must file under Section 10 instead of Section 7. 2. Whether the Section 7 petition was barred by limitation. 3. Whether non-disbursal of an interest tranche of Rs. 10 Crores constituted an engineered default requiring dismissal under Section 65.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial creditor retains its independent statutory status and right to file a Section 7 IBC application notwithstanding temporary acquisition of pledged shares or partial debt-to-equity conversions undertaken to preserve a distressed project; such lender does not become a corporate applicant restricted to Section 10. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Successive written balance sheet entries signed by directors and board meeting resolutions constitute valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, renewing limitation from the date of each acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure to release subsequent loan tranches due to failure of contractual conditions precedent cannot substantiate a plea of fraudulent or malicious initiation under Section 65 when substantial debt and persistent defaults are established on record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor committed substantial defaults exceeding the statutory threshold, the Section 7 petition was within limitation, and the majority decision of NCLT admitting CIRP was fully valid.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs. The Impugned Order dated 27.09.2022 admitting the Section 7 application CP (IB) 111/2018 and initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation Ltd. is upheld. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary: Entegra Limited, promoter of Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation Ltd., appealed against the NCLT order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Power Finance Corporation Ltd. for defaults exceeding Rs. 2,789 Crores. The Promoter contended that lenders held management control, engineered the default by withholding Rs. 10 Crores IDC, and were restricted to Section 10. Following a split verdict referred under Section 419(5) of the Companies Act, NCLAT affirmed the third member's judgment admitting CIRP. It held that lenders retain independent Section 7 rights notwithstanding pledge invocations, debt acknowledgments in balance sheets saved limitation under Section 18, and no ground existed to invoke Section 65.

case_title: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India vs. Reliance Telecom Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 273 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 355 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) is the statutory regulator/Appellant[cite: 7]. Reliance Telecom Ltd. and Reliance Communications Ltd. are the Corporate Debtors under CIRP[cite: 7]. Ericsson India Pvt. Ltd. was the initiating Operational Creditor[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtors operated telecommunication services governed by TRAI Regulations[cite: 7]. Corporate Debtors collected security deposits from post-paid subscribers and held unspent balances of pre-paid subscribers, and discontinued voice services on 29.12.2017[cite: 7]. TRAI directed refunds under MNP Regulations and levied financial disincentives[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: TRAI claimed Rs. 85,10,000/- as statutory financial disincentives (plus Rs. 1,60,000/- imposed on 17.04.2018) along with unquantified unspent balances and security deposits of subscribers[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 15.05.2018[cite: 7]. RP requested TRAI to submit claims via letters dated 14.05.2019 and 03.07.2019, but TRAI filed no claim[cite: 7]. TRAI filed IA No. 4124/2019 and IA No. 88/2020 under Section 60(5) in 2019/2020[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Financial statements of the Corporate Debtor for 2018-19 (Note 2.16 'Other Current Liabilities') reflecting unspent balances, customer advances, and statutory dues as balance sheet liabilities rather than segregated trust accounts[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I on 05.12.2023 and 19.12.2023 allowed the IAs directing that refundable security deposits and unspent balances be admitted as Operational Debt payable to the Telecommunication Consumers Education and Protection Fund, and penalties treated as Operational Debt under the waterfall mechanism, rejecting preferential payment or trust asset exclusion[cite: 7].
legal_issues: 1. Whether subscriber security deposits and unspent prepaid balances are held by a telecom company in constructive trust and excluded from CIRP assets under Section 18(1)(f) of the IBC[cite: 7]. 2. Whether statutory penalties/financial disincentives imposed by TRAI rank higher than operational debt or override the IBC waterfall mechanism under Section 53 via the TRAI Act[cite: 7]. 3. Whether unspent subscriber balances constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13)(c)[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory penalties and commingled customer deposits recorded as liabilities on a corporate debtor's balance sheet constitute operational debts under the IBC rather than trust properties excluded under Section 18(1)(f), and are strictly subject to resolution plan distribution[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC has overriding effect over sectoral statutes like the TRAI Act, 1997; regulatory penalties and statutory liabilities cannot circumvent the Section 53 waterfall mechanism[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To claim property is impressed with a trust under Section 18(1)(f), there must be evidence of a designated trust account, segregation of funds, and legal prohibition against commercial use; absent this, general liabilities remain operational debts[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly classified subscriber balances and TRAI disincentives as operational debt rather than trust assets or CIRP costs[cite: 7].
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 273 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 355 of 2024 are dismissed without costs[cite: 7]. Orders dated 05.12.2023 and 19.12.2023 of NCLT Mumbai Bench-I are affirmed[cite: 7]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are disposed of[cite: 7].
summary: TRAI appealed against orders of NCLT Mumbai Bench-I concerning the CIRP of Reliance Telecom Ltd. and Reliance Communications Ltd., where NCLT held that subscriber security deposits, unspent prepaid balances, and TRAI-levied penalties of Rs. 85.10 lakhs were operational debts payable under the resolution plan rather than trust assets or priority dues[cite: 7]. TRAI contended the TRAI Act as a special law prevailed over the IBC and subscriber funds were held in constructive trust under Section 18(1)(f)[cite: 7]. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, ruling that Section 238 overrides the TRAI Act, unsegregated deposits utilized in ordinary operations are balance sheet liabilities treated as operational debt, and penalty claims cannot bypass the statutory CIRP process[cite: 7].

case_title: Lieutenant Colonel Sandeep Dewan vs. Ootacamund Club & 13 Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Lieutenant Colonel Sandeep Dewan (Retd) is an individual member of Ootacamund Club (Appellant)[cite: 8]. Ootacamund Club is a Section 8 company limited by guarantee with around 900 members (Respondent No. 1), represented by its President and 13 office bearers/committee members (Respondents No. 2-14)[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Membership and club governance rights governed by Articles of Association; Appellant became an active member on 17.10.2016[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-monetary dispute involving challenge to 1-year suspension (and subsequent implied suspension/expulsion) of Appellant's club membership and alleged mismanagement of club funds and fraudulent election practices[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: AGM held on 30.09.2021[cite: 8]. Show-cause notice issued on 26.04.2022[cite: 8]. Appellant filed Civil Suits O.S. No. 65/2022 on 18.05.2022 and O.S. No. 68/2022 on 24.06.2022 before Civil Court[cite: 8]. Appellant filed Section 244(1) waiver application on 08.08.2022 before NCLT[cite: 8]. EGM for expulsion held on 30.06.2023[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Communications dated 30.09.2021, nomination email dated 05.09.2021, show cause notice dated 26.04.2022, civil suit plaints in O.S. No. 65/2022 and O.S. No. 68/2022, and amendment application IA No. 4/2024 challenging EGM expulsion[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected Appellant's application under proviso to Section 244(1) for waiver of the one-fifth membership requirement to maintain a Section 241-242 petition, citing pending identical civil suits, failure to meet statutory thresholds, and dismissal of related injunction appeals[cite: 8].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an individual member of a company limited by guarantee is entitled to a waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241-242[cite: 8]. 2. Whether waiver under Section 244(1) can be granted when the applicant has already instituted parallel civil suits agitating identical grievances regarding membership suspension and expulsion[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 is an exception to the general rule that must be strictly construed; it cannot be claimed as a matter of right to agitate individual grievances or personal vendettas where statutory member thresholds are unmet and identical disputes are sub judice before a civil court[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The word 'may' in the proviso to Section 244(1) confers directory discretion; in a company limited by guarantee, dispensing with the mandatory 1/5th membership threshold requires compelling exceptional circumstances affecting company substratum rather than isolated member disputes[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an applicant is a solitary complainant out of hundreds of members, has been expelled from membership, and has chosen civil forum remedies challenging suspension and expulsion, grant of waiver under Section 244 is impermissible to prevent multiplicity of proceedings[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT rightly denied the waiver under Section 244(1)(b) as Appellant failed to establish exceptional grounds of oppression or satisfy statutory numerical qualifications[cite: 8].
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed[cite: 8]. All connected Interlocutory Applications (IA Nos. 663 & 664/2024) are disposed of[cite: 8].
summary: Lt. Col. Sandeep Dewan appealed against an NCLT order denying him a waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 against Ootacamund Club, a guarantee company with 900 members[cite: 8]. The Appellant alleged proxy irregularities and wrongful suspension/expulsion from membership[cite: 8]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that statutory waivers under Section 244(1) are discretionary exceptions requiring strict justification and exceptional circumstances[cite: 8]. Because the Appellant represented only 1 member out of 900 (failing the 1/5th threshold) and had already instituted parallel civil suits seeking the same declarations, waiver was rightly refused[cite: 8].

case_title: Hari Vitthal Mission vs. Ravi Sethia, Resolution Professional of Suasth Healthcare Foundation & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Hari Vitthal Mission is a Section 8 public charitable company/Financial Creditor (Appellant)[cite: 9]. Suasth Healthcare Foundation is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP[cite: 9]. Ravi Sethia is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 9]. Committee of Creditors comprising Yes Bank and Axis Bank is Respondent No. 2[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor approached Appellant in October 2017 for financial support of Rs. 44.20 Crores to construct a charitable hospital in exchange for reserving 100 hospital beds; Appellant provided Rs. 50 Crores interest-free refundable deposit under agreement dated 10.10.2017[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed by July 2021 due to project delay beyond December 2018; Appellant claimed Rs. 62,16,33,563/- (principal deposit plus 10% interest)[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Voluntary CIRP admitted under Section 10 on 31.08.2021[cite: 9]. Appellant's claim admitted on 15.09.2021 and placed in CoC[cite: 9]. RP replaced IRP on 15.11.2021[cite: 9]. RP issued show cause email on 31.12.2021 and excluded Appellant from CoC on 11.01.2022/07.02.2022[cite: 9]. Appellant filed IA No. 390/KB/2022 on 19.04.2022[cite: 9]. CoC approved Resolution Plan on 06.10.2022[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Shareholding and trust organograms showing Kanoria Foundation (a private trust) owned 99.9% of Appellant and 99.9% of Adisri Commercial, which owned 60.36% of SREI, which held 50.76% in TAIML; TAIML controlled SAIT which owned 99.99% in SIPL and PCPL, holding 100% of the Corporate Debtor; trust deeds and investment management agreements proving control[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed IA No. 390/KB/2022 on 23.09.2022 upholding the RP's decision to disqualify and exclude Appellant from the CoC under Section 21(2) proviso as a related party under Section 5(24)[cite: 9].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Resolution Professional possesses statutory authority to determine whether an admitted financial creditor is a 'related party' and exclude it from the CoC[cite: 9]. 2. Whether a trust (Kanoria Foundation) constitutes a 'person' capable of serving as a holding entity creating related-party affiliation under Section 5(24)(h), (i), and (j) of the IBC[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional has statutory jurisdiction under Section 21 of the IBC to determine the related-party status of financial creditors and reconstitute the CoC to exclude related parties pursuant to the proviso to Section 21(2)[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 2(23) of the IBC, 'person' includes a trust; therefore, where a common parent trust exercises de facto ownership or control exceeding 20% voting power over both the financial creditor and corporate debtor through layered corporate entities, the creditor is a 'related party' under Section 5(24)(h), (i), and (j)[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of intermediary trusts or investment managers does not break the chain of control where constituent contractual agreements confer board nomination, management veto, and voting control back to entities belonging to the same ultimate group[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant is a related party of the Corporate Debtor under Section 5(24) and was lawfully excluded from CoC participation and voting[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 9]. The impugned order of NCLT Kolkata Bench dated 23.09.2022 in IA No. 390/KB/2022 is upheld[cite: 9]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 9].
summary: Hari Vitthal Mission appealed against an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench upholding its exclusion from the Committee of Creditors of Suasth Healthcare Foundation as a 'related party' under Section 5(24) of the IBC[cite: 9]. The Appellant argued that the RP lacked power to determine its status and that its parent entity, Kanoria Foundation, was a trust rather than a corporate holding company[cite: 9]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that Section 21 empowers the RP to verify creditor eligibility for CoC membership[cite: 9]. It held that under Section 2(23) a trust is a 'person', and because Kanoria Foundation exercised indirect de facto control over both the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor through layered entities and management agreements, the exclusion under Section 21(2) was valid[cite: 9].

case_title: Balakrishnan Venkatachalam, RP of Sovereign Developers and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Mro-Tek Realty Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Balakrishnan Venkatachalam is the Resolution Professional of Sovereign Developers & Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 10]. Mr. S. Sankaranarayanan & 32 Ors., and Anand Kumar Iyer & 10 Ors., are Allottees/Homebuyers (Appellants)[cite: 10, 11]. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. is the dissenting Financial Creditor (Intervenor)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of real estate company Sovereign Developers involving multiple stalled housing projects with hundreds of homebuyers[cite: 10]. Resolution plan submitted by consortium of VR Facilities Management Services Bangalore Pvt. Ltd. and K.C. Vijaykumar[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default initiated by Phoenix ARC under Section 7 resulting in admission order on 16.07.2019; CoC approved resolution plan with 88.86% majority[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 16.07.2019[cite: 10]. Plan approved by CoC on 20.10.2021[cite: 10]. RP first e-filed Section 30(6) plan approval application on 18.11.2021 (within CIRP extension granted on 21.04.2022 in IA 291/2021)[cite: 10]. Registry raised defects on 25.11.2021[cite: 10]. RP refiled application as fresh IA No. 570/2022 with delay condonation IA No. 569/2022 (352 days delay) on 23.11.2022[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT Bengaluru Registry report dated 25.10.2024 confirming initial e-filing on 18.11.2021, loss of digital files during portal migration, counsel communication lapses, and Covid-19 limitation exclusion orders[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench on 13.09.2024 dismissed IA No. 569/2022 refusing to condone 352 days delay, and consequentially dismissed plan approval application IA No. 570/2022 without considering merits[cite: 10].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the timeline stipulated in Regulation 39(4) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations for submitting an approved resolution plan to the Adjudicating Authority is directory or mandatory[cite: 10]. 2. Whether delay in refiling/re-presentation of a resolution plan application caused by defect rectification, portal technical glitches, and Covid-19 disruption can be condoned to prevent corporate liquidation[cite: 10]. 3. Whether citing an incorrect provision (Section 198 IBC) invalidates a delay condonation application[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Procedural timelines for refiling or re-presenting an interlocutory application seeking approval of a resolution plan are directory rather than mandatory; procedural defaults in re-presentation should not override the substantive objective of corporate resolution when an overwhelmingly approved plan is at stake[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(4) employs the term 'endeavour', conferring directory flexibility to plan submission timelines; referencing an incorrect statutory provision (such as Section 198) in an interlocutory condonation application does not vitiate the tribunal's inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 and Rule 28 of NCLT Rules[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the initial plan application was filed within the CIRP period, and refiling delays arose from technical portal migration, advocate communication lapses, and fell within the Covid-19 limitation exclusions, sufficient cause is established[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of the delay condonation was erroneous and disproportionately pushed the debtor towards liquidation; delay condoned and plan application remitted for consideration[cite: 10].
operative_order: All 5 Company Appeals are allowed[cite: 10]. The impugned orders dated 13.09.2024 in IA No. 569/2022 and IA No. 570/2022 are quashed and set aside[cite: 10]. The delay of 352 days is condoned, and IA No. 570/2022 is remitted to NCLT Bengaluru Bench for reconsideration of resolution plan approval on merits in accordance with law[cite: 10]. All connected IAs closed[cite: 10].
summary: Resolution Professional Balakrishnan Venkatachalam and homebuyers appealed against NCLT Bengaluru orders dismissing a delay condonation application of 352 days and consequentially rejecting the Section 30(6) application for approval of a resolution plan approved by 88.86% CoC majority[cite: 10]. The NCLT had held the RP could not blame counsel for delayed defect rectification[cite: 10]. NCLAT set aside both orders, ruling that Regulation 39(4) CIRP timelines are directory, the initial filing was within the CIRP period, refiling delays caused by e-portal issues and Covid-19 disruptions constituted excusable re-presentation delay, and citing a wrong section does not extinguish judicial power to advance substantial justice[cite: 10]. The plan application was remitted for decision on merits[cite: 10].

case_title: Anand Kumar Iyer & Ors. vs. Sovereign Developers and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 397 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 398 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anand Kumar Iyer and 10 other Homebuyers of Project 'Sovereign Unnati' are Appellants[cite: 11]. Sovereign Developers and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (through RP Balakrishnan Venkatachalam) is Respondent[cite: 11]. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. is the objecting dissenting Financial Creditor[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allottees entered into agreements for sale of residential apartments in 'Sovereign Unnati'; developer underwent insolvency under Section 7; CoC approved resolution plan of VR Facilities Management Services and K.C. Vijaykumar by 88.86%[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Project stalled with numerous unresolved homebuyer claims and corporate insolvency initiated by Phoenix ARC[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 16.07.2019[cite: 11]. Plan approved by CoC on 20.10.2021[cite: 11]. RP e-filed initial approval application on 18.11.2021[cite: 11]. Defect intimations made on 25.11.2021[cite: 11]. Refiled with delay condonation on 23.11.2022 (fresh IA 570/2022 and IA 569/2022)[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC voting sheets showing 88.86% approval, NCLT Bengaluru Registry report dated 25.10.2024 confirming timely initial submission, and Supreme Court suo motu Covid-19 limitation exclusion orders[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru on 13.09.2024 dismissed IA 569/2022 refusing to condone 352 days delay, and rejected IA 570/2022, pushing hundreds of homebuyers toward corporate liquidation[cite: 11].
legal_issues: 1. Whether delay in refiling an application for approval of a resolution plan voted in favor by 88.86% of the CoC should be condoned to prevent corporate liquidation[cite: 11]. 2. Whether statutory timelines under Regulation 39(4) are directory when balanced against the interests of homebuyers and creditors[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate insolvency proceedings, liquidation is the last resort; where a resolution plan has secured requisite statutory approval from the Committee of Creditors, procedural delays in defect removal or refiling cannot justify dismissing the plan without adjudication on merits[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(4) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations uses the word 'endeavour' and is directory; strict limitation under Section 61 cannot be imported to bar the discretionary condonation of delay in re-presenting an application under Rule 28 of NCLT Rules[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Delay caused by clerical defect communication, IT portal glitches during e-filing modernization, and Covid-19 pandemic protections constitutes genuine cause for condonation[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in taking a hyper-technical approach that would force the corporate debtor into liquidation; delay is condoned and the resolution plan revived for consideration[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 397 of 2024 is allowed[cite: 11]. The order dated 13.09.2024 passed in IA No. 569/2022 is quashed[cite: 11]. Consequently, the order in IA No. 570/2022 is set aside, and the matter is remanded to NCLT Bengaluru to decide the approval of the Resolution Plan on merits[cite: 11]. Connected IAs closed[cite: 11].
summary: Eleven homebuyers of the 'Sovereign Unnati' project appealed against NCLT Bengaluru's dismissal of the RP's application to condone 352 days delay in refiling the application for approval of the Resolution Plan[cite: 11]. The rejection of the condonation application had resulted in dismissal of the plan approval application despite 88.86% CoC approval[cite: 11]. NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that procedural deadlines for removing defects and refiling are directory under Regulation 39(4) and Rule 28 of the NCLT Rules[cite: 11]. The Tribunal held that liquidation must remain a measure of last resort, and remitted the matter to the NCLT for fresh consideration on merits[cite: 11].

case_title: Mr. S. Sankaranarayanan & 32 Ors. vs. Mr. Balakrishnan Venkatachalam, RP of Sovereign Developers and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. S. Sankaranarayanan and 32 other Homebuyers/Financial Creditors in class are Appellants[cite: 12]. Sovereign Developers and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) is represented by RP Balakrishnan Venkatachalam (Respondent)[cite: 12]. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. is the minority dissenting Financial Creditor (Intervenor)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allottees booked residential apartments across projects developed by Sovereign Developers; developer defaulted, leading to Section 7 admission on 16.07.2019; CoC approved resolution plan submitted by consortium of VR Facilities Management Services and K.C. Vijaykumar[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive default on housing projects; CoC approved resolution plan by 88.86% voting share[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 16.07.2019[cite: 12]. Resolution plan approved on 20.10.2021[cite: 12]. RP first filed approval application on 18.11.2021[cite: 12]. Registry raised defects on 25.11.2021[cite: 12]. RP refiled application as fresh IA No. 570/2022 accompanied by delay condonation IA No. 569/2022 on 23.11.2022 (seeking condonation of 352 days)[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registry report from NCLT Bengaluru dated 25.10.2024 confirming original filing on 18.11.2021 within extended CIRP period, lack of direct communication of defects to RP, portal technical upgrade issues, and Supreme Court Covid-19 limitation exclusion orders[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On 13.09.2024, NCLT Bengaluru dismissed IA No. 569/2022 holding the RP could not blame counsel for delayed cure of defects, and consequently dismissed plan approval IA No. 570/2022 as unmaintainable[cite: 12].
legal_issues: 1. Whether delay in refiling/re-presenting an application for approval of a resolution plan under Section 30(6) can be condoned when the original application was filed within the CIRP period[cite: 12]. 2. Whether hyper-technical objections raised by a dissenting minority financial creditor regarding citation of Section 198 of the IBC can defeat an approved resolution plan[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A dissenting financial creditor cannot use technical delays in refiling or defect cure by the RP to defeat a resolution plan approved by an overwhelming CoC majority; refiling delays are matters between the applicant and the tribunal and are liberally condoned to preserve value[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(4) of the CIRP Regulations is directory; the period prescribed for removing registry defects is directory as well. Citing an incorrect provision (Section 198 IBC) does not invalidate an application if the tribunal possesses inherent power under Rule 11 and Rule 28 of NCLT Rules[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where refiling delays overlap with the Covid-19 pandemic exclusion orders and system migration disruptions on the e-filing portal, sufficient justification is established under law[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in adopting an inflexible approach rejecting condonation of delay; the delay is condoned and the plan approval application restored[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 378 of 2024 is allowed[cite: 12]. The order dated 13.09.2024 in IA No. 569/2022 is quashed and the delay of 352 days is condoned[cite: 12]. The consequential order in IA No. 570/2022 is set aside and remitted to NCLT Bengaluru Bench for fresh consideration of the Resolution Plan on merits[cite: 12]. Connected IAs are closed[cite: 12].
summary: Thirty-three homebuyers appealed against NCLT Bengaluru's order dismissing an application for condonation of 352 days delay in refiling the Section 30(6) application for approval of the resolution plan of Sovereign Developers & Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., which had been approved by 88.86% of the CoC[cite: 12]. The NCLT's order had effectively derailed the resolution process and exposed the company to liquidation[cite: 12]. NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that the initial plan submission occurred within the extended CIRP period, re-presentation delays are directory under Regulation 39(4), and Covid-19 exemptions and e-filing technical glitches justified condonation[cite: 12]. The NCLT was directed to reconsider the plan on merits[cite: 12].

case_title: Ashmeet Singh Bhatia vs. Three C Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2021 of 2024 & I.A. No. 7583 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ashmeet Singh Bhatia is an outsider/shareholder in a sister company (GGPPL) of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant). Three C Properties Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. Respondents No. 2 to 35 and other allottees are 51 allottees holding 29 residential units acting as Financial Creditors in class. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was allotted Commercial Plot No. H-10, Sector 98, Noida on 26.04.2011 (revised layout plan comprising 60% commercial and 40% residential use with 2 commercial and 3 residential towers). Corporate Debtor executed Builder Buyer Agreements promising possession of residential apartments within 36 months in project Lotus Isle (Residential), registered with UP RERA on 11.08.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 70,93,58,956/- committed due to failure to deliver possession within the promised timeline. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Revised sanctioned plan dated 19.05.2015; plot bifurcation permitted on 21.01.2017; RERA registration dated 11.08.2017; Section 7 petition CP No. (IB)-597(PB)/2021 filed on 25.09.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: UP RERA project registration details (UPRERAPRJ5442) confirming 'Lotus Isle (Residential)' as an independent ongoing project comprising 255 residential units; Builder Buyer Agreements showing 36-month delivery timeline. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) on 09.08.2024 admitted the Section 7 petition filed by allottees of 29 units and rejected Appellant's objections under Section 65 in IA No. 3816/2022, holding the 10% threshold was satisfied.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a third party who is neither an allottee of the real estate project nor an allottee of the commercial spaces has locus standi to challenge an order admitting a Section 7 application filed by homebuyers in class. 2. Whether the minimum statutory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC is to be calculated against the specific RERA-registered residential real estate project (255 units) or across the entire mixed-use land parcel including commercial spaces.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An external stakeholder or shareholder in a sister entity of the corporate debtor lacks locus standi to challenge the admission of a Section 7 insolvency application filed by genuine allottees of a real estate project. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For determining the threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, the number of allottees must be computed exclusively with reference to the specific real estate project registered under Section 2(zn) of RERA, 2016, and not by aggregating unrelated or distinct commercial developments executed on the same land parcel. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an independent RERA registration establishes 255 residential units, an application joined by allottees of 29 units exceeds the requisite 10% threshold (minimum 25.5 units) required by statute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application satisfied the statutory numerical threshold under Section 7(1), and the Appellant had no legal locus to assail the admission of CIRP.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs. The order dated 09.08.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) admitting the Section 7 petition is upheld, and pending Interlocutory Applications are disposed of.
summary: An outsider who held shares in a sister company of Corporate Debtor Three C Properties Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by homebuyers of 'Lotus Isle (Residential)'. The Appellant contended that the 10% threshold under Section 7(1) was not met because commercial unit allottees across the entire mixed-use commercial plot were excluded from the computation. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the Appellant had no locus standi to challenge the CIRP admission. It further held that per the Supreme Court ruling in Manish Kumar, the 10% threshold must be calculated strictly against the specific RERA-registered real estate project (255 units), which was satisfied by 29 unit holders.

case_title: Mr. Suresh Kumar & Anr. vs. Central Bank of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Suresh Kumar and Mr. Raj Kumar are Personal Guarantors (Appellants). Central Bank of India is the Secured Financial Creditor (Respondent). M/s Ram Hari Auto Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities in 2012 from Central Bank of India, secured by personal guarantees and mortgages of immovable property executed by the Appellants. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: DRT Chandigarh issued Recovery Certificate RC No. 40/2020 on 28.01.2020 against Corporate Debtor and Appellants for unpaid dues; Central Bank of India filed a claim of Rs. 12,15,30,369/- as secured creditor. Appellants did not make any payments towards the debt. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 14.02.2020. Public announcement on 17.02.2020 with last date 02.03.2020. Bank filed claim on 09.03.2020 (admitted on 19.03.2020 with 51.37% voting share). RP reconstituted CoC on 08.06.2020 adding Appellants with 23.85% vote each, reducing Bank's share to 26.86%. Bank filed IA No. 294/2020 challenging the reconstitution. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRT Chandigarh Recovery Certificate RC No. 40/2020 dated 28.01.2020; absence of any receipt, bank transfer, or evidence showing payment or discharge of guaranteed debt by the Appellants. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed Central Bank of India's IA No. 294/2020 on 01.07.2024, directing reconstitution of the CoC by expelling the personal guarantors because they had not discharged the guaranteed debt.
legal_issues: Whether personal guarantors against whom a bank's guarantee has been invoked and a DRT recovery certificate issued can be treated as Financial Creditors of the Corporate Debtor and admitted into the Committee of Creditors without having made any payment or discharge of the debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1.
