ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A surety or guarantor does not acquire the rights of a financial creditor against the principal corporate debtor unless and until the guarantor actually pays or discharges the guaranteed debt under Section 140 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC, a financial debt arises in respect of a guarantee only when there is an actual subsisting liability or payment made; a mere unfulfilled guarantee does not confer a 'right to payment' under Section 3(6) to enable the guarantor to rank as a financial creditor in the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To claim subrogation and voting rights in the CoC, the guarantor must produce concrete evidence of actual payment made to the primary creditor; mere exposure of mortgaged assets or existence of a recovery certificate does not constitute 'performance' under Section 140. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants did not make any payment towards the guaranteed debt and were rightly removed from the CoC; NCLT's direction to reconstitute the CoC is upheld.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs. The Order dated 01.07.2024 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench in IA No. 294/2020 excluding Appellants from the CoC is affirmed, with observation that any post-recovery amounts may be placed before the RP as a contingent claim.
summary: Personal guarantors Suresh Kumar and Raj Kumar appealed against an order of NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowing Central Bank of India's application to remove them from the Committee of Creditors of Ram Hari Auto Pvt. Ltd. The Resolution Professional had admitted the personal guarantors as financial creditors with 23.85% voting share each, based on a DRT recovery certificate, thereby reducing the Bank's majority voting share. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 140 of the Indian Contract Act and Sections 3(6) and 5(8)(i) of the IBC, a surety is invested with creditor rights only upon actual payment or discharge of the debt. Since the guarantors paid nothing, they could not claim status as financial creditors.

case_title: Mr. Bhagawant Narayan Naik vs. Ritesh R. Mahajan, RP of Sovereign Industries Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhagawant Narayan Naik is a third-party purchaser (Appellant). Ritesh R. Mahajan is the Resolution Professional of Sovereign Industries Limited (Respondent No. 1). Sovereign Industries Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2). Basavaraj Ningappa Arekeri is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor operates a sugar and co-generation plant. The disputed land is a narrow strip sandwiched between the sugar plant site and co-generation plant site containing conveyor systems of the factory. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-monetary dispute in CIRP; Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP upon financial debt default under Section 7 on 28.03.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition initiated in October 2022; Corporate Debtor admitted financial stress on 02.12.2022; Suspended Director sold disputed land to Chidanand Sangappa Patil on 23.01.2023; Section 7 orders reserved on 06.02.2023; Patil transferred land to Appellant via registered sale deed on 24.02.2023; Corporate Debtor admitted to CIRP on 28.03.2023; Appellant filed Civil Suit O.S. No. 16/2024 on 16.01.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sale deed map and site photographs showing conveyor belts running across the land for industrial operations of the factory; registered sale deed executed during Section 7 pendency; civil court suit plaint and ex parte injunction obtained without disclosing Section 14 moratorium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 167/2024 (to exclude land from resolution plans) and IA No. 417/2024 (seeking information memorandum and plan copies) under Section 60(5). On 22.10.2024, NCLT Bengaluru rejected both applications, holding the transfer during insolvency proceedings was non-bonafide and sub judice in civil court.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a third-party purchaser who bought land from a suspended director while a Section 7 petition was sub judice can compel the RP to exclude the land from the CIRP and resolution plans under Section 18 of the IBC. 2. Whether an external stranger who instituted a separate civil suit is entitled to access confidential CIRP documents such as the Information Memorandum, Resolution Plan, and CoC minutes.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A third party who acquires property integral to the corporate debtor's operational plant from an insider during the active pendency of Section 7 insolvency proceedings cannot invoke Section 18 or Section 60(5) to derail the CIRP or demand exclusion of assets when title is actively contested in a pending civil suit. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 does not protect transfers lacking bona fides executed to dilute insolvency proceedings; Section 238 overrides civil proceedings and protects the corporate debtor's operational custody. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical incorporation of the property into industrial operations (active conveyor belt infrastructure) coupled with suspicious timeline of sales immediately prior to Section 7 admission negates claims of bona fide third-party purchase free of encumbrances. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of Appellant's applications was justified; the resolution plan's recognition of pending civil litigation sufficiently safeguards legal rights without halting CIRP.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 394 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 395 of 2024 are dismissed without costs. The common order dated 22.10.2024 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench in IA Nos. 167/2024 and 417/2024 is affirmed.
summary: Bhagawant Narayan Naik appealed against NCLT Bengaluru's rejection of his applications seeking to exclude a parcel of land from the CIRP of Sovereign Industries Ltd. and demanding copies of the Information Memorandum and Resolution Plan. The Appellant bought the land from an intermediary who purchased it from the suspended director right after Section 7 orders were reserved. NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that the land was a narrow strip housing conveyor belts essential to the factory's operation and the sale was a non-bona fide attempt to undermine CIRP. As the Appellant had already filed a civil suit regarding title, his rights remained subject to civil court adjudication without interfering with CIRP.

case_title: Jubin Kishore Thakkar vs. Phoenix ARC Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jubin Kishore Thakkar is a Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant). Phoenix ARC Private Limited is the Financial Creditor/Assignee (Respondent No. 1). KLT Automotive & Tubular Products Limited is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP represented by IRP Ashutosh Agarwala (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities between 2005-2012 from Bank of India, Corporation Bank (now Union Bank of India), and KKR Financial Services Ltd. Debts assigned to Phoenix ARC in 2019. Phoenix issued restructuring terms under Letter of Acceptance on 26.04.2019, revoked on 20.03.2020 due to non-compliance. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed in Section 7 application was Rs. 968,20,63,285/- as of 15.05.2023; Date of default asserted was 29.08.2022 based on Recovery Certificate No. 53 of 2022 issued under a DRT Consent Decree. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Accounts declared NPA in 2015, 2017, and 2018. Phoenix issued loan recall notices on 15.09.2020 and filed OA No. 201/2021 before DRT. First Section 7 CP 1207/2021 was filed on 16.10.2021. Parties executed Consent Terms before DRT on 29.08.2022 and DRT issued Consent Decree on 29.08.2022. CP 1207/2021 disposed on 10.10.2022 with liberty to refile upon default. Corporate Debtor defaulted on Consent Terms; fresh Section 7 filed on 03.06.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRT Consent Decree dated 29.08.2022 with Recovery Certificate No. 53 of 2022; NeSL record of default; express terms in Consent Terms authorizing Phoenix to file fresh Section 7 upon default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III on 26.09.2024 admitted Section 7 application CP (IB)-881(MB)/C-III/2023, rejecting Appellant's defense that default was hit by Section 10A.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is barred by Section 10A when the underlying loans were recalled during the Section 10A period but the application is founded upon default of a subsequent DRT Consent Decree and Recovery Certificate issued outside the Section 10A window.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The issuance of a final recovery certificate or consent decree by a competent tribunal creates a fresh cause of action and date of default; where an insolvency application is founded upon the breach of a decree passed outside the Section 10A period, Section 10A cannot operate as a bar. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A prohibits CIRP applications only for defaults occurring within the specified statutory period (25.03.2020 to 24.03.2021); it does not bar applications where pre-10A defaults occurred or where subsequent binding consent decrees crystallize fresh defaults. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A DRT Recovery Certificate paired with an Information Utility (NeSL) Record of Default constitutes conclusive proof of financial debt and default under Section 7. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default arose upon failure to satisfy the Consent Decree dated 29.08.2022; the Section 7 petition was not barred by Section 10A and was properly admitted.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs. The Impugned Order dated 26.09.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III admitting the Section 7 application and initiating CIRP against KLT Automotive & Tubular Products Limited is affirmed.
summary: A suspended director of KLT Automotive & Tubular Products Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Phoenix ARC for default exceeding Rs. 968 Crores. The Appellant argued that the petition was barred under Section 10A because the creditor had issued loan recall notices on 15.09.2020 during the Covid-19 protected period. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that default occurred earlier when accounts became NPA, and independently on 29.08.2022 upon breach of a DRT Consent Decree and Recovery Certificate. Citing Dena Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank, the Tribunal ruled that a recovery certificate creates a fresh cause of action outside Section 10A.

case_title: Apnaghar Builders Pvt. Ltd. vs. Intense Fitness & Spa Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Apnaghar Builders Pvt. Ltd. is a decree-holder landlord/creditor (Appellant). Intense Fitness & Spa Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1). CVR Holdings Pvt. Ltd. is the alleged Financial Creditor/Assignee (Respondent No. 2). Respondent No. 3 is the common director/shareholder. Navayuga Engineering Company Ltd. is the assignor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor leased premises at C-2/10, Safdarjung Development Area, New Delhi from Appellant under a registered lease deed dated 04.01.2016. Alleged unverified loan of Rs. 11,08,94,834/- by Navayuga was assigned to CVR Holdings via assignment agreement dated 10.02.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on rent from 01.11.2018; Delhi High Court passed eviction decree on 19.04.2022 with arrears/mesne profits of Rs. 4,78,85,040/-. CVR claimed default of Rs. 11,08,94,834/- under Section 7. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court decreed eviction on 19.04.2022; CVR filed early hearing application IA No. 2148/2022; Appellant obtained possession via execution on 21.07.2022; NCLT admitted Section 7 on 02.08.2022; Appellant filed Form B claim of Rs. 17,41,09,137/- and filed Section 61 appeal. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audit report dated 04.12.2020 (Note 3) listing the Rs. 11.08 Cr as 'loans and advances from related parties'; common shareholding showing Respondent No. 3 held 21.77% in Navayuga, 33.34% in Corporate Debtor, and 66.66% in CVR Holdings; Corporate Debtor admitted debt and default without contest before NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 228/ND/2022 on 02.08.2022 without investigating collusion or related-party transactions.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an aggrieved third-party creditor can challenge a Section 7 admission order on grounds of fraudulent or collusive initiation under Section 65 in an appeal under Section 61. 2. Whether an application under Section 7 filed by an entity interlinked through common directors and substantial shareholding constitutes a fraudulent or collusive proceeding initiated for a purpose other than insolvency resolution.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application under Section 7 filed collusively between related parties to thwart execution of decrees obtained by genuine creditors constitutes fraudulent initiation under Section 65, rendering the CIRP admission order void and liable to be set aside on appeal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: When common shareholders and directors control more than 20% voting power across assignor, assignee, and debtor entities, the entities are related parties under Section 5(24)(m); loans recorded in balance sheets as 'advances from related parties' and unverified third-party expenses cannot serve as a collusive tool to trigger Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unresisted admission of debt by a corporate debtor, total absence of appeal by suspended directors, and close timing of the petition to evade an impending High Court decree establish conclusive evidence of collusion and gaming. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 proceedings were collusive and initiated with malicious intent for purposes other than resolution; CIRP admission is set aside.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed without costs. The Impugned Order dated 02.08.2022 passed by NCLT New Delhi in CP (IB) No. 228/ND/2022 is set aside, and the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP.
summary: Apnaghar Builders, a landlord holding an eviction and monetary decree from the Delhi High Court, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 petition filed against Intense Fitness & Spa Pvt. Ltd. by CVR Holdings Pvt. Ltd. for an alleged assigned loan of Rs. 11.08 Crores. The Appellant contended that the CIRP was a fraudulent collusion to defeat its decree. NCLAT set aside the admission order, holding that under Section 65, the petition was collusive. Evidence revealed that a common director/shareholder held dominant stakes in the debtor, creditor, and assignor, the debt was booked as a related-party loan, and the debtor conceded default without contest to stall decree execution.

case_title: Sandeep Behl vs. Nirmal Trading Company & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sandeep Behl is the Ex-Director/Shareholder of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant). Nirmal Trading Company is the sole proprietorship Operational Creditor (Respondent No. 1). Printland Digital (India) Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP represented by RP Rajeev Dhingra (Respondent No. 2). Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 3. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of paper and printing materials against purchase orders and invoices for digital printing business. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed default of Rs. 1.67 Crores (Rs. 1.29 Crores principal plus 18% interest) across 70 invoices; earlier demand notices asserted Rs. 1.35 Crores across 53 invoices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 18.03.2019; Second Demand Notice issued on 11.04.2019; Corporate Debtor replied by Notice of Dispute on 24.04.2019. Third Demand Notice issued on 07.01.2020; Corporate Debtor issued second Notice of Dispute on 20.01.2020. Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 1105 of 2020 filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheets for FY 2017-18 and FY 2018-19, Company Secretary certificate dated 24.04.2019 showing Rs. 4,80,954.20 as receivable from the creditor, and ledger showing Rs. 14,09,899/- as credit balance advance; shifting invoice lists between notices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV admitted Section 9 application on 30.10.2023, discounting the replies dated 24.04.2019 and 20.01.2020 on the ground that the cut-off date was the date of the first demand notice.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in fixing the date of the first Section 8 demand notice as an absolute cut-off to disregard notices of dispute issued in response to subsequent demand notices. 2. Whether substantial discrepancies in claimed invoices and documented ledger disputes regarding advances receivable constitute a pre-existing dispute mandating rejection under Section 9(5)(ii)(d).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an operational creditor issues multiple successive demand notices with varying invoice claims, a notice of dispute issued in response to earlier demand notices or within 10 days of the latest demand notice establishes a bona fide pre-existing dispute, barring initiation of Section 9 proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandates rejection of a Section 9 application if a notice of dispute has been received by the operational creditor; the cut-off rule in Naresh Sevantilal Shah does not apply where no Section 9 petition was filed pursuant to the first notice and subsequent notices altered the foundation of the debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, a defense supported by contemporaneous audited balance sheets and shifting invoice amounts is not spurious, hypothetical, or illusory. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Real pre-existing disputes existed between the parties regarding invoice authenticity and account balances prior to the filing of the application; admission of Section 9 was unsustainable.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed without costs. The Impugned Order dated 30.10.2023 is set aside, the Corporate Debtor is released from the rigours of CIRP with immediate effect, and the Operational Creditor is directed to pay the fees and expenses of the Resolution Professional.
summary: An ex-director of Printland Digital (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV's order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Nirmal Trading Company for alleged unpaid invoices totaling Rs. 1.67 Crores. The NCLT had discarded the debtor's notices of dispute on the ground that they followed the first demand notice. NCLAT set aside the admission order, holding that where an operational creditor issues successive demand notices with fluctuating invoice lists and claims, responses asserting receivables based on audited balance sheets establish a genuine pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox doctrine. Section 9 proceedings were held unmaintainable, and the corporate debtor was freed from CIRP.

case_title: Surendra Sancheti vs. Gospell Digital Technologies Co. Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Surendra Sancheti is a Shareholder of Altius Digital Private Limited/Corporate Debtor (Appellant)[cite: 19]. Gospell Digital Technologies Co. Limited is the Chinese supplier/Operational Creditor (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 19]. Dushyant Dave is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of Set Top Boxes (STBs) on credit by Respondent No. 1 to the Corporate Debtor pursuant to purchase orders and commercial invoices[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under Section 9 was USD 129,07,968/- (with Section 8 demand of USD 121,47,968/-); Corporate Debtor signed balance confirmation acknowledging USD 88,81,595/- as on 31.12.2020; date of default asserted was 10.03.2020[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Operational Creditor issued Legal Notice on 07.07.2022; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 18.11.2022; Corporate Debtor sent Notice of Dispute on 01.12.2022; Section 9 application CP (IB) No. 137/MB/C-I/2023 filed on 14.12.2022[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's email dated 21.12.2020 admitting imports of USD 70 million and payments of only USD 57 million citing Covid-19 cash crunch; signed and stamped balance confirmation dated 03.03.2021 confirming USD 8.8 million due; subsequent email dated 03.06.2021 reaffirming outstanding of USD 7-8 million; partial payments of USD 714,699 made between 04.01.2021 and 20.07.2022 post-confirmation; alleged 2015 agreement and unapproved debit notes of USD 4.5 million[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I admitted the Section 9 petition and initiated CIRP on 19.12.2023 holding that undisputed admitted debt exceeded Rs. 1 Crore and alleged disputes were moonshine[cite: 19].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an operational debt can be bifurcated into disputed and undisputed portions to satisfy the Section 4 threshold for admission under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 19]. 2. Whether a Corporate Debtor's belated reliance on unapproved debit notes and an uncorroborated prior agreement constitutes a plausible pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox doctrine[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor repeatedly and unequivocally acknowledges an outstanding operational debt in balance confirmations and emails, and makes post-confirmation part payments, disputes raised as an afterthought or based on unilateral debit notes are spurious and cannot bar Section 9 admission if the undisputed admitted amount exceeds the statutory threshold[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) requires rejection only where a genuine, credible, and plausible dispute truly exists in fact prior to the Section 8 demand notice; spurious or illusory defenses do not constitute a 'dispute' under the Code[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Mobilox standard demands separating the grain from the chaff; an agreement cited for the first time in a Section 9 reply that was absent in contemporaneous correspondence and the Section 8 reply is an implausible afterthought[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor admitted debts far exceeding the Rs. 1 Crore threshold; no bona fide pre-existing dispute was established, and the Section 9 petition was rightly admitted[cite: 19].
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 19]. The Impugned Order dated 19.12.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I admitting the Section 9 application and initiating CIRP against Altius Digital Private Limited is affirmed[cite: 19].
summary: Surendra Sancheti, shareholder of Altius Digital Private Limited, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Chinese manufacturer Gospell Digital Technologies Co. Limited for defaults exceeding USD 12 million for Set Top Box supplies[cite: 19]. The Appellant contended that an alleged 2015 handling agreement, quality defects, and USD 4.5 million in debit notes constituted pre-existing disputes[cite: 19]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the debtor had repeatedly admitted owing over USD 8.8 million in balance confirmations and emails while blaming Covid-19 cash flow constraints, and had made part-payments[cite: 19]. The purported disputes and uncorroborated agreements raised post-demand notice were held to be spurious moonshine defenses under Mobilox[cite: 19].

case_title: Chandrakant Khemka vs. Santanu Bhattacharjee, RP of Nandini Impex Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Chandrakant Khemka is an Ex-Promoter/Director and creditor of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant)[cite: 20]. Santanu Bhattacharjee is the Resolution Professional of Nandini Impex Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 20]. Sincere Securities Pvt. Ltd., Noble Dealcom Pvt. Ltd., and Jodhpur Properties & Finance Pvt. Ltd. are owners/lessors (Respondents No. 2-4)[cite: 20]. UCO Bank is the Financial Creditor/sole CoC member (Respondent No. 5)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CD availed Rs. 6 Crores loans under MoUs in February 2019 secured by mortgage of 'White House' property (1/18-20, Rani Jhansi Road, New Delhi) housing CD's corporate office; upon default, conveyance deeds dated 27.02.2020 were executed transferring portions to Respondents No. 2-4, followed by leave and license agreements leasing it back to CD for Rs. 12 Lakhs/month[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Licensors terminated licenses on 08.05.2020 for non-payment; pre-CIRP license fee arrears and ongoing CIRP occupancy charges of Rs. 3.27 Crores claimed; civil eviction suits pending[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Civil suits filed on 04.09.2020; Commercial Court order for deposit on 09.12.2021; Section 7 CIRP admitted on 20.09.2022[cite: 20]. Respondents No. 2-4 filed eviction applications IA Nos. 1082 & 1083 of 2023 before NCLT in 2023[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered conveyance deeds dated 27.02.2020; leave and license agreements; Tis Hazari Commercial Court orders; minutes of 3rd, 5th, and 6th CoC meetings establishing that the CoC had not formally voted on or resolved to vacate the property pending legal opinion[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench on 07.08.2023 summarily allowed prayer (a) of IA Nos. 1082 and 1083 of 2023, ordering the RP to hand over possession of the corporate office within two weeks based solely on the RP's oral statement that CoC resolved to surrender it[cite: 20].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an owner or lessor can maintain an application before the Adjudicating Authority to recover possession of property occupied by the Corporate Debtor in the face of the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC[cite: 20]. 2. Whether an Adjudicating Authority can order eviction of the Corporate Debtor based on an unvoted CoC discussion without recording reasons or examining the statutory bar under Section 14(1)(d)[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC imposes an absolute, mandatory statutory prohibition against the recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where such property is occupied by or in the physical possession of the corporate debtor; an adjudicating authority cannot direct eviction without addressing this statutory bar[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(d) contains no exceptions permitting third-party owners to initiate possession recovery applications during CIRP; third-party exclusions under Section 18(1) explanation govern the IRP's custody duties but do not weaken the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statements by a Resolution Professional consenting to surrender an occupied office premise cannot override Section 14(1)(d), particularly when CoC minutes reveal that no formal vote was ever conducted and the matter remained postponed for legal opinion[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT passed a non-speaking order in violation of Section 14(1)(d) without adjudicating maintainability; order set aside and matter remanded[cite: 20].
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed[cite: 20]. The Impugned Order dated 07.08.2023 is set aside, and the matter is remanded to NCLT Kolkata Bench to comprehensively decide the eviction applications and IA No. 1412 of 2023 in accordance with law within four weeks[cite: 20]. Parties directed to appear on 26.11.2024[cite: 20].
summary: Chandrakant Khemka, suspended director of Nandini Impex Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order directing the RP to surrender possession of the company's corporate office in the 'White House' building to lessors/purchasers within two weeks[cite: 20]. The NCLT had acted on the RP's oral statement that the CoC did not wish to incur further rental expenses[cite: 20]. NCLAT allowed the appeal and remanded the case, holding that Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC provides an absolute, mandatory statutory bar against owners or lessors recovering possession of premises occupied by a corporate debtor during moratorium[cite: 20]. The Tribunal noted that CoC minutes showed no formal vote had occurred, and the NCLT failed to provide reasons or assess the statutory prohibition[cite: 20].

case_title: Globomet Engineering Private Limited vs. Shri Tejas J Parikh, RP of Unimetal Castings Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Globomet Engineering Private Limited is an investment vehicle formed by promoters/directors and investors (Appellant)[cite: 21]. Unimetal Castings Limited (UCL) is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP represented by RP Tejas J. Parikh (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 21]. Committee of Creditors comprising TJSB Sahakari Bank, Reliance ARC, and M&M Financial Services is Respondent No. 2[cite: 21]. Promoters/Directors of UCL and sister concern Joshi Deodhar Engineering Co. Ltd. (JDECL) are Respondents No. 3 to 6[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Revised MoU dated 07.08.2020 executed between Appellant, CoC, and Promoters for simultaneous resolution of UCL (for Rs. 9.75 Crores via resolution plan) and JDECL (for Rs. 3 Crores via Section 12A withdrawal); Appellant deposited Rs. 3.25 Crores into a no-lien bank account[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rs. 3 Crores was allocated to fully settle JDECL, and Rs. 25 Lakhs was paid as upfront deposit towards UCL upon signing; balance of Rs. 9.50 Crores for UCL was deferred post-NCLT approval[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP of UCL admitted on 25.01.2019[cite: 21]. First MoU signed on 16.03.2020; revised MoU on 07.08.2020[cite: 21]. Section 12A withdrawal for JDECL allowed on 02.11.2020[cite: 21]. UCL resolution plan approved by CoC on 22.12.2020 conditional on Rs. 25 Lakhs performance security, which was never deposited[cite: 21]. Appellant withdrew from settlement and filed IA No. 1370/2021 on 30.06.2021[cite: 21]. NCLT ordered liquidation of UCL on 25.01.2022[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses 11, 13, and VI of revised MoU dated 07.08.2020 containing express undertaking that Rs. 3.25 Crores in the no-lien account shall be refunded if approvals were not obtained by 30.09.2020, without any forfeiture clause for the Rs. 25 Lakhs UCL deposit[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III dismissed IA No. 1370/2021 on 26.07.2022, refusing any refund of the Rs. 3.25 Crores and imposing Rs. 1 Lakh cost, holding the application was non-maintainable and collusive[cite: 21].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an application filed under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC by an investment entity seeking refund of settlement deposits lying in a no-lien escrow account is maintainable[cite: 21]. 2. Whether the applicant is entitled to refund of upfront settlement funds deposited for the CIRP withdrawal of a sister entity (closed under Section 12A) and an unapproved resolution plan of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application seeking adjudication or refund of monies deposited under a multi-party settlement agreement executed to resolve corporate debtor insolvency arises directly out of and in relation to CIRP, and is squarely maintainable under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers broad jurisdiction over all questions of priorities or law and fact arising in relation to insolvency proceedings, notwithstanding arbitration clauses in underlying MoUs[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Funds paid to satisfy third-party debts under Section 12A that successfully resulted in withdrawal of insolvency cannot be refunded as that would permit unjust enrichment; however, upfront earnest amounts deposited toward a resolution plan that was never approved by the adjudicating authority and contained no forfeiture clause cannot be appropriated into the debtor's liquidation estate[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 3 Crores paid for JDECL's Section 12A closure is non-refundable, but the Rs. 25 Lakhs deposited towards the failed UCL plan must be refunded to the Appellant[cite: 21].
operative_order: The Appeal is partly allowed without costs[cite: 21]. The Impugned Order dated 26.07.2022 is modified to the extent that Respondent No. 2 (Financial Creditors/CoC) is directed to refund the sum of Rs. 25 Lakhs to the Appellant within one month via RTGS or bank draft[cite: 21]. The rejection of the refund of Rs. 3 Crores is affirmed[cite: 21].
summary: Globomet Engineering Pvt. Ltd., an investment vehicle formed to revive Unimetal Castings Ltd. (UCL) and its sister firm JDECL, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its application for refund of Rs. 3.25 Crores deposited under an MoU with the CoC[cite: 21]. The deposit comprised Rs. 3 Crores for JDECL's Section 12A withdrawal (which succeeded) and Rs. 25 Lakhs for UCL's resolution plan (which collapsed, leading to liquidation)[cite: 21]. NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, holding that Section 60(5)(c) conferred full jurisdiction over the dispute[cite: 21]. It ruled that while the Rs. 3 Crores utilized for the completed Section 12A exit could not be refunded, the Rs. 25 Lakhs paid toward the unconsummated UCL plan lacked any contractual forfeiture clause and must be refunded by the CoC[cite: 21].

case_title: Pratham Expofab Private Limited vs. Anil Matta, RP of Primrose Infratech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pratham Expofab Private Limited through Ex-Director Brij Bhushan Gupta is the Suspended Management of Corporate Debtor (Appellant)[cite: 22]. Primrose Infratech Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP[cite: 22]. Anil Matta is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 22]. Navneet Arora is the Authorized Representative of Financial Creditors in Class (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 22]. M/s One City Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project undertaken by the Corporate Debtor involving homebuyer allottees[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive default on housing projects; CoC approved SRA's resolution plan with 80.84% voting share in February 2020; Appellant previously offered Rs. 2 Crores upfront against a Rs. 126 Crores project liabilities[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 21.01.2018; SRA submitted plan on 24.01.2020, approved by CoC on 06.02.2020 (80.84%); RP filed approval IA No. 1489/2020; CoC rejected Appellant's second 12A proposal on 19.02.2020 (80.22% dissent); Appellant filed third 12A proposal in IA No. 188/2024 on 11.01.2024[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 8th and 9th CoC meetings establishing rejection of 12A proposals as non-viable; CoC voting record showing 80.84% approval of SRA plan; history of repeated dismissals of withdrawal pleas (IA No. 315/2019 dismissed on 08.04.2019; IA No. 1511/2019 dismissed on 28.02.2020)[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II on 28.08.2024 dismissed IA No. 188 of 2024, refusing to direct the CoC to consider the third Section 12A settlement proposal when the SRA plan had been approved and was awaiting tribunal approval[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can compel the Committee of Creditors to consider a suspended management's Section 12A settlement proposal after the CoC has approved a resolution plan with the requisite statutory majority and submitted it for approval under Section 30(6)[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan submitted by a resolution applicant is approved by the Committee of Creditors with the requisite statutory majority, the plan becomes binding inter se between the CoC and the resolution applicant; the suspended management cannot compel the CoC to entertain or vote on a subsequent Section 12A settlement proposal[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 30A of the CIRP Regulations, read with Section 12A of the IBC, does not contemplate entertaining withdrawal or settlement applications once a resolution plan has already received CoC approval; the commercial wisdom of the CoC rejecting a settlement proposal is supreme and non-justiciable[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Repeated, belated settlement applications submitted by suspended management without demonstrating bona fides or financial capability, following successive rejections by the CoC, constitute vexatious attempts to derail statutory CIRP timelines[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly declined to direct the CoC to consider the belated Section 12A proposal; dismissal of IA No. 188 of 2024 was lawful[cite: 22].
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 22]. The Impugned Order dated 28.02.2024 (pronounced 28.08.2024) in IA No. 188 of 2024 in CP (IB) No. 995 of 2018 is affirmed[cite: 22]. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to proceed expeditiously with the pending plan approval application IA No. 1489 of 2020[cite: 22].
summary: Pratham Expofab Pvt. Ltd., representing the suspended management of Primrose Infratech Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its application (IA No. 188/2024) seeking to force the CoC to consider a fresh Section 12A settlement proposal[cite: 22]. The CoC had approved a resolution plan submitted by One City Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. with 80.84% majority in February 2020, which had been awaiting NCLT approval[cite: 22]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that per the binding precedents in Hem Singh Bharana and Nehru Place Hotels, Section 12A proposals cannot be entertained once a resolution plan has been approved by the CoC[cite: 22]. It reaffirmed that the CoC's commercial wisdom is supreme, and repetitive settlement bids by former promoters cannot be used to derail CIRP[cite: 22].

case_title: Punjab National Bank vs. Walia Traders Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2021 & I.A. No. 1092 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Oriental Bank of Commerce (amalgamated into Punjab National Bank w.e.f. 01.04.2020) is the Financial Creditor (Appellant)[cite: 23]. Walia Traders Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: OBC disbursed two term loans on 26.03.2012 totaling Rs. 21.48 Crores (Term Loan I of Rs. 17.18 Cr and Term Loan II of Rs. 4.30 Cr) at 14.75% interest per annum[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account classified as NPA on 30.09.2014; Date of default asserted in Form 1 was 30.06.2014; Total outstanding claimed as on 31.12.2018 was Rs. 31,42,82,870/- (Term Loan I Rs. 25,14,76,258/- and Term Loan II Rs. 6,28,06,612/-)[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Date of default 30.06.2014; NPA date 30.09.2014; 3-year limitation under Article 137 expired on 29.06.2017 (or 29.09.2017); OBC filed Section 19 DRT recovery application OA No. 227/2016; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 84/Chd/Chd/2019 filed on 04.02.2019 (delay of 493/585 days)[cite: 23]. Appellant filed IA No. 24 of 2021 under Section 5 Limitation Act for condonation of delay[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Absence of any balance confirmation or written acknowledgment of debt within the 3-year limitation period from default; reliance by Bank solely on pendency of DRT proceedings and purported belief that IBC limitation runs from 01.12.2016[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissed IA No. 24 of 2021 refusing to condone the delay of 493 days, and consequentially dismissed Section 7 CP (IB) No. 84/Chd/Chd/2019 as barred by limitation[cite: 23].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the pendency of a recovery application under Section 19 of the RDDBFI Act, 1993 before the DRT constitutes a 'continuous cause of action' under Section 22 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to save limitation for a Section 7 IBC petition[cite: 23]. 2. Whether a financial creditor's mistaken belief that limitation under the IBC commences only from the date of the Code's enforcement (01.12.2016) constitutes 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act to condone inordinate delay[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the right to sue for initiating corporate insolvency under Section 7 of the IBC accrues on the date of default/NPA; the pendency of parallel recovery proceedings before a Debt Recovery Tribunal does not constitute a continuing cause of action or toll the statutory three-year limitation period[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5 of the Limitation Act applies to Section 7 petitions, but delay cannot be condoned on equitable or sympathetic grounds in the absence of a convincing, satisfactory, and bona fide explanation; a creditor cannot plead ignorance or a mistaken legal belief that limitation commenced upon the IBC's notification[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Per B.K. Educational Services, defaults occurring over three years prior to the petition without valid Section 18 acknowledgments render the petition time-barred, and speculative legal beliefs do not satisfy the threshold of sufficient cause[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 petition filed after a delay of 493 days was hopelessly time-barred and rightly dismissed[cite: 23].
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 23]. The Impugned Order of NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissing IA No. 24 of 2021 and rejecting CP (IB) No. 84/Chd/Chd/2019 as barred by limitation is affirmed[cite: 23].
summary: Punjab National Bank (as successor-in-interest to Oriental Bank of Commerce) appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing an application for condonation of 493 days delay and consequentially rejecting its Section 7 IBC petition against Walia Traders Ltd. as time-barred[cite: 23]. The loan account had defaulted on 30.06.2014 and became NPA on 30.09.2014, but the Section 7 petition was filed only on 04.02.2019[cite: 23]. The Bank argued that the delay was caused by its bona fide belief that a pending DRT recovery application constituted a continuing cause of action, and that IBC limitation ran from the date the Code took effect (01.12.2016)[cite: 23]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that DRT proceedings do not toll limitation and mistaken impressions of law cannot constitute sufficient cause under Section 5 of the Limitation Act[cite: 23].

case_title: Dhiren Shantilal Shah, RP of High Ground Enterprise Ltd. vs. Swastik Productions Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 360 of 2024 & Interlocutory Application No. 1223 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dhiren Shantilal Shah is the Resolution Professional of High Ground Enterprise Ltd. (Applicant/Appellant)[cite: 24]. Swastik Productions Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency proceedings involving High Ground Enterprise Limited arising out of Company Petition No. 696 of 2020[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Interlocutory dispute concerning condonation of 5 days delay in filing an appeal under Section 61 against the NCLT order dated 19.12.2023[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT order passed on 19.12.2023; appeal e-filed on 23.01.2024 (5 days beyond the standard 30-day limitation period under Section 61(2))[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Medical ailments of the RP residing in Mumbai delaying legal consultation; delay in online uploading and downloading of the impugned order; time consumed in locating clear, legible copies of Karnataka Bank statements forming part of Company Petition No. 696 of 2020[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 1223 of 2024 under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC seeking condonation of 5 days delay; Respondent opposed relying on Supreme Court limitation precedents[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a delay of 5 days in filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC, attributed to the Resolution Professional's health issues, belated online uploading, and retrieval of legible bank records, constitutes 'sufficient cause' within the permissible 15-day condonation window[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC, the Appellate Tribunal has statutory discretion to condone a delay of up to 15 days upon demonstration of sufficient cause, applying a pragmatic, justice-oriented approach rather than a pedantic rule of rejection[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The expression 'sufficient cause' under Section 61(2) proviso confers discretionary jurisdiction to be exercised on the facts of each case; where the delay is brief (within the statutory 15-day ceiling) and not deliberate, substantial justice must prevail over technical considerations[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Health difficulties of an officer of the court (Resolution Professional) coupled with bona fide administrative efforts to retrieve legible documentary annexures constitute credible sufficient cause for a minor 5-day delay[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Sufficient cause was established; delay of 5 days condoned and appeal admitted for hearing[cite: 24].
operative_order: Interlocutory Application No. 1223 of 2024 is allowed, and the 5 days delay in filing Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 360 of 2024 is condoned[cite: 24]. Appeal listed for admission on 14th November, 2024[cite: 24].
summary: The Resolution Professional of High Ground Enterprise Ltd. filed an interlocutory application (IA No. 1223/2024) seeking condonation of 5 days delay in preferring an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC against an NCLT order dated 19.12.2023[cite: 24]. The RP explained that the delay arose from personal illness in Mumbai, delays in downloading the uploaded order, and efforts to trace legible bank statements from Karnataka Bank[cite: 24]. The Respondent opposed the plea citing strict limitation jurisprudence[cite: 24]. NCLAT allowed the application and condoned the delay, holding that under the proviso to Section 61(2), the Tribunal has discretionary power to condone up to 15 days delay where sufficient cause is shown, and that courts must adopt a pragmatic approach to advance substantial justice[cite: 24].

case_title: Twentyone Sugars Limited vs. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Twentyone Sugars Limited is the Successful Resolution Applicant / SRA (Appellant)[cite: 25]. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. / MSEDCL is the state power distribution utility / Operational Creditor (Respondent)[cite: 25]. M/s Maharashtra Shetkari Sugar Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor revived under CIRP[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor operated a sugar crushing factory in Parbhani, Maharashtra utilizing high-voltage electricity connection No. 536069006330[cite: 25]. SRA took over the factory pursuant to an approved resolution plan requiring electricity restoration for seasonal crushing[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor had pre-CIRP electricity arrears of Rs. 1,81,08,240/- (as of July 2019)[cite: 25]. Respondent filed no claim in CIRP[cite: 25]. SRA paid Rs. 2,11,42,540/- (including initial deposit of Rs. 3,62,165/- under an installment package) under protest to secure connection restoration[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 30.08.2018[cite: 25]. CoC approved resolution plan in August 2019 (95.73%)[cite: 25]. NCLT approved plan on 07.11.2019 directing renewal/restoration of all licenses/approvals at no extra cost[cite: 25]. SRA took over on 09.11.2019; MSEDCL demanded pre-CIRP arrears on 15.11.2019; SRA paid under protest on 25.11.2019[cite: 25]. SRA filed IA No. 32/2021 seeking refund[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT plan approval order dated 07.11.2019; MSEDCL demand letter dated 15.11.2019 threatening disconnection; SRA payment letter dated 25.11.2019 expressly asserting payment made under protest and tribunal protection[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed IA No. 32/2021 on 10.01.2023 holding it lacked privity to post-plan payments and misapplied the clean-slate ratio of Ghanshyam Mishra against the SRA[cite: 25].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an application filed by a Successful Resolution Applicant under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC seeking refund of pre-CIRP electricity dues coerced by a power distribution licensee under protest is maintainable[cite: 25]. 2. Whether an electricity utility can condition the restoration of power supply to an SRA upon the clearance of pre-CIRP dues that were never claimed during CIRP and stood extinguished under Section 31 of the IBC[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Following the approval of a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC, all pre-CIRP claims not incorporated in the plan stand extinguished under the clean slate doctrine; a statutory power distribution utility cannot condition reconnection upon payment of extinguished arrears, and sums extracted under protest are refundable under Section 60(5)(c)[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers jurisdiction over disputes directly impacting the implementation and revival of the corporate debtor; Section 31(1) binds all statutory authorities and extinguishes unfiled pre-commencement operational claims[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where contemporaneous written correspondence establishes payments were made under duress and express protest to avert operational disruption during seasonal production, the payment cannot be treated as voluntary estoppel or a waiver of Section 31 rights[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: MSEDCL unlawfully coerced payment of extinguished pre-CIRP dues; NCLT erred in refusing refund, and MSEDCL must return the entire amount[cite: 25].
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed and the impugned order dated 10.01.2023 is set aside[cite: 25]. IA No. 32/2021 is allowed, and Respondent MSEDCL is directed to refund the sum of Rs. 2,11,42,540/- to the Appellant within six weeks[cite: 25]. Pending applications are disposed of[cite: 25].
summary: Twentyone Sugars Limited, Successful Resolution Applicant of Maharashtra Shetkari Sugar Ltd., appealed against NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of its application seeking refund of Rs. 2.11 Crores coerced by MSEDCL for restoring an essential power connection[cite: 25]. MSEDCL had failed to file a claim in the CIRP but refused reconnection unless pre-CIRP arrears were cleared, forcing the SRA to pay under protest[cite: 25]. NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that under Section 31 and the Supreme Court rulings in Ghanshyam Mishra and Tata Power, all unsubmitted pre-CIRP claims are extinguished and utilities cannot insist on arrears for reconnection[cite: 25]. The dispute was held maintainable under Section 60(5)(c), and MSEDCL was ordered to refund the entire amount within six weeks[cite: 25].

case_title: Ravi Auto Ltd. vs. Surana Mercantiles Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1059 of 2022 & I.A. No. 3090 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ravi Auto Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (Appellant)[cite: 26]. Surana Mercantiles Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disbursement of Rs. 1,00,00,000/- as an Inter-Corporate Deposit (ICD) on 01.11.2016, accompanied by a Demand Promissory Note and an agreement for quarterly interest payments[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor serviced interest regularly till 31.03.2018 and executed a signed balance confirmation for Rs. 1,10,79,999/- on 01.04.2018; default occurred from 01.04.2018, with total claim under Section 7 being Rs. 1,27,74,686/- (principal Rs. 1,00,00,000/- and interest Rs. 27,74,686/- at 12% p.a. through 10.01.2020)[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disbursement on 01.11.2016; interest serviced till 31.03.2018; balance confirmation dated 01.04.2018; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 309/KB/2020 filed on 16.01.2020[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements proving disbursement of Rs. 1 Crore; ledger accounts showing interest receipts up to 31.03.2018; signed balance confirmation dated 01.04.2018; detailed interest computation sheet (Annexure A-9)[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench-I dismissed the Section 7 application on 08.06.2022 on technical grounds: lack of a written loan agreement, non-stamping of the promissory note, and omission of an explicit date of default in Part IV Column 2[cite: 26].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a written loan agreement is mandatory to establish a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 26]. 2. Whether the omission to explicitly state a date of default in Part IV Column 2 of Form 1 is fatal when the date and computation of default are demonstrated in supporting ledgers and balance confirmations[cite: 26]. 3. Whether non-stamping or improper form of a promissory note invalidates a Section 7 petition when disbursement and default are proven through other records[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A formal written loan agreement is not a mandatory prerequisite to prove a financial debt under Section 5(8) if contemporaneous banking transactions, ledger records, and interest servicing establish disbursement for the time value of money[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Omission to specify the date of default in Column 2 of Part IV in Form 1 is directory and not fatal under Section 7(5), provided that supporting pleadings, ledgers, and signed balance confirmations clearly identify the date of default[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Non-stamping of an ancillary promissory note does not render a Section 7 petition non-maintainable when undisputed bank statements and signed balance confirmations independently prove debt and default[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The financial creditor established debt and default w.e.f. 01.04.2018; the rejection of the Section 7 application by the NCLT was erroneous[cite: 26].
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed and the NCLT order dated 08.06.2022 is set aside[cite: 26]. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order admitting the Section 7 application within one month, during which the Corporate Debtor is given liberty to enter into an amicable settlement[cite: 26]. No costs[cite: 26].
summary: Ravi Auto Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench-I dismissing its Section 7 IBC application against Surana Mercantiles Pvt. Ltd. for default on an Inter-Corporate Deposit of Rs. 1 Crore plus interest[cite: 26]. The NCLT had rejected the petition because there was no written loan agreement, the promissory note was unstamped, and Part IV of Form 1 omitted a specific date of default[cite: 26]. NCLAT set aside the rejection, ruling that a written contract is not an absolute prerequisite where bank transfers and interest servicing prove disbursement for the time value of money[cite: 26]. The Tribunal held that omission of the default date in Part IV is directory, and directed admission of the Section 7 petition within one month absent a settlement[cite: 26].

case_title: Mapletree Leather Goods Private Limited vs. Shivadutt Bannanje, Liquidator of Falcon Tyres Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: TA No. 91/2021 (Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 314/2020) & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 329/2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mapletree Leather Goods Private Limited is the sole Prospective Resolution Applicant / Appellant[cite: 27]. Falcon Tyres Limited is the Corporate Debtor (ordered into liquidation)[cite: 27]. Shivadutt Bannanje is the Liquidator (Respondent No. 8 in TA 91/2021 and Respondent No. 1 in CA 329/2022)[cite: 27]. Savan Godiawala was the RP (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 27]. Edelweiss ARC, PNB, SBI, and OBC are Financial Creditors[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Falcon Tyres underwent CIRP initiated by Edelweiss ARC on 01.05.2018 with total financial creditor claims exceeding Rs. 1,512 Crores[cite: 27]. Appellant submitted a resolution plan with 5 addendums across multiple Form G extensions[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive default; financial debt claims admitted totaled Rs. 1,512.63 Crores alongside commercial tax arrears of Rs. 379 Crores; plant operations had been shut since April 2015[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 01.05.2018[cite: 27]. CoC rejected Appellant's revised plan via e-voting on 24.01.2019 and recommended liquidation[cite: 27]. CIRP expired on 26.01.2019[cite: 27]. RP filed liquidation IA No. 47/2019[cite: 27]. NCLT ordered liquidation on 30.12.2019 and dismissed Appellant's modification IA No. 449/2019 and union's IA No. 48/2019 on the same date[cite: 27]. NCLAT refused interim stay on 28.09.2021; e-auction completed and proceeds distributed by July 2023[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC 14th meeting minutes recording rejection of plan for failure to furnish Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) and inadequate upfront funds; NCLT common orders dated 30.12.2019; liquidator status report dated 27.07.2023 confirming completed asset auctions and disbursement[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench on 30.12.2019 allowed RP's IA No. 47/2019 ordering liquidation and rejected Appellant's plan approval application IA No. 449/2019; NCLT later dismissed IA No. 140/2022 (seeking stay of auction) on 24.06.2022 on grounds of res judicata and lack of standing[cite: 27].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant whose plan modification application was dismissed without appeal can maintain a challenge against the liquidation order under Section 33(1)[cite: 27]. 2. Whether an application to stay liquidation auctions and force sale as a going concern under Section 60(5) is barred by res judicata when interim relief has already been denied and liquidation auctions completed[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsuccessful resolution applicant whose challenge to the rejection of its resolution plan has attained finality loses locus standi to challenge the subsequent liquidation order of the corporate debtor or interfere with the liquidator's asset auction[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once a liquidation order under Section 33(1) is passed and an applicant fails to appeal the companion order rejecting its plan modification application under Section 61, no surviving cause of action exists to stall liquidation under Section 60(5)[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The consummation of public e-auctions, receipt of sale considerations, and distribution of proceeds to claimants render appeals seeking restoration of the CIRP or going-concern sale infructuous and barred by res judicata[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of the resolution plan attained finality, auctions were concluded, and both appeals lack merit[cite: 27].
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 314 of 2020 (TA No. 91/2021) and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 329 of 2022 are dismissed without costs[cite: 27].
summary: Mapletree Leather Goods Pvt. Ltd., the sole resolution applicant for Falcon Tyres Ltd., appealed against NCLT Bengaluru orders ordering liquidation under Section 33(1) and refusing to stay the auction of the debtor's immovable assets under Section 60(5)[cite: 27]. The CoC had rejected the plan because the applicant failed to provide a Performance Bank Guarantee and upfront commitment, and the NCLT dismissed its modification plea on 30.12.2019 without any appeal being filed against that dismissal[cite: 27]. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that the rejection of the plan had attained finality, stripping the applicant of standing[cite: 27]. Furthermore, as interim stay was denied in 2021 and the liquidator had completed auctions and distributed sale proceeds, the challenge was infructuous and barred by res judicata[cite: 27].

case_title: Arkay Logistics Limited vs. Mr. Abhijit Guhathakurta, Liquidator of EPC Constructions (India) Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 836 of 2024 & I.A. No. 3021 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arkay Logistics Limited is a third-party affiliate/service provider (Appellant)[cite: 28]. EPC Constructions (India) Ltd. [formerly Essar Projects (India)] is the Corporate Debtor under liquidation (Respondent CD)[cite: 28]. Abhijit Guhathakurta is the Liquidator (Respondent)[cite: 28]. GSPL India Gasnet Ltd. (GIGL) is the project employer[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GIGL awarded a pipeline contract to the Corporate Debtor on 18.01.2017 requiring a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of Rs. 21,17,30,000/-[cite: 28]. At CD's request, Appellant procured the PBG from Axis Bank against a 100% lien marked on Appellant's two Fixed Deposits[cite: 28]. Corporate Debtor deposited Rs. 18.10 Crores net with the Appellant towards margin money between March 2017 and January 2018 under an express agreement to refund upon PBG surrender[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total margin money owed back to the Corporate Debtor was Rs. 18,10,00,000/-; contract was completed, PBG released by GIGL and cancelled by Axis Bank on 24.03.2021, and FD liens were released to the Appellant[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Margin money paid by CD by 18.01.2018; CIRP initiated on 20.04.2018; PBG surrendered on 24.03.2021; Liquidation ordered on 07.05.2021; Liquidator issued legal notice on 09.07.2022; Liquidator filed IA No. 2777 of 2022 under Section 60(5)[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CD's letter dated 18.01.2018 confirming net payment of Rs. 18.10 Crores towards FD margin money; bank statements showing fund transfers; Axis Bank PBG cancellation letter dated 24.03.2021; Appellant filed no reply on merits before NCLT despite four extensions[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-II allowed IA No. 2777 of 2022 on 08.01.2024, directing Appellant to return the Rs. 18.10 Crores to the Corporate Debtor, holding that the summary return of undisputed margin money falls within NCLT jurisdiction[cite: 28].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to direct a third party to refund undisputed margin money paid by the Corporate Debtor for a bank guarantee that has been surrendered and cancelled during liquidation[cite: 28]. 2. Whether such refund constitutes an ordinary recovery of debt requiring the Liquidator to file a civil suit under Section 35(1)(k)[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application filed by a liquidator seeking the refund of proprietary margin money belonging to the corporate debtor following the surrender and cancellation of a third-party bank guarantee arises directly out of and in relation to the liquidation proceedings, and is fully maintainable under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers comprehensive jurisdiction over the assets of the corporate debtor to prevent multiplicity of fora; directing the return of undisputed property held by a third party does not constitute an impermissible summary debt recovery suit[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an appellant fails to deny transaction mechanics before the adjudicating authority and invents an unfiled counterclaim of set-off at the appellate stage without supporting claims lodged in the CIRP, the liability is undisputed on the record[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Rs. 18.10 Crores margin money is an asset of the Corporate Debtor; NCLT had full jurisdiction to direct its return without relegating the liquidator to a civil suit[cite: 28].
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 28]. The order dated 08.01.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-II directing Appellant to return Rs. 18.10 Crores to the Corporate Debtor is affirmed[cite: 28]. IA No. 3536 of 2024 and other pending applications are disposed of[cite: 28].
summary: Arkay Logistics appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing it to refund Rs. 18.10 Crores to EPC Constructions (India) Ltd. (under liquidation)[cite: 28]. The Corporate Debtor had transferred the money to Arkay as margin deposit for securing a performance bank guarantee through Axis Bank, which was subsequently surrendered and cancelled upon contract completion[cite: 28]. Arkay contended that NCLT lacked summary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) and the liquidator had to file a recovery suit under Section 35(1)(k)[cite: 28]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the margin money was an undisputed asset of the debtor arising directly from the liquidation process, and Section 60(5)(c) empowered the NCLT to order its return to avoid multiplicity of fora[cite: 28].

case_title: M/s. Kashyap Infraprojects Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Hi-Tech Sweet Water Technologies Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Kashyap Infraprojects Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Appellant)[cite: 29]. M/s Hi-Tech Sweet Water Technologies Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was awarded a contract by the Government of Bihar for 211 mini piped water supply schemes and placed purchase orders on the Operational Creditor for the supply and installation of solar-powered pump-sets and accessories[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed total outstanding dues of Rs. 1,86,00,000/- (principal Rs. 1.42 Crores and 18% interest Rs. 43.87 Lakhs) against unpaid invoices[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised in 2018-2019; Corporate Debtor sent complaint emails on 07.01.2020; Bihar Govt. cancelled contract on 29.05.2020; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 01.09.2020; Notice of Dispute sent on 18.09.2020; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 349 of 2020 filed on 30.09.2020; settlement meeting held on 26.01.2021[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Contemporaneous emails dated 07.01.2020 detailing non-functioning of pump systems, short running hours, and random controller breakdowns; Government of Bihar order dated 29.05.2020 blacklisting the Corporate Debtor and forfeiting security deposit; Minutes of Meeting dated 26.01.2021 wherein Appellant admitted problems and agreed to replace defective pump sets in lots of 10[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-I dismissed the Section 9 petition on 02.11.2022 on the ground of genuine pre-existing disputes regarding quality and performance of goods[cite: 29].
legal_issues: 1. Whether contemporaneous email complaints regarding quality defects and equipment failures antedating the Section 8 demand notice constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC[cite: 29]. 2. Whether unilateral third-party dispatch inspection reports override proven post-installation defects to invalidate a corporate debtor's defense under the Mobilox standard[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected where contemporaneous correspondence preceding the statutory demand notice demonstrates a plausible, non-spurious dispute regarding goods' functionality and quality that requires substantive inquiry beyond summary insolvency jurisdiction[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d), the Adjudicating Authority is not required to determine the final merits of the dispute or examine whether the defense will succeed, but only to verify whether a plausible contention exists requiring further trial[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Factory dispatch clearance certificates do not negate post-installation failures where subsequent emails and minutes of meetings reveal that equipment failed to function and the operational creditor agreed to replace defective units[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Plausible pre-existing disputes were established prior to the Section 8 notice; dismissal of the Section 9 application was valid[cite: 29].
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 29]. The order dated 02.11.2022 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-I in CP (IB) No. 349 of 2020 is affirmed, leaving it open to the Appellant to pursue other legal remedies[cite: 29].
summary: Kashyap Infraprojects Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against Hi-Tech Sweet Water Technologies Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid invoices of Rs. 1.86 Crores for solar pump sets supplied for a Bihar Government project[cite: 29]. The NCLT found the claim barred by pre-existing disputes[cite: 29]. The Appellant argued that the pump sets had passed third-party inspection prior to dispatch[cite: 29]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that emails dated 07.01.2020 antedating the Section 8 notice proved that the pumps failed after installation, leading to the debtor's blacklisting by the State Government[cite: 29]. Furthermore, meeting minutes showed the creditor agreed to replace defective units[cite: 29]. Under the Mobilox standard, the dispute was genuine and unsuited for summary resolution under the IBC[cite: 29].

case_title: Multiplier Brand Solutions Pvt. Ltd. vs. Amazon Wholesale (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Multiplier Brand Solutions Pvt. Ltd. is the service provider / Operational Creditor (Appellant)[cite: 30]. Amazon Wholesale (India) Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 30]. Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. (ASSPL) is the original contracting affiliate[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Master Services Agreement (MSA) executed on 27.01.2020 (effective 01.05.2019) with ASSPL and Indian affiliates for manpower and field promotional services[cite: 30]. Novation and Substitution Agreement executed on 01.04.2021 transferring all rights, liabilities, and obligations of ASSPL to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 30]. Purchase orders issued for 'Amazon Device Project'[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed Rs. 3,69,57,379/- across 8 invoices dated between 30.03.2023 and 26.05.2023 plus 18% interest[cite: 30]. Amazon claimed to have uncovered inflated invoicing and phantom sales exceeding USD 16.37 million (~INR 136 Crores)[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Amazon flagged 99% data discrepancies on 09.02.2023; Appellant filed police complaint against own staff on 24.02.2023; Corporate Debtor placed all payments on hold on 02.06.2023 and 16.06.2023; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 06.11.2023; Corporate Debtor issued Notice of Dispute on 18.11.2023; Section 9 petition (IB) 757/ND/2023 filed on 29.11.2023; Appellant issued Arbitration Notice on 01.12.2023[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Novation Agreement assigning comprehensive liabilities to Respondent; Appellant's police complaint admitting massive internal employee fraud and manipulated unique IDs; email dated 02.06.2023 from Amazon requisitioning 16 categories of audit data; emails dated 12.06.2023 and 16.06.2023 expressly placing all project payments on hold pending forensic investigation[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II dismissed the Section 9 petition on 05.03.2024 due to substantial pre-existing disputes regarding fraud and invoice legitimacy[cite: 30].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an operational creditor can initiate CIRP under Section 9 for specific project invoices when the corporate debtor had formally placed all payments on hold under the governing Master Services Agreement due to admitted large-scale fraud and inflated billing[cite: 30]. 2. Whether a novated counterparty can raise fraud and discrepancies originating under an overarching Master Services Agreement as a pre-existing dispute against subsequent project invoices[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor formally communicates that payments under an overarching commercial agreement have been placed on hold pending a forensic audit of widespread fraudulent billing and manipulated sales figures (which the creditor itself reported to police), a bona fide pre-existing dispute exists, barring the initiation of Section 9 proceedings[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A Novation Agreement that transfers all rights, interests, and liabilities under a master contract entitles the substituted corporate debtor to assert cross-project billing discrepancies as a defense against operational debt claims arising under that master agreement[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Written email exchanges placing disbursements on hold months prior to the Section 8 notice satisfy the Mobilox threshold, establishing that the defense is neither spurious nor a post-notice contrivance[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A substantial pre-existing dispute existed prior to the demand notice; the NCLT did not err in rejecting the Section 9 application[cite: 30].
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 30]. The Impugned Order dated 05.03.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II in CP (IB) No. 757/ND/2023 is affirmed[cite: 30].
summary: Multiplier Brand Solutions Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 application against Amazon Wholesale (India) Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid invoices of Rs. 3.69 Crores for manpower deployment under the Amazon Device Project[cite: 30]. The Appellant claimed the invoices were undisputed and that allegations of fraud pertained to a separate project[cite: 30]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that both projects were governed by a unified Master Services Agreement novated to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 30]. The record proved that Amazon had placed all payments on hold in June 2023—months before the Section 8 demand notice—after uncovering massive data falsification and phantom billing exceeding Rs. 136 Crores, regarding which the Appellant had lodged police complaints against its own staff[cite: 30]. Under the Mobilox doctrine, these unresolved issues constituted a genuine pre-existing dispute[cite: 30].

case_title: Dr. Aveena Gudapati vs. Katepalli Venkateswara Rao & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 280 of 2024 & IA No. 740 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Aveena Gudapati is a third-party shareholder of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant)[cite: 31]. Katepalli Venkateswara Rao is the initiating Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 31]. Bio Green Papers Limited is the Corporate Debtor represented by RP (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 31]. Jagadish Velamala is the Erstwhile Managing Director of the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 3)[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor and Respondent No. 1 entered into a Memorandum of Understanding on 02.04.2018 for allotment of convertible/redeemable shares within a maximum of one year from payment[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default under financial debt led to admission of Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 97/7/HDB/2022 on 30.05.2023[cite: 31]. Appellant had separately filed Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 337/7/HDB/2021 as a shareholder/creditor which was dismissed on 10.10.2022 and upheld in CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 25/2023 on 09.09.2024[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition admitted on 30.05.2023[cite: 31]. Multiple objection applications filed by Appellant (IA Nos. 405/2022, 453/2022, 1113/2023, 1419/2023) were disposed of/dismissed[cite: 31]. Resolution plan approved in IA(Plan) No. 7/2024 on 28.05.2024[cite: 31]. Unnumbered IA (e-filing No. 1414/2024) under Section 65 dismissed on 28.05.2024[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Orders dismissing Appellant's own Section 7 petition; earlier dismissed IAs challenging admission order; final approval order of Resolution Plan dated 28.05.2024; absence of credible evidence proving fraud under Section 65[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Division Bench-I Hyderabad on 28.05.2024 dismissed Appellant's Section 65 application (e-filing No. 1414/2024) seeking to set aside the admission order dated 30.05.2023 and approved the resolution plan[cite: 31].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a shareholder who previously sought initiation of Section 7 CIRP against the Corporate Debtor can maintain an application under Section 65 of the IBC to recall the admission order granted in favor of another financial creditor after approval of the resolution plan[cite: 31]. 2. Whether an application under Section 65(3) can be used as a substantive vehicle to undo CIRP admission without producing credible evidence of fraud[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A shareholder cannot pursue self-contradictory remedies by seeking to trigger insolvency against a corporate debtor while collaterally attacking a valid CIRP admission order initiated by another creditor, especially after earlier objection applications and appeals have attained finality[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 65 of the IBC is an enabling penal provision for imposing penalties on fraudulent initiation rather than a substantive mechanism to recall concluded admission orders; unsubstantiated allegations lacking credible evidence do not satisfy Section 65[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an applicant files repeated interlocutory objections against CIRP admission that are dismissed, and allows those orders to achieve finality, principles analogous to res judicata bar belated re-litigation under Section 65 after the resolution plan has been approved[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT rightly dismissed the unnumbered IA challenging CIRP admission; the appeal lacks merit[cite: 31].
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 31]. The Impugned Order dated 28.05.2024 passed by NCLT Division Bench-I Hyderabad in unnumbered IA (e-filing No. 1414 of 2024) in CP(IB) No. 97/7/HDB/2022 is affirmed[cite: 31]. All pending applications are closed[cite: 31].
summary: Dr. Aveena Gudapati, a shareholder of Bio Green Papers Limited, appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing his Section 65 application which sought to recall the Section 7 CIRP admission order dated 30.05.2023 and stop approval of the resolution plan[cite: 31]. The Appellant alleged that the financial debt claimed by Katepalli Venkateswara Rao was fraudulent[cite: 31]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Appellant had engaged in self-contradictory litigation after his own Section 7 petition had been dismissed[cite: 31]. The Tribunal held that his previous objection applications had attained finality, Section 65 could not be invoked as an unsubstantiated afterthought post-plan approval, and no credible proof of fraud was provided[cite: 31].

case_title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. vs. Sandeep Goyal, Liquidator for Chaudhary Ingots Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1081 of 2024 & I.A. No. 3905 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. (PVVNL) is the state electricity distribution utility / Operational Creditor (Appellant)[cite: 32]. Chaudhary Ingots Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor in liquidation[cite: 32]. Sandeep Goyal is the Liquidator (Respondent)[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of high-tension industrial electricity to the Corporate Debtor's manufacturing unit in Muzaffarnagar under an electricity supply agreement against cash security deposit of Rs. 1,04,00,000/-[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on electricity bills, accumulating arrears of Rs. 4,04,19,294/- (principal Rs. 3,48,44,219/- plus interest Rs. 55,75,075/-) as of the liquidation commencement date[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor entered liquidation; Appellant submitted Form C proof of claim on 24.12.2021 explicitly recording adjustment/set-off of the Rs. 1.04 Crores security deposit; Liquidator filed IA No. 147/2022 seeking refund of the security deposit[cite: 32]. 5.
