FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Schedule II Form C claim dated 24.12.2021 explicitly stating in Clause 8 that the security deposit of Rs. 1,04,00,000/- had been adjusted against the gross claim of Rs. 4.04 Crores; consumer ledgers and electricity bills[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT on 03.04.2024 allowed the Liquidator's IA No. 147/2022 relying on Bharti Airtel vs. Vijaykumar V. Iyer, directing PVVNL to refund the security amount of Rs. 1,04,00,000/- (totaling Rs. 1,15,33,600/- with interest/charges), holding set-off impermissible during liquidation[cite: 32].
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor is legally entitled under Regulation 29 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 to set off and adjust a pre-existing cash security deposit against its crystallized unpaid operational claims when filing its proof of claim in liquidation proceedings[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate liquidation proceedings, mutual credits, debts, and cross-dealings between the corporate debtor and a creditor are permitted to be set off under Regulation 29 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 to arrive at the net payable amount[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 29 explicitly allows mutual set-off in liquidation, distinguishing liquidation proceedings from the CIRP moratorium where statutory set-off is circumscribed; the prohibition on set-off articulated in Bharti Airtel does not bar adjusting cash security deposits in a liquidation claim form[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an operational creditor submits Form C explicitly demonstrating the adjustment of security against crystallized, non-contingent electricity bill arrears, the set-off is valid and not an impermissible adjustment against an anticipated claim[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the refund of the adjusted security deposit; the set-off under Regulation 29 was lawful[cite: 32].
operative_order: The Appeal is partly allowed[cite: 32]. The Impugned Order dated 03.04.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in IA No. 147/2022 directing the Appellant to pay Rs. 1,15,33,600/- is set aside[cite: 32]. Pending applications are disposed of[cite: 32].
summary: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order directing it to refund a security deposit of Rs. 1.04 Crores to the Liquidator of Chaudhary Ingots Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 32] The utility had adjusted the security against electricity arrears of Rs. 4.04 Crores in its Form C claim[cite: 32]. The NCLT held the set-off impermissible based on the Supreme Court ruling in Bharti Airtel[cite: 32]. NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, ruling that while set-off is restricted during CIRP, Regulation 29 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations expressly authorizes mutual dealings and set-off in liquidation[cite: 32]. Because PVVNL adjusted the deposit against an actual, crystallized debt, the direction ordering refund was set aside[cite: 32].

case_title: M/s. Vedic Projects Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shri Sutanu Sinha, RP for M/s. Simplex Projects Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Vedic Projects Pvt. Ltd. is an MSME sub-contractor / Operational Creditor (Appellant)[cite: 33]. M/s Simplex Projects Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor under CIRP (Respondent CD)[cite: 33]. Shri Sutanu Sinha is the Resolution Professional (Respondent)[cite: 33]. State Bank of India is the initiating Financial Creditor[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor and Appellant entered into a Sub-contract Agreement dated 16.06.2010 for the construction work of Kabrai Feeder Channel awarded by Irrigation Department, Govt. of U.P., containing payment deductions and margin clauses but no delayed payment interest clause[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant raised bills totaling Rs. 41,53,95,348/- between 2010 and 2014, leaving Rs. 10,36,47,148/- unpaid; Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 23,42,42,554/- (principal Rs. 10.36 Cr plus interest of Rs. 13,05,95,406/- calculated under Section 16 of the MSMED Act)[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 27.04.2022; public announcement on 29.04.2022; RP initially admitted Rs. 2,76,67,940/-; following joint reconciliation on 16.05.2022, RP admitted full principal of Rs. 10,36,30,064/- and rejected interest on 18.01.2023; Appellant filed IA (IB) No. 1033/KB/2023[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sub-contract Agreement dated 16.06.2010 lacking any interest clause on delayed payment; MSME registration certificate; Corporate Debtor's financial statements showing no interest liability acknowledged[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench Court No. II dismissed IA (IB) No. 1033/KB/2023 on 06.08.2024, holding that NCLT is not the appropriate forum to claim statutory compound interest under the MSMED Act in the absence of a contractual interest stipulation[cite: 33].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a Resolution Professional acting under Regulations 13 and 14 of the IBBI CIRP Regulations is bound to admit statutory compound interest claimed under Section 16 of the MSMED Act when the underlying commercial contract contains no interest clause[cite: 33]. 2. Whether an operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC includes statutory penal interest in the absence of an express contractual agreement[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC includes interest only if interest is expressly payable under the terms of the commercial contract between the parties; in the absence of a contractual stipulation, an operational creditor cannot compel the Resolution Professional to collate statutory compound interest under the MSMED Act[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The definition of 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) does not inherently include interest, in contrast to 'financial debt' under Section 5(8); the Resolution Professional performs an administrative, facilitative role and cannot adjudicate unliquidated statutory interest claims under Section 16 of the MSMED Act[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the sub-contract agreement contains no provision for delayed interest and the debtor's balance sheets omit interest liabilities, the RP properly admits only the verified principal amount[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of the interest component by the RP and NCLT was lawful; the NCLT is not the forum to enforce MSMED Act interest claims[cite: 33].
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 33]. The Impugned Order dated 06.08.2024 passed by NCLT Division Bench Court No. II Kolkata in IA (IB) No. 1033/KB/2023 is affirmed[cite: 33].
summary: M/s Vedic Projects Pvt. Ltd., an MSME sub-contractor, appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order affirming the Resolution Professional's rejection of its claim for Rs. 13.05 Crores as compound interest under Section 16 of the MSMED Act in the CIRP of Simplex Projects Ltd.[cite: 33] The RP had admitted the entire principal operational claim of Rs. 10.36 Crores but rejected interest because the 2010 sub-contract lacked an interest clause[cite: 33]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that per Krishna Enterprises, an operational debt does not include interest unless explicitly agreed to in the contract[cite: 33]. The Tribunal ruled that the RP acts as an administrative facilitator and NCLT is not the forum to determine statutory interest liabilities under the MSMED Act[cite: 33].

case_title: Sunil Kumar Sharma Suspended Board of Director of Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. & Anr. vs. ICICI Bank Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 197 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 199 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sunil Kumar Sharma is the Suspended Director/Appellant of Corporate Debtor Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. (JAL); ICICI Bank Ltd. is the Lead Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Jaypee Infratech Ltd. (JIL) is a subsidiary; YEIDA is a statutory authority/lessor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debt realignment scheme of arrangement trifurcated JAL's debt into three buckets, proposing under Bucket-2B to hive off Rs. 11,689 Crore debt along with 950.35 acres of SEZ land to an SPV (Jaypee Infrastructure Development Ltd./JIDL) under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: JAL was classified as SMA-II on 03.10.2014 and declared NPA on 31.03.2015; default involved Rs. 11,689 Crore under Bucket-2B out of total multi-crore liabilities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RBI directed ICICI Bank on 14.08.2017/14.08.2018 to initiate CIRP pursuant to IAC recommendations; ICICI Bank filed Section 7 petition on 06.09.2018/07.09.2018; Supreme Court in Chitra Sharma declined to stay CIRP or fast-track scheme on 09.08.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ICICI Bank letter dated 19.01.2018 giving only conditional in-principle approval subject to Supreme Court leave; YEIDA order dated 12.02.2020 cancelling the lease allotment of the entire 1,000 hectares/950.35 acres of SEZ land; interim status quo order dated 25.02.2020 of Allahabad High Court in WP No. 6049/2020 conditional upon depositing Rs. 100 Crore. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: First motion CA No. 174 of 2017 filed on 20.11.2017 and allowed on 08.01.2018/08.12.2017; Second Motion CP (CAA) No. 19/ALD/2018 filed on 22.01.2018/23.01.2018; NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed Second Motion and IA No. 18 of 2024 on 03.06.2024 because the underlying asset was cancelled/under litigation and Section 7 CIRP was admitted against JAL on the same date.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in rejecting the Second Motion Petition under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 for sanctioning a scheme of arrangement on the grounds of subsequent cancellation and litigation over the primary demerged asset and the simultaneous admission of a Section 7 IBC application against the corporate debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Company Court/Tribunal sanctioning a scheme of arrangement is not a mere rubber stamp bound solely by majority creditor approval; it has the power and duty to evaluate whether the scheme remains viable, fair, just, and aligned with public interest in light of material subsequent events occurring after the initial motion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The supervisory jurisdiction under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires looking beyond the ipse dixit of consenting majorities; where subsequent developments eliminate or cloud the foundation of the scheme, sanction cannot be granted automatically. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Subsequent changed circumstances (cancellation of core project land by an authority and the admission of a Section 7 IBC application) must be evaluated to decide whether the relief sought has become unviable, inappropriate, or unworkable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The cancellation of the underlying 950.35 acres of land by YEIDA and the admission of JAL into CIRP under Section 7 on 03.06.2024 constituted valid and sustainable grounds for the NCLT to reject the Second Motion Scheme of Arrangement and dismiss the deferment application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 197 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 199 of 2024 are dismissed; orders of NCLT dated 03.06.2024 rejecting CP (CAA) No. 19/ALD/2018 and IA No. 18 of 2024 are affirmed.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed appeals filed by the suspended director of Jaiprakash Associates Limited challenging NCLT orders dated 03.06.2024 that rejected a second motion scheme of arrangement under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 and dismissed an application seeking deferment of pronouncement. The proposed scheme sought to transfer Rs. 11,689 Crore debt and 950.35 acres of land to an SPV. NCLAT held that the NCLT is not a mere rubber stamp and must consider material subsequent events. Since YEIDA cancelled the underlying land allotment, rendering the asset subject to ongoing litigation, and JAL was admitted into CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC, the scheme became unviable and legally unfeasible.

case_title: NCC Ltd. vs. Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: NCC Ltd. is an Operational Creditor/contractor; M/s Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co. II (NQ) Pte. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA); Committee of Creditors (CoC) consists of Financial Creditors; Telangana State Tourism Corporation Ltd. (TSTCL/YATCL) and Shilparamam Arts, Crafts & Cultural Society are land lessors classified as 'Special Operational Creditors'. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor developed and operated a 5-star hotel (Trident, Hyderabad) under a PPP model and BOT agreement with YATCL and Society on leased land; NCC Ltd. provided construction and engineering services. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following initiation of Section 7 CIRP, NCC submitted an operational debt claim of Rs. 51,75,95,253 in Form B on 14.03.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Public notice issued on 01.03.2018; CoC approved SRA's Resolution Plan on 21.12.2018 with 68.26% majority. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Plan earmarked Rs. 41.99 Crore ('Society Claim') to YATCL/Society with up to 100% payout while providing Nil payment to other Operational Creditors based on Nil liquidation value; Corporate Debtor had an Arbitral Award dated 25.02.2020 for Rs. 25.95 Crore against YATCL challenged under Section 34. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditors filed IA No. 950/2019 and related objections alleging illegality in creating 'Special Operational Creditors' and paying them 100% while giving others Nil; NCLT Hyderabad Bench approved the Resolution Plan on 07.02.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan can provide differential treatment by paying 100% of dues to certain operational creditors essential to the corporate debtor's business continuity (lessors/GoT) while providing Nil payment to other operational creditors whose liquidation value is Nil, and whether condition precedents for governmental approval invalidate the plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the CoC is supreme and non-justiciable regarding fund distribution in a resolution plan; differential treatment within the class of operational creditors is permissible where an intelligible differentia exists linked to the corporate debtor's business survival, provided dissenting or other operational creditors receive not less than their liquidation value under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'fair and equitable' in Explanation 1 to Section 30(2)(b) does not mandate identical or proportionate distribution among all operational creditors; meeting the liquidation value benchmark satisfies Section 30(2)(b). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Differential treatment requires a rational business nexus to keeping the corporate debtor a going concern (such as securing title/lease rights to the sole operational asset). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because liquidation value to operational creditors was Nil and full payment to land lessors was critical to operating the hotel, CoC's exercise of commercial wisdom was lawful and valid.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2020 is dismissed. The order of NCLT Hyderabad dated 07.02.2020 approving the Resolution Plan is affirmed with no order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by operational creditor NCC Ltd. challenging the approval of the resolution plan for Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. by SRA BREP Asia II. NCC contended that classifying land lessors (YATCL and Shilparamam Society) as 'Special Operational Creditors' and granting them up to 100% payment while giving other operational creditors Nil was illegal and discriminatory. The Tribunal held that CoC's commercial wisdom is paramount. Since the liquidation value for operational creditors was Nil, Section 30(2)(b) was met, and differential treatment was justified to preserve the leased land vital to the hotel's operation.

case_title: Infinity Interiors Private Limited vs. Subodh Kumar Agarwal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Infinity Interiors Private Limited is an MSME-registered Operational Creditor; Subodh Kumar Agrawal is former RP/Respondent No. 1; M/s Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2; BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co. II (NQ) Pte. Ltd. is SRA/Respondent No. 3; Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 4. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor engaged Appellant for interior decoration works and supply of materials for its hotel project built on PPP-leased land. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 4,87,39,050 and additional claim of Rs. 1,85,00,000 on 20.07.2018, which was admitted by RP to the revised amount of Rs. 4,40,24,552. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7; CoC approved SRA's Resolution Plan on 21.12.2018 with 68.26% majority. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan allocated Rs. 41.99 Crore to lessors YATCL and Society as 'Special Operational Creditors' while allocating Nil payment to Appellant and other operational creditors whose liquidation entitlement was Nil under Section 53. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 961 of 2019 challenging the resolution plan as discriminatory against MSME operational creditors; NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed objections and approved the plan on 07.02.2020.
legal_issues: Whether an MSME operational creditor is entitled to statutory priority or pro-rata parity under MSMED Act in a resolution plan when liquidation value is Nil, and whether CoC's commercial wisdom can prioritize essential land lessor claims over ordinary MSME operational debts.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Non-obstante Section 238 of the IBC overrides provisions of the MSMED Act, 2006, leaving MSME operational creditors without any statutory priority in CIRP plan distributions over other creditors beyond what Section 30(2)(b) provides. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 54A and 240A of the IBC protect MSMEs only in their capacity as corporate debtors, not as operational creditors; Section 30(2)(b) is satisfied if operational creditors receive their liquidation value. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where liquidation value of operational creditors is Nil, the allotment of Nil payment to trade creditors alongside full payment to indispensable project lessors is legally valid under the commercial wisdom of the CoC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan did not contravene any statutory requirement of the IBC, and the tribunal possesses no equity jurisdiction to mandate redistributions to MSME suppliers.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 432 of 2020 is dismissed. Impugned order of NCLT dated 07.02.2020 is affirmed without costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Infinity Interiors Pvt. Ltd., an MSME operational creditor with an admitted claim of Rs. 4.40 Crore against Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd., challenging the approved resolution plan. The Appellant argued that giving Nil payment to MSME suppliers while according 100% payout to government lessors was illegal and violated the MSMED Act. The Tribunal held that Section 238 of the IBC overrides the MSMED Act, and IBC provisions like Section 240A protect MSMEs only as corporate debtors, not creditors. Since the liquidation value was Nil, CoC acted within its commercial wisdom in prioritizing lease dues essential for hotel survival.

case_title: Ahuja Furnishers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Subodh Kumar Agarwal Former Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ahuja Furnishers Pvt. Ltd. is an MSME-registered Operational Creditor; Subodh Kumar Agrawal is former RP/Respondent No. 1; M/s Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2; BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co II (NQ) PTE. Ltd. is SRA/Respondent No. 3; IBBI is Respondent No. 4; Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 5. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of furniture to Corporate Debtor for hotel project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 29,83,025.69 in Form B on 08.03.2018; RP admitted Rs. 29,08,729 on 24.08.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7; CoC approved the resolution plan with 68.26% majority on 21.12.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved plan provided 100% payment to land lessors (YATCL and Society) under 'Special Operational Creditor' category but Nil payment to supplier operational creditors; liquidation value payable to operational creditors was Nil under Section 53. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant objected to CA No. 32 of 2019 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench arguing discriminatory allocation; NCLT approved the plan on 07.02.2020.
legal_issues: Whether the approval of a resolution plan that provides Nil payment to operational creditors who supplied furniture while allocating full payment to special operational creditors (lessors) violates Section 30(2) or Section 53 of the IBC, and whether the adjudicating authority holds equity jurisdiction to reallocate amounts.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The adjudicating authority and appellate authority possess no equity jurisdiction to alter or modify the distribution matrix approved by the CoC in its commercial wisdom, provided statutory minimum requirements under Section 30(2)(b) are met. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) mandates payment to operational creditors not less than the amount payable under Section 53 in liquidation; where that amount is Nil, an allocation of Nil complies fully with the law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: CoC may differentiate between subclasses of operational debts based on commercial logic, business continuity, and preservation of the going concern without rendering the plan unfair or inequitable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC approving full payment for land-lease dues while giving Nil to furniture suppliers cannot be interfered with, as liquidation value to operational creditors was Nil.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 710 of 2020 is dismissed. The order dated 07.02.2020 passed by NCLT Hyderabad is affirmed with no costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal preferred by Ahuja Furnishers Pvt. Ltd. challenging the NCLT order dated 07.02.2020 approving BREP Asia II's resolution plan for Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant, an MSME supplier with admitted claims of Rs. 29.08 Lakhs, challenged the Nil payment allotted to it while project lessors received full satisfaction. The Tribunal held that neither the Adjudicating Authority nor NCLAT possesses equity-based jurisdiction to modify commercial distributions approved by the CoC. Because the liquidation value was Nil, allocating Nil to the Appellant complied with Section 30(2)(b), and prioritizing lessors was a valid business decision to safeguard corporate assets.

case_title: Consolidated Engineering Company vs. Subodh Kumar Agarwal Former Resolution Professional & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Consolidated Engineering Company is an MSME partnership firm/Operational Creditor; Subodh Kumar Agrawal is former RP/Respondent No. 1; M/s Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 2; BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co. II (NQ) Pte. Ltd. is SRA/Respondent No. 3; Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 4. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Designing, fabrication, and installation of building facade and allied works for Trident (Tower-I) and Oberoi Hotel (Tower-II) of Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 20,02,07,912 in Form B on 14.03.2018; RP admitted Rs. 10,52,37,168 initially, plus Rs. 21,54,575 post-reconciliation on 08.09.2018, and Rs. 5,18,56,248 as contingent liability (Rs. 3,84,32,558 rejected, leading to IA No. 264/2018). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7; CoC approved SRA's plan on 21.12.2018 with 68.26% votes. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved plan provided Nil payment to trade operational creditors but earmarks Rs. 41.99 Crore for government lessors (YATCL/Society); Corporate Debtor obtained an Arbitral Award on 25.02.2020 for Rs. 25.95 Crore against YATCL which was challenged under Section 34. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 960 of 2019 challenging the plan as discriminatory and conditional; NCLT Hyderabad Bench approved the plan on 07.02.2020.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan is invalid if it provides conditional implementation based on obtaining governmental lessor approval, gives Nil payment to MSME operational creditors while paying 100% to project land lessors, and whether surplus from post-CIRP arbitral awards must be distributed to operational creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A condition precedent in a resolution plan that is integral and essential for the recommencement or continuity of the corporate debtor's business operations is legally valid and does not render the plan conditional under the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Future receivables such as arbitral awards remain the property and asset of the corporate debtor under Section 31; operational creditors have no independent statutory right to claim such surplus outside the approved plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Differential distribution by CoC between lessor operational creditors and contracting operational creditors is valid as long as the liquidation value floor under Section 30(2)(b) is satisfied. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The condition precedent requiring GoT's approval for change of control was necessary since the D&M Agreement was co-terminus with the lease, and allocating Nil payment to operational creditors complied with Section 30(2)(b).
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 430 of 2020 is dismissed. The order dated 07.02.2020 of the NCLT Hyderabad Bench is upheld without costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Consolidated Engineering Company against the approval of the resolution plan for Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant, who executed facade works and held admitted claims of over Rs. 10.73 Crore, challenged the plan for paying Nil to trade creditors while giving 100% to lessors, imposing condition precedents, and retaining arbitral award benefits. NCLAT held that obtaining lessor consent was an indispensable condition precedent for business continuity and did not invalidate the plan. Furthermore, arbitral recoveries vest in the corporate debtor, and CoC's commercial decision to allocate Nil to operational creditors whose liquidation value was Nil complied with Section 30(2)(b).

case_title: Puneet P. Bhatia vs. ASREC (India) Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Puneet P. Bhatia is the Suspended Director/Appellant of Corporate Debtor Barracks Retail India Pvt. Ltd.; ASREC (India) Ltd. is the Assignee Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Ganesh Venkata Siva Rama Krishna Remani is the IRP/Respondent No. 2; Bharat Co-operative Bank (Mumbai) Ltd. is the original assignor lending bank[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bharat Co-operative Bank originally sanctioned a Rs. 5 Crore Term Loan and Rs. 25 Lakh Cash Credit on 21.03.2017 secured by mortgage over 41 plots in Vikramgarh, renewed loans on 08.06.2018 with an additional loan of Rs. 1.91 Crore to acquire Eye Catch Fashions, and subsequently restructured/sanctioned revised facilities on 17.03.2020 including CC of Rs. 300 Lakh, WCTL-1 of Rs. 800 Lakh, FITL of WCTL-1 of Rs. 122.90 Lakh, and Term Loan of Rs. 505.40 Lakh[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount was Rs. 21,37,94,606 as on 30.09.2022; default date was initially filed as 31.10.2020 and later amended to 02.08.2019 following RBI inspection classifying the account as NPA on 01.11.2019 (aggregate principal outstanding Rs. 16,21,73,514)[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall notice was issued by the Bank on 07.12.2020 demanding clearance within 7 days; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice was issued on 19.03.2021 demanding clearance within 60 days; debt assignment to ASREC took place on 25.03.2021[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter of acknowledgment of debt and securities executed by CD on 01.09.2020; RBI inspection report of September-October 2020 revealing failure to bring promoter's contribution of 15% under RBI IRAC guidelines rendering 17.03.2020 restructuring void ab-initio; NeSL database records confirming default prior to Section 10A period[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed by ASREC on 18.02.2023; NCLT Mumbai Bench-I allowed amendments to Form 1 Part IV to change the default date to 02.08.2019 on 13.10.2023 and 24.11.2023, and subsequently admitted the Section 7 petition on 09.01.2024[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor can amend the date of default in an application filed under Section 7 of the IBC prior to final admission, and whether the default committed by the Corporate Debtor fell outside the protective moratorium period under Section 10A of the IBC[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant in a Section 7 proceeding is legally entitled to amend pleadings or file additional documents before the final order of admission or rejection is made, provided it complies with due procedure and natural justice and does not manipulate the period of limitation[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A of the IBC applies strictly and exclusively to defaults occurring within the protected period between 25.03.2020 and 25.03.2021; an earlier, unrectified default predating this statutory window is not shielded, and an invalid or failed debt restructuring does not erase an antecedent default or reset the default timeline into the Section 10A period[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Regulatory audit findings (RBI IRAC classification establishing NPA date 90 days following non-payment) substantiated by Information Utility (NeSL) records serve as valid evidence proving that default occurred prior to the onset of the COVID-19 relief period[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The amendment of the default date to 02.08.2019 was validly allowed by the Adjudicating Authority, and because this date predated the Section 10A moratorium window, the Section 7 petition was fully maintainable[cite: 6].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 139 of 2024 is dismissed; the order of admission dated 09.01.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in CP (IB)/280(MB)2023 is affirmed without costs[cite: 6].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by the suspended director of Barracks Retail India Pvt. Ltd. challenging the admission of a Section 7 IBC application by ASREC (India) Ltd.[cite: 6]. The appellant contended that the initial default date of 31.10.2020 fell within the Section 10A protected COVID-19 period and that amending the default date to 02.08.2019 was impermissible[cite: 6]. NCLAT held that, under the principles of Dena Bank, the Adjudicating Authority has the discretion to allow amendments to Section 7 pleadings prior to final orders[cite: 6]. Since the borrower failed to fulfill mandatory RBI conditions for loan restructuring, the restructuring was void and the default dated back to 02.08.2019, falling entirely outside Section 10A[cite: 6].

case_title: Sanjeeb Kumar Jha vs. Yogesh Gupta & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 295 of 2024, Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 296 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 298 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sanjeeb Kumar Jha, Rohit Kumar, and Arun Kumar Bag are the Appellants/alleged Financial Creditors[cite: 7]; Shraddha Health & Fitness Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (operating a Gold's Gym franchise in Patna)[cite: 7]; Yogesh Gupta is the IRP/RP (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 7]; M/s J.N. Hotels Private Limited is the original Section 9 Operational Creditor/Respondent No. 2[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported cash loans of Rs. 2 Lakh each allegedly advanced by Sanjeeb Kumar Jha and Rohit Kumar under loan agreements dated 28.09.2022/30.09.2022[cite: 7]; purported loan of Rs. 3,84,540 claimed by Arun Kumar Bag under agreement dated 22.08.2022 stemming from unpaid supply material[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claims filed in Form C for Rs. 2 Lakh each (with 25.53% CoC voting rights each claimed) by Sanjeeb Kumar Jha and Rohit Kumar, and Rs. 3,84,540 (claiming 48.92% voting share) by Arun Kumar Bag[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application heard and orders reserved by NCLT on 02.08.2022; CIRP admitted against Corporate Debtor on 28.10.2022; public announcement on 10.11.2022; tentative CoC formed on 20.11.2022/28.11.2022[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants' alleged loan agreements were executed in cash immediately after Section 9 order was reserved[cite: 7]; Appellants resided 1,650 km away in Chamba, Himachal Pradesh with no prior commercial relationship with the Patna gym[cite: 7]; ITRs revealed modest annual incomes of Rs. 5.8 Lakh to Rs. 7.37 Lakh without bank disbursal evidence[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: When Appellants sought to replace IRP with Mr. Umesh Kumar, IRP withheld voting rights and de-listed them for lack of verifiable proof; Appellants filed IAs 1645, 1646, and 1647 of 2022; NCLT Kolkata Bench-I on 19.01.2024 held IRP formed CoC hastily on preliminary examination and directed IRP to re-examine the claims and reconstitute CoC[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the Resolution Professional to re-examine the claims and legal credentials of purported financial creditors whose claims arose from undocumented cash agreements executed after orders were reserved in the Section 9 petition, and whether provisional admission in Form C vests an indefeasible right to participate in the CoC[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The collation or provisional verification of claims by an Interim Resolution Professional does not confer an irrevocable right upon a claimant to be permanently seated on the Committee of Creditors; the RP and Adjudicating Authority retain the jurisdiction and legal duty to verify whether claimed debts satisfy the substantive statutory tests of financial debt under Section 5(8)[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A valid financial debt under Section 5(8) requires satisfactory proof of actual disbursal of funds against the consideration for the time value of money; cash entries and unilateral conversions of trade debts lacking evidentiary corroboration do not establish financial creditor status[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where transactions bear hallmarks of being collusive, sham, or executed after judicial orders are reserved to capture CoC voting share, the tribunal can direct rigorous re-examination including production of financial capacity, bank records, and regulatory compliance[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no illegality in ordering the RP to re-verify the claims and reconstitute the CoC, and the appeals are without merit[cite: 7].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 295, 296, and 298 of 2024 are dismissed without costs; the matters in I.A. Nos. 1645, 1646, and 1647 of 2022 are remanded to NCLT Kolkata Bench for final consideration on 08.01.2025[cite: 7].
summary: NCLAT dismissed three appeals filed by individuals claiming to be Financial Creditors of Shraddha Health & Fitness Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 7]. The Appellants claimed voting shares in the CoC based on purported cash loans of Rs. 2 Lakh each and a converted operational debt of Rs. 3.84 Lakh, all executed under private agreements right after the NCLT had reserved orders admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP[cite: 7]. After the Appellants sought to replace the IRP, the IRP scrutinized the claims, found lack of banking trail and violations of money lending statutes, and withheld their participation[cite: 7]. NCLAT affirmed the NCLT order directing the RP to re-examine the validity of the claims and reconstitute the CoC[cite: 7].

case_title: Abhijit Realtors & Infraventures Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Rohit Mehra & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Abhijit Realtors & Infraventures Pvt. Ltd. and Entertainment Network (India) Ltd. (ENIL) form an Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant Consortium[cite: 8]; Reliance Broadcast Network Limited (operating Big FM) is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 8]; Rohit Mehra is the Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1)[cite: 8]; Committee of Creditors is Respondent No. 2[cite: 8]; Sapphire Media Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3)[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP process for revival and transfer of radio broadcasting business holding 58 FM radio licenses across India[cite: 8, 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP under Section 7 on 24.02.2023 on application by IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd.[cite: 8]; challenge process started with a base price of Rs. 240 Crore[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form G issued on 14.04.2023; RFRP issued on 15.06.2023; Challenge Process Document issued on 12.10.2023; Challenge Process conducted on 27.10.2023; final financial proposals submitted on 04.11.2023; CoC approved SRA plan by 88.97% on 16.11.2023[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: In Challenge Process Round 1, SRA bid Rs. 241 Crore and Consortium bid Rs. 240 Crore; in Round 2, Consortium bid Rs. 242 Crore (failing to give the mandatory incremental bid in multiples of Rs. 10 Crore under Clause 7 of the Process Note) and was deemed exited; SRA bid Rs. 251 Crore in Round 3; subsequent negotiations yielded final bids of Rs. 261 Crore from SRA and Rs. 248 Crore from Consortium[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 5572 of 2023 challenging the challenge process; NCLT Mumbai Bench-V dismissed the IA and approved SRA's plan in IA No. 5391 of 2023 on 06.05.2024[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether the challenge process and subsequent negotiation rounds conducted by the RP and CoC violated Regulation 39(1A) of the CIRP Regulations and the Process Note, and whether the RP committed material irregularity in exiting the Consortium after Round 2 for non-compliance with the minimum bid increment[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Conducting further negotiations with prospective resolution applicants for value maximization following the conclusion of a challenge mechanism does not violate Regulation 39(1A) of the CIRP Regulations, provided the RFRP reserves the CoC's right to negotiate[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1A) is not a fetter on the commercial wisdom and authority of the CoC to seek improved financial proposals from resolution applicants[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Adherence to express terms of the process note (requiring bids to increase in stipulated minimum increments) is strictly enforceable by the RP, and a bidder failing to comply with mandatory bidding increments is properly deemed to have exited the challenge rounds[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP acted strictly in accordance with Clause 7 of the Process Note in eliminating the Consortium after Round 2, and the CoC lawfully exercised its powers to negotiate improved proposals, resulting in no material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii)[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 923 of 2024 is dismissed; the order dated 06.05.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-V in IA No. 5572 of 2023 is affirmed without costs[cite: 8].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Abhijit Realtors & Infraventures Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT's rejection of its application alleging irregularities in the challenge process for Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd.[cite: 8]. Appellant contended that its elimination after Round 2 of the bidding was improper and that adopting both a challenge process and subsequent negotiations violated CIRP Regulation 39(1A)[cite: 8]. The Tribunal affirmed that the Appellant was rightly exited for failing to bid in multiples of Rs. 10 Crore as mandated by the Process Note[cite: 8]. Following Vistra ITCL, NCLAT reiterated that the CoC retains inherent authority to negotiate further with applicants for value maximization[cite: 8].

case_title: Dinesh Kumar vs. Narendra Kumar Sharma & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1422 of 2024, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1434 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1573 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dinesh Kumar is Suspended Director of Developer Mist Direct Sales Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant in 1422/2024); Aman Sehgal is Suspended Director of land-owning company Anand Infoedge Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant in 1434/2024); Ravi Kumar is Suspended Director of erstwhile developer Mist Avenue Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant in 1573/2024); Narendra Kumar Sharma is IRP (Respondent No. 1); Respondents 2 to 4 are Homebuyers representing 115 allottees in a class[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development of commercial/residential project 'Festival City' at Plot No. 1, Sector 143, Noida on 90-year lease land from NOIDA; BBAs executed in 2012 providing possession within 36 months plus 12 months grace period[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Project stalled for over a decade with roughly 50% construction; Developer failed to hand over units; Developer subsequently offered Rs. 22,10,43,647 via Demand Draft covering principal and delayed interest, which allottees rejected as inadequate[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: UP RERA issued show cause and deregistered project on 07.12.2019; Section 7 joint petition filed by 115 allottees in October 2021; Supreme Court on 11.12.2023 upheld maintainability and directed disposal within 2 months[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Allottees deposited booking amounts in 2012; CAG audit confirmed Rs. 401 Crore collected from allottees and Rs. 302 Crore diverted to sister concerns; pending civil title suit No. 662/2017 and Allahabad HC WP No. 15503/2019 concerning two middle khasras; Developer filed FIR No. 102/2024 alleging 20 forged affidavits[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-VI held joint petition maintainable on 21.10.2022 (affirmed by NCLAT on 17.11.2023 and Supreme Court on 11.12.2023); Developer's Section 340 CrPC fraud applications were dismissed on 05.01.2024 (affirmed by NCLAT on 29.01.2024); NCLT admitted Section 7 petition and rejected settlement IAs on 19.07.2024[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by real estate allottees against three interwoven companies despite defenses of non-fulfillment of the 100-allottee threshold based on police status reports alleging forged affidavits, force majeure title disputes over project land, and unaccepted unilateral refund offers[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once debt and default are established under Section 7 of the IBC, admission is mandatory under the rule of M. Suresh Kumar Reddy; pendency of collateral criminal investigations, title disputes, or unilateral settlement offers rejected by the class of creditors cannot preclude admission[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory threshold of 100 allottees or 10% under Section 7 is determined at the threshold stage; once affirmed by superior appellate forums, it cannot be relitigated via police status reports in collateral FIRs filed by the promoter[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Force majeure cannot be established when project delay stems from internal mismanagement, diversion of funds, and regulatory cancellations rather than insurmountable external events[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because default in delivering units spanning over a decade was indisputable and maintainability had attained finality, the Section 7 petition was rightly admitted[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1422, 1434, and 1573 of 2024 are dismissed; order dated 19.07.2024 admitting Section 7 CIRP is affirmed; Rs. 22,10,43,647 deposited by the Appellant pursuant to interim orders is directed to be refunded to the Appellant without costs[cite: 9].
summary: NCLAT dismissed appeals preferred by the suspended directors of Mist Direct Sales, Anand Infoedge, and Mist Avenue challenging the admission of a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by 115 allottees of the 'Festival City' project[cite: 9]. The developers contended that the 100-allottee threshold was vitiated due to alleged forged affidavits flagged in an FIR status report, that project delay was caused by force majeure land title disputes with NOIDA, and that they offered to deposit Rs. 22.10 Crore to settle[cite: 9]. NCLAT held that maintainability had attained finality up to the Supreme Court[cite: 9]. Since debt and default in handing over possession were admitted, the NCLT had no discretion but to admit the CIRP[cite: 9].

case_title: Creative Channel Advertising & Marketing Pvt. Ltd. vs. Rohit Ramesh Mehra & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 980 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 981 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Creative Channel Advertising & Marketing Pvt. Ltd. is an Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant[cite: 10]; Reliance Broadcast Network Limited is Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]; Rohit Ramesh Mehra is RP[cite: 10]; Sapphire Media Ltd. is Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA)[cite: 10]; CoC represents lenders[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution of Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd. under CIRP; invitation for EoI issued for PRAs having minimum net worth of Rs. 50 Crore at group level or consolidated average group turnover of Rs. 75 Crore[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 7 CIRP initiated on 24.02.2023 on application of IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd.[cite: 10]; final plan approved by CoC was for Rs. 261 Crore[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form G issued 14.04.2023; RFRP issued 15.06.2023; challenge process held on 27.10.2023; revised bids submitted on 04.11.2023; CoC approved SRA's plan on 16.11.2023 by 88.97% majority[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Creative did not participate in challenge rounds but submitted a revised bid of Rs. 240 Crore on 04.11.2023; SRA was incorporated on 21.10.2022 taking over sole proprietorship of Sahil Mangla who held 99.99% equity; CA certificate dated 08.05.2023 and updated certificate dated 04.11.2023 demonstrated net worth of Rs. 85.04 Crore to Rs. 175 Crore and turnover exceeding Rs. 75 Crore[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Creative filed IA No. 290 of 2024 challenging SRA's eligibility alleging it was a newly incorporated shell company and promoter's personal net worth could not be counted under 'group'; NCLT Mumbai Bench-V dismissed IA No. 290 of 2024 and approved SRA's plan in IA No. 5391 of 2023 on 06.05.2024[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether the word 'entity' in the definition of 'group' within an Invitation for Expression of Interest encompasses an individual promoter holding 99.99% shares, and whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant can challenge the eligibility of the SRA at the plan approval stage after failing to object within statutory timelines[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The author of a tender or process document (the CoC and RP) is the best judge of its interpretation, and where terms are framed broadly to advance value maximization and competition, an interpretation permitting an individual promoter's net worth and turnover to be included at the 'group' level is valid and lawful[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'entity' used in an invitation for EoI is expansive and is not legally restricted to corporate entities or bodies corporate unless explicitly stated[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance with eligibility criteria is assessed from certified financial statements and statutory auditor certificates prescribed under the EoI, and third-party attempts to introduce confidential tax and GST returns barred under Section 138 Income Tax Act and Section 151 CGST Act cannot be entertained[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA fulfilled the net worth and turnover criteria at the group level through its 99.99% promoter, suffered no disqualification, and the CoC's commercial wisdom approving the plan cannot be faulted[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 980 and 981 of 2024 are dismissed; the orders of NCLT Mumbai Bench-V dated 06.05.2024 in IA No. 290 of 2024 and IA No. 5391 of 2023 are upheld[cite: 10].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeals filed by Creative Channel Advertising & Marketing Pvt. Ltd. challenging the approval of Sapphire Media Ltd.'s resolution plan for Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd.[cite: 10]. Creative contended that Sapphire Media was ineligible under Section 25(2)(h) as it was incorporated merely months prior and the RP erroneously counted the individual net worth and turnover of its 99.99% promoter Sahil Mangla under 'group'[cite: 10]. NCLAT held that the term 'entity' in the EoI is expansive and encompasses individuals[cite: 10]. The CoC correctly interpreted its own process criteria to foster competition and asset maximization, warranting no interference with its commercial wisdom[cite: 10].

case_title: Abhijit Realtors & Infraventures Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Rohit Mehra & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 924 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 925 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Abhijit Realtors & Infraventures Pvt. Ltd. and ENIL (Consortium) are the Appellants/Unsuccessful Resolution Applicants[cite: 11]; Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd. is Corporate Debtor[cite: 11]; Rohit Mehra is RP[cite: 11]; Sapphire Media Ltd. is SRA[cite: 11]; CoC represents financial institutions[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency resolution of Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd. (Big FM); Invitation for EoI required minimum group net worth of Rs. 50 Crore or average turnover of Rs. 75 Crore[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to Section 7 CIRP admission on 24.02.2023 on petition of IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd.[cite: 11]; SRA final plan approved at Rs. 261 Crore[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Final PRA list published 25.06.2023; Challenge process conducted 27.10.2023; revised bids submitted 04.11.2023; CoC approval achieved on 16.11.2023 with 88.97% vote[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SRA was corporatized on 21.10.2022 by Sahil Mangla holding 99.99% shares; CA certificate dated 08.05.2023 showed Rs. 84 Crore net worth and updated certificate dated 04.11.2023 showed Rs. 175 Crore net worth; blacklisting by IOC was quashed by Allahabad HC Lucknow Bench; two administrative letters dated 18.10.2023 and 19.10.2023 uploaded on VDR on 03.11.2023 did not cause prejudice as bidding was on 'as is where is' basis[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Consortium filed IA No. 614 of 2024 challenging SRA eligibility; NCLT Mumbai Bench-V rejected IA No. 614 of 2024 and approved plan in IA No. 5391 of 2023 on 06.05.2024[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether SRA Sapphire Media Ltd. was ineligible under Clause 3 of the Invitation for EoI for taking into account the net worth and turnover of its promoter, whether prior blacklisting by IOC disqualified the SRA, and whether delayed uploading of certain correspondence on the Virtual Data Room vitiated the plan approval[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Although an unsuccessful resolution applicant is barred from raising belated objections regarding the provisional list after final PRA publication, the Adjudicating Authority retains jurisdiction to examine fundamental eligibility under Section 30(2) at the time of plan approval[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 3 and Note 5(a) of the Invitation for EoI defining 'group' to include an 'entity' holding 26% or more shares or controlling management properly includes an individual promoter, in harmony with commercial practice and Ministry guidelines[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disqualification clauses restricting entities barred by the Central/State Government or statutory regulators do not apply to commercial contracts with public sector corporations like IOC, particularly where such debarment has been set aside by a High Court[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA fulfilled all eligibility criteria, no material irregularity existed under Section 61(3)(ii), and the commercial approval of the plan by an 88.97% CoC majority is sacrosanct[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 924 and 925 of 2024 are dismissed; IA Nos. 4691 and 4692 of 2024 for additional documents are rejected; the NCLT orders dated 06.05.2024 are affirmed without costs[cite: 11].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeals filed by the Consortium of Abhijit Realtors and ENIL challenging the approval of Sapphire Media Ltd.'s resolution plan for Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd. and the rejection of its objections to the SRA's eligibility[cite: 11]. The Appellants claimed the SRA was a newly formed company that impermissibly aggregated its promoter's personal net worth and had been blacklisted by IOC[cite: 11]. NCLAT held that 'entity' in the EoI includes individual promoters holding 99.99% equity, and IOC debarment did not trigger government regulatory disqualifications[cite: 11]. As all mandatory statutory criteria under Section 30(2) were satisfied, the CoC's commercial approval with an 88.97% majority was upheld[cite: 11].

case_title: Aramco Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ideal Real Estates Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Aramco Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Appellant; Ideal Real Estates Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan extended by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor for which resolution was sought under Section 7 IBC[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount was Rs. 1,92,88,886; under a settlement agreement, the debt was agreed to be paid in 35 monthly instalments commencing from 10.08.2022 with an interest rate of 18% p.a. payable immediately on default[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Settlement agreement executed on 07.06.2022; Section 7 petition disposed of as withdrawn on 08.06.2022; default occurred on instalment payments; revival application RST.A (IBC)/17(KB) 2023 was subsequently filed before NCLT[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement agreement dated 07.06.2022 was taken on record by the NCLT on 08.06.2022; Clause 9 of the agreement explicitly provided that in default of performance, the creditor would be free to apply to NCLT Kolkata to restore CP(IB) No. 1066/KB/2019[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed restoration application RST.A (IBC)/17(KB) 2023 on 03.04.2024 on the ground that the Section 7 petition had been dismissed as withdrawn without explicit liberty granted in the order to revive[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition withdrawn pursuant to a settlement agreement taken on record can be revived upon default by the corporate debtor when the settlement agreement contains an express revival clause, notwithstanding the absence of explicit words granting liberty to revive in the withdrawal order[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where an insolvency petition is withdrawn on the basis of a settlement agreement that is formally placed and taken on record, and the settlement agreement incorporates an explicit clause entitling the creditor to seek revival upon default, the creditor has a right to restore the petition upon breach without being precluded by the non-mention of explicit liberty in the order of withdrawal[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: When an Adjudicating Authority takes a settlement agreement on record and disposes of a petition as withdrawn on that basis, the consent terms—including the revival clause—form an integral part of the record; a withdrawal based on terms placed on record stands on a fundamentally different legal footing from a withdrawal simpliciter[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted failure by the corporate debtor to honour the payment schedule stipulated in the settlement agreement taken on record establishes a valid ground for revival[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of the revival application denied the Financial Creditor its rightful remedy against a dishonest corporate debtor; the revival application was maintainable and CP (IB) No. 1066/KB/2019 stood revived[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1137 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT dated 03.04.2024 is set aside; CP (IB) No. 1066/KB/2019 is revived before the Adjudicating Authority to proceed in accordance with law; cost of Rs. 2,00,000 is imposed on the Respondent payable to the Appellant via Bank Draft within one month[cite: 12].
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by Financial Creditor Aramco Pvt. Ltd. against NCLT Kolkata's order dated 03.04.2024 which had refused to revive a Section 7 petition against Ideal Real Estates Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 12]. The original petition was withdrawn after a settlement agreement for Rs. 1.92 Crore was taken on record[cite: 12]. The CD defaulted on instalments, and the NCLT rejected revival on the premise that explicit liberty was not reserved in the withdrawal order[cite: 12]. Reversing the decision, NCLAT held that because the settlement containing an express revival clause was brought on record, the creditor had the legal right to seek revival, and imposed Rs. 2 Lakh costs on the CD[cite: 12].

case_title: Mavjibhai Nagarbhai Patel vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1702 of 2024, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1711 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1712 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mavjibhai Nagarbhai Patel, Jayantibhai Nagarbhai Patel, and Narayanbhai N. Patel are Appellants/Personal Guarantors; Vrundavan Ceramic Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Debtor; State Bank of India (SAMB Ahmedabad) is Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Dharit K. Shah is RP/Respondent No. 2[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI extended credit facilities (Cash Credit, WCTL, FITL) to the Corporate Debtor, secured by a continuing Deed of Guarantee dated 09.04.2005 and supplemental guarantees up to 2010 executed by the Personal Guarantors[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Loan account declared NPA on 31.07.2013; Demand Notice under Section 13(2) SARFAESI claimed Rs. 32.60 Crore as on 30.04.2021; Section 95 Form-C claimed unpaid debt in default amounting to Rs. 33,51,62,406[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted into CIRP on 21.01.2020; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued on 04.06.2021 demanding payment within 60 days (default date 04.08.2021); Rule 7(1) demand notice issued on 28.09.2021; Section 95 petition filed on 18.06.2022[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Guarantee clauses 8 and 20 provided for a continuing on-demand guarantee payable upon notice; Gazette of India Notification dated 02.05.1987 under Regulation 76(1) of SBI General Regulations authorized officers of SMGS-IV and above to sign legal documents; settlement proposal dated 11.01.2022[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed Section 95(1) petitions; RP submitted report under Section 99 recommending admission; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-I admitted the petitions on 27.06.2024[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 95 IBC application against a personal guarantor is barred by limitation when the borrower account was declared NPA in 2013 but the on-demand continuing personal guarantee was invoked in 2021, and whether an Assistant General Manager holding SMGS-V rank was competent to sign and institute the Section 95 petition on behalf of State Bank of India[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The liability of a principal borrower and a guarantor are co-extensive, but a guarantor's liability is governed by the specific terms of the guarantee contract; where a deed of guarantee is a continuing on-demand guarantee, the cause of action and limitation period against the guarantor accrue only upon invocation of the guarantee and expiry of the demand notice period, not on the date the principal borrower defaulted or was declared NPA[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In Section 95 proceedings, the date of default for a guarantor is legally distinct from that of the corporate debtor if the contract of guarantee prescribes a formal demand notice as a prerequisite for payment[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An Assistant General Manager of SBI is statutorily authorized to institute legal petitions under Gazette of India Notification dated 02.05.1987 issued pursuant to Regulation 76(1) of SBI General Regulations, 1955, without requiring a specific standalone board resolution[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Invocation on 04.06.2021 with default occurring on 04.08.2021 rendered the Section 95 petition filed on 18.06.2022 well within the three-year limitation period, and institution by the AGM was legally valid[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1702, 1711, and 1712 of 2024 are dismissed; orders of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-I dated 27.06.2024 admitting Section 95 applications are affirmed without costs[cite: 13].
summary: NCLAT dismissed three appeals filed by personal guarantors of Vrundavan Ceramic Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT Ahmedabad's orders admitting SBI's Section 95 insolvency applications[cite: 13]. Appellants contended that since the CD was declared NPA in 2013, the Section 95 petitions filed in 2022 were barred by limitation, and that the AGM was unauthorized to file them[cite: 13]. NCLAT held that because the guarantee was a continuing on-demand contract, the cause of action qua the guarantors arose only when the guarantee was invoked on 04.06.2021 under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, making the 2022 petitions timely[cite: 13]. Additionally, the AGM possessed statutory signing authority under the 1987 Gazette Notification[cite: 13].

case_title: Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited vs. Waaree Energies Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA) is Financial Creditor/Appellant; Waaree Energies Limited is Financial Creditor/Debenture Holder/Respondent No. 1; M/s Taxus Infrastructure and Power Projects Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Debtor; Darshan Singh Anand is RP/Respondent No. 2[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Waaree subscribed to 1,00,000 secured Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) of face value Rs. 1,000 each for Rs. 10 Crore under Debenture Subscription Agreement (DSA) dated 16.10.2012 to fund CD's projects[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 21,45,42,466 (comprising Rs. 10,00,00,000 principal and Rs. 11,45,42,466 interest) based on arbitral award dated 31.12.2021 granting Rs. 10 Crore plus 24% p.a. interest[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Letter issued by Waaree on 08.12.2017 demanding repayment of Rs. 15,63,86,301 or conversion into 49.93% equity; Arbitral Award rendered 31.12.2021; Section 7 CIRP initiated by IREDA on 10.10.2022; public announcement on 12.10.2022; RP filed Section 34 challenge on 20.01.2023[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DSA Clause 1.1 made conversion optional at investor's discretion; Clause 7.1(XVI) identified failure to redeem debentures as Event of Default; Clause 8.1 mandated payment of defaulted amounts with 24% p.a. interest from due date[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP initially admitted Waaree as FC with 23.50% CoC voting share but subsequently excluded it citing pending Section 34 petition; Waaree filed IA No. 2068 of 2023; NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) allowed the IA on 29.05.2024, holding that CCDs carried time value of money and restoring Waaree to the CoC[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) that provide an option to the investor for conversion and incorporate default clauses mandating repayment with penal interest at 24% per annum qualify as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(c) of the IBC, and whether the pendency of a Section 34 petition against an arbitral award bars recognition of a financial creditor's claim[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An instrument labeled as a Compulsorily Convertible Debenture constitutes a 'financial debt' within the meaning of Section 5(8)(c) where contractual terms reveal that conversion is at the investor's option and the issuer is obligated to pay interest upon default in repayment/redemption, thereby embodying the time value of money[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(c) expressly encompasses any amount raised pursuant to the issue of debentures; where redemption or interest payments are contractually stipulated upon failure of conversion, the instrument operates as debt rather than pure equity[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To determine whether an investment is equity or debt, tribunals must interpret the specific provisions of the subscription agreement as a whole rather than relying on nomenclature alone[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The DSA between the parties established time value of money, the failure to redeem or convert triggered an event of default carrying 24% interest, and the pendency of a Section 34 challenge did not wipe out the claim; the NCLT properly restored Respondent No. 1 as a Financial Creditor[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1380 of 2024 is dismissed; order of NCLT New Delhi Bench dated 29.05.2024 in IA No. 2068 of 2023 is affirmed without costs[cite: 14].
summary: NCLAT dismissed IREDA's appeal challenging NCLT New Delhi's order that recognized Waaree Energies Ltd. as a Financial Creditor of Taxus Infrastructure and Power Projects Pvt. Ltd. and restored its 23.50% seat in the CoC[cite: 14]. IREDA argued that Waaree's investment in CCDs was pure equity and that an arbitral award challenged under Section 34 could not create a financial debt[cite: 14]. Interpreting the Debenture Subscription Agreement, NCLAT held that conversion was at the investor's option and default clauses mandated repayment with 24% interest[cite: 14]. Thus, the instrument had time value of money and constituted financial debt under Section 5(8)(c) of the IBC[cite: 14].

case_title: Mr. Pankaj Dhanuka, Liquidator of Lanco Kondapalli Power Limited vs. Lanco Kondapalli Power Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Pankaj Dhanuka is Liquidator of Lanco Kondapalli Power Limited (Appellant); Lanco Kondapalli Power Limited through Director Sunil Saraf is Respondent No. 1; MCM Pacific Pte Limited (Singapore) is Successful Auction Purchaser/Respondent No. 2[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Auction sale of corporate debtor's plant goods/assets lying on land sold to a third-party land purchaser, involving terms for remittance of rent for use and occupation of land[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Landowner demanded occupation rent of approx. Rs. 1.5 Crore per month; alleged non-compliance with NCLT directions dated 02.08.2023 passed in IA No. 1221/2023[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Direction issued on 02.08.2023 permitting the auction purchaser to seek liquidator's assistance to work out rent terms by separate agreement; Contempt Application Cont. A(IBC)/02/2024 filed in 2024[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order dated 02.08.2023 left it open to the Successful Auction Purchaser to get assistance of the liquidator to negotiate rent terms; the alleged contemnor impleaded was an inanimate Singapore corporate entity without naming an individual responsible[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed Cont. A(IBC)/02/2024 under Section 60(5) IBC read with Section 425 Companies Act, 2013; NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed the contempt petition on 04.10.2024 holding that no deliberate or intentional contempt was established[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC read with Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 is maintainable against an order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing a contempt petition and declining to initiate contempt proceedings, and whether a contempt petition is tenable against an inanimate juristic person[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 lies exclusively against an order or decision imposing punishment for contempt; no appeal lies as of right against an order rejecting, dropping, or declining to initiate contempt proceedings[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) of the IBC is a residual savings clause and cannot be deployed to circumvent statutory mechanisms where a specific procedure is provided under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contempt is a matter between the court and the alleged contemnor; the initiator acts merely as an informer and acquires no personal right to appeal a dismissal unless an inextricably linked final decision on substantive inter se rights is made[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the NCLT merely refused to initiate contempt and imposed no punishment, the appeal is not maintainable under Section 19; furthermore, a contempt petition impleading only an inanimate corporate entity without an individual contemnor is untenable[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 438 of 2024 and IA No. 1194 of 2024 are dismissed for lack of merit and maintainability[cite: 15].
summary: NCLAT Chennai dismissed an appeal filed by the Liquidator of Lanco Kondapalli Power Ltd. challenging NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 04.10.2024 which dismissed a contempt petition against auction purchaser MCM Pacific Pte Ltd. for alleged non-compliance with directions regarding site occupation rent[cite: 15]. NCLAT held that under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 read with Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, an appeal lies solely against an order imposing punishment, and never against an order dropping or refusing to initiate contempt[cite: 15]. Furthermore, contempt proceedings cannot lie against an inanimate company without joining responsible individuals[cite: 15].

case_title: Mr. Rakesh Kumar Jain vs. M/s ADTV Communications Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rakesh Kumar Jain is the Financial Creditor/Decree Holder/Appellant; M/s ADTV Communications Private Limited (formerly M/s AEZ Infratech Private Limited) is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Long-standing debt recovery disputes referred to Delhi High Court Mediation and Conciliation Centre, resulting in a Settlement Agreement dated 11.09.2014 whereby the Respondent agreed to pay Rs. 15,23,00,000 in four instalments via cheques, upon which a consent decree was passed in CS(OS) No. 2183/2013[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rs. 5.23 Crore was paid, but the post-dated cheque for the balance amount of Rs. 10,00,00,000 bounced upon presentation on 07.04.2016[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheque dishonoured on 07.04.2016; Execution Petition Ex. P. No. 133/2016 filed on 20.09.2016; written objections acknowledging debt filed by CD on 23.08.2018; further acknowledgments recorded in High Court orders dated 04.09.2018 and 17.09.2018; Section 7 petition filed on 11.10.2019/15.10.2019[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Objections dated 23.08.2018 admitting liability for Rs. 10 Crores; High Court orders recording CD's requests for 6 months time to pay; High Court attachment of CD's bank accounts and 19,795 sq. meter freehold plot in Ghaziabad[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT-III New Delhi dismissed Section 7 CP (IB) No. 3083/ND/2019 on 24.04.2023, holding that a Decree Holder cannot be a Financial Creditor and the application was barred by limitation[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a Decree Holder whose decree crystallizes an underlying financial debt qualifies as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7) of the IBC, and whether written acknowledgments made in execution proceedings extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A decree holder falls within the definition of 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7) read with Section 3(10) of the IBC if the underlying decree arises from a financial debt; a consent decree formalizing a financial debt does not change its character into an unexecutable non-financial claim[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: By virtue of the non-obstante effect of Section 238, the pendency of execution proceedings does not bar initiation of Section 7 CIRP; Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings, and unequivocal written acknowledgments of liability made in court or pleadings before the expiration of the 3-year period renew the limitation period[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the rule in Dena Bank and Laxmi Pat Surana, written pleadings in court and statements recorded in judicial orders within three years from dishonour constitute valid acknowledgments of liability under Section 18[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application filed in October 2019 was well within the extended limitation period, the Appellant was a bona fide Financial Creditor, and the NCLT's dismissal was erroneous[cite: 16].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 849 of 2023 is allowed; impugned order of NCLT-III New Delhi dated 24.04.2023 is set aside; Section 7 petition is admitted; NCLT directed to appoint an IRP and issue consequential admission orders within 15 days without costs[cite: 16].
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by Rakesh Kumar Jain setting aside NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of his Section 7 petition against ADTV Communications Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 16]. The claim arose from a mediated consent decree where a Rs. 10 Crore settlement cheque was dishonoured on 07.04.2016[cite: 16]. The NCLT had held that a decree holder cannot initiate CIRP as a financial creditor and that the claim was time-barred[cite: 16]. Relying on Dena Bank, NCLAT ruled that a decree holder remains a Financial Creditor if the underlying transaction is a financial debt[cite: 16]. Furthermore, multiple written admissions made by the CD in High Court execution proceedings in August and September 2018 extended limitation under Section 18[cite: 16].

case_title: Laxmi Narayan Sharma vs. Subodh Kumar Agrawal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Laxmi Narayan Sharma is Suspended Director/Promoter holding 84% shares of Corporate Debtor Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (GJHPL); Subodh Kumar Agrawal is former RP/Respondent No. 1; Bank of Baroda is lead lender among eight Financial Creditors (Respondents 2 to 9); BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co. II (NQ) Pte. Ltd. is SRA/Respondent No. 10; EIH Limited is 16% shareholder/operator (Respondent No. 11)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GJHPL developed and operated the 5-star hotel 'Trident' in Hyderabad under lease agreements with YATCL and Shilparamam Society, funded by consortium credit facilities[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted Financial Creditor claims were Rs. 949 Crore; Operational Creditor claims were Rs. 106.57 Crore (Rs. 60.14 Crore admitted); Liquidation value was Rs. 448-458 Crore; approved SRA resolution plan value was Rs. 584.02 Crore[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Admission under Section 7 on 27.02.2018 (affirmed on 06.09.2018); Appellant submitted OTS proposal for Rs. 430 Crore on 31.10.2018; CoC approved SRA plan with 68.26% vote on 18.12.2018[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved plan earmarked Rs. 41.99 Crore in full for land lessors as 'Special Operational Creditors' while allocating Nil to trade operational creditors based on Nil liquidation value under Section 53; SRA plan contained a condition precedent requiring lessor consent for shareholding transfer within one year[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed multiple IAs challenging non-furnishing of the plan, rejection of OTS, discriminatory distribution, and inclusion of condition precedents; NCLT Hyderabad Bench rejected objections and approved the plan on 07.02.2020[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether the approval of a resolution plan is vitiated because a copy was not furnished to the suspended director prior to CoC voting, whether the CoC was bound to accept the promoter's OTS proposal over the SRA's plan, and whether differential treatment of operational creditors and condition precedents invalidate the plan[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the CoC in evaluating the feasibility, viability, and fund distribution of a resolution plan is non-justiciable, and the promoter possesses no statutory entitlement to compel the CoC to accept an OTS proposal in lieu of a compliant resolution plan[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Post-CIRP settlement can only occur under Section 12A with a 90% CoC voting majority; furthermore, non-furnishing of a resolution plan prior to the Supreme Court's ruling in Vijay Kumar Jain causes no prejudice where the director actively participated in all CoC deliberations and the plan was subsequently supplied[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Condition precedents necessary for legal continuity of operations (such as obtaining lessor consent under a co-terminus BOT project) are legally permissible under the rule in Jet Airways[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Allocating 100% to project lessors while trade operational creditors received Nil complied with Section 30(2)(b) since liquidation entitlement was Nil, and the promoter's challenge to the approved plan was devoid of merit[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 438 of 2020 is dismissed; order dated 07.02.2020 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench approving the resolution plan is affirmed without costs[cite: 17].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Laxmi Narayan Sharma, the 84% promoter of Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd., challenging the approval of BREP Asia II's resolution plan[cite: 17]. The promoter alleged procedural violations including non-furnishing of the plan before CoC voting, rejection of his Rs. 430 Crore OTS, and discriminatory full payment to land lessors versus Nil to other operational creditors[cite: 17]. NCLAT held that no prejudice occurred regarding plan supply as the promoter attended all meetings, the CoC was not obliged to accept an unapproved OTS lacking Section 12A's 90% majority, and differential payout to essential land lessors was a lawful exercise of commercial wisdom[cite: 17].

case_title: Devkaran & Co. Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shashi Tanna & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Devkaran & Co. Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant Company; Shashi Tanna (Plaintiff No. 2/Petitioner No. 1) and Nikhil Sayta are legal representatives/Respondents 1 and 2; Late Smt. Tarla Girish Tanna was an erstwhile majority shareholder; Respondent No. 3 is a minority shareholder/director in control. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Shareholding in Appellant Company historically held in a 2:1 ratio between Tannas (667 shares) and Respondent No. 3 (333 shares); after Smt. Tarla Tanna died on 22.08.2012, paid-up capital was increased in 2014 by allotting 9,000 shares without notice, drastically reducing her estate's holding from 66.7% to 6.67%. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement alleged under Sections 241 and 242 based on dilution of 667 equity shares from 66% to 6% following the member's death. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Smt.
