Tarla passed away on 22.08.2012 leaving a Will dated 16.07.2010; Consent Terms executed on 26.04.2017 in High Court Suit No. 1210/2009; Testamentary Suit No. 887/2014 disposed of on 04.05.2017 recording settlement; CP(IB) No. 21/MB/2024 filed before NCLT Mumbai in 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent Terms dated 26.04.2017 vested ownership and authority over the 667 shares in Plaintiffs and Defendants 3 to 12 as Class II legal heirs and authorized Shashi Tanna to hold and administer the shares; pending High Court Suit No. 1075/2019 challenging Consent Terms was confined strictly to two immovable properties and did not seek relief qua the 667 shares. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant Company raised preliminary objections under Section 244(1) that Respondents 1 and 2 lacked locus standi as they had not obtained a Letter of Administration/Probate under Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act; NCLT Mumbai rejected the objection on 05.08.2024.
legal_issues: Whether the legal representatives of a deceased shareholder who derive authority from High Court consent terms have locus standi to maintain a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Section 241 without first obtaining a formal Letter of Administration or Probate under Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon the demise of a company member, their estate immediately vests in their legal representatives, who are legally entitled to maintain an application alleging oppression and mismanagement to protect the deceased's shareholding from illegal dilution or wrongful expropriation, standing in the shoes of the deceased member. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241 read with Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be interpreted with hyper-technical rigidity to bar legal representatives holding authority under valid judicial consent terms from protecting the estate, particularly where the requirement of probate was dispensed with by court order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where consent terms conferring administrative and beneficial authority over shares remain unsuspended, unstayed, and unchallenged by any competent civil court or appellate forum, they constitute sufficient evidentiary authorization to establish locus standi. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The reduction of the deceased member's shareholding from 66% to 6% post-mortem justified legal representation by Respondents 1 and 2 to defend the estate under the rule in Worldwide Agencies; NCLT's finding on maintainability was legally sound.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 361 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai dated 05.08.2024 is affirmed; pending applications are disposed of.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Devkaran & Co. Pvt. Ltd. challenging an NCLT Mumbai order that upheld the locus standi of legal representatives of Late Smt. Tarla Tanna to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241. The company argued that the petitioners were Class II heirs who lacked probate or letters of administration as mandated in Mumbai under Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act. NCLAT held that, under Worldwide Agencies, succession is not kept in abeyance and the estate must be protected by legal representatives where shareholding was drastically diluted from 66% to 6% post-death, affirming the validity of authority derived from subsisting High Court consent terms.

case_title: Commercial Tax Department vs. Mr. Mangesh Vitthal Kekre & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Commercial Tax Department (Indore Circle-15) is the Appellant; Mr. Mangesh Vitthal Kekre is Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); M/s Bhagwan Motors Private Limited is Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2); VE Commercial Vehicles Limited is the third-party debtor/dealer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial dealings between Corporate Debtor and VE Commercial Vehicles Limited wherein VE Commercial Vehicles availed Input Tax Credit (ITC) on transactions, but Corporate Debtor failed to deposit corresponding VAT/GST with tax authorities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: VAT dues of Rs. 17,12,094 for Assessment Year 2014-15 owed by Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 21.06.2019; Commercial Tax Department issued statutory notice under Section 28(1) MP VAT Act to VE Commercial Vehicles on 03.07.2019; VE Commercial Vehicles deposited Rs. 17,12,094 with the tax department shortly thereafter; RP filed avoidance application IA/131/MP/2020 in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statutory garnishee notice dated 03.07.2019 demanding payment from third-party debtor under Section 28(1); proof of independent deposit by VE Commercial Vehicles to reverse ITC benefits; no transfer of assets or funds made from the Corporate Debtor's bank accounts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA/131/MP/2020 under Section 43 read with Section 60(5) IBC alleging preferential transaction and violation of moratorium; NCLT Indore Special Bench-I on 01.09.2023 held recovery during moratorium was invalid and ordered tax authorities to refund Rs. 17,12,094.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory recovery of VAT dues made by the tax department from a third-party debtor under Section 28(1) of the MP VAT Act during the CIRP moratorium constitutes a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC or violates Section 14 moratorium.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For a transaction to be challenged as an avoidable preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC, there must be an actual transfer of property or interest of the corporate debtor made by the corporate debtor itself; payments made independently by third parties under separate statutory liabilities do not qualify. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The moratorium under Section 14(1) operates strictly to protect the corporate debtor and its own property and assets; it does not extend to third-party entities discharging their statutory obligations or reversing unremitted input tax credits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where recovery is effected not from the corporate debtor's accounts or assets but from a third-party debtor reversing an unremitted tax benefit under state revenue law, no breach of moratorium or preference is established. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The deposit of Rs. 17,12,094 by VE Commercial Vehicles Limited was not a transfer by the Corporate Debtor and did not violate Section 14; the NCLT's direction compelling the tax department to refund the amount was erroneous.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 232 of 2024 is allowed; the order dated 01.09.2023 passed by NCLT Indore Special Bench in IA/131/MP/2020 is set aside; IA/131/MP/2020 filed by the RP is dismissed with parties bearing their own costs.
summary: NCLAT allowed an appeal filed by the Commercial Tax Department against an NCLT Indore order that directed the department to refund Rs. 17,12,094 recovered from VE Commercial Vehicles Ltd. towards VAT dues of Corporate Debtor Bhagwan Motors Pvt. Ltd. The RP had challenged the recovery under Section 43 and Section 14 of the IBC as an unlawful preference and moratorium violation. Reversing the decision, NCLAT held that Section 43 requires a transfer of property by the corporate debtor itself, which was absent here. Furthermore, Section 14 moratorium shields only the corporate debtor's assets and does not prohibit statutory third-party adjustments reversing input tax credits.

case_title: Bikram Bhadur vs. Union Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bikram Bhadur is Suspended Director/Appellant of Corporate Debtor M/s I World Business Solutions Pvt. Ltd.; Union Bank of India (formerly Andhra Bank) is Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Interim Resolution Professional is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities including Cash Credit of Rs. 50 Crore, Bank Guarantee renewal of Rs. 10 Crore, Funded Interest Term Loan (FITL) of Rs. 3,21,63,265 sanctioned on 16.09.2020, and GECL facility of Rs. 10 Crore. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed in Section 7 petition was Rs. 76,61,82,565 as on 30.06.2022; default date cited was 31.03.2021 (the date account was classified as NPA), with an overdue amount of Rs. 1,09,28,247 on FITL as on 31.03.2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Revival letter admitting Rs. 50.73 Crore outstanding executed on 30.08.2019; FITL sanctioned on 16.09.2020; NPA declared on 31.03.2021; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued on 09.06.2021; Section 7 petition filed on 24.09.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's revival letter dated 30.08.2019 acknowledging liability of Rs. 50.73 Crore prior to Section 10A period; bank account statements establishing ongoing default of over Rs. 1 Crore outside 10A period; corporate debtor's own EMI repayment chart showing Rs. 1.09 Crore default as on 31.03.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor resisted Section 7 admission arguing default occurred during Section 10A period; NCLT Court-V New Delhi Bench admitted Section 7 application on 04.06.2024.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application is barred by Section 10A when the date of default is stated as 31.03.2021 (the date of NPA classification), where defaults existed both prior to and continuously subsequent to the Section 10A statutory window in amounts exceeding the threshold of Rs. 1 Crore.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While Section 10A permanently bars filing an application under Section 7 for defaults occurring between 25.03.2020 and 25.03.2021, an application is maintainable if independent actionable defaults exceeding the statutory threshold occurred prior to the 10A period and continued after its expiry. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Declaration of an account as NPA on 31.03.2021 can be reckoned as a valid date of default under Section 7, and the accrual of unpaid debt exceeding Rs. 1 Crore beyond the 10A period maintains the actionability of the claim. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bank statements and loan revival letters executed prior to the pandemic acknowledging liabilities establish antecedent default; at admission, the adjudicating authority examines only whether actionable default exceeds the threshold, leaving exact quantum reconciliation to the RP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because actionable default exceeding Rs. 1 Crore existed independently of the 10A period, Section 10A did not bar admission of the CIRP.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1289 of 2024 is dismissed; order dated 04.06.2024 passed by NCLT Court-V New Delhi Bench admitting Section 7 application is affirmed with observations that default amounts during 10A period be excluded by RP upon claim collation.
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by the suspended director of M/s I World Business Solutions Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT New Delhi's order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Union Bank of India. The Appellant argued that the default date of 31.03.2021 fell within the Section 10A COVID-19 relief period and arose out of an emergency FITL facility. NCLAT held that the Corporate Debtor had executed acknowledgments of debt exceeding Rs. 50 Crore prior to the 10A period and continued to remain in default well beyond the 10A window in excess of the Rs. 1 Crore threshold, rendering the Section 7 petition maintainable.

case_title: Anshuman Warehousing Private Limited vs. M/s K.V. Developers (P) Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anshuman Warehousing Private Limited is the Appellant; M/s K.V. Developers (P) Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1; M/s Brijkishor Trading Pvt. Ltd., Mr. Sumit Kumar Khanna, and Rearco (P) Ltd. are Successful Resolution Applicants (Respondents 2 to 4); Monitoring Agency is Respondent No. 5; Substituted RP is Respondent No. 6. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Challenge to orders passed in IA Nos. 3447/2021 and 3583/2022 during the corporate insolvency resolution process of K.V. Developers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Inordinate procedural delay of 156 days in re-filing the Memo of Appeal after defects were notified by the Registry. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal originally e-filed on 01.06.2023; Registry notified defects on 12.06.2023; 7-day cure window expired on 19.06.2023; appeal re-filed on 22.11.2023 after 156 days; condonation application IA No. 5648 of 2023 filed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Defect sheets issued on 12.06.2023; Appellant cited counsel travel, court summer vacations, loss of courier containing signed affidavit on 04.08.2023 (supported by NCR dated 29.08.2023), clerk leaving employment, registry queries regarding challenging two IAs together, and festive court vacations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 5648 of 2023 seeking condonation of 156 days delay in re-filing; Respondent No. 6 opposed on grounds of strict statutory timelines under Section 61 IBC.
legal_issues: Whether an inordinate delay of 156 days in re-filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC can be condoned on grounds of administrative convenience, counsel travel, clerk turnover, and lost courier affidavits.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is a self-contained code designed for strict time-bound resolution; an applicant seeking condonation of an inordinate re-filing delay must demonstrate bona fide diligence and establish compelling sufficient cause. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Timelines under Section 61 of the IBC are strict and sacred; routine administrative excuses or procedural laxity do not constitute sufficient cause to grant condonation where the delay hinders the finality of the resolution process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Generic assertions regarding summer breaks, advocate travel, logistical disruptions of clerks, and misplacement of internal correspondence fail the legal standard of vigilance required in commercial insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay of 156 days in re-filing was unjustified, displayed a total lack of vigilance, and could not be condoned; the application for condonation and consequently the appeal were liable to dismissal.
operative_order: IA No. 5648 of 2023 is rejected; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1583 of 2023 along with other pending interlocutory applications is dismissed without costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed an application seeking condonation of a 156-day delay in re-filing an appeal against K.V. Developers (P) Ltd. and its Successful Resolution Applicants. The Appellant attributed the delay to advocate travel, clerk resignation, court vacations, and a misplaced courier affidavit. Reaffirming Supreme Court precedents in Essar Steel, Ebix Singapore, and Gujarat Urja, the Appellate Tribunal held that strict adherence to timelines is foundational to the IBC regime. Because the Appellant failed to show sufficient cause and demonstrated complete lack of vigilance, the condonation application was rejected and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Desana Impex Limited vs. Brick and Mortar Realty Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Desana Impex Limited is an RBI-registered NBFC/Financial Creditor/Appellant; Brick and Mortar Realty Private Limited is a real estate developer/Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Oral agreement for an Inter-Corporate Loan facility of Rs. 1,50,00,000 extended to the Corporate Debtor carrying interest at 12% per annum payable on demand. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal loan amount disbursed was Rs. 1,50,00,000; total default claimed in Demand Notice dated 12.03.2022 was Rs. 2,31,44,999 (comprising Rs. 1.5 Crore principal and Rs. 81,44,999 unpaid interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disbursals occurred in five tranches between 24.05.2013 and 05.09.2015; interest paid up to 31.03.2017; formal Demand Notice issued on 12.03.2022; reminder sent 04.05.2022; legal notice sent 26.05.2022; Section 7 petition filed on 02.12.2022/14.12.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements establishing 5 disbursements of Rs. 1.5 Crore; interest payment of Rs. 14,69,688 reflected on 14.02.2017; TDS deducted under Section 194A reflected in Form 26AS from FY 2014-15 through FY 2020-21; Confirmation of Accounts signed and emailed by group accountant Dilip Mohanty for FY 2014-15, 2016-17, 2017-18, 2018-19, and 2020-21. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed Section 7 CP (IB) 342/KB/2022 on 21.11.2023, ruling that RBI NBFC guidelines mandate written contracts, loan was booked as 'Other Liabilities', and no valid debt was proved.
legal_issues: Whether the absence of a written loan agreement precludes an NBFC from establishing a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether TDS deductions in Form 26AS and account confirmation emails extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A written loan agreement is not a mandatory pre-condition to prove the existence of a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC; disbursement of money with an agreed interest component (time value of money) can be fully established through bank statements, ledger confirmations, and tax filings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Non-obstante Section 238 of the IBC overrides RBI regulatory circulars prescribing written contracts for NBFCs; failure to comply with internal circulars does not invalidate an otherwise proved financial debt under the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Deductions of tax at source under Section 194A of the Income Tax Act reflected in Form 26AS coupled with ledger confirmation letters constitute valid written acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, renewing limitation from the date of the latest deduction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default were conclusively established, the Section 7 petition was filed within three years of the FY 2020-21 acknowledgment, and the NCLT's dismissal of the petition was unsustainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 318 of 2024 is allowed; the order of NCLT Kolkata Bench dated 21.11.2023 is set aside; Corporate Debtor is ordered to be proceeded against under Section 7; NCLT directed to pass consequential admission orders within 30 days.
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by NBFC Desana Impex Limited setting aside NCLT Kolkata's dismissal of its Section 7 petition against Brick and Mortar Realty Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had rejected the petition on grounds that RBI guidelines mandate written loan contracts for NBFCs and that the funds were recorded as 'Other Liabilities'. NCLAT held that Section 238 overrides RBI circulars and that a formal written agreement is not mandatory to prove financial debt. Because bank statements proved disbursement, interest was paid at 12%, and continuous TDS deductions in Form 26AS up to FY 2020-21 extended limitation under Section 18, debt and default were established.

case_title: Archangles Distributors Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ideal Financing Corporation Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Archangles Distributors Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Appellant; Ideal Financing Corporation Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility extended by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 2,31,60,579, which was agreed under a formal settlement agreement dated 07.06.2022 to be paid in 27 instalments starting from 10.08.2022, with default interest at 18% p.a.[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Settlement agreement executed on 07.06.2022; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 598/KB/2019 was disposed of as withdrawn on 08.06.2022; Corporate Debtor subsequently defaulted on instalment payments; revival application RST.A (IBC)/16(KB) 2023 was filed in 2023[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement agreement was taken on record by the NCLT on 08.06.2022; Clause 9 of the agreement explicitly provided that in default of performance, the creditor would be free to apply to NCLT Kolkata to restore CP(IB) No. 598/KB/2019[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the restoration application on 03.04.2024 holding that the main Section 7 petition was dismissed as withdrawn without explicit liberty granted in the order to revive[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition disposed of as withdrawn pursuant to a settlement agreement taken on record by the Adjudicating Authority can be revived upon default by the corporate debtor when the settlement agreement contains an express revival clause, notwithstanding the absence of explicit words granting liberty to revive in the withdrawal order[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where an insolvency petition under Section 7 is withdrawn pursuant to a settlement agreement brought on record, and that agreement contains an explicit clause permitting revival in the event of default, the creditor is entitled to restore the petition without requiring a specific grant of liberty in the withdrawal order[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A withdrawal based on settlement terms taken on record by the Tribunal stands on a fundamentally different legal footing from a withdrawal simpliciter, and the agreed terms (including the right of revival) form an operative basis of the disposal[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted failure by the corporate debtor to honour the payment schedule stipulated in the settlement agreement taken on record establishes a valid ground for revival[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The non-mention of specific liberty in the order of withdrawal is inconsequential in light of the clear terms of settlement on record; rejecting the revival application improperly denied the Financial Creditor its rightful legal remedy[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1143 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Kolkata dated 03.04.2024 is set aside; CP (IB) No. 598/KB/2019 is revived before the Adjudicating Authority to proceed in accordance with law; cost of Rs. 2,00,000 is imposed on the Respondent payable to the Appellant via Bank Draft within one month[cite: 24].
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by Financial Creditor Archangles Distributors Pvt. Ltd., setting aside NCLT Kolkata's order that refused to revive a Section 7 petition against Ideal Financing Corporation Ltd.[cite: 24]. The original petition had been disposed of as withdrawn after taking on record a settlement agreement for Rs. 2.31 Crore which expressly provided for revival upon default[cite: 24]. When the Corporate Debtor failed to pay instalments, NCLT rejected restoration because explicit liberty was not stated in the withdrawal order[cite: 24]. Reversing this, NCLAT held that bringing the settlement on record gave the creditor an inherent right to revive upon breach, and penalized the Corporate Debtor with Rs. 2 Lakh costs[cite: 24].

case_title: Yashdeep Sharma vs. Tara Chand Meenia & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Yashdeep Sharma is Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Maha Associated Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant); Tara Chand Meenia is Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 1); Punjab & Sind Bank is Secured Financial Creditor/CoC member (Respondent No. 2); Trufalir Buildwell LLP is Successful Resolution Applicant/SRA (Respondent No. 3)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution of hotel corporate debtor during CIRP initiated under Section 9; project involved land leased by RIICO[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation value estimated at Rs. 4.8 Crore by RP; SRA's revised resolution plan approved by CoC offering substantial value over liquidation estimates[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant belatedly submitted an uninvited plan without EMD on 26.04.2024 (rejected 22.05.2024); CoC adopted Swiss Challenge Method on 09.05.2024; revised resolution plans received 22.05.2024; CoC approved Trufalir Buildwell LLP's plan by 100% vote share in 54th meeting; NCLT approved plan on 13.08.2024[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SRA submitted revised offer via email as a word document screen-shared during the 54th CoC meeting; Trufalir Buildwell cured conditional clauses by removing lease resumption contingencies with RIICO and increased plan value by Rs. 1.50 Crore; Appellant was a competing resolution applicant who failed to file an EoI or pay EMD[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 353 of 2024 objecting to plan approval; NCLT Jaipur Bench rejected objections and approved SRA's resolution plan in IA No. 06/JPR/2024 on 13.08.2024[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether the adoption of the Swiss Challenge method violated Regulation 39(1A), whether the non-furnishing of the SRA's resolution plan in advance to the suspended management who was also a competing resolution applicant vitiated the approval process, and whether the RP's assistance in scoring evaluation matrix parameters constituted a material irregularity[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While suspended management generally possesses a right to attend CoC meetings and access resolution plans under Vijay Kumar Jain, that right does not extend to a suspended director who has entered the fray as a competing resolution applicant, as sharing competitors' confidential resolution plans creates an untenable conflict of interest and breach of commercial sensitivity[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1A) does not restrict the CoC from conducting negotiations or employing a Swiss Challenge mechanism for value maximization[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unsuccessful resolution applicants cannot challenge the scoring of the evaluation matrix prepared and applied by the CoC, as the evaluation and interpretation of process documents lie within the non-justiciable business domain of the CoC[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC unanimously approved the resolution plan with 100% voting share in exercise of its commercial wisdom, no violation of Section 30(2) or Section 61(3) occurred, and the NCLT's approval was lawful[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1906 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Jaipur Bench dated 13.08.2024 is affirmed without costs[cite: 25].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by the suspended director of Maha Associated Hotels Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT Jaipur's approval of Trufalir Buildwell LLP's resolution plan[cite: 25]. The Appellant alleged procedural irregularities, including the use of the Swiss Challenge method, screen-sharing of an unsigned plan, and failure to supply him with a copy of the SRA's plan under the Vijay Kumar Jain principle[cite: 25]. NCLAT held that because the Appellant was himself a competing bidder in the fray, sharing competing resolution plans was barred by commercial confidentiality and conflict of interest[cite: 25]. The Swiss Challenge method and the CoC's unanimous 100% approval reflected a valid exercise of commercial wisdom[cite: 25].

case_title: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Jyoti Structures Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India & Consortium Lenders are Appellants/Secured Financial Creditors; Jyoti Structures Ltd. (EPC company) is Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1; Sharad Sanghi is SRA; Respondents 2 to 12 are Investors[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approved resolution plan for EPC company providing for debt restructuring, payout of Rs. 3,674 Crore over 15 years from business cash flows, and continuance/roll-over of Non-Fund Based (NFB) limits (Bank Guarantees/Letters of Credit) to the extent of existing lender exposure[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Lenders refused to disburse/roll over NFB limits across 14 new contracts valued at Rs. 1,162 Crore won by the revived company post-implementation, demanding re-assessment of the borrower's overall financial viability under RBI circulars[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 04.07.2017; Plan approved by NCLT on 27.03.2019; NFB Agreement executed 15.09.2021; Closing date achieved 09.11.2021; Tripartite Agreement completed 23.11.2022; repayment exclusion granted up to 23.11.2022; IA No. 4959 of 2023 filed by CD on 27.10.2023[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Schedule VI Clause F of Resolution Plan mandated roll-over of BG/LC limits based on project evaluation, stipulating that approval should not be unreasonably withheld; NFB Agreement Recital D specified execution was solely to implement the approved plan; company infused Rs. 170 Crore equity and had not defaulted on any issued BG/LC[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-1 on 20.08.2024 directed lenders to release NFB limits at the first instance based on project appraisal, while reserving lenders' right to monitor performance and review financial documents subsequently[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether lenders who approved a resolution plan stipulating the roll-over of Non-Fund Based (NFB) facilities can demand a re-assessment of the borrower company's overall financial viability under RBI circulars prior to releasing bank guarantees for individual viable projects[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved by the CoC and the Adjudicating Authority, its terms bind all stakeholders, including assentor lenders; lenders cannot evade their implementation obligations or renegotiate commercial terms under the pretext of re-evaluating borrower viability[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Viability and feasibility of the corporate debtor are evaluated by the CoC at the stage of plan approval under Section 30(4); post-approval, lenders cannot reopen borrower viability as a condition precedent to honoring commitments stipulated in the plan[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where contractual agreements executed pursuant to a plan specify that project appraisal governs the issuance of rolled-over credit facilities, terms must be construed harmoniously with the plan so as not to render its operational clauses otiose or paralyze the company's business[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's direction ordering the release of NFB limits upon project appraisal at the first instance while allowing ongoing performance monitoring strikes a balanced implementation approach and warrants no interference[cite: 26].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1962 & 1963 of 2024 are dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai Bench-1 dated 20.08.2024 is affirmed without costs[cite: 26].
summary: NCLAT dismissed appeals filed by the State Bank of India and consortium lenders challenging NCLT Mumbai's order directing them to operationalize Non-Fund Based (NFB) limits for Jyoti Structures Ltd.[cite: 26]. The lenders had withheld bank guarantees required for the company's EPC projects, claiming a right under RBI circulars to re-appraise the financial viability of the borrower itself[cite: 26]. NCLAT held that the feasibility and viability of the company were conclusively determined when the CoC approved the resolution plan[cite: 26]. Since the business required bank guarantees to generate revenue for debt servicing, lenders could not frustrate the plan by withholding limits where individual projects were sound[cite: 26].

case_title: Fintech Restructuring LLP vs. M/s Fairdeal Multifilament Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1823 of 2024, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1824 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1915 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Fintech Restructuring LLP is the erstwhile Resolution Professional (Appellant in 1823 & 1824/2024); Saraswat Co-operative Bank Ltd. is the Secured Financial Creditor holding 41.95% voting share (Appellant in 1915/2024); M/s Fairdeal Multifilament Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Debtor; Manoj Shanklecha is Suspended Director/PRA; Parth Poly Coat Yarn Pvt. Ltd. is PRA; Ravindra Kumar Goyal is new RP[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Corporate Debtor; CoC approved e-bidding process held on 29.03.2024 wherein Parth bid Rs. 9.36 Crore and Sanklecha bid Rs. 9.26 Crore[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In post-bidding negotiations during the 15th CoC meeting on 02.04.2024, PRAs were invited to submit revised plans by 03.04.2024; Sanklecha increased bid to Rs. 9.76 Crore while Parth remained at Rs. 9.36 Crore; upon e-voting, Parth's plan was approved by 84.52% vote share[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 21.02.2023; Fintech appointed RP on 09.10.2023; e-voting concluded 08.04.2024; IA (Plan)/18/2024 filed 24.04.2024; NCLT passed impugned order on 03.09.2024[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT found irregularities: multiple revisions under Regulation 39(1A), e-voting by 50 members when only 9 physically attended the 15th CoC meeting under Regulation 25(3), and evaluation matrix marking completed on 02.04.2024 prior to receiving revised plans on 03.04.2024[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-I dismissed the plan approval application, ordered fresh CIRP from Form G within 90 days, replaced the RP with Ravindra Kumar Goyal, and recorded adverse remarks against Fintech[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether the RP committed material irregularities by permitting multiple revisions of resolution plans, enabling electronic voting by absent CoC members under Regulation 25(5)(b), and whether adverse remarks against the RP should be expunged[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An RP acting in obedience to the collective commercial directions of the CoC to negotiate for value maximization does not commit a statutory infraction under Regulation 39(1A), as the CoC retains the inherent right to negotiate for higher value[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 25(5)(b) of the CIRP Regulations explicitly authorizes the RP to seek the votes of CoC members who did not vote or were not physically present at the meeting through an electronic voting system; confining voting rights solely to attendees under Regulation 25(3) ignores the mandate of sub-regulation (5)(b)[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under amended Regulation 39(3)(B), the resolution plan receiving the highest requisite votes is considered approved, rendering procedural evaluation matrix scoring non-fatal to the commercial outcome[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The adverse observations against the RP were unwarranted and are expunged; however, because the fresh 90-day CIRP initiated by the newly appointed RP had reached an advanced stage with six new bidders, the substantive direction to conclude the fresh CIRP is sustained to prevent value destruction[cite: 27].
operative_order: Appeals are disposed of; the impugned order dated 03.09.2024 is modified to the extent that adverse remarks in paragraph 27 regarding the conduct of erstwhile RP Fintech Restructuring LLP are expunged, while the ongoing fresh CIRP under the new RP is maintained without costs[cite: 27].
summary: NCLAT disposed of appeals filed by erstwhile RP Fintech Restructuring LLP and Saraswat Co-operative Bank challenging NCLT Ahmedabad's order which set aside the approval of Parth Poly Coat's resolution plan, removed the RP with adverse remarks, and restarted CIRP[cite: 27]. NCLT had cited irregularities in electronic voting by absent members and multiple plan revisions[cite: 27]. NCLAT held that Regulation 25(5)(b) expressly allows electronic voting by members not present in the meeting, and negotiations for plan improvement are lawful under CoC's commercial wisdom[cite: 27]. While expunging all adverse remarks against Fintech, NCLAT declined to cancel the ongoing fresh CIRP since it was near completion with multiple new bidders[cite: 27].

case_title: B. D. Agarwal vs. Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: B.D. Agarwal is the Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor/Appellant; Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (SASF) is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1; Interim Resolution Professional is Respondent No. 2[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debt recovery and insolvency proceedings initiated under Section 7 of the IBC against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appeal filed with an alleged delay of 12 days (if Section 14 exclusion applied) or 163 days (actual delay)[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order pronounced in open court on 03.05.2024 and uploaded on 06.05.2024; earlier appeal Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1086 of 2024 filed by CD on 22.05.2024 and dismissed on merits as not maintainable on 16.10.2024; present appeal e-filed by the Suspended Director on 12.11.2024[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant sought benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act to exclude 148 days (22.05.2024 to 16.10.2024) spent prosecuting the earlier appeal filed by the company through himself[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 8330 of 2024 seeking condonation of delay in filing the fresh appeal; Respondent opposed on the ground that Section 14 conditions were not met and the appeal was filed beyond the condonable period[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether a suspended director can claim exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act for the period during which an earlier appeal filed by the corporate debtor against the same order was prosecuted and dismissed on merits, and whether limitation runs from the date of open-court pronouncement or the date the order is uploaded[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 14 of the Limitation Act applies exclusively to exclude time spent prosecuting a prior proceeding in good faith before a forum that failed to decide the matter due to defect of jurisdiction or cause of a like nature; it does not apply where the prior proceeding was heard by a court of competent jurisdiction and dismissed on merits or maintainability[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 30-day statutory limitation period under Section 61(2) of the IBC begins from the date of pronouncement of the order in open court, not from the date the order is uploaded on the portal[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the rule in Consolidated Engineering Enterprises, five conditions must strictly co-exist to attract Section 14, none of which are satisfied when a prior appeal in the same appellate court was dismissed on its merits[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Even assuming arguendo that 148 days were excluded, the appeal was e-filed on the 46th day following pronouncement, placing it outside the maximum 15-day condonation window permissible under the proviso to Section 61(2)[cite: 28].
operative_order: IA No. 8330 of 2024 for condonation of delay is rejected; Memo of Appeal is rejected; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2220 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 28].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by B.D. Agarwal, suspended director of the Corporate Debtor, seeking to challenge an order dated 03.05.2024 with an inordinate delay of 163 days[cite: 28]. The Appellant sought exclusion of 148 days under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, arguing that an earlier appeal filed by the Corporate Debtor was pending before NCLAT until 16.10.2024[cite: 28]. Rejecting the plea, NCLAT held that Section 14 applies only when a proceeding fails due to a defect of jurisdiction, which was not the case here[cite: 28]. Moreover, limitation commences from the date of open-court pronouncement, and the appeal was filed well past the outer 45-day limit allowed under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 28].

case_title: Shikshak Sahakari Bank Ltd. vs. Mr. Jagdish Kumar Parulkar Liquidator
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shikshak Sahakari Bank Ltd. is the Secured Financial Creditor/Appellant; Mr. Jagdish Kumar Parulkar is the Liquidator of Narendra Solvex Private Limited (Respondent)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by the Appellant bank to the Corporate Debtor, secured by a mortgage over 1.10 hectares of land at Amravati, Maharashtra[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim submitted in Form D was Rs. 5,95,45,557; Appellant opted not to relinquish security interest and set reserve price at Rs. 2,24,15,000 under Section 52(1)(b) to realize the asset via SARFAESI; Liquidator demanded fee of Rs. 14,48,965 and CIRP/liquidation costs totaling Rs. 15,68,326, which later accrued to Rs. 25,47,229[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation ordered on 27.01.2024 (rectified 28.03.2023); public announcement on 06.04.2023; Appellant intimated intent to realize security interest on 11.05.2023; 90-day compliance period under Regulation 21A expired without payment; Liquidator filed IA No. 785/2024 on 19.01.2024[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Exchange of emails where Appellant agreed to pay out-of-pocket costs but refused to pay the Liquidator's fee, citing that the Liquidator did not directly realize or distribute the asset under Regulation 4(2)(b)[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 785/MB/2024 under Section 60(5) seeking payment of fees; NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV allowed the application on 30.08.2024 and directed the bank to pay the Liquidator's fee under Regulation 4(1A)[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether a secured creditor that chooses not to relinquish its security interest under Section 52 and realizes the secured asset independently under the SARFAESI Act is statutorily obligated under Regulation 21A(2)(a) to pay its proportionate share of liquidation costs, including the liquidator's fee, even if the liquidator did not directly sell or distribute the asset[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A secured creditor who elects to realize its security interest outside the liquidation estate under Section 52 is mandatorily obligated under Regulation 21A(2) of the Liquidation Process Regulations to pay to the liquidator its proportionate share of liquidation costs and the liquidator's fee within 90 days from the liquidation commencement date[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The requirement to contribute towards the liquidator's fee under Regulation 21A(2)(a) read with Section 53(1)(a) operates independently of whether the liquidator personally sold or distributed the secured asset under the sliding scale in Regulation 4(2)(b); the liquidator remains responsible for verifying claims and coordinating the realization process[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a secured creditor defaults in remitting the estimated liquidation costs within the mandatory 90-day window despite repeated demands, the Adjudicating Authority possesses full jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to compel payment[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant's refusal to pay the liquidator's fee was contrary to Regulation 21A, and the NCLT's order enforcing payment was legally sound and valid[cite: 29].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2023 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dated 30.08.2024 directing payment of the Liquidator's fee within three weeks is affirmed without costs[cite: 29].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Shikshak Sahakari Bank Ltd. challenging NCLT Mumbai's order directing it to pay Rs. 25.47 Lakh towards the Liquidator's fee for Corporate Debtor Narendra Solvex Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 29]. The bank, a secured creditor, opted not to relinquish its mortgage and realized the asset independently under the SARFAESI Act, arguing that the Liquidator was disentitled to fees under Regulation 4(2)(b) because he neither sold nor distributed the asset[cite: 29]. Relying on SBI v. Navjit Singh and SIDBI v. Vijender Sharma, NCLAT held that Regulation 21A(2) mandatorily obligates non-relinquishing secured creditors to pay their share of liquidation costs and liquidator's fees within 90 days, irrespective of direct asset realization[cite: 29].

case_title: Sunil Kumar Sharma Suspended Board of Director of Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. & Anr. vs. ICICI Bank Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 197 of 2024 & I.A. No. 6806 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) No. 199 of 2024 & I.A. No. 6807 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sunil Kumar Sharma, Suspended Board Member of Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Demerged Company/Appellant); ICICI Bank Ltd. (Lead Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1); Jaypee Infrastructure Development Limited (JIDL/Transferee SPV). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debt realignment scheme involving the demerger and hiving-off of JAL's Bucket-2B residual debt aggregating to Rs. 11,689 Crores along with 950.35 acres of Special Development Zone (SDZ) land to SPV JIDL under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: JAL was classified under SMA-II on 03.10.2014 and declared NPA by lenders on 31.03.2015 with multi-thousand crore aggregate debt default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Joint Lenders Meeting approved debt realignment on 22.06.2017; First Motion CA No. 174 of 2017 filed on 20.11.2017 and accepted on 08.01.2018; Second Motion CP (CAA) No. 19/ALD/2018 filed on 23.01.2018; RBI directed ICICI Bank to initiate CIRP on 14.08.2017/14.08.2018; ICICI Bank filed Section 7 IBC petition on 06.09.2018/07.09.2018; YEIDA cancelled SEZ/SDZ land allotment on 12.02.2020; Allahabad High Court granted interim status quo in WP No. 6049/2020 on 25.02.2020 subject to deposit of Rs. 100 Crores. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter dated 19.01.2018 by ICICI Bank granting conditional approval subject to Supreme Court leave; orders of Supreme Court in Chitra Sharma v. UOI refusing to direct NCLT to sanction scheme and granting RBI leave to initiate CIRP; YEIDA lease cancellation order dated 12.02.2020 knocking out underlying assets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench on 03.06.2024 admitted Section 7 petition in CP (IB) No. 330/ALD/2018, rejected IA No. 18 of 2024 seeking deferment of pronouncement, and rejected Second Motion Petition CP (CAA) No. 19/ALD/2018 on grounds that underlying assets were disputed/cancelled by YEIDA and Section 7 CIRP stood admitted against JAL.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in rejecting the Second Motion Petition for sanction of a Scheme of Arrangement under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 on the grounds of subsequent material adverse changes—specifically the cancellation of the underlying land parcel by YEIDA and the simultaneous admission of a Section 7 IBC application against the Corporate Debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Company Court/Tribunal scrutinising a scheme of compromise or arrangement is not a mere rubber stamp; it possesses the jurisdiction and duty to take cognizance of subsequent events and material adverse changes impacting the feasibility, viability, and public interest of the scheme prior to sanction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 230-232 require the Tribunal to ensure that the proposed arrangement is fair, viable, and not contrary to public interest or statutory discipline under the IBC; pendency or propounding of a Section 230 scheme cannot halt or override insolvency resolution under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the core foundational asset forming the bedrock of the demerger and debt hive-off is cancelled by a statutory authority and remains sub-judice under writ proceedings, the viability of the scheme is fatally prejudiced. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because JAL was admitted into CIRP under Section 7 and the primary security/land parcel stood cancelled, the NCLT committed no error in rejecting the Second Motion scheme petition and refusing deferment.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) No. 197 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 199 of 2024 are dismissed. All pending interlocutory applications are disposed of.
summary: Sunil Kumar Sharma, suspended director of Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. (JAL), appealed NCLT Allahabad orders rejecting a Second Motion petition under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 for hiving off Rs. 11,689 Crore debt into an SPV, and refusing deferment of pronouncement. ICICI Bank and SBI opposed, citing JAL's CIRP admission and YEIDA's cancellation of the underlying 950.35-acre land allotment. NCLAT held that the Tribunal is not a rubber stamp and must evaluate subsequent adverse material changes affecting scheme viability and public interest. Finding the underlying asset disputed and CIRP initiated, NCLAT affirmed the rejection and dismissed both appeals.

case_title: NCC Ltd. vs. Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2020 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 430 of 2020, Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 432 of 2020 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 710 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: NCC Ltd., Operational Creditor (Appellant); M/s Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1); Committee of Creditors (Respondent No. 2); Telangana State Tourism Corporation Ltd./YATCL and Shilparamam Arts, Crafts & Cultural Society (Land Lessors/Special Operational Creditors/Respondents No. 3 & 4); BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co. II (NQ) Pte. Ltd., Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/services by Operational Creditors for construction/facade/interiors of hotel properties; project lands leased under PPP/BOT concessions by YATCL and Society to Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant NCC Ltd. filed Form B claim of Rs. 51,75,95,253/-; total OC admitted claims stood at Rs. 50.07 Crores; Financial Creditor admitted claims totaled Rs. 949.83 Crores; Corporate Debtor's liquidation value was Nil. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 in CP (IB) No. 248/7/HDB/2017; Form B claims submitted in March 2018; CoC approved SRA Resolution Plan on 21.12.2018 with 68.26% voting share; NCLT approved plan on 07.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Plan earmarking upfront payment of Rs. 41.99 Crores ('Society Claim') to YATCL/Society to maintain going-concern status under BOT/lease agreements, while proposing Nil payout to other OCs given Nil liquidation value. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved the Resolution Plan via order dated 07.02.2020 in IA No. 32 of 2019 and rejected OCs' objection applications (IA No. 950 of 2019) on grounds of commercial wisdom and compliance with Section 30(2)(b).
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan can lawfully differentiate within the category of Operational Creditors by according 100% payment to 'Special Operational Creditors' (land lessors essential for going-concern operations) while providing Nil payment to other Operational Creditors when the liquidation value is Nil, and whether MSMED Act provisions override IBC distribution priorities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Differential treatment inter se operational creditors is legally permissible under the commercial wisdom of the CoC provided there exists an intelligible differentia linked to the survival and going-concern viability of the corporate debtor, and every operational creditor receives at least its liquidation entitlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) read with Explanation 1 mandates 'fair and equitable' distribution rather than mathematical parity; Operational Creditors are statutorily entitled only to the minimum liquidation value under Section 53. Section 238 of the IBC overrides the provisions of the MSMED Act, 2006. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Rational nexus to business continuity—securing critical leased premises under BOT agreements without which the enterprise cannot operate justifies preferential full allocation funded via reduction of Financial Creditors' realizations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because liquidation value for Operational Creditors was Nil, no statutory floor was breached, and commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving the plan cannot be interfered with under equity.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2020 and connected appeals (Nos. 430, 432, and 710 of 2020) are dismissed without costs. Suggestion made to IBBI to examine calibrated waterfall options for Operational Creditors.
summary: Operational Creditor NCC Ltd. challenged the NCLT Hyderabad order approving BREP Asia's resolution plan for Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd., contending that creating a sub-category of 'Special Operational Creditors' (land lessors YATCL and Society) entitled to full payments while allocating 'Nil' to other operational creditors was illegal and discriminatory. NCLAT held that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is non-justiciable and permits differential distribution among creditors within a class based on intelligible business rationale to maintain going-concern viability. Since the liquidation value for operational creditors was Nil, the plan complied with Section 30(2)(b), and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Infinity Interiors Private Limited vs. Subodh Kumar Agrawal & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 432 of 2020 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2020, Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 430 of 2020 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 710 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Infinity Interiors Private Limited, Operational Creditor/Small Enterprise under MSMED Act (Appellant); Subodh Kumar Agrawal, Former RP (Respondent No. 1); M/s Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2); BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co. II (NQ) Pte. Ltd., SRA (Respondent No. 3); Committee of Creditors (Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of interior decoration works and materials for hotel properties of the Corporate Debtor (Trident and Oberoi Hotel towers). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted initial Form B claim of Rs. 4,87,39,050/- and additional claim of Rs. 1,85,00,000/-; RP admitted claim of Rs. 4,40,24,552/-; Corporate Debtor's liquidation value was Nil. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in CP (IB) No. 248/7/HDB/2017; additional claim filed 20.07.2018; CoC approved SRA Resolution Plan on 21.12.2018 with 68.26% voting share; NCLT approved plan on 07.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan allocated 100% dues (Rs. 41.99 Crores) to 'Special Operational Creditors' (land lessors YATCL and Society) to preserve leasehold rights, while allocating Nil to other operational creditors including registered MSMEs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 07.02.2020 approved the Resolution Plan in IA No. 32 of 2019 and dismissed Appellant's objection application IA No. 961 of 2019.
legal_issues: Whether an Operational Creditor registered as an MSME is entitled to mandatory payment under a Resolution Plan ahead of or at par with other operational creditors, and whether classification of land lessors as 'Special Operational Creditors' receiving full payment violates Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the CoC in distributing funds under a resolution plan is non-justiciable; MSME status under the MSMED Act confers no priority or preferential claim over the waterfall mechanism of the IBC in CIRP proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC has overriding effect over the MSMED Act, 2006. Sections 54A and 240A protect MSMEs strictly in their capacity as corporate debtors, not as operational creditors. Explanation 1 to Section 30(2)(b) ensures equity within liquidation thresholds, not absolute mathematical parity. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Priority granted to project land lessors is sustained by an intelligible differentia directly linked to enterprise survival, where other operational creditors suffer Nil payout due to Nil liquidation value. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan satisfied the mandate of Section 30(2)(b) since the liquidation value payable to the Appellant was Nil, making the approval unassailable.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 432 of 2020 is dismissed alongside companion appeals without costs. All interim applications are closed.
summary: Infinity Interiors Pvt. Ltd., an MSME operational creditor with an admitted claim of Rs. 4.40 Crores, appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's approval of the resolution plan for Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. It argued that the plan unlawfully created a sub-class of 'Special Operational Creditors' (land lessors) who received 100% payout while MSME vendors received Nil. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT held that the MSMED Act is overridden by Section 238 of the IBC and offers no priority to MSME creditors. CoC's commercial wisdom in treating indispensable land lessors differently to preserve going-concern status was upheld, as the Appellant's liquidation value was Nil.

case_title: Ahuja Furnishers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Subodh Kumar Agrawal & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 710 of 2020 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2020, Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 430 of 2020 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 432 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ahuja Furnishers Pvt. Ltd., Operational Creditor/Registered Small Enterprise under MSMED Act (Appellant); Subodh Kumar Agrawal, Former RP (Respondent No. 1); Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2); BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co. II (NQ) Pte. Ltd., SRA (Respondent No. 3); IBBI (Respondent No. 4); Committee of Creditors (Respondent No. 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of furniture to Corporate Debtor for hotel operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted Form B claim for Rs. 29,83,025.69/-; RP admitted Rs. 29,08,729/- on 24.08.2018; Corporate Debtor's liquidation value was Nil. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 in CP (IB) No. 248/7/HDB/2017; Form B claim submitted on 08.03.2018; CoC approval of Resolution Plan on 21.12.2018; NCLT approval order on 07.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Plan providing 100% payment to Special Operational Creditors (YATCL/Society) to secure land leases, while allocating Nil to trade suppliers and furniture vendors; subsequent arbitral award dated 25.02.2020 awarding Corporate Debtor Rs. 25.95 Crores against YATCL. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved the Resolution Plan via order dated 07.02.2020 in CA No. 32 of 2019 and rejected operational creditors' objections.
legal_issues: Whether the approval of a Resolution Plan offering Nil payment to trade operational creditors while fully paying government land lessors violates the IBC or MSMED Act, and whether a post-CIRP arbitral award in favour of the Corporate Debtor must be redistributed to operational creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the CoC cannot be subjected to equity-based judicial review to reallocate funds, and post-resolution arbitral assets or windfalls belong exclusively to the revived corporate debtor as structured under the plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) requires only that operational creditors receive not less than their liquidation value under Section 53. MSMED Act protections cannot alter the priority waterfall in view of Section 238 IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Differentiation between trade vendors and lessor-authorities is founded on intelligible differentia crucial to keeping the corporate debtor a going concern. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan strictly fulfilled all legal conditions under Section 30(2); since liquidation entitlement was Nil, the plan could not be faulted for providing Nil payout to the Appellant.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 710 of 2020 is dismissed alongside companion appeals without costs. All pending IAs are closed.
summary: Ahuja Furnishers Pvt. Ltd., an MSME supplier with an admitted operational debt of Rs. 29.08 Lakhs, challenged the NCLT Hyderabad order approving the resolution plan for Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd., alleging illegal preference to land lessors (YATCL/Society) and seeking redistribution of post-CIRP arbitral award receivables. NCLAT held that neither the Tribunal nor Appellate Tribunal possesses equity jurisdiction to interfere with the CoC's commercial wisdom. Because the liquidation value for operational creditors was Nil, the plan complied with Section 30(2)(b). The MSMED Act is overridden by Section 238, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Consolidated Engineering Company vs. Subodh Kumar Agrawal & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 430 of 2020 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2020, Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 432 of 2020 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 710 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Consolidated Engineering Company, Operational Creditor/Registered MSME Partner Firm (Appellant); Subodh Kumar Agrawal, Former RP (Respondent No. 1); Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2); BREP Asia II Indian Holding Co. II (NQ) Pte. Ltd., SRA (Respondent No. 3); Committee of Creditors (Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Designing, fabrication, and installation of building facades and allied works for Trident and Oberoi Hotel towers of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim submitted for Rs. 20,02,07,912/-; RP admitted Rs. 10,52,37,168/-, further admitted Rs. 21,54,575/- post-reconciliation, and Rs. 5,18,56,248/- as contingent liability; Corporate Debtor's liquidation value was Nil. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 in CP (IB) No. 248/7/HDB/2017; Form B submitted on 14.03.2018; IA No. 264 of 2018 filed for unadmitted claim of Rs. 3.84 Crores; SRA plan approved by CoC on 21.12.2018 with 68.26% votes; IA No. 960 of 2019 filed on 31.10.2019; NCLT approved plan on 07.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan providing 100% payment to land lessors (YATCL and Society) under condition precedent of obtaining lease continuation consents, while providing Nil payment to general OCs and leaving unadmitted claim IA undecided. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved the Resolution Plan via order dated 07.02.2020 in IA No. 32 of 2019 and disposed of IA No. 960 of 2019 without modifying the plan.
legal_issues: Whether the inclusion of condition precedents (procuring lessor consents) invalidates a Resolution Plan, and whether the CoC's allocation of Nil payout to an operational creditor whose liquidation value is Nil can be interfered with under Section 61(3) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Conditions precedent in a resolution plan that are essential and critical for the implementation of the plan and revival of business operations are legally valid and do not render the plan conditional or invalid. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) requires payment to operational creditors of not less than the liquidation value under Section 53; when that value is Nil, zero allocation does not violate the statute. Section 238 overrides MSMED Act protections. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Necessity test—conditions requiring consent of statutory lessors for change of control are indispensable when BOT agreements are co-terminus with underlying leases. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC in approving the plan and accepting haircuts on financial debt to pay lessors is non-justiciable, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 430 of 2020 is dismissed alongside companion appeals without costs. All pending IAs are disposed of.
summary: Consolidated Engineering Company, an MSME operational creditor with over Rs. 10.73 Crores in admitted facade work claims, appealed against the approval of the resolution plan for Golden Jubilee Hotels Pvt. Ltd. It challenged the plan's condition precedents and discriminatory full settlement of 'Special Operational Creditors' (land lessors) versus 'Nil' payment to vendors. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that condition precedents vital to business continuity are valid and that commercial wisdom of the CoC is supreme. As liquidation value was Nil, zero payment satisfied Section 30(2)(b), and MSMED protections yielded to Section 238 of the IBC.

case_title: Mr. Puneet P. Bhatia vs. Asrec (India) Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Puneet P. Bhatia, Suspended Director of Barracks Retail India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Appellant); ASREC (India) Limited (Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1); Mr. Ganesh Venkata Siva Rama Krishna Remani (IRP/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan of Rs. 5 crores and cash credit limit of Rs. 25 lakhs sanctioned on 21.03.2017 by Bharat Co-operative Bank (Mumbai) Limited, subsequently reviewed, renewed, and revised via sanction letter dated 17.03.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed for Rs. 21,37,94,606/- as on 30.09.2022, with default date subsequently amended to 02.08.2019 (90 days prior to NPA date of 01.11.2019). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan accounts declared NPA as on 01.11.2019; RBI inspection conducted in Sept-Oct 2020; Recall notice issued by bank on 07.12.2020; SARFAESI notice issued on 19.03.2021; Assignment agreement executed on 25.03.2021 in favor of ASREC; Section 7 petition filed on 18.02.2023; Adjudicating Authority allowed amendment of default date on 13.10.2023 and 24.11.2023; CIRP admitted on 09.01.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letters, restructuring documents, RBI risk assessment report classifying account as NPA on 01.11.2019, and NESL database records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I admitted the Section 7 application on 09.01.2024, prompting the suspended director to file the present appeal challenging the admission and the amendment of the default date.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in allowing the amendment of the date of default to pre-date the Section 10A moratorium period, and whether the CIRP petition was maintainable under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Pleadings and particulars regarding the date of default in a Section 7 petition under the IBC can be amended before the final order is passed, provided the amendment is processed fairly and does not abuse the legal process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A shields defaults occurring exclusively during the COVID-19 pandemic window; where the original default occurred and was fixed prior to the protected period (e.g., 02.08.2019), Section 10A protection is inapplicable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Regulatory inspection findings by the RBI establishing non-compliance with restructuring conditions render purported restructuring ineffective, restoring the original NPA and default timeline. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the amended default date of 02.08.2019 predates the Section 10A exemption window and the debt and default are fully established, the NCLT's admission order is legally sound.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and pending interlocutory applications are disposed of accordingly, with no order as to costs.
summary: Mr. Puneet P. Bhatia, suspended director of Barracks Retail India Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 application filed by ASREC (India) Ltd. The appellant contended that the default fell within the Section 10A COVID-19 moratorium period and that the default date was improperly altered. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority is empowered to allow amendments to the date of default prior to final adjudication. Since the regulatory audit established the true default date as 02.08.2019 (predating Section 10A), the protections under Section 10A did not apply, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Sanjeeb Kumar Jha vs. Yogesh Gupta & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 295 of 2024 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 296 of 2024 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 298 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sanjeeb Kumar Jha, Rohit Kumar, Arun Kumar Bag (Appellants/Alleged Financial Creditors); Yogesh Gupta (IRP/Respondent No. 1); Committee of Creditors (Respondent No. 2); J.N. Hotels Private Limited (Operational Creditor/Respondent No. 2 impleaded). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged cash loans of Rs. 2 Lakhs each advanced by Sanjeeb Kumar Jha and Rohit Kumar under loan agreements dated 30.09.2022/28.09.2022, and conversion of operational dues of Rs. 3,84,540/- into a financial loan by Arun Kumar Bag under agreement dated 22.08.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim amounts of Rs. 2 Lakhs, Rs. 2 Lakhs, and Rs. 3,84,540/- filed in Form C during CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Shraddha Health & Fitness Private Limited; public announcement made on 10.11.2022; claims filed and provisionally admitted; first CoC meeting scheduled for 27.11.2022; NCLT Kolkata Bench passed impugned order on 19.01.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form C claim filings, cash loan agreements executed shortly after Section 9 order was reserved on 02.08.2022, income tax returns showing low income, and lack of bank transfer records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench vide order dated 19.01.2024 in IA Nos. 1645, 1646, 1647 of 2022 directed the IRP to re-examine the constitution of the CoC and properly verify financial credentials, prompting the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether the IRP/Resolution Professional is empowered to re-verify and re-examine the financial credentials and admissibility of claims of alleged financial creditors who claim debt via cash transactions executed close to the initiation of CIRP, and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in directing re-constitution of the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim resolution professional or resolution professional has the duty and authority to properly verify claims and examine financial credentials to ensure the genuine constitution of the Committee of Creditors free from sham or collusive transactions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisional admission of claims for collation does not bar subsequent detailed verification and scrutiny by the RP before or during CoC constitution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Cash loan agreements executed immediately after the judgment reservation date in a Section 2/Section 9 proceeding, unsupported by adequate bank trails or justifiable financial capacity, warrant strict re-examination. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no illegality in directing the RP to re-examine the CoC constitution and verify the claims in accordance with law.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 295 of 2024 and connected appeals are dismissed. The original interlocutory applications are remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: Appellants claiming to be financial creditors based on recent cash loan agreements and converted operational debt appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dated 19.01.2024 directing the IRP to re-examine the constitution of the CoC and verify financial credentials[cite: 7]. NCLAT held that the IRP is fully empowered to rigorously verify claims to prevent collusive entries into the CoC, especially when agreements are executed right after insolvency proceedings are reserved[cite: 7]. Finding no infirmity, NCLAT dismissed the appeals and remanded the matter to the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 7].

case_title: Abhijit Realtors & Infraventures Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Rohit Ramesh Mehra (RP of Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd.) & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 923 of 2024 with 924 of 2024, 925 of 2024, 980 of 2024 & 981 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Abhijit Realtors & Infraventures Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. and Creative Channel Advertising & Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicants/Appellants); Rohit Ramesh Mehra, RP of Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Committee of Creditors (Respondent No. 2); Sapphire Media Ltd., Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd., involving invitation of Expression of Interest (EoI), RFRP, a challenge bidding process, and subsequent negotiations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. initiated CIRP under Section 7 on 24.02.2023; SRA's final approved plan value stood at INR 261 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-G issued on 14.04.2023; challenge process conducted on 27.10.2023; CoC approved Sapphire Media's plan with 88.97% vote share on 16.11.2023; NCLT Mumbai approved the plan and dismissed objectors' IAs on 06.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Challenge process documents, bidding rounds where Sapphire Media bid INR 251 Crores and consortium bid INR 242 Crores (exited for non-compliance with Rs. 10 Crore increment rules), followed by CoC negotiations resulting in SRA's final bid of INR 261 Crores and CA certificates verifying SRA's net worth and turnover including promoter Sahil Mangla. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench on 06.05.2024 dismissed unsuccessful RAs' IAs challenging the challenge process and SRA eligibility, and approved the resolution plan in IA No. 5391 of 2023.
legal_issues: Whether the challenge bidding process and subsequent CoC negotiations violated CIRP regulations and process notes, and whether the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) was eligible under the EOI criteria by including the promoter's net worth and turnover.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The CoC retains full authority to conduct post-challenge process negotiations for value maximization, and the author of tender/EOI documents is the best judge of their interpretation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1A) of CIRP Regulations does not fetter the CoC's power to negotiate further after a challenge mechanism. The term 'entity' in group definitions can encompass individual promoters holding controlling shares. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict adherence to bidding increment rules justifies the elimination of bidders who fail to comply, and commercial wisdom of the CoC in evaluating financial viability and eligibility must not be disturbed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The challenge and negotiation processes were legally sound, the SRA was fully eligible, and the CoC's commercial approval of the plan is unassailable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 923 of 2024 and connected appeals (924, 925, 980, 981 of 2024) are dismissed. Additional document applications (IA 4691 and 4692) are rejected.
summary: Unsuccessful resolution applicants Abhijit Realtors and Creative Channel Advertising appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders dated 06.05.2024 approving Sapphire Media's resolution plan for Reliance Broadcast Network Ltd. and dismissing their challenges to the bidding process and SRA eligibility[cite: 8]. NCLAT held that the challenge process and subsequent CoC negotiations were fully valid under RFRP and CIRP regulations, and that the SRA's inclusion of the promoter's net worth and turnover complied with the EOI criteria[cite: 8]. Upholding the CoC's commercial wisdom, NCLAT dismissed all appeals[cite: 8].

case_title: Dinesh Kumar vs. Narendra Kumar Sharma & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1422 of 2024 with 1434 of 2024 & 1573 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dinesh Kumar, Aman Sehgal, Ravi Kumar, Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtors (Appellants); Narendra Kumar Sharma & Ors., Financial Creditors in a class/Allottees (Respondents); Mist Direct Sales Pvt. Ltd., Anand Infoedge Pvt. Ltd., Mist Avenue Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtors/Developers/Land Owners). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of residential/commercial units in the real estate project 'Festival City' at Sector 143, Noida, under Builder-Buyer Agreements starting from 2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Project stalled for over a decade with no possession delivered; joint Section 7 petition filed by 115 allottees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Joint Section 7 application filed in October 2021; NCLT admitted maintainability on 21.10.2022; NCLAT dismissed appeals on 17.11.2023; Supreme Court dismissed appeals on 11.12.2023 directing disposal within two months; NCLT admitted CIRP on 19.07.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder-buyer agreements, non-delivery of possession after 12 years, rejected settlement proposals, and unsubstantiated allegations of forged affidavits via police FIRs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Court VI, New Delhi on 19.07.2024 dismissed developers' IAs (IA 293 and 2497) seeking settlement/dismissal and admitted the joint Section 7 application, leading to the suspended directors' appeals.
legal_issues: Whether a joint Section 7 application filed by allottees against multiple interconnected corporate debtors (land owner and developers) is maintainable, and whether unsubstantiated allegations of forged affidavits can defeat an admitted debt and default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a default in delivering real estate units and refunding or fulfilling contractual terms is established, the NCLT is bound to admit a Section 7 application, and pending or subsequent criminal FIRs or status reports cannot override clear default metrics. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interconnected corporate entities forming part of a single real estate project can be jointly proceeded against under Section 7 when their obligations are interwoven. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unsubstantiated claims of forged affidavits, previously raised and rejected in dedicated interlocutory proceedings and appeals up to the Supreme Court, cannot be re-agitated to stall insolvency admission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt and default were fully established, threshold requirements were met, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted the Section 7 application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1422 of 2024 and connected appeals (1434 and 1573 of 2024) are dismissed. Interim deposits ordered to be refunded to the appellant.
summary: Suspended directors of three real estate companies (Mist Direct Sales, Anand Infoedge, and Mist Avenue) appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated 19.07.2024 admitting a joint Section 7 application filed by homebuyers of the 'Festival City' project[cite: 9]. NCLAT held that issues of maintainability and threshold had already been conclusively settled up to the Supreme Court, and subsequent criminal status reports alleging forged affidavits could not alter the proven debt and default[cite: 9]. Finding the corporate debtors in persistent default over a decade, NCLAT dismissed the appeals[cite: 9].

case_title: Renuka Devi Rangaswamy vs. State Bank of India
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 442 of 2024 & IA No. 1212 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Renuka Devi Rangaswamy, Resolution Professional for Regen Powertech Private Limited and Regen Infrastructure and Services Private Limited (Appellant); State Bank of India (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes of Regen Powertech Private Limited and Regen Infrastructure and Services Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from reference made to IBBI by the Adjudicating Authority against the RP). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order rendered by NCLT Chennai on 14.10.2023/14.10.2024 in IA (IBC)/2329/2023 in CP (IBA)/1099/CHE/2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Observations and directions in paragraph 4.15 of the Adjudicating Authority's order referring the matter to the IBBI against the RP for alleged non-compliance of NCLAT and NCLT orders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench passed an order on 14.10.2024 referring the RP's conduct to the IBBI, prompting the RP to file the present appeal under Section 61 of the IBC.
