legal_issues: Whether a direction by the Adjudicating Authority referring the conduct of a Resolution Professional to the IBBI for disciplinary action is appealable under Section 61 of the IBC, and whether such reference constitutes a conclusive determination of guilt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is maintainable only against orders falling within the scope of Part II of the Code, and a procedural reference of a professional's conduct to the IBBI for inquiry does not amount to a conclusive finding of guilt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 196, 207, and 208 of the IBC empower the IBBI to regulate resolution professionals and conduct disciplinary inquiries, meaning a reference by the Adjudicating Authority is a preliminary recommendation rather than a binding verdict. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Observations reflecting the application of judicial mind to justify a reference to a regulatory body do not prejudice or pre-determine the outcome of an independent disciplinary inquiry. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the order referring the matter to the IBBI is not an appealable order under Section 61 of the IBC and does not constitute a conclusive judgment against the RP, the appeal is not maintainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 442 of 2024 is dismissed as not maintainable.
summary: Renuka Devi Rangaswamy, Resolution Professional, appealed against paragraph 4.15 of an NCLT Chennai order dated 14.10.2024 which referred her conduct to the IBBI for disciplinary action due to alleged non-compliance with earlier tribunal orders[cite: 18]. NCLAT Chennai held that the appeal is not maintainable under Section 61 of the IBC since a reference to the IBBI is a preliminary administrative step rather than a conclusive finding of guilt, leaving the professional's defense open before the regulatory body[cite: 18]. The appeal was accordingly dismissed[cite: 18].

case_title: Omkara Assets Reconstruction Private Limited vs. Mr. Yadavalli Sai Karunakar & Anr.
appeal_number: IA No. 1012 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 368 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Secured Financial Creditor); Mr. Yadavalli Sai Karunakar, Erstwhile Liquidator of B.S. Limited (Respondent No. 1); Bank of India (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation of B.S. Limited; assignment of debts and secured assets by IFCI to the Appellant on 14.02.2023. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Estimated surplus amount of Rs. 96.28 Crores directed to be tendered to the liquidation account, along with preservation costs of Rs. 90,70,048/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad passed the impugned order on 29.07.2024; appeal e-filed on 14.09.2024 with a reported delay of 16 days; exemption application filed for certified copy; certified copy application filed on 08.10.2024/09.10.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's IA No. 1378 of 2024 seeking distribution of surplus realization from unsold secured assets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad allowed Liquidator's IA on 29.07.2024 directing first charge holders to deposit surplus funds; Appellant filed appeal on 14.09.2024 along with a delay condonation application (IA 1012 of 2024).
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed beyond the 30-day limitation period under Section 61(2) of the IBC, and exceeding the total 45-day outer limit including the proviso, can be entertained when the appellant claims knowledge from a later date and fails to apply for a certified copy within limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is strict, and a party cannot extend limitation unilaterally by claiming a later date of knowledge while failing to apply for a certified copy within the statutory period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) prescribes a 30-day limitation period extendable by a maximum of 15 days under the proviso, beyond which the appellate tribunal lacks jurisdiction to condone delay. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of evidence showing uploading delays, knowledge is computed from the date of the order, and failure to apply for a certified copy within limitation disentitles the appellant to exclusion under Section 12 of the Limitation Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appeal was filed beyond the absolute outer limit of 45 days from the date of the impugned order, the delay condonation application cannot be allowed.
operative_order: IA No. 1012 of 2024 (condone delay application) is rejected, and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 368 of 2024 stands dismissed as time-barred.
summary: Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. filed an appeal along with a delay condonation application (IA 1012 of 2024) against an NCLT Hyderabad order dated 29.07.2024 directing first charge holders to deposit surplus liquidation funds[cite: 19]. NCLAT Chennai held that the appeal was filed beyond the absolute outer limit of 45 days prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC, and the appellant could not claim extended limitation based on a delayed application for a certified copy[cite: 19]. The delay condonation application was rejected and the appeal dismissed as time-barred[cite: 19].

case_title: Straw Commodities LLP vs. Anram Agro Trading Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Straw Commodities LLP (Operational Creditor/Appellant); Anram Agro Trading Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Three sale contracts dated 21.04.2021, 19.11.2021, and 14.02.2022 for the supply of Tanzania and Ethiopian origin Soya Bean and Soya Bean Meal, involving advance payments made by the appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding balance claim of Rs. 1,01,89,178.77/- demanded under Section 8 notice dated 18.09.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice issued on 18.09.2023; Section 9 application filed and subsequently dismissed by NCLT Mumbai on 25.10.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: WhatsApp chats and email communications between parties showing that commodity delivery failed because market prices plummeted and the appellant's buyer backed out, leading to discussions on sharing losses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the Section 9 application on 25.10.2024, holding that there was a pre-existing dispute and that the IBC was being used for debt recovery against a solvent company, prompting the operational creditor's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether WhatsApp chat records relied upon to establish a pre-existing dispute must strictly comply with Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where the genuineness and occurrence of WhatsApp communications between parties are undisputed, technical objections regarding Section 65B compliance cannot invalidate their use to establish a pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC mandates the rejection of an application if a pre-existing dispute is demonstrated, and the IBC cannot be utilized as a recovery forum for disputed commercial claims against a solvent corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Communications showing that an operational creditor failed to lift goods due to falling market prices and backing buyers constitute clear evidence of a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The evidence established a genuine pre-existing dispute and proved that the corporate debtor was solvent, rendering the Section 9 application inadmissible.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 2292 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Straw Commodities LLP appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated 25.10.2024 dismissing its Section 9 application against Anram Agro Trading Pvt. Ltd. for default on agricultural commodity supply contracts[cite: 20]. NCLAT held that WhatsApp conversations between the parties clearly established a pre-existing dispute arising from falling market prices and the operational creditor's buyers backing out[cite: 20]. Ruling that the IBC cannot be used as a debt recovery forum against a solvent company, NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 20].

case_title: Tajinder Singh Bhathal vs. MRF Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 94 of 2023 & IA No. 1191 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tajinder Singh Bhathal (Appellant); MRF Limited (Respondent No. 1); K. B. Munivenkata Reddy & Kumar V Jahgirdar (Respondents No. 2 & 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase of 100 equity shares of MRF Limited in 1987 in the name of the Appellant and his late mother, which were later transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) and claimed by competing lodgers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (dispute regarding share transmission, duplicate share issuance, and rectification of the register under Section 59). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Shares purchased in 1987; information regarding IEPF transfer received on 16.10.2018; FIR lodged on 06.12.2018; Civil suits filed in Pune and Bengaluru; Company Petition No. 106(CHE)/2021 filed on 28.07.2021; NCLT Chennai dismissed petition on 10.08.2022; civil suit withdrawn on 13.08.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share certificates, IEPF transfer notices, police FIRs for lost shares, and competing title claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench dismissed the appellant's Section 59 company petition on 10.08.2022 because a parallel civil suit (RCS 123/2020) was pending, despite an undertaking to withdraw it. The civil suit was subsequently withdrawn on 13.08.2022, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a company petition under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 should be dismissed permanently when a parallel civil suit is pending, and whether the subsequent withdrawal of the civil suit revives the right to seek adjudication under Section 59.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Procedural technicalities or minor delays in withdrawing a parallel civil suit should not bar a litigant from pursuing statutory remedies under Section 59 of the Companies Act once the civil suit is unconditionally withdrawn. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013 bars civil court jurisdiction over matters triable by the NCLT, making NCLT the appropriate forum for share rectification disputes once civil litigation is removed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Showing bona fides through the filing of a withdrawal application in the civil court satisfies the requirement of removing parallel litigation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the civil suit was successfully withdrawn shortly after the NCLT's dismissal order, the bar of parallel proceedings no longer applies, and the company petition must be restored for adjudication on merits.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 94 of 2023 is allowed, the impugned order dated 10.08.2022 is quashed, and Company Petition No. 106(CHE)/2021 is revived for adjudication on merits subject to payment of costs.
summary: Tajinder Singh Bhathal appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated 10.08.2022 dismissing his Section 59 company petition for share rectification because a parallel civil suit was pending[cite: 21]. NCLAT Chennai held that since the civil suit was formally withdrawn on 13.08.2022 (three days after the NCLT order), the procedural hurdle of parallel proceedings no longer existed[cite: 21]. Setting aside the dismissal, NCLAT revived the company petition for adjudication on merits upon payment of nominal costs[cite: 21].

case_title: Bank of India vs. Mr. Naren Sheth (Resolution Professional)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of India (Appellant); Mr. Naren Sheth, Resolution Professional of Jaybharat Textiles & Real Estate Ltd. (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Deposit of Rs. 1 Crore paid by the Corporate Debtor (via third party Wellworth Apparels Private Limited) into a bank account with Bank of India to show bona fides towards an One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor admitted into CIRP on 03.01.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: OTS payment made on 16.07.2017; CIRP initiated on 03.01.2020; 3rd CoC meeting held on 05.09.2020; RP filed IA No. 696 of 2020; NCLT Ahmedabad passed impugned order allowing release of funds on 03.05.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Cheque No. 852249 dated 16.07.2017 issued by Wellworth Apparels on account of Jaybharat Textiles, letter dated 12.07.2017 specifying that funds be adjusted upon OTS approval, and failure of the OTS proposal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 03.05.2021 allowed IA No. 696 of 2020 filed by the RP, directing Bank of India to release the Rs. 1 Crore held in the 'No Lien Account' to the corporate debtor, prompting the bank's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an amount deposited by a corporate debtor into a 'No Lien Account' to show bona fides for a failed OTS proposal constitutes an asset of the corporate debtor under Section 18(f) of the IBC, or whether the bank can exercise a banker's lien over it after moratorium commences.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Funds deposited for a specific unmaterialized purpose such as an OTS proposal become assets of the corporate debtor upon the failure of the settlement, and a bank cannot appropriate them after the commencement of CIRP moratorium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(f) read with Section 3(27) of the IBC obligates the RP to take control and custody of all assets and properties, including money belonging to the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a third-party cheque is issued specifically on account of the corporate debtor for a conditional settlement that ultimately fails, the bank retains no general lien to withhold the funds once CIRP begins. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the OTS failed and CIRP commenced, the Adjudicating Authority correctly ruled that the Rs. 1 Crore deposit is an asset of the corporate debtor. and the bank must release it.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 533 of 2021 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Bank of India appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 03.05.2021 directing it to release Rs. 1 Crore held in a 'No Lien Account' to the Resolution Professional of Jaybharat Textiles & Real Estate Ltd[cite: 22]. The amount had been deposited by a third party on behalf of the corporate debtor to show bona fides for an OTS proposal that eventually failed[cite: 22]. NCLAT held that since the OTS failed and moratorium commenced, the funds belonged to the corporate debtor as an asset under Section 18(f) of the IBC, and the bank had no right to retain or appropriate them[cite: 22]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 22].

case_title: Archangles Distributors Private Limited vs. Ideal Financing Corporation Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1143 of 2024 & IA No. 4101 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Archangles Distributors Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor); Ideal Financing Corporation Limited / Ideal Real Estates Private Limited (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 petition filed for resolution of an amount of Rs. 2,31,60,579/-, followed by a settlement agreement dated 07.06.2022 providing for payment in 27 installments. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by corporate debtor in honoring installment payments under the settlement agreement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Settlement agreement executed on 07.06.2022; Section 7 petition disposed of as withdrawn on 08.06.2022; revival application (RST.A (IBC)/16(KB) 2023) dismissed by NCLT Kolkata on 03.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement terms containing explicit clauses (Clause 9) permitting the financial creditor to restore the company petition upon default, and joint statements recorded by NCLT Kolkata on 08.06.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the appellant's revival application on 03.04.2024 solely because explicit liberty to revive was not written into the short withdrawal order of 08.06.2022, leading to the financial creditor's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor is entitled to seek revival of a withdrawn Section 7 petition when the underlying settlement agreement brought on record explicitly provides for restoration upon default, notwithstanding the absence of express revival liberty in the brief withdrawal order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a settlement agreement containing an explicit clause for the revival of insolvency proceedings upon default is submitted and taken on record by the Adjudicating Authority, the absence of express revival wording in the brief withdrawal order does not bar the financial creditor from seeking restoration. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 proceedings withdrawn on the strength of a recorded settlement preserve the creditor's right to execute or revive the petition if the debtor breaches the agreed payment schedule. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of default under a court-recorded settlement agreement triggers the automatic contractual right to restore the original company petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing revival on technical grounds, and the appellant is entitled to restore the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1143 of 2024 is allowed, the impugned order dated 03.04.2024 is set aside, and the underlying company petition is revived, accompanied by a cost of Rs. 2 Lakhs imposed on the respondent corporate debtor.
summary: Archangles Distributors Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dated 03.04.2024 dismissing its application to revive a withdrawn Section 7 petition against Ideal Real Estates Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 23]. The petition had been withdrawn on 08.06.2022 based on a settlement agreement that explicitly permitted revival upon default[cite: 23]. NCLAT held that since the settlement terms were brought on record and accepted by the tribunal, the absence of formal revival wording in the brief withdrawal order could not defeat the creditor's rights[cite: 23]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT revived the company petition and imposed a cost of Rs. 2 Lakhs on the corporate debtor[cite: 23].

case_title: Mamtha Steels Corporation vs. Yosmite Engineering Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mamtha Steels Corporation, proprietary concern represented by proprietor Mr. Vasanram (Operational Creditor/Appellant); Yosmite Engineering Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business relationship for the supply of stainless steel sheets, rods, and pipes from March 2018 to June 2018, amounting to Rs. 1,14,70,735.98/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total principal amount due and outstanding stood at Rs. 57,16,918.10/- prior to the issuance of the demand notice. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Business transactions occurred between March 2018 and June 2018; demand notice under Section 8 issued on 05.12.2018; Section 9 application filed and subsequently rejected by NCLT Chennai Special Bench-I on 27.07.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices, partial payments made up to June 2018, and numerous subsequent WhatsApp and email communications between June 2018 and December 2018 where the corporate debtor acknowledged the debt and promised repayment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Special Bench-I dismissed the Section 9 application on 27.07.2023 on the ground of a pre-existing dispute regarding product quality, prompting the operational creditor's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether WhatsApp and email communications acknowledging a debt and promising payment establish the existence of an operational debt and default, and whether a quality dispute raised belatedly constitutes a valid pre-existing dispute under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: WhatsApp and email communications containing clear acknowledgments of liability and promises to pay override vague, belated contentions of material quality defects raised without contemporaneous proof. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC requires a pre-existing dispute to be real and supported by evidence prior to the Section 8 notice, rather than a spurious defense or afterthought. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Utilization of supplied goods in manufacturing operations without raising contemporaneous quality objections creates a strong presumption of satisfactory quality, rendering subsequent quality disputes illusory. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the corporate debtor repeatedly acknowledged the debt and promised payment via electronic messages without a valid pre-existing dispute, the Section 9 application is maintainable and must be admitted.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 381 of 2023 is allowed, the impugned order dated 27.07.2023 is quashed, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to appoint an Interim Resolution Professional and proceed with CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC.
summary: Mamtha Steels Corporation appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated 27.07.2023 dismissing its Section 9 application against Yosmite Engineering Pvt. Ltd. for default on steel supplies[cite: 29]. NCLAT Chennai held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in finding a pre-existing dispute, as numerous WhatsApp messages and emails showed the corporate debtor consistently acknowledging the debt and promising payment without raising timely quality issues[cite: 29]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT set aside the dismissal and directed the initiation of CIRP[cite: 29].

case_title: Prio S.A. vs. Mr. Pravin R. Navandar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: PRIO S.A. (Appellant/Prospective Resolution Applicant); Mr. Pravin R. Navandar, RP of VOVL Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); BPRL Ventures BV (Respondent No. 2); Committee of Creditors of VOVL Limited (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of VOVL Limited, involving submission of multiple offers by PRIO S.A. for participating interests in the Wahoo Field/IBV, and subsequent agreement between CoC and BPRL based on a Right of First Refusal (ROFR). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP commenced against VOVL Limited vide NCLT Mumbai order dated November 8, 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EOI submitted on May 7, 2020; third revised offer submitted on November 21, 2022; RP filed IA No. 2787 of 2023 for approval of BPRL's offer on July 5, 2023; PRIO filed IA No. 3363 of 2023 for intervention; NCLT Mumbai dismissed intervention on October 9, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Quotaholders' Agreement dated September 12, 2008 containing ROFR provisions, and successive commercial offers submitted by PRIO S.A. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Court-II dismissed PRIO S.A.'s intervention application (IA No. 3363 of 2023) in IA No. 2787 of 2023 on October 9, 2023 on the ground that the applicant lacked locus standi, prompting PRIO's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a prospective resolution applicant who has actively participated in negotiations and submitted successive offers during CIRP has the requisite locus standi to intervene and oppose an application filed by the RP for approval of another entity's competing offer.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A prospective resolution applicant who has participated in the resolution process and submitted offers possesses sufficient locus standi under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to intervene and contest applications relating to the approval of rival proposals. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC grants wide jurisdiction to the NCLT to entertain any question of law or facts arising out of or in relation to the insolvency resolution process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Active participation in negotiations and submission of binding financial offers creates a direct stake in the outcome of the resolution process, precluding a summary dismissal on grounds of 'no locus'. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that the appellant lacked locus standi, and the appellant must be permitted to file objections and participate in the hearing of the approval application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1650 of 2023 is allowed. The impugned order dated October 9, 2023 is set aside, and the appellant is permitted to file objections/affidavits to IA No. 2787 of 2023 for a fresh decision on merits.
summary: PRIO S.A., a prospective resolution applicant, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated October 9, 2023 rejecting its intervention application (IA 3363 of 2023) filed against the RP's application to approve a competing offer from BPRL[cite: 24]. NCLAT held that since PRIO had submitted multiple binding offers and actively participated in negotiations, it had a clear legal stake and locus standi under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC[cite: 24]. Setting aside the dismissal, NCLAT directed the Adjudicating Authority to hear PRIO's objections on merits[cite: 24].

case_title: Parikshit Madanmohan Sharma vs. M.S. Gopikrishnan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Parikshit Madanmohan Sharma, Suspended Director (Appellant); M.S. Gopikrishnan & Ors., Homebuyers/Financial Creditors (Respondents No. 1-8, 10, 11, 13-20); Arihant Nenawati, IRP (Respondent); K.D. Lite Developers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of residential/commercial units in a real estate project developed by K.D. Lite Developers Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 7 application filed by home buyers for initiation of CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 application on February 8, 2023; appeal filed subsequently. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Disputed figures regarding total allottees (appellant claiming 209 allottees and respondents claiming 124 allottees), raising questions on whether the statutory threshold under Section 7(1) second proviso was met. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 7 application on February 8, 2023 without recording any findings on vital contested issues like threshold compliance and limitation, leading to the suspended director's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an order admitting a Section 7 application filed by homebuyers is legally sustainable when the Adjudicating Authority fails to record findings on core contested issues of fact and law such as the statutory threshold requirement and limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order of admission under Section 7 of the IBC must be a speaking order containing clear findings on material contested issues, especially threshold requirements for homebuyer applications and limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC mandates strict threshold compliance (100 allottees or 10% of total allottees) which must be judicially verified when disputed on facts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A total failure by the adjudicating tribunal to discuss and resolve conflicting factual assertions regarding total allottee counts renders the decision a non-speaking order violating natural justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Adjudicating Authority omitted all discussion on limitation and threshold compliance, the admission order is vitiated and must be remanded for a fresh, reasoned decision.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 206 of 2023 is allowed, the impugned order dated February 8, 2023 is set aside, and CP (IB) No. 1420/MB-IV/2020 is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority for a fresh speaking order within two months.
summary: Parikshit Madanmohan Sharma, suspended director of K.D. Lite Developers, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated February 8, 2023 admitting a Section 7 application filed by homebuyers[cite: 25]. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority failed to record findings on core contested issues such as limitation and whether the mandatory homebuyer threshold (100 allottees or 10%) was fulfilled amidst conflicting numbers[cite: 25]. Setting aside the non-speaking order, NCLAT remanded the matter back for a fresh adjudication[cite: 25].

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited (Assignee) vs. Mr. Sandeep Goel (Resolution Professional)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 140 of 2024 & IA No. 445 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited (Appellant/Assignee); Sandeep Goel, Resolution Professional of Sarvottam Realcon Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Assignment of debt dated March 4, 2023 taken by Kotak Mahindra Bank from PNB Housing, relating to a flat mortgaged by a homebuyer (Atul Jaidka) whose payments were reflected in corporate debtor records. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP commenced on July 9, 2021; public announcement made on July 14, 2021; Resolution Plan approved by CoC on December 24, 2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on July 9, 2021; Resolution Plan approved on December 24, 2022; debt assignment taken on March 4, 2023; claim filed by appellant in August 2023; NCLT rejected application on November 21, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assignment agreement executed long after CoC approval of the resolution plan, and delayed claim filing in August 2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected Kotak Mahindra Bank's application seeking condonation of a 738-day delay in filing its claim and a direction to the RP to admit it, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in RPS Infrastructure Limited v. Mukul Kumar.
legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor/assignee who takes an assignment of debt after the approval of the resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors can seek condonation of massive delay to compel the resolution professional to admit a belated claim.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assignee of debt stepping into the shoes of a creditor after the approval of the resolution plan by the CoC cannot claim the benefit of belated claim condonation to reopen finalized insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Timelines prescribed under the IBC for submission of claims to the resolution professional are mandatory to ensure certainty and prevent disruption of approved resolution plans. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Taking an assignment of debt with constructive or actual notice of ongoing CIRP after the resolution plan has already been approved precludes the admission of belated claims. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the belated claim application filed months after CoC plan approval.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 140 of 2024 is dismissed.
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank, as an assignee of PNB Housing, appealed against an NCLT order dated November 21, 2023 rejecting its application to condone a 738-day delay and admit a claim in the CIRP of Sarvottam Realcon Pvt. Ltd[cite: 26]. NCLAT held that since the bank took the debt assignment in March 2023—months after the resolution plan was approved by the CoC on December 24, 2022—and filed its claim only in August 2023, the Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the belated claim[cite: 26]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 26].

case_title: JK Jute Mills Mazdoor Morcha vs. Kaledonia Jute and Fibres Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1407 of 2023 & IA No. 5034 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: JK Jute Mills Mazdoor Morcha (Appellant); Kaledonia Jute and Fibres Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 application proceedings and transferred winding-up petition from the Allahabad High Court pursuant to Supreme Court directions in Kaledonia Jute and Fibres (P) Ltd. v. Axis Nirman and Industries Ltd. [(2021) 2 SCC 403]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 7 application (CP No. 25(ALD)/2020) disposed of on February 3, 2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Supreme Court transferred winding-up proceedings on November 19, 2020; Section 7 application disposed of on February 3, 2022; NCLT Allahabad dismissed IA No. 319 of 2023 on August 22, 2023; appeal filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: High court winding-up petition (Company Petition No. 24 of 2015) transferred to NCLT Allahabad but remaining dormant post-transfer. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed the appellant's IA No. 319 of 2023 seeking to declare the CIRP initiation fraudulent, prompting the trade union's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal seeking to declare a CIRP fraudulent is sustainable when the principal grievance is merely the delayed adjudication of a winding-up petition transferred from a High Court to the NCLT.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not keep an appeal challenging a CIRP admission alive when the underlying grievance is resolved by directing the Adjudicating Authority to expeditiously dispose of a transferred winding-up petition. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Pursuant to Supreme Court mandates transferring pending winding-up proceedings to the NCLT under the IBC framework, such proceedings must be brought to a logical conclusion alongside or subsequent to insolvency resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Inaction or delay in processing a transferred High Court winding-up petition warrants a directive for final disposal rather than entertaining speculative challenges to the CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal lacks grounds to challenge the CIRP as fraudulent, but is appropriately disposed of with a mandate for the NCLT to finalize the transferred winding-up petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1407 of 2023 is disposed of with an observation that the winding-up petition transferred from the Allahabad High Court be finally disposed of by the Adjudicating Authority without expressing any opinion on merits.
summary: JK Jute Mills Mazdoor Morcha appealed against an NCLT Allahabad order dated August 22, 2023 dismissing its application (IA 319 of 2023) which sought to declare the CIRP of Kaledonia Jute and Fibres fraudulent[cite: 27]. During hearings, the appellant sought a direction for the disposal of a pending winding-up petition transferred from the Allahabad High Court pursuant to Supreme Court orders[cite: 27]. NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the Adjudicating Authority to finally dispose of the transferred winding-up petition[cite: 27].

case_title: Varun Gupta vs. ISINOX Pvt. Ltd. through the IRP Mr. Manishkumar R. Patel & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Varun Gupta, Suspended Director of ISINOX Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); ISINOX Pvt. Ltd. through IRP Manishkumar R. Patel (Respondent No. 1); Somesh A. Naik & 44 Others (Financial Creditors/Respondents No. 2 to 46). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Invoice discounting and reverse invoice discounting transactions facilitated through the KredX platform (managed by Minion Ventures Pvt. Ltd.), where raw material supplier Manohar Manak Alloys Pvt. Ltd. sold unpaid invoices to investors/financers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 7 application filed by 45 invoice purchasers claiming Rs. 4,37,14,449/- (including principal of Rs. 2,34,17,965/- and interest), with default date cited as October 31, 2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices and COR agreements executed in August-September 2019; Section 7 petition filed on December 30, 2021; NCLT Mumbai admitted Section 7 application on March 17, 2023; NCLAT stayed order on April 11, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Creation of Rights (COR) agreement dated August 13, 2019 among Manohar Alloys (seller), investors (buyers), ISINOX (buyer), and Minion Ventures (platform provider), escrow account records at Yes Bank. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted CP (IB) No. 216 of 2022 filed by Somesh A. Naik & Ors. under Section 7 on March 17, 2023, treating invoice discounting as a financial debt under Section 5(8)(e), prompting the suspended director's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether invoice discounting transactions where investors purchase unpaid trade invoices through a fintech platform constitute a 'financial debt' maintainable under Section 7 of the IBC, or whether they represent an 'operational debt' under Section 9.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Invoice discounting arrangements where financiers purchase unpaid trade invoices do not constitute a financial debt under Section 5(8)(e) of the IBC, but rather represent an operational debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Financers in invoice discounting platforms step into the shoes of the supplier/operational creditor pursuant to Sections 5(20) and 21(5), making Section 9 the appropriate remedy rather than Section 7. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Transactions arising directly from underlying goods supply contracts and trade invoice financing without a direct time-value-of-money loan disbursement cannot be categorized as financial debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Following binding precedent in Minions Ventures Pvt. Ltd. v. TDT Copper Ltd., the Section 7 application was not maintainable, and the financers must be relegated to seek remedies under Section 9.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 430 of 2023 is allowed, the impugned order dated March 17, 2023 admitting the Section 7 application is set aside, and the respondents/financers are relegated to file an application under Section 9 of the IBC in accordance with law.
summary: Varun Gupta, suspended director of ISINOX Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated March 17, 2023 admitting a Section 7 application filed by 45 investors who had purchased trade invoices through the KredX platform[cite: 28]. NCLAT held, following its precedent in Minions Ventures Pvt. Ltd. v. TDT Copper Ltd., that invoice discounting transactions do not qualify as financial debt under Section 5(8)(e), but are operational debts[cite: 28]. Setting aside the admission order, NCLAT relegated the financers to pursue remedies under Section 9[cite: 28].

case_title: Mamtha Steels Corporation vs. Yosmite Engineering Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mamtha Steels Corporation, proprietary concern represented by proprietor Mr. Vasanram (Operational Creditor/Appellant); Yosmite Engineering Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent). 2. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices, partial payments made up to June 2018, and numerous subsequent WhatsApp and email communications between June 2018 and December 2018 where the corporate debtor acknowledged the debt and promised repayment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Special Bench-I dismissed the Section 9 application on 27.07.2023 on the ground of a pre-existing dispute regarding product quality, prompting the operational creditor's appeal.

ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: WhatsApp and email communications containing clear acknowledgments of liability and promises to pay override vague, belated contentions of material quality defects raised without contemporaneous proof. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC requires a pre-existing dispute to be real and supported by evidence prior to the Section 8 notice, rather than a spurious defense or afterthought. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Utilization of supplied goods in manufacturing operations without raising contemporaneous quality objections creates a strong presumption of satisfactory quality, rendering subsequent quality disputes illusory. 4. operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 381 of 2023 is allowed, the impugned order dated 27.07.2023 is quashed, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to appoint an Interim Resolution Professional and proceed with CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC.
summary: Mamtha Steels Corporation appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated 27.07.2023 dismissing its Section 9 application against Yosmite Engineering Pvt. Ltd. for default on steel supplies[cite: 29]. NCLAT Chennai held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in finding a pre-existing dispute, as numerous WhatsApp messages and emails showed the corporate debtor consistently acknowledging the debt and promising payment without raising timely quality issues[cite: 29]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT set aside the dismissal and directed the initiation of CIRP[cite: 29].

case_title: Md. Sadique Islam & Ors. vs. Niraj Kumar Agarwal & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1081 of 2022 & I.A. No. 3178 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Md. Sadique Islam & Ors. (Appellants/Respondents No. 3 to 7); Niraj Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business transactions of the corporate debtor scrutinized via a transaction audit report leading to an avoidance application. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order on avoidance of preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench on 06.07.2022 in I.A. No. 314/KB/2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Composite application filed by the RP under Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC based on a Transaction Audit Report. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata allowed the RP's composite application without filing of replies by appellants and without analyzing separate ingredients of preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions, prompting the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can pass a composite order under Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC without separately analyzing the distinct statutory ingredients and pleadings for preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority must separately analyze and record distinct findings on the statutory ingredients for preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions rather than issuing a generalized conclusion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 contemplate entirely different legal parameters, standards of intent, and scopes of inquiry which cannot be lumped together without specific pleadings and evidence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying solely on the RP's opinion without independently evaluating the material facts and statutory requirements for each category of avoided transaction violates basic principles of adjudication. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Adjudicating Authority failed to independently evaluate the specific ingredients for each provision and denied the appellants an opportunity to file a reply, the impugned order is unsustainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1081 of 2022 is allowed, the impugned order dated 06.07.2022 is set aside, and I.A. No. 314/KB/2021 is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority for a fresh decision after permitting appellants to file their reply within two weeks.
summary: Md. Sadique Islam and others appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dated 06.07.2022 allowing an avoidance application filed by the Resolution Professional under Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC[cite: 30]. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority committed a patent error by issuing a generalized conclusion without analyzing the distinct statutory ingredients for preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions, and without affording the appellants an opportunity to file a reply[cite: 30]. Setting aside the order, NCLAT remanded the matter for fresh adjudication[cite: 30].

case_title: Ajay Singal vs. Gaurav Katiyar (IRP) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ajay Singal, Suspended Director of GRJ Distributers and Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant); Gaurav Katiyar, IRP (Respondent No. 1); Homebuyers/Financial Creditors in a class (Respondents No. 2 to 47); Tata Capital Housing Finance Ltd., Secured Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 48). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project known as 'Avalon Regal Court Project' at Bhiwadi, Rajasthan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 7 application filed by Devinder Yadav & Ors. for debt resolution. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Delhi admitted Section 7 application on June 3, 2022; appellant submitted project completion proposal and settlement affidavits on August 24, 2023, September 4, 2023, and December 23, 2023; voting conducted between March 10 and March 13, 2024; compliance report filed on March 14, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Project completion proposal submitted by the suspended director, Authorized Representative voting results showing 99% agreement among homebuyers and 45.7% from Tata Capital, culminating in a 100% majority resolution approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Delhi admitted the Section 7 petition on June 3, 2022; during the appeal, the appellant moved IA No. 546/2024 seeking implementation of a 'Reverse CIRP' project completion proposal based on unanimous creditor approval.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can permit the implementation of a 'Reverse CIRP' project completion proposal submitted by a suspended director when both the real estate allottees and secured financial creditors have voted in favor of it with 100% majority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When financial creditors and allottees unanimously approve a project completion proposal submitted by a promoter under the principles of 'Reverse CIRP', the appellate tribunal can permit its implementation to ensure project completion and prevent corporate liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25A(3) of the IBC governs voting by authorized representatives of financial creditors in a class, which aligns with commercial consensus for project-based resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance reports demonstrating 100% creditor approval for a settlement proposal provide a robust foundation for invoking Reverse CIRP principles. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because all classes of creditors overwhelmingly approved the project completion proposal, the appellant is permitted to execute the proposal under the guidance of the IRP.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 676 of 2022 is disposed of, allowing the appellant to complete the project under the guidance of the IRP in terms of the submitted affidavits and on the principles of 'Reverse CIRP'.
summary: Ajay Singal, suspended director of GRJ Distributers and Developers, appealed against an NCLT Delhi order dated June 3, 2022 admitting a Section 7 application for the 'Avalon Regal Court Project'[cite: 31]. During the appeal, the appellant proposed a settlement and project completion plan which was overwhelmingly approved with 100% majority voting by both homebuyers and the secured financial creditor (Tata Capital)[cite: 31]. Accepting the compliance report, NCLAT disposed of the appeal by permitting the suspended director to complete the project under the IRP's guidance on 'Reverse CIRP' principles[cite: 31].

case_title: Union Bank of India vs. Resolution Applicant of M/s. Bheema Cements Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 84 of 2023 & Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 391 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union Bank of India (Appellant in 84/2023); Resolution Applicant of M/s. Bheema Cements Limited (Appellant in 391/2023); G. Madhusudhan Rao, Former RP (Respondent); JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation of an approved resolution plan for M/s. Bheema Cements Limited by a consortium comprising Fortuna Engi Tech and Structurals (India) Pvt. Ltd. and Murgud Vincom Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Delays in resolution plan implementation caused by power supply disconnection and lack of regulatory approvals. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad granted initial extension on October 10, 2022 (IA 634/2022); further 8-month extension granted on January 4, 2023 (IA 1538/2022); civil appeal pending before Supreme Court (CA No. 4587/2022); settlement affidavit filed by SRA on January 18, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Non-restoration of power supply by SPDCTL until Supreme Court intervention, and a revised payment proposal submitted by the SRA on January 18, 2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Union Bank of India challenged an NCLT Hyderabad order dated January 4, 2023 granting an 8-month extension for plan implementation, while the SRA cross-appealed seeking longer timelines, culminating in a consent settlement before NCLAT Chennai.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can exercise inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules to record a consent-based restructuring proposal modifying resolution plan implementation timelines to prevent corporate liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal can exercise powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules to endorse consensual settlement proposals regarding plan implementation timelines to fulfill the objective of avoiding corporate liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) and Rule 11 permit flexible timeline adjustments when delays stem from external infrastructural impediments like power disconnections resolved via Supreme Court intervention. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consent given by major financial creditors (Union Bank of India and JM Financials) to an undertaking by the SRA to clear dues in structured tranches provides a workable mechanism for plan execution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals are disposed of in terms of the consensual payment proposal, with strict default stipulations triggering immediate deemed dismissal and liquidation orders.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 84 of 2023 and 391 of 2023 are disposed of in terms of the SRA's settlement proposal dated January 18, 2024, with default resulting in deemed dismissal of the SRA's appeal and allowance of UBI's appeal seeking liquidation.

During appellate proceedings, the SRA submitted a revised payment undertaking, to which Union Bank and JM Financial consented[cite: 32]. NCLAT Chennai disposed of both appeals in terms of the consensual proposal under Rule 11, stipulating that any default in tranches would trigger automatic liquidation[cite: 32].

case_title: Resolution Applicant of M/s. Bheema Cements Limited vs. G. Madhusudhan Rao & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 391 of 2023 with Comp. App. (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 84 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Resolution Applicant of M/s. Bheema Cements Limited (Appellant); G. Madhusudhan Rao, Former RP (Respondent No. 1); JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (Respondent No. 2); Union Bank of India (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation of an approved resolution plan for M/s. Bheema Cements Limited by a consortium comprising Fortuna Engi Tech and Structurals (India) Pvt. Ltd. and Murgud Vincom Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Implementation delays arising from power supply disconnection by Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Limited (SPDCTL). 4. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interlocutory applications for timeline extension, Supreme Court intervention restoring power supply, and SRA's undertaking dated January 18, 2024 to clear dues in specific tranches. 6. Appeal 84/2023), resulting in a unified disposal based on a consented restructuring proposal.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can modify implementation timelines for a resolution plan beyond statutory limits based on infrastructural delays, and whether a consensual repayment schedule can be adopted under Rule 11.

ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The primary objective of the IBC is to avoid corporate liquidation, and the Appellate Tribunal can exercise Rule 11 powers to adopt consensual restructuring timelines when implementation is hampered by external infrastructural hurdles. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules of Procedure allows courts to make necessary orders to prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice. 3. case_title: Solen Renewable Energy DMCC vs. BETA Infratech Pvt. Ltd. Through Mr. T.S.N. Raja (Liquidator) & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1444 of 2023 & I.A. No. 5168, 5169 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Solen Renewable Energy DMCC (Appellant/Purchaser); BETA Infratech Pvt. Ltd. through Liquidator T.S.N. Raja (Respondent No. 1); Aksa Energy/Respondent No. 2 (Unsuccessful/Late Bidder). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Private sale of corporate debtor's power plant assets (77MWx2 Gas Turbine and 74 MW Steam Turbine located in Uttarakhand) following failed e-auctions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Reserve price reduced to Rs. 202 Crores in failed auction on 27.02.2023; Appellant submitted private sale offer of Rs. 202.01 Crores on 23.04.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EMD of Rs. 20.20 Crores deposited by appellant between 24.04.2023 and 06.05.2023; Respondent No. 2 expressed initial interest on 05.05.2023 and revised non-binding offer on 14.05.2023; 21st SCC meeting approved sale to appellant on 15.05.2023; sale letter issued on 17.05.2023 and accepted on 18.05.2023; Respondent No. 2 made higher offer on 19.05.2023 and deposited EMD on 22.05.2023; NCLT passed impugned order on 31.10.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's repeated emails to Respondent No. 2 stating that non-binding offers without EMD would not be entertained; EMD deposit records of the appellant; SCC meeting minutes approving the private sale. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court No. IV disposed of Respondent No. 2's IA No. 3049 of 2023 on October 31, 2023, directing the liquidator and SCC to hold competitive bidding between the appellant and respondent No. 2, prompting the appellant's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can direct the reopening of a concluded private sale of liquidation assets through competitive bidding upon receiving a higher unsolicited offer from a third party who failed to deposit EMD within the stipulated process timelines.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A concluded private sale of liquidation assets approved by the Stakeholders' Consultation Committee (SCC) and finalized with a compliant bidder who deposited EMD cannot be reopened merely because a third party subsequently submits a higher, unsolicited offer without timely EMD deposit. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation read with Schedule I of the Liquidation Process Regulations provides strict procedural discipline for private sales which must be respected to maintain auction sanctity. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Express communication from the liquidator warning a prospective bidder that non-binding expressions of interest without EMD will be ignored establishes that the later offer is legally inconsequential after contract conclusion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a patent error in reopening a concluded private sale, and the impugned order directing competitive bidding must be set aside.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1444 of 2023 is allowed, and the impugned order dated October 31, 2023 directing reconsideration and competitive bidding is set aside.
summary: Solen Renewable Energy DMCC appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated October 31, 2023 directing the liquidator of BETA Infratech to hold competitive bidding between the appellant and a late bidder (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 34]. NCLAT held that since the appellant had successfully completed a private sale by depositing the required EMD and executing a concluded contract approved by the SCC, a subsequent higher offer by a party who failed to submit timely EMD could not reopen the finalized sale[cite: 34]. The appeal was allowed and the impugned order set aside[cite: 34].

case_title: Srigopal Choudhary vs. SREI Equipment Finance Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Srigopal Choudhary, Ex-Resolution Professional (Appellant); SREI Equipment Finance Limited, Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2); Corporate Debtor: M/s Ortel Communications Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of M/s Ortel Communications Limited, where Srigopal Choudhary was confirmed as RP on 01.02.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order dismissing an application to recall an ex-parte order removing the RP). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 27.11.2018; CoC approved resolution plan on 20.08.2019; Financial creditors requested CoC meetings in August and October 2021 which the RP refused; NCLT issued notice on IA 2121/2023 on April 25, 2023; ex-parte removal order passed on June 7, 2023; recall application (IA 3216/2023) dismissed on December 12, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Emails from financial creditors demanding CoC meetings, RP's refusal letter dated 11.08.2021 stating CoC meetings are not contemplated post-plan approval, and case diary entries showing counsel's failure to appear on June 7, 2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III dismissed the appellant's recall application (IA No. 3216 of 2023) under Rule 49 of NCLT Rules on December 12, 2023, upholding his ex-parte removal as RP, prompting the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an ex-parte order removing a Resolution Professional for failing to convene CoC meetings can be set aside under Rule 49 of the NCLT Rules when the appellant fails to demonstrate sufficient cause for non-appearance.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An ex-parte order passed by an Adjudicating Authority will not be recalled under Rule 49 of the NCLT Rules unless the applicant satisfies the tribunal that notice was unserved or that they were prevented by genuine, sufficient cause from appearing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 49(2) of the NCLT Rules requires strict proof of sufficient cause, and mere clerical errors in noting hearing dates by counsel when service is undisputed do not mandate ex-parte recall. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Actual knowledge of hearing dates coupled with failure to file mandatory replies within granted timelines and unexcused absence on the date of hearing defeats an application for ex-parte setting aside. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in concluding that the appellant failed to show sufficient cause under Rule 49, making the dismissal of the recall application unassailable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1690 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Srigopal Choudhary, former Resolution Professional of Ortel Communications, appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated December 12, 2023 dismissing his application (IA 3216 of 2023) to recall an ex-parte order removing him as RP[cite: 35]. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the recall application under Rule 49 of the NCLT Rules because the appellant failed to show 'sufficient cause' for his non-appearance on the date of the removal order, having been duly served and aware of proceedings[cite: 35]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 35].

case_title: RCC Infraventures Limited vs. Union Bank of India
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 390 & 391 of 2024 & I.A. No. 1338, 1339 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: RCC Infra Ventures Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Union Bank of India (Respondent/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 application filed by Union Bank of India against the corporate debtor in CP (IB) No. 239/CHD/HRY/2023. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on credit facilities extended by Union Bank of India. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority passed orders on October 11, 2023 and November 28, 2023; corporate debtor filed Writ Petition No. 28528 of 2023 before Punjab & Haryana High Court (dismissed on January 8, 2024); SLP dismissed on February 5, 2024; appeal e-filed on February 10, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Orders dated October 11, 2023 and November 28, 2023 expressing prima facie views on limitation and default by the Adjudicating Authority. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor appealed against the NCLT orders; NCLAT dismissed Company Appeal No. 390 of 2024 as time-barred beyond the 15-day condonable limit, and disposed of Company Appeal No. 391 of 2024 on merits, clarifying that prima facie observations do not bar raising limitation objections in the reply.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed beyond the 15-day condonable period under Section 61(2) of the IBC is maintainable even after excluding time spent in writ proceedings, and whether an Adjudicating Authority's prima facie view on limitation restricts the corporate debtor from raising limitation as a substantive defense in its reply.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal filed beyond the absolute outer limit of limitation (30 days plus the permissible 15-day extension) must be dismissed as time-barred, and a tribunal's prima facie observations do not bar a party from raising legal objections in its final reply. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) proviso strictly restricts the appellate tribunal's power to condone delay beyond 15 days following the expiration of the initial 30-day appeal period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Even after granting the benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act for time spent prosecuting writ petitions, if the appeal remains outside the condonable statutory window, it cannot be entertained. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Company Appeal No. 390 of 2024 is time-barred and dismissed, while Company Appeal No. 391 of 2024 is disposed of with clarification that the corporate debtor is fully entitled to raise limitation in its substantive reply.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 390 of 2024 is dismissed as barred by time, and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 391 of 2024 is disposed of with the clarification that prima facie observations on limitation shall not prejudice the corporate debtor's defense.
summary: RCC Infra Ventures Ltd. appealed against two NCLT orders dated October 11, 2023 and November 28, 2023 passed in a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by Union Bank of India[cite: 37]. NCLAT held that the appeal against the October order was barred by time even after excluding the period spent prosecuting a writ petition and SLP, while the appeal against the November order was disposed of with a clarification that the corporate debtor's right to contest limitation in its reply remains unfettered by earlier prima facie observations[cite: 37].

case_title: M/s. Bharat Steel Rolling Mills Unit-1 vs. Revital Reality Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bharat Steel Rolling Mills Unit-1 (Appellant/Operational Creditor); Revital Reality Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods (TMT Steel Bars) under a running account from 2017 to 2021, with invoices raised between August 23, 2017 and July 22, 2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Demand notice dated September 30, 2021 claiming principal of Rs. 1,95,89,098/- and interest of Rs. 13,41,218/- (totaling Rs. 2,09,30,316/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised; default occurred within 15 days; Section 10A barred period spanned March 25, 2020 to March 24, 2021; Section 9 petition filed on December 20, 2021; NCLT dismissed petition on March 16, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statement of accounts showing part payments made and adjusted against earlier invoices, demand notice covering 17 invoices (12 of which fell within the Section 10A barred window). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Section 9 application on March 16, 2023 on the ground that 12 out of 17 invoices fell under Section 10A, and excluding those invoices left the remaining claim below the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC, prompting the operational creditor's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether invoices falling within the Section 10A COVID-19 default exclusion period can be counted toward meeting the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC in a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Defaults occurring during the Section 10A exclusion period cannot form the basis of a CIRP application, and part payments made by a running account corporate debtor are adjusted against the earliest invoices in time, extinguishing older debts first. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A of the IBC imposes a strict legislative embargo on initiating CIRP for defaults occurring between March 25, 2020 and March 24, 2021, and excluding such invoices reduces actionable debt below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Standard accounting practices dictate that part payments in a running account clear older invoices first, leaving defaults within the Section 10A window as the primary unpaid component. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because 12 out of 17 invoices were barred by Section 10A and the remaining valid invoices fell below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4, the Section 9 petition was rightly dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 666 of 2023 is dismissed, and the impugned order dated March 16, 2023 is upheld.
summary: Bharat Steel Rolling Mills Unit-1 appealed against an NCLT order dated March 16, 2023 dismissing its Section 9 application against Revital Reality Pvt. Ltd. for default on steel supplies[cite: 38]. NCLAT held that 12 out of the 17 claimed invoices fell squarely within the Section 10A COVID-19 exclusion period, and part payments made by the corporate debtor had cleared earlier pre-10A invoices[cite: 38]. Excluding the barred invoices left the remaining claim below the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC, leading to the dismissal of the appeal[cite: 38].

case_title: Md. Sadique Islam & Ors. vs. Niraj Kumar Agarwal & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1081 of 2022 & I.A. No. 3178 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Md. Sadique Islam & Ors. (Appellants/Respondents No. 3 to 7); Niraj Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Avoidance application filed by the Resolution Professional regarding transactions of the corporate debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an avoidance application order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench on July 6, 2022 in I.A. No. 314/KB/2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Composite application filed under Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC based on a Transaction Audit Report. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata allowed the RP's composite avoidance application without giving appellants an opportunity to file a reply and without analyzing separate statutory ingredients for preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions, prompting the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can pass a composite avoidance order under Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC without separately analyzing the distinct statutory ingredients and pleadings for each category of transaction.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority must separately analyze and record distinct findings on the statutory ingredients for preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions rather than issuing a generalized conclusion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 contemplate entirely different legal parameters, standards of intent, and scopes of inquiry which cannot be lumped together. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying solely on the RP's opinion without independently evaluating the material facts and statutory requirements for each category of avoided transaction violates basic principles of adjudication. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Adjudicating Authority failed to independently evaluate the specific ingredients for each provision and denied the appellants an opportunity to file a reply, the impugned order is unsustainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1081 of 2022 is allowed, the impugned order dated July 6, 2022 is set aside, and I.A. No. 314/KB/2021 is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority for a fresh decision after permitting appellants to file their reply within two weeks.
summary: Md. Sadique Islam and others appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dated July 6, 2022 allowing an avoidance application filed by the Resolution Professional under Sections 43, 45, 49, and 66 of the IBC[cite: 39]. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority committed a patent error by issuing a generalized conclusion without analyzing the distinct statutory ingredients for preferential, undervalued, and fraudulent transactions, and without affording the appellants an opportunity to file a reply[cite: 39]. Setting aside the order, NCLAT remanded the matter for fresh adjudication[cite: 39].

case_title: Ajay Singal vs. Gaurav Katiyar (IRP) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ajay Singal, Suspended Director of GRJ Distributers and Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant); Gaurav Katiyar, IRP (Respondent No. 1); Homebuyers/Financial Creditors in a class (Respondents No. 2 to 47); Tata Capital Housing Finance Ltd., Secured Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 48). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development project known as 'Avalon Regal Court Project' at Bhiwadi, Rajasthan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 7 application filed by Devinder Yadav & Ors. for debt resolution. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Delhi admitted Section 7 application on June 3, 2022; appellant submitted project completion proposal and settlement affidavits on August 24, 2023, September 4, 2023, and December 23, 2023; voting conducted between March 10 and March 13, 2024; compliance report filed on March 14, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Project completion proposal submitted by the suspended director, Authorized Representative voting results showing 99% agreement among homebuyers and 45.7% from Tata Capital, culminating in a 100% majority resolution approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Delhi admitted the Section 7 petition on June 3, 2022; during the appeal, the appellant moved IA No. 546/2024 seeking implementation of a 'Reverse CIRP' project completion proposal based on unanimous creditor approval.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can permit the implementation of a 'Reverse CIRP' project completion proposal submitted by a suspended director when both the real estate allottees and secured financial creditors have voted in favor of it with 100% majority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When financial creditors and allottees unanimously approve a project completion proposal submitted by a promoter under the principles of 'Reverse CIRP', the appellate tribunal can permit its implementation to ensure project completion and prevent corporate liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25A(3) of the IBC governs voting by authorized representatives of financial creditors in a class, which aligns with commercial consensus for project-based resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compliance reports demonstrating 100% creditor approval for a settlement proposal provide a robust foundation for invoking Reverse CIRP principles. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because all classes of creditors overwhelmingly approved the project completion proposal, the appellant is permitted to execute the proposal under the guidance of the IRP.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 676 of 2022 is disposed of, allowing the appellant to complete the project under the guidance of the IRP in terms of the submitted affidavits and on the principles of 'Reverse CIRP'.
summary: Ajay Singal, suspended director of GRJ Distributers and Developers, appealed against an NCLT Delhi order dated June 3, 2022 admitting a Section 7 application for the 'Avalon Regal Court Project'[cite: 40]. During the appeal, the appellant proposed a settlement and project completion plan which was overwhelmingly approved with 100% majority voting by both homebuyers and the secured financial creditor (Tata Capital)[cite: 40]. Accepting the compliance report, NCLAT disposed of the appeal by permitting the suspended director to complete the project under the IRP's guidance on 'Reverse CIRP' principles[cite: 40].

case_title: SP Probuild LLP vs. Rabindra Kumar Mintri & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 795 of 2024 with 816 of 2024 & 817 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SP Probuild LLP, Yashveer Singh, Reena (Appellants/Homebuyers/Allottees); Rabindra Kumar Mintri, RP of Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Noida Authority (Respondent No. 2); Consortium of One Group, Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of flats in the real estate project 'Ridge Residency', Sector-135, Noida, developed by Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor admitted into insolvency on August 20, 2019; CoC approved resolution plan submitted by One Group on March 3, 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved by CoC on March 3, 2020; RP filed IA No. 2518/2021 under Section 30(2); claims filed by appellants in 2022 and 2023 rejected by RP; Adjudicating Authority remitted plan back to CoC on March 5, 2024 pursuant to Supreme Court judgment in Greater Noida v. Prabhjit Singh Soni. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Rejection emails issued by the RP stating claims were time-barred due to prior CoC plan approval, and Greater Noida Supreme Court ruling mandating secured status for statutory authorities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi disposed of approval applications on March 5, 2024 by sending the plan back to the CoC for resubmission while deferring other IAs to April 30, 2024, prompting appeals by homebuyers seeking mandatory claim consideration.
legal_issues: Whether the remand of a resolution plan back to the Committee of Creditors (CoC) for resubmission opens a window for belated homebuyers whose claims were earlier rejected due to prior plan approval to compel the RP and SRA to consider and admit their claims.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The remand of a resolution plan back to the CoC for specific rectifications does not automatically reopen the CIRP process for fresh claim admissions or override final judicial rejections of belated claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12 of CIRP Regulations and statutory timelines strictly govern claim submissions, and previous final rejections confirmed up to the Supreme Court constitute a bar against re-agitating claim admissions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Remission of a plan limited to addressing secured creditor statutory dues (Noida/Greater Noida mandates) does not constitute a wholesale reopening of the resolution process for late creditors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellants' earlier claim-rejection orders attained finality up to the Supreme Court, the remand order does not create a fresh right for claim consideration, and pending applications must be decided on their own merits.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 795, 816, and 817 of 2024 are disposed of with directions that the Adjudicating Authority expedite pending applications, and the SRA await those decisions before resubmitting the plan to the CoC.
summary: SP Probuild LLP, Yashveer Singh, and Reena appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated March 5, 2024 which disposed of resolution plan approval applications for Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd. and remitted the plan back to the CoC following the Supreme Court's Greater Noida judgment[cite: 42]. The appellants argued that the remand revived their right to have their belated claims considered[cite: 42]. NCLAT held that the remand was limited to specific statutory rectifications and did not reopen finalized claim rejections, disposing of the appeals with directions for the Adjudicating Authority to expedite pending interlocutory applications[cite: 42].

case_title: Yashveer Singh vs. Rabindra Kumar Mintri & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 816 of 2024 with 795 of 2024 & 817 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Yashveer Singh (Appellant/Allottee of Unit J-0606); Rabindra Kumar Mintri, RP (Respondent No. 1); Noida Authority (Respondent No. 2); Consortium of One Group, SRA. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment and payment of Rs. 41,17,773/- towards Unit J-0606 in the 'Ridge Residency' project of Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP on August 20, 2019; CoC approved resolution plan on March 3, 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claim filed on September 6, 2023; rejected by RP on September 9, 2023 due to delay and prior CoC plan approval; IA No. 5923 of 2023 filed before NCLT; NCLT passed order on March 5, 2024 remitting plan to CoC. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP's rejection email stating claim was time-barred post-CoC approval, and pending IA No. 5923 of 2023 seeking condonation of delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi on March 5, 2024 remitted the resolution plan back to the CoC pursuant to the Supreme Court's Greater Noida ruling while deferring Yashveer Singh's claim condonation application (IA 5923/2023) to April 30, 2024, prompting the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an allottee whose claim was rejected by the RP for delay and prior CoC plan approval can demand direct admission of the claim upon the remand of the resolution plan back to the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The remand of a resolution plan for specific rectifications does not dispense with the requirement to adjudicate pending delay condonation applications on their individual merits. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12 of the CIRP Regulations governs late claims, requiring formal condonation of delay by the Adjudicating Authority rather than automatic absorption upon plan remittal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pending applications for claim condonation must be decided independently by the Adjudicating Authority before a resubmitted resolution plan is finalized by the CoC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is premature since the appellant's delay condonation application is already pending before the Adjudicating Authority for adjudication.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 816 of 2024 is disposed of, directing the Adjudicating Authority to expedite the pending delay condonation application and requiring the SRA to await that decision before resubmitting the plan to the CoC.
summary: Yashveer Singh appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated March 5, 2024 passed in the CIRP of Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd[cite: 42]. The appellant sought directions for the admission of his belated claim after the resolution plan was remitted back to the CoC[cite: 42]. NCLAT held that his pending application for delay condonation (IA 5923/2023) must be adjudicated by the Adjudicating Authority independently, disposing of the appeal with instructions for expedited consideration[cite: 42].

case_title: Reena vs. Rabindra Kumar Mintri & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 817 of 2024 with 795 of 2024 & 816 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Reena (Appellant/Allottee of Unit I-1406); Rabindra Kumar Mintri, RP (Respondent No. 1); Noida Authority (Respondent No. 2); Consortium of One Group, SRA. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment and payment of Rs. 32,11,234/- towards Unit I-1406 in the 'Ridge Residency' project of Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP on August 20, 2019; CoC approved resolution plan on March 3, 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claim filed in Form-CA on August 11, 2023; rejected by RP on September 9, 2023 due to delay and prior CoC plan approval; IA No. 4906 of 2023 filed before NCLT; NCLT passed order on March 5, 2024 remitting plan to CoC. 5.
