FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP's rejection email citing delay and prior CoC plan approval, and pending IA No. 4906 of 2023 seeking condonation of delay and setting aside of the resolution plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi on March 5, 2024 remitted the resolution plan back to the CoC pursuant to the Supreme Court's Greater Noida ruling while deferring Reena's claim application (IA 4906/2023) to April 30, 2024, prompting the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an allottee filing a belated claim after CoC plan approval is entitled to automatic admission upon the subsequent remand of the resolution plan back to the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The remand of a resolution plan does not bypass the statutory requirement for the Adjudicating Authority to adjudicate pending delay condonation and claim admission applications. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12 of the CIRP Regulations requires judicial determination of delay condonation for belated claims before they can be mandated for inclusion in a resubmitted resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pending interlocutory applications seeking claim condonation must be heard and decided on their merits rather than being presumed allowed by a general plan remand order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is premature because the appellant's delay condonation application is already pending before the Adjudicating Authority for a reasoned decision.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 817 of 2024 is disposed of, directing the Adjudicating Authority to expedite the pending delay condonation application and requiring the SRA to await that decision before resubmitting the plan to the CoC.
summary: Reena appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated March 5, 2024 passed in the CIRP of Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd[cite: 42]. The appellant sought directions for the admission of her belated claim following the remission of the resolution plan back to the CoC[cite: 42]. NCLAT held that her pending application for delay condonation (IA 4906/2023) must be adjudicated by the Adjudicating Authority independently, disposing of the appeal with instructions for expedited consideration[cite: 42].

case_title: Metamorphosis Trading LLP vs. Sankalp Engineering & Services Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Metamorphosis Trading LLP (Appellant/Financial Creditor/Assignee); Sankalp Engineering and Services Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor); Innoventive Industries Ltd. (IIL/Assignor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial assistance allegedly provided by IIL (wholly owning subsidiary Sankalp Engineering) during November 2013 to March 2014, and subsequent assignment of receivables by the Liquidator of IIL to the Appellant via Deed of Assignment dated July 21, 2021 for Rs. 25 Lakhs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 7 application filed for default on an assigned debt of Rs. 5.10 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IIL admitted into CIRP on January 23, 2017; liquidation ordered on December 8, 2017; debt assigned to appellant on July 21, 2021; legal notice sent on September 16, 2021; Section 7 petition rejected by NCLT Mumbai on December 9, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated May 24, 2014 confirming Rs. 5.58 Crores due, IIL balance confirmation letter dated April 12, 2017 (unresponded by Sankalp), statutory auditor affidavits showing balance written off via journal entry on April 1, 2017, and IIL financial statements showing derecognition of subsidiary assets from 2017-18 onwards. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV rejected CP (IB) 970/MB-IV/2022 on December 9, 2023, holding that the appellant failed to prove the existence of a financial debt and default, prompting the assignee's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether trade receivables assigned on an 'as is where is' and 'no recourse' basis without proof of disbursement against time value of money constitute a 'financial debt' maintainable under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For a debt to qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, there must be a clear disbursal of debt against the consideration for the time value of money, and an assignee cannot elevate trade receivables into a financial loan without underlying loan contracts and disbursement proof. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(7) and 5(8) require strict proof of disbursement and time value of money; trade receivables assigned under a 'no recourse' and 'as is where is' deed lack financial debt trappings unless proven otherwise. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The absence of balance confirmations post-2017, the writing off of the balance via journal entries in the corporate debtor's books, and the classification of exposure as trade receivables rather than intercorporate loans defeat the Section 7 claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant failed to establish disbursement against time value of money and the existence of a subsisting financial debt, the Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the Section 7 application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 460 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Metamorphosis Trading LLP appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated December 9, 2023 dismissing its Section 7 application against Sankalp Engineering & Services Pvt. Ltd[cite: 44]. The appellant claimed to be a financial creditor by virtue of a deed of assignment acquiring receivables from the liquidator of Innoventive Industries Ltd.[cite: 44]. NCLAT held that the assigned dues represented trade receivables rather than a financial loan, lacked proof of disbursal against time value of money, and had been written off in the corporate debtor's books since 2017[cite: 44]. Upholding the dismissal, NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 44].

case_title: Anton Engineering vs. Sherisha Technologies Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 79 of 2024 & IA Nos. 229, 230, 231 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anton Engineering, represented by Proprietrix Zita Vija (Appellant/Successful Auction Purchaser); Sherisha Technologies Private Limited (Respondent No. 1); V.M. Gurusamy, Liquidator of Balasara Engineering Products Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); E-Procurement Technologies Ltd. (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: E-auction liquidation sale of Balasara Engineering Products Ltd., where Anton Engineering emerged as the successful auction purchaser. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order setting aside an e-auction sale without hearing the successful auction purchaser). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chennai Special Bench-I directed impleadment of the successful auction purchaser on January 30, 2024; impugned order passed on February 9, 2024 setting aside the auction without formal impleadment or opportunity of hearing. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT order sheets showing direction for impleadment on January 30, 2024, failure of the applicant to file a formal impleadment application, and the subsequent order on February 9, 2024 ordering a fresh e-auction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench-I passed an order on February 9, 2024 in IA No. 346 of 2024 ordering a fresh e-auction without formally impleading or hearing the successful auction purchaser, prompting the purchaser's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can set aside a completed e-auction sale and order a fresh auction without formally impleading and affording an opportunity of hearing to the successful auction purchaser, in violation of principles of natural justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful auction purchaser is a necessary and proper party whose rights are directly affected, and no order setting aside an auction sale can be passed without formal impleadment and a full opportunity of hearing in accordance with natural justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Principles of natural justice require that before any adverse order affecting property rights or auction confirmation is passed, the affected party must be formally arrayed and heard. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure by an applicant to file a formal impleadment application despite tribunal directions, resulting in an ex-parte or non-participatory adverse order against a successful bidder, vitiates the proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the successful auction purchaser was not formally impleaded or heard before the auction was cancelled, the impugned order violates natural justice and must be set aside for de novo consideration.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 79 of 2024 is allowed, the impugned order dated February 9, 2024 is set aside, and the matter is remitted back to NCLT Chennai for de novo consideration after proper impleadment and hearing, with e-auction proceedings deferred in the interim.
summary: Anton Engineering, the successful auction purchaser in the liquidation of Balasara Engineering, appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated February 9, 2024 which ordered a fresh e-auction without formally impleading or hearing the purchaser[cite: 45]. NCLAT Chennai held that the failure to formally implead the successful bidder despite earlier tribunal directions violated the principles of natural justice[cite: 45]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT set aside the impugned order and remanded the matter back for de novo consideration after proper impleadment[cite: 45].

case_title: Paisalo Digital Limited vs. Uniglobal Ventures LLP
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 589 of 2023 & I.A. No. 1958 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Paisalo Digital Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor); Uniglobal Ventures LLP (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 insolvency application filed by Paisalo Digital Ltd. claiming a default amount of Rs. 10,92,05,184/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed for Rs. 10,92,05,184/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed; notices issued on July 1, 2022; NCLT directed paper publication on August 11, 2022; corporate debtor appeared through counsel on September 16, 2022 and sought time to file vakalatnama and counter affidavit; fresh notice issued on December 5, 2022; NCLT dismissed application on February 2, 2023 for alleged non-compliance of service orders. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Affidavit of service filed on August 8, 2022, order sheets showing counsel appearance for the corporate debtor on September 16, 2022, and failure of corporate debtor to file vakalatnama or counter. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Section 7 application on February 2, 2023 due to non-compliance with service orders (dated August 11 and December 5, 2022), overlooking the fact that the corporate debtor had already entered appearance through counsel, prompting the financial creditor's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can dismiss a Section 7 insolvency application for non-compliance with service orders when the corporate debtor has already entered appearance through counsel and sought time to file a reply.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate debtor enters appearance through counsel in response to Section 7 proceedings and seeks time to file a reply, technical defaults regarding prior service modes or paper publication become inconsequential, and the application cannot be dismissed for non-prosecution or service non-compliance. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 proceedings must be adjudicated on merits once the corporate debtor has notice and representation, avoiding hyper-technical dismissals. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunal order sheets reflecting counsel appearance and requests for time to file a vakalatnama establish that the corporate debtor had full knowledge of the proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a patent error in dismissing the Section 7 petition for service non-compliance when the corporate debtor had already appeared, necessitating the revival of the petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 589 of 2023 is allowed, the impugned order dated February 2, 2023 is set aside, and the Section 7 application is revived before the Adjudicating Authority for adjudication on merits.
summary: Paisalo Digital Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order dated February 2, 2023 dismissing its Section 7 application against Uniglobal Ventures LLP for default on a financial debt of Rs. 10.92 Crores[cite: 46]. NCLT had dismissed the petition citing non-compliance with service publication orders[cite: 46]. NCLAT held that since the corporate debtor's counsel had already appeared before the tribunal and sought time to file a counter affidavit, service defects were cured, and the dismissal was erroneous[cite: 46]. Setting aside the dismissal, NCLAT revived the Section 7 application for a decision on merits[cite: 46].

case_title: IIFL Home Finance Ltd. vs. Shiv Nandan Sharma (Resolution Professional of Saha Infratech Pvt. Ltd.)
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 856 of 2024 & I.A. No. 2958, 3089 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IIFL Home Finance Ltd. (Appellant/Lender); Shiv Nandan Sharma, Resolution Professional of Saha Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent); Mr. Vikas Pandhi and Mr. Vinod Kumar (Flat Buyers/Borrowers). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Home loans advanced by IIFL Home Finance Ltd. to flat buyers for purchasing residential units in the 'Amadeus' project developed by Saha Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), secured by equitable mortgages and quadripartite agreements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP initiated against the corporate debtor under Section 7 on February 28, 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on February 28, 2020; claim of Rs. 2,31,50,653/- filed in Form C by IIFL on August 17, 2023; IA No. 6104 of 2023 dismissed by NCLT on January 23, 2024; appeal filed with 7 days' condoned delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tripartite/quadripartite loan agreements, demand letters, allotment letters, and mortgage documents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed IIFL's IA No. 6104 of 2023 on January 23, 2024 seeking admission of its claim as a secured financial creditor, prompting the lender's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a bank or financial institution that has advanced home loans to flat buyers, secured by mortgages and quadripartite agreements, can be categorized as a 'Secured Financial Creditor' and included in the Committee of Creditors (CoC) of the corporate debtor developer.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Banks and financial institutions that advance housing loans to individual home buyers do not qualify as 'Financial Creditors' or 'Secured Financial Creditors' of the corporate debtor developer, as the primary repayment liability rests on the individual home buyers. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Home buyers are the financial creditors of the real estate corporate debtor regardless of whether they self-financed or took bank loans; a tripartite or quadripartite agreement does not alter the underlying character of the home buyer's borrowing. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of default and financial debt under a home loan is strictly between the home allottee and the lending bank, and including banks in the CoC would defeat the IBC's objective of corporate resolution and asset maximization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the liability to repay the home loan lies with the individual home buyers and not the corporate debtor developer, the appellant cannot be admitted as a secured financial creditor in the CIRP.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 856 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: IIFL Home Finance Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated January 23, 2024 dismissing its application (IA 6104 of 2023) to admit its claim as a secured financial creditor in the CIRP of Saha Infratech Pvt. Ltd[cite: 48]. The lender had advanced home loans to flat buyers secured by mortgages and quadripartite agreements[cite: 48]. NCLAT held, relying on precedent, that financial institutions lending to home buyers cannot be included as financial creditors in the CoC because the repayment liability rests on the individual buyers, and tripartite agreements do not change this legal character[cite: 48]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 48].

case_title: Devesh Raminklal Thakker vs. Arun Kapoor (Resolution Professional of Monarch Brookefields LLP)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 808 of 2024 & I.A. No. 2633, 2914 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Devesh Raminklal Thakker (Appellant/Homebuyer); Arun Kapoor, Resolution Professional of Monarch Brookefields LLP (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement for Sale dated January 13, 2016 for Flat No. 603, Wing Arizona, Sector 20, Kalamboli, Navi Mumbai. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Homebuyer claim filed in CIRP of Monarch Brookefields LLP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreement executed on January 13, 2016; NCLT rejected IA No. 2218 of 2022 on December 19, 2023; appeal filed with 12 days' condoned delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement for Sale showing payment mode via A/c Payee cheques, attached receipt listing three specific Indian Bank cheques totaling Rs. 27 Lakhs, and the appellant's contradictory pleading claiming cash payment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai rejected the appellant's IA No. 2218 of 2022 seeking acceptance of his homebuyer claim because the payment proof contradicted his assertion of cash payment, prompting the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution professional and adjudicating authority are justified in rejecting a homebuyer's claim when the agreement and attached receipt explicitly specify payment by cheques while the claimant contends payment was made in cash without supporting proof.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A claimant seeking admission of a debt or homebuyer claim must produce reliable proof of payment corresponding to the contractual terms, and uncorroborated assertions of cash payments that contradict written agreement receipts justify claim rejection. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Verification of claims by a resolution professional requires substantiation through verifiable banking or financial records matching transaction documents. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an Agreement for Sale and its receipt record specific cheque numbers and bank branches for consideration, a later unverified claim of cash payment unsupported by material evidence is rightly rejected. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant failed to prove payment of consideration in accordance with the contract or via verifiable records, the Resolution Professional and Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the claim.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 808 of 2024 is dismissed.
summary: Devesh Raminklal Thakker appealed against an NCLT order dated December 19, 2023 rejecting his application (IA 2218 of 2022) for the acceptance of his homebuyer claim in the CIRP of Monarch Brookefields LLP[cite: 49]. The resolution professional had rejected the claim because the appellant claimed cash payment, whereas the Agreement for Sale and attached receipt explicitly recorded payment via three specific cheques[cite: 49]. NCLAT held that the appellant failed to prove payment of consideration, and the rejection was fully justified[cite: 49].

case_title: SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. vs. Harsh Arora & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 721 of 2024 & I.A. No. 2590, 2592 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (Appellant/CoC Member); Harsh Arora & Anr., Resolution Professional and ex-Directors (Respondents); Punjab National Bank (PNB/Applicant in IA 3151/2022). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of the corporate debtor under CP (IB) No. 271/PB/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from interlocutory orders regarding CoC reconstitution and transaction audits). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved by CoC in June 2022; PNB filed IA 3151/2022 seeking transaction audits and CoC reconstitution; NCLT passed interim directions on January 29, 2024; subsequent order passed on March 11, 2024 directing notice and replies from all CoC members. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interlocutory applications and subsequent NCLT order dated March 11, 2024 reopening the matter for fresh hearing after issuing notice to all CoC members. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SREI appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated January 29, 2024 which directed the RP to examine CoC reconstitution, but given a subsequent order on March 11, 2024 setting a de novo hearing schedule, the appeal was rendered infructuous.
legal_issues: Whether an interlocutory order directing a resolution professional to examine CoC reconstitution issues warrants appellate interference when a subsequent order by the Adjudicating Authority opens up all issues for fresh consideration after issuing notice to all parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not entertain an appeal against an interlocutory order when the Adjudicating Authority subsequently issues comprehensive directions for a fresh hearing, affording all affected parties an opportunity to file replies and contest the issues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) and Section 61 permit interlocutory challenges, but appellate intervention is unwarranted when the trial forum itself supersedes the prior interim step with a de novo notice and reply schedule. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Subsequent procedural orders directing formal notice and reply submissions to all CoC members cure any interim procedural grievances. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because all contentions remain open for fresh adjudication before the Adjudicating Authority pursuant to the subsequent March 11, 2024 order, the appeal need not be entertained.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 721 of 2024 is disposed of, with all contentions left open for fresh determination by the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order dated January 29, 2024 passed in IA 3151/2022 which directed the RP to examine CoC reconstitution issues[cite: 50]. During proceedings, it was noted that the Adjudicating Authority subsequently passed an order on March 11, 2024 issuing formal notice and calling for replies from all CoC members for a fresh adjudication[cite: 50]. NCLAT disposed of the appeal, holding that all issues were open for de novo consideration before the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 50].

case_title: Shrenik Ashokbhai Morakhia vs. Reliance Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shrenik Ashokbhai Morakhia, Personal Guarantor (Appellant); Reliance Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor); Mahesh R. Sureka, Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2); Morakhia Metals and Alloy Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facility of Rs. 32.15 Crores sanctioned by Dena Bank on June 18, 2012 to the corporate debtor, secured by a joint deed of guarantee executed by the appellant and Pankaj Kumar Morakhia on July 25, 2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor account declared NPA on May 31, 2015; personal guarantee invoked via recall notice dated March 4, 2016 demanding Rs. 26.68 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NPA on May 31, 2015; guarantee invoked on March 4, 2016; Declaration-cum-Undertaking executed by appellant acknowledging debt on January 29, 2018; corporate debtor CIRP admitted on February 19, 2020; Section 95 demand notice issued on July 12, 2021; Section 95 application filed on August 10, 2021; NCLT Ahmedabad admitted Section 95 application on March 20, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Recall notice dated March 4, 2016, signed Declaration-cum-Undertaking dated January 29, 2018 creating a charge on joint property for corporate dues, and Form A consent of the resolution professional. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitted the Section 95 insolvency application against the personal guarantor on March 20, 2024 under Section 100, prompting the guarantor's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 95 insolvency application against a personal guarantor is barred by limitation when filed more than three years after initial guarantee invocation, and whether an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act extends limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of debt in writing signed by a guarantor before the expiration of the limitation period extends the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and the Supreme Court's Suo Motu COVID-19 exclusion period applies to suspend limitation calculations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 95(1) permits filing an application through a resolution professional who submits written consent in Form A. Section 18 of the Limitation Act gets attracted upon written acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Executing a formal Declaration-cum-Undertaking acknowledging debt and creating a lien on property constitutes a valid acknowledgment extending limitation by a further three years. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the limitation period was successfully extended by the 2018 undertaking and further protected by the Supreme Court's Suo Motu COVID-19 exclusion order, the Section 95 application is well within limitation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 719 of 2024 is dismissed.
summary: Shrenik Ashokbhai Morakhia, personal guarantor of Morakhia Metals and Alloy Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dated March 20, 2024 admitting a Section 95 insolvency application filed by Reliance Asset Reconstruction Company[cite: 51]. The appellant argued that the petition was barred by limitation since the guarantee was invoked on March 4, 2016[cite: 51]. NCLAT held that the appellant's execution of a Declaration-cum-Undertaking on January 29, 2018 constituted a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, extending limitation, and that the petition was further protected by the Supreme Court's Suo Motu COVID-19 exclusion period[cite: 51]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 51].

case_title: Peanance Commercial Private Limited & Anr. vs. Mamta Binani (Resolution Professional for Rolta India Limited)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Peanance Commercial Private Limited (Appellant No. 1/Assignee); Rolta Private Limited (Appellant No. 2/Assignor/Related Party); Mamta Binani, Resolution Professional for Rolta India Limited (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Rolta India Limited, where Rolta Private Limited filed a claim of Rs. 634,55,43,228/- which was admitted but denied CoC representation as a related party; subsequent Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) dated January 15, 2024 between Rolta Private Limited and Peanance Commercial Private Limited for debt assignment for Rs. 50 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP commenced against Rolta India Limited on January 19, 2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on January 19, 2023; MoU executed on January 15, 2024; letters sent to RP seeking advance confirmation on February 6, 2024; RP's replies issued on February 8 and February 15, 2024 refusing confirmation; NCLT Mumbai dismissed IA 724 of 2024 on April 24, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU defining purchase consideration to be payable only upon RP's approval recognizing the assignee as an unrelated secured financial creditor with full voting rights. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I dismissed IA 724 of 2024 filed by the appellants on April 24, 2024, refusing to direct the RP to pre-approve the assignment as converting a related party claim into an unrelated voting claim, prompting the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution professional can be compelled to pre-approve a debt assignment agreement whose very effectiveness is contingent upon recategorizing a related party creditor into an unrelated voting member of the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assignment agreement structured to take effect only upon obtaining advance judicial or professional confirmation that a related party's debt will acquire voting rights constitutes a device to circumvent the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The exclusion under the first proviso to Section 21(2) bars related party financial creditors from CoC participation, and related parties cannot sanitize their disqualified status through staged assignment agreements designed solely to acquire voting power. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where purchase consideration is expressly contingent on gaining CoC voting rights, the transaction lacks bona fides and amounts to an attempt to manipulate CoC constitution. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the assignment arrangement was a malafide device to smuggle a related party into the CoC, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 905 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Peanance Commercial Pvt. Ltd. and Rolta Private Limited appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated April 24, 2024 dismissing IA 724 of 2024[cite: 52]. Rolta Pvt. Ltd., a related party creditor, had executed an MoU to assign its admitted claim of Rs. 634 Crores to Peanance Commercial, seeking advance confirmation from the RP that the assignee would enjoy voting rights in the CoC[cite: 52]. NCLAT held that the assignment was a conditional, malafide device designed to circumvent the related-party voting bar under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC, as expounded by the Supreme Court in Phoenix ARC v. Spade Financial Services[cite: 52]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 52].

case_title: R.B. Singh & Anr. vs. Rashmi Cement Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: R.B. Singh and Alok Gaur, Erstwhile Directors/Shareholders of Bhilai Jaypee Cement Limited (Appellants/Corporate Debtors); Rashmi Cement Limited (Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor); Gunjan Poddar, IRP (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply contract for cement clinker, where Rashmi Cement Limited (RCL) made advance payments for three rakes, but Bhilai Jaypee Cement Limited (BJCL) failed to supply the third rake and did not refund the advance. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid advance principal of Rs. 1.83 Crores plus interest, totaling Rs. 1.96 Crores claimed in Section 8 notice and Section 9 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice sent on September 15, 2022; Section 9 application filed; NCLT Cuttack reserved orders on August 7, 2023; BJCL refunded the entire Rs. 1.96 Crores via RTGS on August 10, 2023; BJCL filed IAs on August 11, 2023 to bring payment on record; NCLT admitted CIRP on September 5, 2023 without addressing the IAs. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RTGS transfer receipt dated August 10, 2023 for Rs. 1.96 Crores, IAs filed on August 11, 2023 apprising the tribunal of full debt satisfaction, and RCL's email claiming unpaid GST return/ITC losses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench admitted the Section 9 petition on September 5, 2023 without considering pending interlocutory applications reporting full debt repayment prior to judgment pronouncement, prompting the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can admit a Section 9 application and initiate CIRP when the entire crystallized operational debt claimed in Form 3 and Form 5 has been fully paid and satisfied prior to the pronouncement of the order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the entire crystallized operational debt claimed in the Section 8 demand notice and Section 9 application is fully paid and satisfied prior to the admission of the petition, no 'default' subsists, and CIRP cannot be initiated. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 6 and Section 9(5) mandate that default is a sine qua non for admitting insolvency applications, and unpleaded collateral claims like unrefunded GST/ITC amounts cannot be introduced at the final stage to manufacture a default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Proof of an RTGS transfer clearing the exact principal and interest claimed in Form 3 and Form 5 prior to judgment pronouncement extinguishes the operational debt and renders the insolvency petition infructuous. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the entire operational debt stood fully satisfied before the admission order was passed, the Adjudicating Authority committed a grave error in ignoring pending satisfaction applications and admitting the petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1187 of 2023 is allowed, the impugned order dated September 5, 2023 admitting CIRP is set aside, the corporate debtor is released from CIRP, and RCL is directed to pay the IRP's fee of Rs. 1 Lakh within 15 days.
summary: R.B. Singh and Alok Gaur, erstwhile directors of Bhilai Jaypee Cement Limited, appealed against an NCLT Cuttack order dated September 5, 2023 admitting a Section 9 petition filed by Rashmi Cement Limited[cite: 53]. The appellants argued that the entire operational debt of Rs. 1.96 Crores claimed in the petition had been fully refunded via RTGS prior to the pronouncement of the order, but the Adjudicating Authority ignored their pending satisfaction applications[cite: 53]. NCLAT held that full debt satisfaction extinguished the default, making the admission unsustainable, and set aside the CIRP[cite: 53].

case_title: M/s. C Mahendra Exports Limited vs. Bank of Baroda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. C Mahendra Exports Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Bank of Baroda (Respondent/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 insolvency proceedings pending before the Adjudicating Authority, Mumbai Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an interlocutory procedural order directing production of documents). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority directed production on April 1, 2024 and June 26, 2024; appeal filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bombay High Court winding-up order referencing the existence of the corporate debtor's annual report for the financial year 2014-15. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench directed the corporate debtor on June 26, 2024 to place on record its annual report for 2014-15, prompting the corporate debtor's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority has the statutory power to direct a corporate debtor to produce relevant financial records and annual reports during the pendency of a Section 7 insolvency application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory powers under Rule 43 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 to direct any party to produce relevant documents necessary for adjudication. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act and NCLT Rule 43 grant tribunals broad procedural powers to summon records and direct document production to ascertain facts like limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where judicial records (such as a Bombay High Court winding-up order) establish the existence of a specific annual report, the tribunal can validly direct its production. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in directing the corporate debtor to produce the 2014-15 annual report, and all parties remain free to argue merits including limitation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1407 of 2024 is dismissed.
summary: M/s. C Mahendra Exports Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated June 26, 2024 directing it to place on record its annual report for the financial year 2014-15[cite: 55]. NCLAT held that tribunals are statutorily empowered under Rule 43 of the NCLT Rules and Section 424 of the Companies Act to direct parties to produce relevant documents like annual reports[cite: 55]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT noted that no final issue on limitation had been decided yet[cite: 55].

case_title: Kairav Anil Trivedi (IRP for Parenteral Drugs India Ltd.) vs. Punjab National Bank & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 760 of 2024 & I.A. No. 2623, 2730 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kairav Anil Trivedi, IRP of Parenteral Drugs India Ltd. (Appellant); Punjab National Bank & Anr. (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Parenteral Drugs India Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order dismissing a delay condonation application). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on December 4, 2023; uploaded on December 7, 2023; certified copy applied on December 15, 2023 and delivered on December 20, 2023; appeal filed on January 26, 2024 with a delay beyond the condonable statutory window. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Date of order (December 4, 2023), date of uploading (December 7, 2023), and date of appeal filing (January 26, 2024). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed an order on December 4, 2023; the IRP filed an appeal on January 26, 2024 along with an application for delay condonation (IA 2730/2024) citing medical exigencies and counting limitation from the uploading date.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can condone a delay in filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC when the total elapsed time exceeds the absolute outer limit of 30 days plus the permissible 15-day extension under Section 61(2) proviso.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The appellate tribunal's jurisdiction to condone delay under Section 61(2) proviso is strictly restricted to a maximum of 15 days following the expiration of the initial 30-day limitation period, and limitation commences from the date of the order, not the date of uploading or knowledge. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC sets a mandatory limitation framework which cannot be bypassed using general limitation principles or date-of-knowledge arguments settled in V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Limited. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Even after granting exclusions for the time taken to obtain certified copies, if the appeal is filed beyond 45 days from the order date, it is time-barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appeal was filed beyond the absolute statutory cap of 45 days, the delay condonation application cannot be entertained.
operative_order: IA No. 2730 of 2024 (delay condonation application) is dismissed, and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 760 of 2024 stands rejected as time-barred.
summary: Kairav Anil Trivedi, IRP for Parenteral Drugs India Ltd., appealed against an NCLT order dated December 4, 2023, filing the appeal on January 26, 2024[cite: 56]. NCLAT held that even after factoring in certified copy preparation time, the appeal was filed beyond the absolute outer limit of 45 days prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 56]. Reaffirming that limitation runs from the date of the order and the tribunal's power to condone delay is strictly capped at 15 days post-limitation, NCLAT dismissed the delay application and rejected the appeal[cite: 56].

case_title: Asha Apartments Pvt. Ltd. vs. Gospell Digital Technology Co. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 915 of 2024 & I.A. No. 3316, 3319 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Asha Apartments Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Creditor); Gospell Digital Technology Co. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Arun Bagaria, Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2/Incoming RP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Gospell Digital Technology Co. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order appointing a new resolution professional and directing claim verification). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority passed order on March 4, 2024 in IA No. 503 of 2024 giving the incoming RP 30 days to verify the appellant's claim; appeal filed after two months. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Adjudicating Authority's directions discharging the previous RP and appointing Arun Kisanlal Bagadia with a mandate to verify Asha Apartments' claim within 30 days. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed an order on March 4, 2024 replacing the RP and directing claim verification within 30 days; the appellant filed an appeal complaining of delay, prompting NCLAT's directions.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should interfere with an order directing a newly appointed resolution professional to verify a pending creditor claim within a stipulated timeframe.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an Adjudicating Authority directs a newly appointed resolution professional to verify a pending creditor claim within a specific timeframe, appellate interference is unwarranted provided the process is expedited. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19 and general CIRP provisions empower the Adjudicating Authority to streamline resolution professionals and ensure pending claims are duly verified from corporate debtor records. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Delays in verification caused by non-cooperation or missing records from suspended directors justify granting reasonable timeline extensions for claim processing under RP supervision. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error, and the appeal is appropriately disposed of with instructions for the RP to complete verification within two months.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 915 of 2024 is disposed of, directing the Resolution Professional to complete the claim verification process as per corporate debtor records preferably within two months.
summary: Asha Apartments Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order dated March 4, 2024 (IA 503 of 2024) which replaced the resolution professional and directed the incoming RP to verify the appellant's claim within 30 days[cite: 57]. The appellant complained that more than two months had passed without verification[cite: 57]. NCLAT disposed of the appeal by noting that the RP faced hurdles due to missing records from suspended directors and directed him to complete the verification within two months[cite: 57].

case_title: Partha Sarathy Sarkar vs. Union of India through Secretary & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Partha Sarathy Sarkar, Erstwhile Resolution Professional (Appellant/In Person); Union of India & Ors. (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process where the appellant served as the initial Resolution Professional before being replaced. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order disposing of an interlocutory application as infructuous). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: I.A. No. 463/JPR/2023 filed by erstwhile RP; new RP appointed; Adjudicating Authority passed impugned order on January 15, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: New Resolution Professional's statement before the Adjudicating Authority declining to further prosecute I.A. No. 463/JPR/2023 (an application to summon UTI officials and produce documents). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench disposed of I.A. No. 463/JPR/2023 as infructuous on January 15, 2024 after the new RP stated he did not wish to prosecute it, prompting the erstwhile RP's personal appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an erstwhile, replaced Resolution Professional has the locus standi to challenge an order disposing of an interlocutory application as infructuous when the active, incumbent Resolution Professional explicitly states he does not wish to prosecute it.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An erstwhile, replaced Resolution Professional has no independent locus standi to challenge the withdrawal or disposal of an interlocutory application when the incumbent, active Resolution Professional leading the CIRP decides not to prosecute it. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once an RP is replaced, control of ongoing litigation and procedural steps vests solely in the new RP acting for the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A statement by the new Resolution Professional declining to pursue a discovery application renders the application infructuous, precluding the former RP from contesting the decision. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal filed by the erstwhile RP lacks substance and standing, as decisions regarding the prosecution of pending applications rest with the incumbent resolution professional.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 576 of 2024 is dismissed.
summary: Partha Sarathy Sarkar, an erstwhile Resolution Professional, appealed in person against an NCLT order dated January 15, 2024 disposing of an interlocutory application (IA 463/JPR/2023) as infructuous[cite: 58]. The application had sought to summon UTI officials, but the newly appointed Resolution Professional stated he no longer wished to prosecute it[cite: 58]. NCLAT held that once an RP is replaced, the former RP cannot challenge procedural litigation decisions made by the incumbent RP, and dismissed the appeal[cite: 58].

case_title: Optinova AB vs. Bio-Med Health Care Products Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 3897 of 2024 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1359 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Optinova AB (Appellant/Operational Creditor); Bio-Med Health Care Products Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational debt dispute settled between the parties following NCLAT's earlier judgment dated May 1, 2024 which set aside the dismissal of a Section 9 application and granted 30 days for payment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid operational debt subject to mutually agreed settlement terms. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLAT judgment delivered on May 1, 2024; settlement agreement executed between the parties on May 20, 2024; IA 3897 of 2024 filed on May 28, 2024 seeking timeline extension up to August 10, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Agreement dated May 20, 2024 executed between Optinova AB and Bio-Med Health Care Products Pvt. Ltd. providing a revised payment schedule. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following NCLAT's judgment on May 1, 2024 allowing the operational creditor's appeal and giving 30 days to pay, the parties entered into a formal settlement on May 20, 2024 and filed an interlocutory application (IA 3897/2024) to take the settlement on record and extend the payment deadline.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can take a post-judgment settlement agreement on record and extend the operational debt payment deadline mutually agreed upon by the parties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal can take a post-judgment settlement agreement on record and extend payment timelines mutually agreed upon by the parties to foster amicable debt resolution under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules and inherent powers permit the tribunal to modify operational debt payment schedules to reflect out-of-court settlements reached after an appellate ruling. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Express consent from both the operational creditor and corporate debtor to an updated settlement agreement providing a revised payment schedule justifies timeline modifications. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The settlement agreement is taken on record, and the payment deadline is extended in accordance with the terms mutually agreed upon by the parties.
operative_order: I.A. No. 3897 of 2024 is allowed; the Settlement Agreement dated May 20, 2024 is taken on record, and the time for releasing payment of the unpaid operational debt is extended to August 10, 2024.
summary: Optinova AB and Bio-Med Health Care Products Pvt. Ltd. filed an interlocutory application (IA 3897 of 2024) in a disposed-of Section 9 insolvency appeal (Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1359 of 2022) to take a fresh settlement agreement on record[cite: 59]. Following NCLAT's earlier judgment on May 1, 2024 which gave 30 days to pay the operational debt, the parties executed an out-of-court settlement on May 20, 2024 extending the payment schedule to August 10, 2024[cite: 59]. NCLAT took the settlement on record and extended the payment deadline accordingly[cite: 59].

case_title: Asif Balwa vs. Bank of India Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 18 of 2024 with 1701 of 2023, 1702 of 2023, 819 of 2023, 820 of 2023 & 821 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Asif Balwa, Vinod Goenka, Shahid Balwa, Imtiyaz Javed Siddiqui, Hifzurrehman Abdullah, Nabil Yusuf Patel (Appellants/Corporate Debtors/Guarantors/Personal Guarantors); Bank of India (Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by Bank of India, resulting in Section 7 insolvency applications and Section 95 personal guarantor proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by principal borrower and guarantors under credit facilities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on July 4, 2023; OTS proposal of Rs. 387.44 Crores submitted on May 30, 2023; Bank of India approved OTS on March 21, 2024; settlement agreement and OTS approval brought on record on March 22, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement agreement, Bank of India's OTS approval letter dated March 21, 2024, and token deposit of Rs. 10 Crores in the 'No Lien Account'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeals filed against the admission of Section 7 proceedings were subsequently resolved as the parties entered into a One Time Settlement (OTS) approved by Bank of India, leading to a joint request for closing the CIRP.
legal_issues: Whether corporate insolvency resolution processes and personal guarantor insolvency proceedings should be closed when the financial creditor accepts a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal and enters into a settlement agreement with the debtors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a financial creditor accepts a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal and enters into a binding settlement agreement, ongoing insolvency and personal guarantor proceedings must be closed in accordance with the terms of settlement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Settlement of debt under an approved OTS supersedes the continuance of CIRP, fulfilling the primary objective of the IBC to revive corporate entities and resolve distressed debts consensually. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Formal acceptance of an OTS proposal by the competent authority of a financial institution together with execution of a settlement agreement provides sufficient ground to set aside admission orders. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Bank of India approved the OTS proposal, the settlement agreement is taken on record, the CIRP and Section 95 proceedings are closed, and the debtors are freed from insolvency.
operative_order: All connected appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 18 of 2024, 1701, 1702 of 2023, 819, 820, and 821 of 2023) are disposed of. The settlement agreement is taken on record, the impugned admission orders are set aside, and the CIRP against corporate and personal guarantors is closed with liberty reserved to the bank.
summary: Asif Balwa and other related corporate and personal guarantors appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders admitting Section 7 and Section 95 insolvency proceedings initiated by Bank of India[cite: 36]. During the appeal, the parties reported that Bank of India had approved a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal of Rs. 387.44 Crores on March 21, 2024[cite: 36]. NCLAT took the settlement agreement on record, set aside the admission orders, and closed the CIRP and personal guarantor proceedings[cite: 36].

case_title: Vijaypal Kishorilal Sharma vs. Amit Mittal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vijaypal Kishorilal Sharma (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Amit Mittal (Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor); Kanhaiya Maheshwari (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods or services resulting in a Section 9 application filed by Respondent No. 1 for an amount of Rs. 1,03,37,635/- (including principal of Rs. 84,19,041/- and interest at 24% p.a. from default date September 21, 2019). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Original principal of Rs. 84,19,041/-; prior to Section 9 filing, a civil suit was filed in the Bombay High Court which was decreed on December 14, 2022 for Rs. 61,08,217/- (including principal of Rs. 23,70,417/- and interest at 18% p.a. on principal from date of suit till realization, giving credit for a Rs. 34 Lakh part payment). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default date September 21, 2019; High Court suit decreed on December 14, 2022; NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted Section 9 application on March 24, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bombay High Court decree and the operational creditor's deposition in the civil suit acknowledging part payment and quantifying the remaining principal and interest at 18% p.a. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 petition on March 24, 2023[cite: 60], prompting the corporate debtor's appeal where it argued that the decreasement in claim via High Court judgment brought the total due below the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 insolvency application is maintainable when the principal debt and interest, as subsequently quantified and decreed by a civil court, fall below the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold prescribed under Section 4 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an operational creditor's claim is adjudicated and decreed by a civil court with a specific quantification of principal and interest, the adjudicated figures and interest rates bind the parties, and if the total amount falls below the statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC, the Section 9 application is not maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4 of the IBC mandates a minimum monetary threshold (originally Rs. 1 Crore) for triggering CIRP, which must be strictly satisfied based on legally recoverable and adjudicated dues. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An operational creditor's own admissions and calculations in a prior civil suit regarding principal amounts and interest rates override subsequent inflated claims in an insolvency petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the recalculated total dues based on the High Court's decreed interest rate of 18% fell short of the Rs. 1 Crore threshold, the Section 9 petition was non-maintainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 489 of 2023 is allowed, and the impugned admission order dated March 24, 2023[cite: 60] is set aside.
summary: Vijaypal Kishorilal Sharma appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated March 24, 2023[cite: 60] admitting a Section 9 application filed by Amit Mittal for over Rs. 1.03 Crores[cite: 60]. The appellant argued that a prior decree by the Bombay High Court had crystallized the principal and restricted interest to 18% p.a., bringing the total claim below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 60]. NCLAT accepted the calculation, held that the claim fell short of the statutory threshold, and set aside the admission order[cite: 60].

case_title: Devendra Singh vs. Homebuyers of Sidhartha Buildhome Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 3557 of 2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 791 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Devendra Singh (Appellant); Homebuyers of Sidhartha Buildhome Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., including Punjab National Bank and Punjab & Sind Bank (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Sidhartha Buildhome Pvt. Ltd., specifically concerning the 'Estella Project'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (application seeking correction of an inadvertent error in a previously delivered appellate judgment). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original appellate judgment delivered on February 16, 2024; rectification application (IA 3557 of 2024) filed subsequently. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC composition records for the Estella Project confirming that Punjab & Sind Bank was not a member of the Estella Project CoC, though it was part of another project (NCR Green). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Punjab National Bank filed IA No. 3557 of 2024 seeking correction of paragraph 38 of NCLAT's judgment dated February 16, 2024, which had mistakenly included Punjab & Sind Bank in the CoC of the Estella Project.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can correct an inadvertent factual error in its judgment regarding the composition of a project-specific Committee of Creditors under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal possesses inherent power to correct inadvertent errors in its judgments regarding factual aspects such as the composition of a project-specific Committee of Creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Administrative and typographical corrections can be made to ensure judgments accurately reflect undisputed factual records. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontested admissions by financial institutions regarding their non-membership in a specific project's CoC warrant the deletion of their names from directions concerning that project. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Punjab & Sind Bank was admittedly not part of the Estella Project CoC, paragraph 38 of the judgment stands corrected.
operative_order: I.A. No. 3557 of 2024 is allowed, and paragraph 38 of the judgment dated February 16, 2024 is corrected to remove references to Punjab & Sind Bank in relation to the Estella Project CoC.
summary: Punjab National Bank filed an interlocutory application (IA 3557 of 2024) seeking correction of an inadvertent error in paragraph 38 of NCLAT's judgment dated February 16, 2024[cite: 61]. The judgment had mistakenly included Punjab & Sind Bank alongside Punjab National Bank in the CoC of the Estella Project[cite: 61]. As Punjab & Sind Bank conceded it was not part of that project's CoC, NCLAT allowed the application and corrected the judgment accordingly[cite: 61].

case_title: Mr. Kamma Srinivasa Rao vs. Raghu Babu Gunturu (RP) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Kamma Srinivasa Rao, Trichy-Thanjavur Expressways Ltd. (Appellant); Raghu Babu Gunturu, RP (Respondent No. 1); National Highways Authority of India (NHAI/Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Trichy-Thanjavur Expressways Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an interlocutory order taking creditor lists on record). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order rendered by NCLT Chennai on May 29, 2024 allowing IA (IBC) 982 of 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP's application IA (IBC) 982 of 2024 taking on record lists of creditors dated February 16, 2024 and March 5, 2024, including an undecided Rs. 500 Crore claim from NHAI subject to pending arbitral proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai allowed the RP's interlocutory application on presentation without issuing notice or affording an opportunity of hearing to affected parties, prompting the appellant's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can allow an interlocutory application on presentation without issuing notice or hearing affected parties, in violation of Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and principles of natural justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority violates principles of natural justice and Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 when it allows an interlocutory application on presentation without issuing notice or hearing affected parties. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 mandates that the tribunal shall issue a show cause notice accompanied by a copy of the application and supporting documents to respondents before deciding a petition or application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Adjudicating an application that impacts creditor lists and involves major disputed claims without serving notice creates a fatal procedural defect. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the impugned order was passed ex-parte without notice or hearing in clear violation of Rule 37, it must be set aside and remanded for a fresh, reasoned decision after notice.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 240 of 2024 is allowed, the impugned order dated May 29, 2024 is set aside, IA (IBC) 982 of 2024 is restored, and the matter is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority to decide afresh after issuing notice and giving an opportunity of hearing.
summary: Mr. Kamma Srinivasa Rao of Trichy-Thanjavur Expressways Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dated May 29, 2024 allowing the RP's application (IA 982 of 2024) to take on record creditor lists containing an undecided Rs. 500 Crore claim from NHAI[cite: 63]. NCLAT Chennai held that the Adjudicating Authority committed a fundamental procedural error by allowing the application on presentation without issuing notice or hearing affected parties, in direct violation of Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules and principles of natural justice[cite: 63]. Setting aside the order, NCLAT remanded the matter back for fresh adjudication[cite: 63].

case_title: M/s. C Mahendra Exports Limited vs. Bank of Baroda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. C Mahendra Exports Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Bank of Baroda (Respondent/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 insolvency proceedings pending before the Adjudicating Authority, Mumbai Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an interlocutory procedural order directing production of documents). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority directed production on April 1, 2024 and June 26, 2024; appeal filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bombay High Court winding-up order referencing the existence of the corporate debtor's annual report for the financial year 2014-15. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench directed the corporate debtor on June 26, 2024 to place on record its annual report for 2014-15, prompting the corporate debtor's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority has the statutory power to direct a corporate debtor to produce relevant financial records and annual reports during the pendency of a Section 7 insolvency application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory powers under Rule 43 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 to direct any party to produce relevant documents necessary for adjudication. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act and NCLT Rule 43 grant tribunals broad procedural powers to summon records and direct document production to ascertain facts like limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where judicial records (such as a Bombay High Court winding-up order) establish the existence of a specific annual report, the tribunal can validly direct its production. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in directing the corporate debtor to produce the 2014-15 annual report, and all parties remain free to argue merits including limitation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1407 of 2024 is dismissed.
summary: M/s. C Mahendra Exports Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated June 26, 2024 directing it to place on record its annual report for the financial year 2014-15[cite: 64]. NCLAT held that tribunals are statutorily empowered under Rule 43 of the NCLT Rules and Section 424 of the Companies Act to direct parties to produce relevant documents like annual reports[cite: 64]. Dismissing the appeal, NCLAT noted that no final issue on limitation had been decided yet[cite: 64].

case_title: Kairav Anil Trivedi (IRP for Parenteral Drugs India Ltd.) vs. Punjab National Bank & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 760 of 2024 & I.A. No. 2623, 2730 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kairav Anil Trivedi, IRP of Parenteral Drugs India Ltd. (Appellant); Punjab National Bank & Anr. (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Parenteral Drugs India Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order dismissing a delay condonation application). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on December 4, 2023; uploaded on December 7, 2023; certified copy applied on December 15, 2023 and delivered on December 20, 2023; appeal filed on January 26, 2024 with a delay beyond the condonable statutory window. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Date of order (December 4, 2023), date of uploading (December 7, 2023), and date of appeal filing (January 26, 2024). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed an order on December 4, 2023; the IRP filed an appeal on January 26, 2024 along with an application for delay condonation (IA 2730/2024) citing medical exigencies and counting limitation from the uploading date.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can condone a delay in filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC when the total elapsed time exceeds the absolute outer limit of 30 days plus the permissible 15-day extension under Section 61(2) proviso.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The appellate tribunal's jurisdiction to condone delay under Section 61(2) proviso is strictly restricted to a maximum of 15 days following the expiration of the initial 30-day limitation period, and limitation commences from the date of the order, not the date of uploading or knowledge. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC sets a mandatory limitation framework which cannot be bypassed using general limitation principles or date-of-knowledge arguments settled in V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Limited. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Even after granting exclusions for the time taken to obtain certified copies, if the appeal is filed beyond 45 days from the order date, it is time-barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appeal was filed beyond the absolute statutory cap of 45 days, the delay condonation application cannot be entertained.
operative_order: IA No. 2730 of 2024 (delay condonation application) is dismissed, and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 760 of 2024 stands rejected as time-barred.
summary: Kairav Anil Trivedi, IRP for Parenteral Drugs India Ltd., appealed against an NCLT order dated December 4, 2023, filing the appeal on January 26, 2024[cite: 65]. NCLAT held that even after factoring in certified copy preparation time, the appeal was filed beyond the absolute outer limit of 45 days prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 65]. Reaffirming that limitation runs from the date of the order and the tribunal's power to condone delay is strictly capped at 15 days post-limitation, NCLAT dismissed the delay application and rejected the appeal[cite: 65].

case_title: Khozim Yusuf Nagarwala vs. Satyendra Prasad Khorania (Erstwhile RP of Raj Buildhome Pvt. Ltd.)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 871 of 2023 & I.A. No. 2962 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Khozim Yusuf Nagarwala (Appellant/Financial Creditor); Satyendra Prasad Khorania, Erstwhile RP of Raj Buildhome Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 insolvency proceedings filed by the financial creditor against Raj Buildhome Pvt. Ltd., which were initially admitted on May 3, 2019, but subsequently quashed and set aside by NCLAT on December 11, 2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order determining CIRP costs and fees payable to the erstwhile RP). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on May 3, 2019; NCLAT set aside CIRP on December 11, 2019; NCLT dismissed company petition on December 12, 2019; RP claimed fee of Rs. 17,68,67,767/-; NCLT passed impugned order on February 22, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP's fee and expense claims, prior NCLAT directions mandating financial creditor liability for CIRP costs, and duplicate bills submitted for certain expenses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench passed an order on February 22, 2023 in IA No. 71/JPR/2021 & Contempt Petition No. 168/JPR/2020 determining RP fees and expenses, prompting the financial creditor's appeal against the quantum and specific bill items.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to compute and determine CIRP costs and professional fees payable to an erstwhile resolution professional when a corporate debtor is released from CIRP by appellate orders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority has ample jurisdiction to examine, compute, and determine the entitlement of fees and CIRP expenses payable by a financial creditor when an appellate tribunal sets aside a Section 7 admission and directs cost recovery. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 33(2) of the CIRP Regulations and specific appellate remands empower the Adjudicating Authority to fix reasonable fees and verify expenses supported by actual records. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Adjudication of RP fees must rest strictly on verified materials and records, requiring the disallowance of duplicate or unsubstantiated bills (such as duplicate expense claims). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the Adjudicating Authority has full jurisdiction to determine fees and verified expenses, unverified or duplicate bill items must be set aside.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 871 of 2023 is disposed of; the appellant is directed to pay Rs. 7,30,000/- towards fees plus Rs. 2,41,512/- towards verified expenses (minus any amounts already paid) to the RP within four weeks.
summary: Khozim Yusuf Nagarwala appealed against an NCLT Jaipur order dated February 22, 2023 determining the professional fees and CIRP expenses payable to the erstwhile Resolution Professional after an insolvency admission was quashed[cite: 66]. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority had full jurisdiction under Regulation 33(2) and prior appellate orders to determine reasonable fees and verified expenses[cite: 66]. However, NCLAT set aside unsubstantiated duplicate bill items and modified the payable amount to Rs. 7,30,000 in fees plus Rs. 2,41,512 in verified expenses[cite: 66].

case_title: Arvind Garg (Liquidator of Moser Baer Solar Ltd.) vs. Palika Towns LLP & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1207 of 2024 & I.A. Nos. 4323 & 4324 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arvind Garg, Liquidator of Moser Baer Solar Ltd. (Appellant); Palika Towns LLP (Respondent No. 1); Liquidator of Moser Baer India Limited (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings of Moser Baer Solar Ltd. (MBSL) involving unutilized utilities and machinery lying idle since 2018, subject to rival ownership claims between MBSL and Moser Baer India Limited (MBIL). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an interlocutory order directing asset sale through an Advocate Commissioner). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority passed interim suggestions order on March 6, 2024; liquidator filed response on April 17, 2024; impugned order passed on June 12, 2024 in IA 5733/2023 and IA 1802/2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Advocate Commissioner suggestions regarding scrap value and escrow accounts for idle utilities, and pending substantive applications (IA 581/2023) regarding going-concern sale and asset ownership disputes. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi passed an order on June 12, 2024 permitting an Advocate Commissioner to sell unutilized utilities and deposit proceeds in an escrow account, prompting the liquidator's appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can direct the sale of unutilized liquidation assets through an Advocate Commissioner before adjudicating pending substantive applications concerning going-concern sale and conflicting ownership claims over the liquidation estate.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority cannot direct the piecemeal sale of liquidation assets through an Advocate Commissioner without first deciding pending substantive applications regarding going-concern sales and rival ownership disputes over the liquidation estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Liquidation asset sales must strictly follow the statutory framework of the IBC under liquidator supervision, ensuring all estate ownership and going-concern questions are resolved beforehand. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Premature orders directing asset sales while foundational ownership applications (IA 581/2023) remain undecided are legally unsustainable and liable to be set aside. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because core ownership and going-concern sale applications were pending, the direction for sale by an Advocate Commissioner was premature and must be set aside for a comprehensive decision.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1207 of 2024 is allowed, the impugned order dated June 12, 2024 is set aside, and IA 5733/2023, IA 1802/2024, IA 581/2023, and related liquidator applications are revived before the Adjudicating Authority for expedited disposal within 6 months.
summary: Arvind Garg, Liquidator of Moser Baer Solar Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order dated June 12, 2024 which permitted an Advocate Commissioner to sell unutilized utilities and deposit proceeds in an escrow account[cite: 67]. NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in ordering asset sales before adjudicating pending foundational applications concerning going-concern sales and rival ownership claims between MBSL and MBIL[cite: 67]. Setting aside the order, NCLAT remanded all related interlocutory applications for a joint, expedited decision within six months[cite: 67].

case_title: Vijaypal Kishorilal Sharma vs. Amit Mittal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vijaypal Kishorilal Sharma (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); Amit Mittal (Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor); Kanhaiya Maheshwari (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods or services resulting in a Section 9 application filed by Respondent No. 1 for an amount of Rs. 1,03,37,635/- (including principal of Rs. 84,19,041/- and interest at 24% p.a. from default date September 21, 2019). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Original principal of Rs. 84,19,041/-; prior to Section 9 filing, a civil suit was filed in the Bombay High Court which was decreed on December 14, 2022 for Rs. 61,08,217/- (including principal of Rs. 23,70,417/- and interest at 18% p.a. on principal from date of suit till realization, giving credit for a Rs. 34 Lakh part payment). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default date September 21, 2019; High Court suit decreed on December 14, 2022; NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV admitted Section 9 application on March 24, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bombay High Court decree and the operational creditor's deposition in the civil suit acknowledging part payment and quantifying the remaining principal and interest at 18% p.a. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 petition on March 24, 2023[cite: 68], prompting the corporate debtor's appeal where it argued that the decreasement in claim via High Court judgment brought the total due below the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 insolvency application is maintainable when the principal debt and interest, as subsequently quantified and decreed by a civil court, fall below the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold prescribed under Section 4 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an operational creditor's claim is adjudicated and decreed by a civil court with a specific quantification of principal and interest, the adjudicated figures and interest rates bind the parties, and if the total amount falls below the statutory threshold under Section 4 of the IBC, the Section 9 application is not maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4 of the IBC mandates a minimum monetary threshold (originally Rs. 1 Crore) for triggering CIRP, which must be strictly satisfied based on legally recoverable and adjudicated dues. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An operational creditor's own admissions and calculations in a prior civil suit regarding principal amounts and interest rates override subsequent inflated claims in an insolvency petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the recalculated total dues based on the High Court's decreed interest rate of 18% fell short of the Rs. 1 Crore threshold, the Section 9 petition was non-maintainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 489 of 2023 is allowed, and the impugned admission order dated March 24, 2023[cite: 68] is set aside.
summary: Vijaypal Kishorilal Sharma appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated March 24, 2023[cite: 68] admitting a Section 9 application filed by Amit Mittal for over Rs. 1.03 Crores[cite: 68]. The appellant argued that a prior decree by the Bombay High Court had crystallized the principal and restricted interest to 18% p.a., bringing the total claim below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 68]. NCLAT accepted the calculation, held that the claim fell short of the statutory threshold, and set aside the admission order[cite: 68].

case_title: Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association vs. Mr. Ashish Chhawchharia (Resolution Professional of Jet Airways (India) Ltd.)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1705 of 2023 & I.A. No. 6137 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association (Appellant); Mr. Ashish Chhawchharia, Resolution Professional of Jet Airways (India) Ltd. (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Jet Airways (India) Ltd., where an Asset Preservation Team (APT) consisting of 103 employees was constituted in June 2019 to handle compliances and asset preservation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (appeal arises from an order dismissing an application seeking directions against the RP regarding lump-sum payments made to APT members). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on June 20, 2019; APT formed in June/July 2019; CoC approved CIRP costs including APT payments on July 19, 2019; MA No. 3387 of 2019 filed by association; NCLT Mumbai passed impugned order on September 26, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC approval of operational budget for APT payments, waiver agreements signed by 103 APT employees giving up pre-CIRP dues totaling approximately Rs. 7.9 Crores in exchange for lump-sum payments of Rs. 5.4 Crores, and List of Creditors version 3A reflecting employee claims. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Court Room No. 1 dismissed MA No. 3387 of 2019 on September 26, 2019/2023, prompting the association's appeal challenging the legitimacy of APT payments and seeking the RP's personal liability.
legal_issues: Whether payments made to an Asset Preservation Team (APT) during CIRP with CoC approval and accompanied by a waiver of pre-CIRP dues constitute double payment or illegal diversion of funds, and whether the Resolution Professional can be held personally liable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Payments made to key employees forming an Asset Preservation Team during CIRP with the explicit approval of the CoC as operational/CIRP costs are valid, and obtaining waivers of pre-CIRP claims in exchange for such payments benefits the corporate debtor without causing double payment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 and CIRP cost provisions empower the resolution professional to incur necessary expenses for asset preservation and value maximization during insolvency. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear affidavits and accounting records demonstrating that 103 APT employees waived their pre-CIRP salary claims in exchange for operational lump-sum payments dispel allegations of double payment or preferential treatment. 4.
