DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the APT payments were approved by the CoC as CIRP costs and secured valuable waivers for the estate, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the association's application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1705 of 2023 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Jet Aircraft Maintenance Engineers Welfare Association appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dated September 26, 2023 dismissing MA 3387 of 2019[cite: 69]. The association challenged lump-sum payments made by the RP to 103 employees who formed an Asset Preservation Team during CIRP, alleging double payment[cite: 69]. NCLAT held, based on detailed affidavits from the RP, that the CoC had approved the payments as CIRP costs and that the 103 employees had validly waived their pre-CIRP claims exceeding the payout, resulting in a net benefit to the corporate debtor[cite: 69]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 69].

case_title: Supertech Realtors Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Supertech Realtors Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. (Appellants/Appellants in Company Appeal); Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. & Anr. (Respondents); IRP (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 rejected by NCLT. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law appeal). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed impugned order on February 7, 2024; Appellant No. 1 admitted into insolvency on June 12, 2024; Appellant No. 2 admitted into insolvency on June 4, 2024; appeal heard in July 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admission of insolvency orders against both appellant companies during the pendency of the appeal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Supertech Realtors and another appealed against an NCLT order dated February 7, 2024 rejecting their Section 213 company petition; during appellate hearings, it was revealed that both appellants had entered insolvency, prompting the closure of the appeal with liberty to revive.
legal_issues: Whether a company law appeal filed under Section 213 of the Companies Act can be prosecuted by erstwhile management when the corporate appellants have subsequently been admitted into corporate insolvency resolution processes.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When corporate appellants are admitted into insolvency under the IBC, management control vests in the Interim Resolution Professional, and erstwhile management lacks instructions or standing to prosecute company law appeals without IRP authorization. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 17 of the IBC suspends the powers of the board of directors upon insolvency commencement, transferring authority over company litigation to the IRP/RP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure of erstwhile management to obtain instructions or authorization from the appointed IRP to continue an appeal requires closing the proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because both appellants were admitted into insolvency and no authorization from their respective IRPs was forthcoming, the appeal is closed with liberty to revive if appropriate occasions arise.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 103 of 2024 is dismissed/closed, with liberty granted to the appellants to revive the appeal in accordance with law if such an occasion arises.
summary: Supertech Realtors Pvt. Ltd. and another appealed against an NCLT order dated February 7, 2024 rejecting their application under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 71]. During appellate proceedings, it was noted that both appellant companies had subsequently been admitted into insolvency (on June 4 and June 12, 2024)[cite: 71]. As erstwhile management had no instructions from the respective IRPs to prosecute the appeal, NCLAT closed the appeal with liberty to revive if circumstances warranted[cite: 71].

case_title: Employees' Provident Fund Organization vs. Jaykumar Pesumal Arlani
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1062 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1065 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: In Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1062 of 2024, the Appellant is Employees' Provident Fund Organization (EPFO) Regional Office, Vashi, Navi Mumbai (Statutory Operational Creditor), the Corporate Debtor is M/s Decent Laminates Pvt. Ltd., and the Respondent is Jaykumar Pesumal Arlani (Resolution Professional). In Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1065 of 2024, the Appellant is EPFO Regional Office, Vashi, Navi Mumbai, the Corporate Debtor is Apollo Soyuz Electricals P. Ltd., and the Respondents are Sanjay Kumar Lalit (Resolution Professional) & Anr. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matters involve statutory provident fund contributions, interest under Section 7Q, and damages under Section 14B of the Employees' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 assessed against the Corporate Debtors for pre-CIRP employment periods. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: For Decent Laminates Pvt. Ltd., an initial claim of Rs. 76,09,494/- was lodged on 11.05.2023, subsequently revised to Rs. 1,58,90,685/- on 31.08.2023 following orders under Sections 14B and 7Q dated 16.08.2023, totaling Rs. 2,35,00,179/-. For Apollo Soyuz Electricals P. Ltd., an assessment order was passed on 29.08.2022 determining statutory PF dues of Rs. 10,89,938/-. Specific defaults occurred during pre-CIRP periods prior to CIRP initiation on 03.05.2021 and 12.07.2021, respectively. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In Decent Laminates, CIRP commenced on 03.05.2021; Section 7A summons were issued on 22.06.2022; Section 14B and 7Q show-cause notice was issued on 09.05.2023; claims were submitted on 11.05.2023 and 31.08.2023; the RP rejected the claim on 05.09.2023. In Apollo Soyuz, CIRP commenced on 12.07.2021; IRP sent letter inviting claims on 18.10.2021; CoC approved the Resolution Plan on 23.06.2022; IRP informed EPFO of plan approval on 12.07.2022; Section 7A assessment order was passed on 29.08.2022; IA No. 743 of 2023 was filed on 30.01.2023; NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the Resolution Plan on 13.04.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Summons and assessment orders under Sections 7A, 14B, and 7Q of the EPF & MP Act issued during the currency of the moratorium; correspondence between the RPs and EPFO establishing that EPFO had knowledge of CIRP initiation (via emails dated 11.06.2021 and 16.06.2021 in Decent Laminates, and letters dated 18.10.2021 and 12.07.2022 in Apollo Soyuz) prior to finalizing assessments and lodging claims post-CoC plan approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In Decent Laminates, EPFO filed IA No. 1111(AHM)/2023 in CP(IB) 387 of 2020 seeking admission of Rs. 2,35,00,179/-, which NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed on 19.10.2023 because assessment orders were passed during moratorium and the claim was submitted belatedly after CoC approval. In Apollo Soyuz, EPFO filed IA No. 743 of 2023 in CP(IB) 3484(MB)/2019 seeking admission of Rs. 10,89,938/-, which NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed on 22.08.2023 holding the assessment order dated 29.08.2022 void under Section 14 moratorium and barred due to approval of the plan by CoC.
legal_issues: 1. Whether after imposition of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, assessment proceedings can be carried on by the EPFO under Section 7A, 14B and 7Q of the EPF & MP Act, 1952. 2. Whether any claim on the basis of assessment, subsequent to imposition of moratorium, can be admitted in the CIRP. 3. Whether claims, which were filed by the Appellant(s), subsequent to the approval of Resolution Plan by the CoC, could have been admitted in the CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon declaration of moratorium under Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC, an absolute statutory freeze prohibits the institution or continuation of any proceedings, including quasi-judicial statutory assessment proceedings that create fresh pecuniary liabilities against the Corporate Debtor, during the CIRP. In contrast, under Section 33(5) during liquidation, the statutory bar applies only to a 'suit or other legal proceeding', which does not bar statutory assessments. Consequently, any assessment completed in violation of Section 14 moratorium is void, and no claim based on such post-moratorium assessments or lodged after approval of a resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors can be admitted in CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted the word 'proceedings' in Section 14(1)(a) broadly as unqualified by civil court constraints, covering any proceedings that deplete debtor assets or impose liabilities, intentionally distinguished from the restrictive phrase 'suit or other legal proceeding' used in Section 33(5) of the IBC and Section 446(1) of the Companies Act, 1956. By virtue of Section 238 of the IBC, Section 14 moratorium acts as an absolute protective shield to preserve corporate assets as a going concern, overriding conflicting provisions of the EPF & MP Act during CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court applied a strict chronological and statutory-temporal bar test: examining whether quasi-judicial assessment orders were finalized after the insolvency commencement date without statutory sanction, and whether claims were lodged prior to approval of the resolution plan by the CoC. Relying on RPS Infrastructure Ltd. v. Mukul Kumar, post-moratorium assessments and post-CoC plan approval filings were held legally untenable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that EPFO lacked jurisdiction to continue or conclude assessment proceedings under Sections 7A, 14B, and 7Q during the Section 14 moratorium, that claims founded upon prohibited assessments cannot be admitted in CIRP, and that belated claims lodged post-CoC approval are impermissible, thereby justifying dismissal of both appeals.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1062 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1065 of 2024 are dismissed. Pending Interlocutory Applications, if any, are disposed of. There shall be no order as to costs.
summary: The EPFO appealed against orders of NCLT Ahmedabad and Mumbai dismissing its applications for admission of provident fund claims of Rs. 2.35 crores and Rs. 10.89 lakhs against Decent Laminates Pvt. Ltd. and Apollo Soyuz Electricals P. Ltd., respectively. In both cases, EPFO finalized statutory assessments under Sections 7A, 14B, and 7Q of the EPF & MP Act during the CIRP moratorium and submitted claims after the Committee of Creditors approved resolution plans. The NCLAT held that Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC imposes an absolute statutory freeze barring continuation or completion of assessment proceedings during CIRP, unlike Section 33(5) during liquidation. Relying on RPS Infrastructure, belated claims submitted after CoC approval cannot be admitted. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Ms. Vineeta Maheshwari vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ms. Vineeta Maheshwari, erstwhile Resolution Professional (RP) for Corporate Debtor Raj Rayon Industries Limited and Resolution Professional appointed in insolvency proceedings against Personal Guarantor Gourishankar Poddar. Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Gourishankar Poddar (Personal Guarantor/Erstwhile Director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working capital and term loan facilities extended by SBI to Raj Rayon Industries Limited, secured by personal guarantee agreements executed by Gourishankar Poddar on 10.07.2013 and 29.03.2014 securing limits enhanced up to Rs. 398.64 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor was declared NPA on 30.11.2013; recall notice dated 18.01.2018 demanded Rs. 998.52 crores (default occurring on 25.01.2018); statutory demand notice dated 08.03.2021 under Rule 7(1) demanded Rs. 1854 crores inclusive of accrued interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Personal Guarantor resigned on 06.03.2014 (accepted 18.03.2014); SBI issued recall notice on 18.01.2018; Section 7 CIRP admitted against CD on 23.01.2020; SBI issued Form B Demand Notice under Rule 7(1) on 08.03.2021; Guarantor replied on 25.03.2021; SBI filed Section 95 petition on 24.03.2021; RP submitted Section 99 Report on 19.10.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 99 Report dated 19.10.2021 wherein the RP reproduced an event list from SBI's Section 95 petition containing an inadvertent typographical error stating that guarantor Gourishankar Poddar executed a revival letter dated 06.02.2016, accompanied by an explicit disclaimer stating that the list was framed strictly as per information available in SBI's application; SBI acknowledged the typographical error and tendered an apology before the Appellate Tribunal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in CP (IB) No. 80 (AHM) 2021, vide order dated 23.02.2024, dismissed SBI's Section 95 petition and in paragraph 13(k) made adverse observations against the RP for allegedly making a false statement regarding execution of the revival letter, directing an inquiry by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) without issuing notice or hearing the RP.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in making adverse observations against the Resolution Professional and referring her conduct to the IBBI for inquiry without affording an opportunity of being heard in accordance with the principles of natural justice. 2. Whether the inadvertent reproduction of an erroneous event list from the creditor's application with an explicit disclaimer constituted deliberate false statement or professional misconduct by the Resolution Professional.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adverse remarks, strictures, or directions for regulatory inquiry cannot be recorded by a judicial or quasi-judicial authority against an insolvency professional or officer of the court without issuing a show-cause notice and affording an effective opportunity of hearing, as doing so violates fundamental principles of natural justice. Where an inaccuracy in a statutory report is bona fide, non-deliberate, and accompanied by an express disclaimer citing reliance on creditor-provided pleadings, such remarks are legally unsustainable and liable to be expunged. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The reporting duty of a Resolution Professional under Section 99 of the IBC requires collation and examination of material, but reproduction of dates from creditor filings does not constitute making a deliberate 'false statement' under regulatory standards when accompanied by a source disclaimer and absent mala fides. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated whether the RP acted with deliberate dishonesty or mala fides by examining the Section 99 report's explicit disclaimer, the source pleadings of the Financial Creditor where the error originated, and the concession and apology tendered by the Financial Creditor confirming the typographical error was solely at its behest. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Adjudicating Authority condemned the RP without hearing her explanation and overlooked the explicit disclaimer demonstrating the mistake was non-deliberate and not mala fide, the adverse findings and IBBI referral in paragraph 13(k) violated natural justice, requiring the appeal to be allowed and all adverse remarks expunged.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 663 of 2024 is allowed. All adverse remarks against the Appellant in Para 13(k) of the impugned order dated 23.02.2024 are expunged. The Registry is directed to send a copy of this order to the IBBI not to proceed with the enquiry against the Appellant. Pending Interlocutory Applications, if any, are closed. No order as to costs.
summary: Resolution Professional Ms. Vineeta Maheshwari appealed against the order dated 23.02.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad in CP (IB) No. 80 (AHM) 2021, which dismissed SBI's Section 95 petition and passed adverse observations in paragraph 13(k) referring her conduct to IBBI for inquiry. The NCLT alleged she made a false statement that personal guarantor Gourishankar Poddar signed a debt revival letter dated 06.02.2016. The NCLAT observed that the error was non-deliberate, originated from SBI's petition, and was accompanied by an explicit disclaimer in the RP's Section 99 report. Holding that the NCLT violated principles of natural justice by condemning the RP without affording her a hearing, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, expunged all adverse remarks, and directed IBBI not to proceed.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Gourishankar Poddar & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Gourishankar Poddar (Personal Guarantor and erstwhile Chairman/Managing Director of the Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 2 is Ms. Vineeta Maheshwari (Resolution Professional for Corporate Debtor Raj Rayon Industries Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Raj Rayon Industries Limited availed term loan and working capital credit facilities from SBI starting in 1999, secured by Working Capital Consortium Agreements and Joint Deeds of Hypothecation. On 10.07.2013, Gourishankar Poddar executed an irrevocable, unconditional, continuing Deed of Guarantee securing enhanced limits of Rs. 292 crores under the 6th Supplemental Consortium Agreement. On 29.03.2014, he executed a second Deed of Guarantee containing continuing coverage clauses and an explicit waiver of rights under Section 133 of the Indian Contract Act. The 7th Supplemental Consortium Agreement dated 25.07.2014 restructured facilities to Rs. 106.64 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor's account was classified as NPA on 30.11.2013. On 18.01.2018, SBI issued a Recall Notice demanding payment of Rs. 998.52 crores outstanding as of 31.12.2017 plus interest and costs within 7 days, resulting in default on 25.01.2018. Subsequent statutory Demand Notice dated 08.03.2021 demanded Rs. 1854 crores inclusive of accrued interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Gourishankar Poddar resigned as director on 06.03.2014 (accepted 18.03.2014); sent guarantee revocation letters on 24.03.2014, 01.04.2014, 02.04.2014, and 24.04.2014; SBI rejected revocation vide letter dated 12.03.2014; CD executed Revival Letter on 06.02.2016; SBI issued Recall Notice on 18.01.2018 (default on 25.01.2018); SBI filed OA No. 185 of 2018 before DRT-II Ahmedabad on 15.02.2018; Section 7 CIRP admitted against CD on 23.01.2020; SBI issued Form B Demand Notice under Rule 7(1) on 08.03.2021; Guarantor replied on 25.03.2021; SBI filed Section 95 petition on 24.03.2021; CD's resolution plan was approved on 05.10.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deeds of Guarantee dated 10.07.2013 (Clauses 2, 8, 11, 12, 14, 19, 26) and 29.03.2014 (Clauses 5, 14, 26) establishing irrevocable and continuing guarantee liabilities, waiver of Section 133 protections against facility variations, and stipulations that CD acknowledgments constitute agency acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act; balance confirmation letter dated 08.08.2016 and account ledger reflecting last transaction on 03.02.2017; DRT-II Ahmedabad order-sheets in OA No. 185/2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed CP (IB) No. 80 (AHM) 2021 under Section 95 of the IBC against Gourishankar Poddar. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed the petition on 23.02.2024 holding that the guarantee was revoked under Section 130 of the Contract Act, that non-signing of the revival letter dated 06.02.2016 discharged guarantor liability, and that the petition was barred by limitation.
legal_issues: 1. Whether unilateral revocation of a continuing guarantee by a personal guarantor through resignation and intimation letters is legally valid when the deed of guarantee is express, unconditional, and irrevocable, and has not been released by the creditor. 2. Whether subsequent variations, extensions, or restructuring of credit facilities without the guarantor's signature on a revival letter discharge the guarantor under Section 133 of the Indian Contract Act when the guarantee deed contains express waivers. 3. Whether the Section 95 insolvency resolution petition against the personal guarantor was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unconditional and irrevocable continuing guarantee cannot be unilaterally revoked by a guarantor under Section 130 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 without the express consent or release by the creditor; resignation from the corporate debtor's directorship does not absolve personal guarantee liability. Where a guarantor explicitly waives statutory protections under Section 133 of the Contract Act, subsequent variations or restructuring of the debtor's debt do not discharge the surety, and the surety remains bound up to the agreed or beneficial outstanding liability. Under the Limitation Act, 1963, limitation against a personal guarantor commences upon issuance of a specific demand notice invoking the guarantee; additionally, acknowledgments of debt by the principal borrower bind the guarantor under Section 18, and limitation is extended by statutory Covid-19 exclusion periods. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal interpreted Sections 128, 130, and 133 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 alongside Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963, holding that party autonomy permits contractual waiver of Section 133 protections, and that continuing guarantees under Section 129 survive until full debt discharge. Under Section 95 of the IBC read with Rule 7, the cause of action crystallizes upon default following statutory demand. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict contractual construction of express guarantee terms (Clauses 2, 8, 12, 14, 19, and 26 of 2013/2014 deeds) establishing irrevocability, continuing coverage, agency acknowledgment, and Section 133 waiver, evaluated alongside the chronology of invocation (recall notice dated 18.01.2018, default on 25.01.2018, demand notice dated 08.03.2021) and Supreme Court Covid-19 limitation exclusion orders. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The guarantor's unilateral letters did not revoke the irrevocable guarantees; variations in credit facilities did not discharge liability in light of explicit contractual waivers; and the Section 95 petition was filed well within limitation (having accrued on 25.01.2018 and benefited from Covid-19 exclusion), thereby vitiating the Adjudicating Authority's dismissal and necessitating restoration of the insolvency petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 689 of 2024 is allowed, and the impugned order dated 23.02.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench is set aside. CP (IB) No. 80 (AHM) 2021 is restored to the file of the Adjudicating Authority. The parties are directed to appear before the Tribunal on 16.01.2025. Pending Interlocutory Applications, if any, are closed. No order as to costs.
summary: State Bank of India appealed against an order dated 23.02.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad dismissing its Section 95 insolvency petition against personal guarantor Gourishankar Poddar for credit facilities availed by Corporate Debtor Raj Rayon Industries Limited. The NCLT had dismissed the petition holding the guarantee was revoked upon resignation and the claim was time-barred. The NCLAT set aside the order and restored the petition, holding that an unconditional and irrevocable continuing guarantee cannot be unilaterally revoked without the creditor's consent. Furthermore, contractual waivers of Section 133 of the Indian Contract Act prevent discharge upon loan restructuring, and the Section 95 petition was filed well within limitation computed from demand invocation and Covid-19 exclusion periods.

case_title: Super Floorings Pvt. Ltd. vs. Napin Impex Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1928 of 2024 & I.A. No. 7115 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Super Floorings Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Purchaser) and the Respondent is Napin Impex Limited (Operational Creditor/Supplier), a manufacturer and exporter of PVC vinyl floorings, multipurpose sheets, and insulation products[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of PVC vinyl floorings, multipurpose sheets, and insulation products by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor under various invoices raised during the period from 03.01.2018 to 16.08.2018, with invoices stipulated to be payable within 3 days[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed operational debt was Rs. 2,14,16,735/-[cite: 4]; payments were made from time to time, with the last part-payment of Rs. 3,00,000/- made on 26.08.2019 via bank transfer, which was treated as the date of default[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a Section 8 demand notice on 16.09.2022 demanding Rs. 2,14,16,735/-[cite: 4]; the Corporate Debtor replied to the demand notice on 28.09.2022[cite: 4]; the Section 9 application was filed on 29.11.2023[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor's ledger account showing periodic payments and a bank receipt entry of Rs. 3,00,000/- on 26.08.2019[cite: 4]; written admission and acknowledgment in paragraph 3 of the Corporate Debtor's reply dated 28.09.2022 expressly admitting that the last payment towards the price of goods was made on 26.08.2019[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Napin Impex Ltd. filed Section 9 application CP (IB) No. 23/Chd/Hry/2024 on 29.11.2023[cite: 4]. The Corporate Debtor raised a preliminary objection that the application was barred by limitation under Article 137[cite: 4]. The NCLT Chandigarh Bench (Court-I) vide order dated 05.07.2024 rejected the objection, holding the application to be within limitation by extending limitation from 26.08.2019 under Section 19 of the Limitation Act and applying the Supreme Court's Suo Motu Covid-19 extension order[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether the Operational Creditor was entitled to the benefit of Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to extend the limitation period from the date of the last part-payment (26.08.2019) when acknowledged in writing in the Corporate Debtor's reply to the Section 8 demand notice, thereby bringing the Section 9 application within limitation under Article 137 alongside Covid-19 exclusion orders[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a fresh period of limitation is computed from the date a part-payment on account of a debt is made, provided such payment occurs before the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation and is acknowledged in writing signed by the payer; the written acknowledgment need not be contemporaneous with the payment and may come into existence subsequently before the filing of the petition, including in a written reply to a statutory demand notice[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 applications under the IBC are governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, where limitation runs from the date the right to apply accrues upon default[cite: 4]. The bench held that Section 19 requires two cumulative conditions: (i) payment made within the prescribed period of limitation, and (ii) an acknowledgment of payment in writing signed by the debtor[cite: 4]. Following Shanti Conductors and Sant Lal Mahton, while payment must be made within the 3-year limitation period, the statute does not require that the signed written acknowledgment itself must also be made within that initial 3-year period, so long as it exists at or before the filing of the petition[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal verified whether the payment of Rs. 3,00,000/- on 26.08.2019 occurred within three years of the 2018 invoices and whether it was acknowledged in signed writing; the written admission in paragraph 3 of the Corporate Debtor's reply dated 28.09.2022 to the Section 8 notice constituted valid signed written acknowledgment under Section 19[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because both conditions of Section 19 were satisfied, limitation ran afresh from 26.08.2019; after excluding 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 under the Supreme Court's Suo Motu Covid order, the balance limitation expired on 10.08.2024, making the application filed on 29.11.2023 timely and justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 4].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1928 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 4]. Pending Interlocutory Applications, if any, are closed[cite: 4]. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 4].
summary: Corporate Debtor Super Floorings Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Chandigarh Bench's order dated 05.07.2024 rejecting its preliminary objection that Napin Impex Ltd.'s Section 9 IBC application was time-barred[cite: 4]. The Operational Creditor supplied goods under invoices from January to August 2018, and received a last payment of Rs. 3 lakhs via bank transfer on 26.08.2019, which the Corporate Debtor admitted in its reply dated 28.09.2022 to the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 4]. The NCLAT held that under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963, part-payment made within limitation and acknowledged in writing—even in a subsequent demand notice reply—renews limitation[cite: 4]. Factoring in the Supreme Court's Covid-19 exclusion period, the petition filed on 29.11.2023 was timely, leading to dismissal of the appeal[cite: 4].

case_title: Anita Goyal vs. Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2282 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2283 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Anita Goyal (in Comp. App. 2282/2024) and Ayush Goel (in Comp. App. 2283/2024), Personal Guarantors[cite: 5]. Respondent No. 1 is Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Debenture Trustee)[cite: 5]. Respondent No. 2 is Vikram Bajaj (Resolution Professional)[cite: 5]. The Principal Borrower/Corporate Debtor is Nivaya ASL Pvt. Ltd., an SPV incorporated to finance the resolution of Allied Strips Ltd[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debenture subscription/financial credit facilities extended by Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. to Nivaya ASL Pvt. Ltd., secured by personal guarantees executed by Anita Goyal and Ayush Goel[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayment occurred by Nivaya ASL Pvt. Ltd., leading to invocation of personal guarantees and filing of insolvency petitions under Section 95 against both guarantors[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Vistra ITCL filed petitions under Section 95; NCLT appointed RP Vikram Bajaj on 29.04.2024; earlier appeals challenging RP appointment were dismissed by NCLAT on 19.07.2024; RP submitted report recommending admission; NCLT admitted Section 95 petitions under Section 100 on 04.12.2024[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-C submitted by the Resolution Professional conveying statutory consent and certifying no disciplinary proceedings were pending[cite: 5]; deeds of personal guarantee; Section 99 Report recommending admission of insolvency resolution process against the Personal Guarantors[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Vistra ITCL filed CP(IB) No. 214/(PB)/2024 against Anita Goyal and CP(IB) No. 213/(PB)/2024 against Ayush Goel under Section 95[cite: 5]. The guarantors objected, contending NCLT lacked jurisdiction as no CIRP or liquidation was pending against Corporate Debtor Nivaya ASL Pvt. Ltd. and that DRT had exclusive jurisdiction under Section 179[cite: 5]. NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi admitted both applications on 04.12.2024 under Section 100, which was challenged in these appeals[cite: 5].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has jurisdiction under Section 60(1) of the IBC to entertain an application under Section 95 initiating insolvency resolution against a personal guarantor of a corporate debtor when no CIRP or liquidation proceeding is pending against the principal corporate debtor[cite: 5]. 2. Whether the appointment of the Resolution Professional by the Adjudicating Authority violated Section 97(3) of the IBC by relying on Form-C and IBBI panel guidelines[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 60(1) of the IBC, the National Company Law Tribunal has exclusive territorial jurisdiction over insolvency resolution and liquidation of corporate persons, including corporate debtors and personal guarantors thereof, irrespective of whether an insolvency resolution process or liquidation proceeding is currently pending against the corporate debtor[cite: 5]. Section 60(2) is supplemental and without prejudice to Section 60(1), and the jurisdiction of the Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 179(1) is expressly subject to Section 60[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The words 'Without prejudice to sub-section (1)' in Section 60(2) do not cut down the generality of Section 60(1); sub-section (2) merely serves as an allocation provision requiring that when a CIRP is already pending before a particular NCLT bench, the guarantor's proceedings must be filed before that identical bench[cite: 5]. In Section 179(1), the opening phrase 'Subject to the provisions of section 60' subordinates DRT jurisdiction over individuals to NCLT's exclusive jurisdiction over personal guarantors to corporate debtors under Section 60(1)[cite: 5]. Furthermore, appointment of an RP based on Form-C and an IBBI-shared panel complies fully with Section 97(3) read with Rule 8 of the 2019 Rules[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following the Supreme Court's decisions in Lalit Kumar Jain and Mahendra Kumar Jajodia, the court tested whether the existence of an ongoing CIRP against the corporate debtor is a condition precedent to invoking Section 95 against a personal guarantor before the NCLT, answering conclusively in the negative[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT has complete jurisdiction under Section 60(1) to entertain Section 95 applications against personal guarantors regardless of whether proceedings are pending against the corporate debtor, and the RP was lawfully appointed, warranting dismissal of both appeals[cite: 5].
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2282 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2283 of 2024 are dismissed[cite: 5]. The order dated 04.12.2024 passed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi admitting the applications under Section 100 is affirmed[cite: 5]. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 5].
summary: Personal Guarantors Anita Goyal and Ayush Goel appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench's order dated 04.12.2024 admitting Section 95 IBC insolvency applications filed by Financial Creditor Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd. under Section 100[cite: 5]. The Appellants contended that NCLT lacked jurisdiction under Section 60(2) because no CIRP or liquidation proceeding was pending against the Corporate Debtor, Nivaya ASL Pvt. Ltd., and that jurisdiction lay before the DRT under Section 179[cite: 5]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that Section 60(1) confers plenary jurisdiction on NCLT over personal guarantors of corporate debtors irrespective of pending CIRP against the corporate debtor, since Section 60(2) is supplemental and Section 179 is expressly subject to Section 60[cite: 5].

case_title: Canara Bank vs. Sh. Vivek Kumar, Resolution Professional of M/s AVJ Developers (India) Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Canara Bank (Lender/Financial Creditor)[cite: 6]. The Corporate Debtor is M/s AVJ Developers (India) Private Limited (Real Estate Developer/Builder)[cite: 6]. The Respondent is Sh. Vivek Kumar (Resolution Professional, replacing erstwhile RP Anil Tayal)[cite: 6]. The Intervenor is the suspended director of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Canara Bank disbursed housing loans totaling Rs. 17.46 Crores directly to the Corporate Debtor on behalf of individual homebuyers for purchasing flats in the AVJ Heights project[cite: 6]. The transactions were executed through tripartite agreements among Canara Bank, individual borrowers, and the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on construction and failed to deliver possession of the dwelling units[cite: 6]. Canara Bank filed a total claim of Rs. 17.46 Crores as of 21.10.2019 for 59 accounts, later pursued for 32 defaulting accounts before NCLT[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against Corporate Debtor on 21.10.2019[cite: 6]; Canara Bank filed Form C claim on 25.02.2021[cite: 6]; CoC approved resolution plan on 11.10.2021[cite: 6]; RP filed plan approval application IA No. 5385/2021 on 09.11.2021[cite: 6]; erstwhile RP rejected Bank's claim on 01.09.2022[cite: 6]; Canara Bank filed IA No. 836/2023 before NCLT[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tripartite agreements featuring Clause 16 stipulating that in the event of default or builder's failure to complete the project/pass title, the entire amount advanced by the Bank on account of the borrower shall be refunded by the builder to the Bank[cite: 6]; DRT-II Delhi decrees/recovery orders obtained by Canara Bank against 18 accounts and the Corporate Debtor (including OA No. 356/2019)[cite: 6]; CERSAI registration of security interest[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Canara Bank filed IA No. 836/2023 in CP (IB) No. 654(PB)/2019 before NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench[cite: 6]. NCLT dismissed it on 10.02.2023 relying on Axis Bank v. Value Infracon[cite: 6]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal on 19.12.2023[cite: 6]. On appeal, the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 7311 of 2024 set aside NCLAT's order on 27.09.2024 and remanded the appeal for fresh adjudication on merits to interpret developer liability under the specific contractual clauses[cite: 6].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a lending bank that disburses housing loans directly to a real estate developer/corporate debtor under a Tripartite Agreement containing a specific covenant (Clause 16) making the developer primarily liable to refund the advance upon default or project failure qualifies as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(8) read with Section 5(7) of the IBC[cite: 6]. 2. Whether the alleged non-registration of charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 invalidates the bank's status as a secured creditor or extinguishes its right to claim in CIRP[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a lender disburses loan funds directly to a corporate debtor/developer on behalf of homebuyers under a tripartite agreement containing an explicit covenant that places primary liability on the corporate debtor to refund all advances directly to the lender upon loan default, builder failure, or non-delivery of units, such liability constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8) read with Section 3(33) and Section 3(6) of the IBC[cite: 6]. This distinguishes the transaction from ordinary tripartite arrangements where the sole repayment obligation rests on the homebuyer, thereby clothing the lending bank with locus standi as a Financial Creditor[cite: 6]. Additionally, non-registration of mortgage under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not nullify the lender's status as a secured creditor[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) as broad and inclusive, extending beyond direct borrower relationships where a promise by the debtor to refund money disbursed against time value of money creates an independent debt under Section 5(8)(i) read with 'transaction' under Section 3(33)[cite: 6]. Axis Bank v. Value Infracon was distinguished on facts because there the builder had no repayment liability, whereas here Clause 16 imposed a direct, primary refund obligation on the builder[cite: 6]. Non-registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act does not defeat security rights under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act or SARFAESI Act[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the contractual covenants of the Tripartite Agreement, specifically Clause 16, finding that the builder undertook a direct refund obligation, supported by DRT recovery certificates and decrees against the Corporate Debtor, satisfying the evidentiary requirement for a financial debt[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Clause 16 created a primary contractual obligation of the Corporate Debtor to refund the loan disbursements directly to Canara Bank, the Bank's claim qualifies as a financial debt, rendering the RP's rejection and NCLT's dismissal erroneous, warranting allowance of the appeal and remand of IA No. 836/2023 for reassessment[cite: 6].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 390 of 2023 is allowed[cite: 6]. The Impugned Order dated 10.02.2023 is set aside, and I.A No. 836/2023 in C.P. (IB) No. 654(PB)/2019 is restored to its original number and remanded back to the Tribunal for reassessment in accordance with law[cite: 6]. Parties are directed to appear before the Adjudicating Authority on 27.01.2025[cite: 6]. Interlocutory Applications, if any, are closed[cite: 6]. No costs[cite: 6].
summary: Canara Bank appealed against NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of IA No. 836/2023 in the CIRP of builder M/s AVJ Developers (India) Pvt. Ltd., which rejected its Rs. 17.46 crore financial claim for home loans disbursed directly to the developer under Tripartite Agreements[cite: 6]. Following remand from the Supreme Court, NCLAT distinguished Axis Bank v. Value Infracon, holding that Clause 16 of the Tripartite Agreement created a direct contractual obligation making the developer primarily liable to refund all disbursed loan amounts to the Bank upon default or project failure[cite: 6]. This obligation constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 6]. NCLAT set aside the impugned order and remanded the matter to NCLT for reassessment[cite: 6].

case_title: State Bank of India, Singapore Branch vs. Shantanu Prakash & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is State Bank of India, Singapore Branch (Secured Financial Creditor)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 1 is Shantanu Prakash (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Educomp Solutions Limited)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 2 is Mahendar Singh Khandelwal (Resolution Professional)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 4 is State Bank of India[cite: 7]. Educomp Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd. (EAPPL) is a foreign wholly-owned subsidiary of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 16.05.2008, EAPPL obtained a loan facility of USD 20 million from Appellant to acquire a 51% stake (18,173 unlisted shares) in US-based The Learning Internet Inc. (TLI)[cite: 7]. On 22.05.2008, the Corporate Debtor executed a Deed of Guarantee securing the loan[cite: 7]. On 23.07.2008, EAPPL pledged the 18,173 TLI shares to the Appellant under a Stock Pledge Agreement[cite: 7]. On 03.11.2014, the loan was restructured with outstanding dues of USD 14.72 million[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EAPPL defaulted on USD 14.72 million[cite: 7]; Appellant originally lodged a claim against Corporate Debtor as guarantor for Rs. 112,82,42,159.97 (USD 17,455,969.65), which was subsequently reduced to Rs. 67,17,18,480.81 (USD 10,392,713.40) following share sale realization[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against Corporate Debtor on 30.05.2017[cite: 7]; Singapore High Court ordered liquidation of EAPPL on 30.06.2017[cite: 7]; Singapore liquidators issued no-objection email on 12.02.2020[cite: 7]; Appellant executed share sale on 03.09.2021[cite: 7]; Respondent No. 1 filed IA No. 187/ND/2022 in 2022[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Stock Pledge Agreement dated 23.07.2008[cite: 7]; Corporate Guarantee dated 22.05.2008 containing express waiver in Clause 5[cite: 7]; valuation report estimating TLI shares at USD 5.31 to 8.16 million[cite: 7]; liquidator's written consent dated 12.02.2020 confirming absence of better offers[cite: 7]; Share Sale Agreement dated 03.09.2021 realizing USD 7.10 million[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed IA No. 187/ND/2022 under Section 60(5) read with Section 47 alleging the share sale was an undervalued transaction[cite: 7]. NCLT New Delhi Bench-II vide order dated 25.08.2023 held the shares were not the Corporate Debtor's assets, but directed the RP to approach IBBI to appoint two registered valuers under IBBI Liquidation Regulations and ordered that if the valuation exceeded USD 7.10 million, Appellant's claim against the Corporate Debtor would stand reduced accordingly[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possessed jurisdiction under Section 60(5) or Section 47 of the IBC to order a fresh valuation of pledged shares held by a foreign subsidiary in liquidation abroad under IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations, and to conditionally reduce the admitted financial claim of the secured creditor against the corporate debtor based on such valuation[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate debtor and its subsidiary are distinct legal entities, and assets owned by a subsidiary do not constitute assets of the holding company corporate debtor under Section 18 Explanation (b) or Section 36(4) of the IBC[cite: 7]. The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to supervise or revalue the realization of pledged assets belonging to a foreign subsidiary undergoing court-monitored liquidation under foreign law, nor can it apply IBBI Liquidation Regulations during the CIRP stage of the corporate debtor to alter an admitted financial claim[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 Explanation (b) expressly excludes assets of any Indian or foreign subsidiary from the control and custody of the RP[cite: 7]. Sections 45 and 47 apply strictly to transactions entered into by the corporate debtor transferring its own assets, not to sales of assets owned by a subsidiary executed by a secured pledgee[cite: 7]. Regulation 21A of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 applies exclusively to the liquidation process of the corporate debtor itself and has no applicability during CIRP[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated whether any prima facie evidence of undervaluation or fraud existed under Indian insolvency law, noting that the sale was conducted at a negotiated price exceeding contemporaneous valuation estimates and with the written consent of court-appointed liquidators in Singapore[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the pledged shares were assets of the Singapore subsidiary and the sale was completed under Singapore liquidation proceedings, the NCLT had no jurisdiction to direct fresh valuation through IBBI or reduce the creditor's claim, warranting the setting aside of paragraph 27(a), (b), and the second sentence of (c)[cite: 7].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1351 of 2023 is allowed[cite: 7]. The Impugned Order contained in Para 27(a) & (b) and the second sentence of Para 27(c) ('The secured financial claim of the State Bank of India (Singapore) qua the CD would be subject to the outcome of the valuation result/report') is set aside[cite: 7]. The remaining portions of the Impugned Order survive and remain applicable[cite: 7]. Pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 7]. No costs[cite: 7].
summary: State Bank of India Singapore Branch appealed against an order of NCLT New Delhi in IA No. 187/ND/2022 directing a fresh valuation by IBBI of pledged shares of US-based The Learning Internet Inc., owned by Educomp Solutions Ltd.'s subsidiary (EAPPL) and sold by SBI for USD 7.10 million during Singapore liquidation[cite: 7]. The NCLT directed that SBI's claim against corporate debtor Educomp would be reduced if the fresh valuation exceeded the sale price[cite: 7]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the valuation directives, holding that subsidiary assets do not belong to the corporate debtor under Section 18, the NCLT lacks extraterritorial jurisdiction over foreign liquidation sales, and IBBI Liquidation Regulation 21A is inapplicable during CIRP[cite: 7].

case_title: Arvind Gulsia vs. Om Sai Boxes & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Arvind Gulsia (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s C & A Farm Fresh Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 1 is Om Sai Boxes (Operational Creditor, an unregistered partnership firm)[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 2 is Paresh Mehta (Interim Resolution Professional)[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of packaging boxes by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor under 13 invoices raised between 26.09.2016 and 30.11.2016 subject to a 30-day credit period[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of 13 invoices totaling principal operational debt of Rs. 11,69,999/- and interest of Rs. 8,96,029.76/-, aggregating to Rs. 20,66,028.76/-, exceeding the then-applicable threshold of Rs. 1 lakh[cite: 8]. First invoice default occurred on 26.10.2016, last invoice default on 30.12.2016, and the last part-payment of Rs. 1,34,892/- was made by Corporate Debtor on 17.02.2017[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice dated 15.01.2020 was dispatched on 22.01.2020 and delivered on 28.01.2020[cite: 8]; Corporate Debtor sent reply dated 07.02.2020 via speed post on 08.02.2020[cite: 8]; Section 9 petition was filed on 17.02.2020 and refiled on 03.03.2020[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices and delivery challans establishing receipt of goods with VAT/CENVAT levies[cite: 8]; bank statement evidencing part-payment of Rs. 1,34,892/- on 17.02.2017[cite: 8]; Corporate Debtor's ledger statement acknowledging principal debt payable as of 01.04.2018[cite: 8]; unverified cash ledger entries without cash receipts produced by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Om Sai Boxes filed Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 226/CHD/PB/2020 on 17.02.2020[cite: 8]. The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh Bench) vide order dated 23.08.2023 admitted the Corporate Debtor to CIRP, rejecting preliminary objections regarding limitation, unregistered partnership status, and pre-existing dispute[cite: 8].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an unregistered partnership firm is barred under Section 69(2) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 from filing an application under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 8]. 2. Whether the Section 9 application was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 8]. 3. Whether the Corporate Debtor raised a plausible pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the IBC are applications governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act and are not suits; therefore, the statutory bar under Section 69(2) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not apply to an unregistered partnership firm maintaining an IBC petition[cite: 8]. Part-payment made on account of debt within three years extends limitation under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, and if the final limitation date falls on a court holiday, Section 4 allows filing on the next working day[cite: 8]. A dispute raised for the first time after statutory demand without prior contemporaneous evidence is a moonshine defense[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 69(2) of the Indian Partnership Act applies exclusively to suits to enforce contract rights in civil court[cite: 8]. Following Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave and B.K. Educational Services, IBC petitions fall under Article 137 residuary limitation, and Section 5 applies, confirming they are not suits[cite: 8]. Under Section 12(1) and Section 4 of the Limitation Act read with Rule 3 of NCLT Rules, the day of reckoning is excluded and expiry on a Sunday extends filing to Monday[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The bench examined whether any contemporaneous written communication regarding inferior quality existed before the Section 8 notice, finding only contradictory pleas of dispute and unsupported cash repayments[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was legally maintainable by the unregistered firm, within statutory limitation, and free of any genuine pre-existing dispute, justifying CIRP admission and appeal dismissal[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 41 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 8]. The Section 9 Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against the Corporate Debtor must go on[cite: 8]. No orders as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Suspended Director Arvind Gulsia appealed against NCLT Chandigarh's order admitting Corporate Debtor C & A Farm Fresh Pvt. Ltd. to CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC on an application filed by unregistered partnership firm Om Sai Boxes for default of Rs. 20.66 lakhs[cite: 8]. The Appellant contended that Section 69(2) of the Indian Partnership Act barred the application, that the claim was time-barred, and that defective box quality constituted a pre-existing dispute[cite: 8]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that Section 69(2) applies only to suits and not IBC petitions[cite: 8]. Limitation was extended under Sections 18 and 19 by part-payment on 17.02.2017, and the uncorroborated quality issues constituted an illusory defense[cite: 8].

case_title: Anil Kumar (Resolution Professional) vs. Mukund Choudhary
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Anil Kumar (Resolution Professional in the Personal Insolvency Resolution Process of Mukund Choudhary)[cite: 9]. The Respondent is Mukund Choudhary (Personal Guarantor)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Mukund Choudhary executed a personal guarantee securing credit facilities availed by a corporate debtor[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment occurred, prompting the Personal Guarantor to initiate personal insolvency proceedings under Section 94(1) of the IBC[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 08.04.2021, the Adjudicating Authority declared interim moratorium under Section 96 upon Section 94 filing and appointed RP[cite: 9]; on 30.04.2024, NCLT admitted the Section 94 petition under Section 100 and declared fresh moratorium under Section 101 for 180 days[cite: 9]; public announcement issued on 03.05.2024[cite: 9]; first creditors' meeting held on 23.10.2024[cite: 9]; on 28.10.2024, creditors authorized RP to seek 90-day extension[cite: 9]; 180-day moratorium expired on 28.10.2024[cite: 9]; RP filed IA No. 5719/2024; NCLT passed order on 04.12.2024[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Professional's Section 99 Report[cite: 9]; Draft Repayment Plan submitted by the Personal Guarantor[cite: 9]; minutes of creditors' meeting dated 23.10.2024 requesting modification of the repayment plan[cite: 9]; creditors' authorization resolution dated 28.10.2024[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 5719/2024 in (IB)-202(PB)/2021 before NCLT New Delhi Court-V seeking extension of PIRP by 90 days from 29.10.2024[cite: 9]. NCLT vide order dated 04.12.2024 granted 90 days extension to complete the process but expressly stated that no view was expressed on extending the moratorium under Section 101[cite: 9]. RP appealed seeking extension of the Section 101 moratorium[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether the statutory 180-day period for moratorium under Section 101(1) of the IBC in a Personal Insolvency Resolution Process is mandatory with automatic cessation upon expiry, or whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal has jurisdiction to extend the moratorium beyond 180 days[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium prescribed under Section 101(1) of the IBC during personal insolvency resolution is strictly mandatory and subject to automatic statutory cessation upon the expiration of 180 days from the date of admission or upon an order on the repayment plan under Section 114, whichever is earlier[cite: 9]. The Adjudicating Authority and the Appellate Tribunal have no jurisdiction, power, or discretion to extend the Section 101 moratorium beyond the statutorily fixed outer limit of 180 days, even when an extension of time is granted to complete the resolution process[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 101(1) uses the phrase 'shall cease to have effect at the end of the period of one hundred and eighty days... whichever is earlier'[cite: 9]. Applying the literal rule of interpretation (citing Babu Ram Upadhyay, Newtech Promoters, and Kotak Mahindra Bank), clear statutory language providing specific consequences of nullification or cessation must be construed as mandatory[cite: 9]. Section 101(1) is distinguishable from Section 54D (PPIRP), which contains no automatic statutory termination[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the statutory timeline from the admission date of 30.04.2024, confirming that the 180-day moratorium period expired on 28.10.2024 by operation of law[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The moratorium under Section 101(1) ended automatically on 28.10.2024 and cannot be judicially extended; the NCLT committed no error in omitting to extend the moratorium, requiring dismissal of the appeal[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 38 of 2025 is dismissed[cite: 9]. No extension of moratorium under Section 101 of the IBC can be allowed[cite: 9].
summary: The Resolution Professional of Personal Guarantor Mukund Choudhary appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 04.12.2024 in IA No. 5719/2024, which granted a 90-day extension to complete the Personal Insolvency Resolution Process (PIRP) but declined to extend the statutory moratorium under Section 101 of the IBC[cite: 9]. The Appellant contended that the 180-day moratorium limit is directory and that continuing PIRP without a moratorium defeats the process[cite: 9]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 101(1) prescribes mandatory automatic cessation of the moratorium at the end of 180 days or upon an order under Section 114, and courts possess no statutory power to extend it[cite: 9].

case_title: Sumati Suresh Hegde & Ors. vs. Anand Sonbhadra, RP of Champalalji Finance Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Sumati Suresh Hegde & Ors. (legal heirs and successors-in-interest of Late Suresh Padmanabha Hegde, monthly tenant)[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 1 is Anand Sonbhadra (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Champalalji Finance Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 10]. Respondent No. 2 is the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Predecessor Late Suresh Padmanabha Hegde was inducted as a monthly tenant at Rs. 500/- per month in premises 'Villa Mohindra Outhouse', Khar (W), Mumbai, by erstwhile owners Prem and Dilip Mohindra, from whom the Corporate Debtor subsequently purchased the property subject to the existing tenancy[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Tenancy dispute; Corporate Debtor claimed bonafide requirement for demolition and reconstruction and alleged rent non-payment; no financial debt default between tenant and Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 26.11.2009, Small Causes Court Bandra decreed RAD Suit No. 916/2005 declaring monthly tenancy[cite: 10]; Corporate Debtor filed eviction suit RAE No. 149/2011 on 23.12.2016[cite: 10]; tenant died on 11.10.2016[cite: 10]; CIRP commenced against CD on 17.03.2023[cite: 10]; RP appointed on 26.04.2023[cite: 10]; RP filed IA No. 4632/2023[cite: 10]; civil eviction suit dismissed for non-prosecution on 16.11.2024[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Civil court decree dated 26.11.2009 in RAD Suit No. 916/2005 declaring monthly tenancy and restraining eviction without due process of law[cite: 10]; admissions in plaint of RAE Suit No. 149/2011 admitting predecessor was inducted as monthly tenant at Rs. 500/- per month[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 4632 of 2023 under Section 60(5) read with Section 25(2)(a) seeking eviction and possession[cite: 10]. NCLT Mumbai Bench C-IV allowed the IA on 05.04.2024, holding that under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 25 RP can take custody of assets under lease and Section 238 overrides the Maharashtra Rent Control Act[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) read with Section 25(2)(a) of the IBC possesses jurisdiction to summarily order the eviction of a statutory monthly tenant protected under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 from property owned by the Corporate Debtor, or whether the RP must pursue regular eviction proceedings under Section 25(2)(b)[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) of the IBC has no jurisdiction to summarily evict a protected statutory monthly tenant from property owned by the corporate debtor[cite: 10]. Under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 25 of the IBC, the duty of the RP to take control and custody of debtor assets does not empower the RP to summarily remove a tenant[cite: 10]. Rather, under Section 25(2)(b), the RP must represent the corporate debtor before the appropriate civil/rent control court to seek eviction in accordance with due process of law[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5)(c) confers residuary jurisdiction only over questions arising solely from or directly related to the insolvency resolution process (following Embassy Property Developments and Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam); tenancy disputes under State Rent Control Acts exist dehors insolvency and cannot be adjudicated by NCLT[cite: 10]. Section 238 of the IBC cannot be invoked to override statutory tenancy protections[cite: 10]. A statutory monthly tenancy is distinct from an expired short-term lease or license[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tenancy was established by a binding Small Causes Court decree dated 26.11.2009 and affirmed in the debtor's own eviction suit, confirming that under the principle 'once a tenant, always a tenant', dispossession requires due process under rent control legislation[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed a patent error in treating statutory tenancy as a lease and ordering summary eviction; the RP cannot short-circuit civil remedies, warranting that the appeal be allowed and the eviction order set aside[cite: 10].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 884 of 2024 is allowed[cite: 10]. The Impugned Order dated 05.04.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench C-IV is set aside[cite: 10]. Pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 10]. No costs[cite: 10].
summary: Legal heirs of protected statutory tenant Suresh Hegde appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order allowing an application under Section 60(5) and Section 25(2)(a) filed by the RP of Champalalji Finance Pvt. Ltd. for summary eviction from premises owned by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the eviction order, holding that the NCLT is not a civil court and lacks jurisdiction to summarily evict a monthly tenant protected under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999[cite: 10]. Following Supreme Court rulings in Embassy Property and Gujarat Urja, the Tribunal held that tenancy disputes arise dehors the insolvency process, and under Section 25(2)(b), the RP must pursue eviction through competent rent control courts[cite: 10].

case_title: Ravi Raman vs. RR Info Park Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ravi Raman (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor RR Info Park Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 11]. Respondent No. 1 is RR Info Park Private Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 11]. Respondent No. 2 is JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (Financial Creditor/Assignee of Oriental Bank of Commerce)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed consortium financial facilities totaling Rs. 270 Crores (including Rs. 70 Crores from Oriental Bank of Commerce), secured by Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds (MODT) dated 01.06.2007[cite: 11]. OBC assigned the debt to Respondent No. 2 on 07.03.2014[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default led to DRT-III Chennai OA No. 121/2011 order dated 13.12.2012; Recovery Certificate DRC No. 73/2013 issued on 21.05.2013 for Rs. 107,46,91,420.28 plus interest at 16% p.a., totaling Rs. 198,31,59,760/-[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Recovery Certificate issued on 21.05.2013[cite: 11]; SARFAESI auction initiated in 2019[cite: 11]; CD offered OTS on 30.01.2019 in SA No. 42/2019 (rejected 06.02.2019)[cite: 11]; Section 7 filed on 27.06.2019[cite: 11]; CD proposed settlement on 18.03.2020[cite: 11]; Memorandum of Compromise filed on 21.12.2020[cite: 11]; NCLT allowed withdrawal with liberty on 22.12.2020[cite: 11]; CD defaulted on 15.11.2021[cite: 11]; Restoration Application RST No. 2/2022 allowed on 04.03.2022[cite: 11]; Section 7 admitted on 12.12.2023[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheets for FY 2014-15 to 2017-18 acknowledging consortium debts[cite: 11]; written OTS proposals dated 30.01.2019 and 18.03.2020[cite: 11]; signed Memorandum of Compromise dated 21.12.2020[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 2 filed Section 7 petition IBA/930(CHE)/2019, withdrawn upon compromise on 22.12.2020 and restored upon default on 04.03.2022[cite: 11]. NCLT Chennai admitted the petition on 12.12.2023, rejecting the defense that limitation began exclusively on 21.05.2013[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition was barred by limitation under Article 137 on the ground that it was initiated beyond three years from the date of issuance of the DRT Recovery Certificate (21.05.2013), or whether successive acknowledgments in balance sheets, OTS proposals, and the signed Memorandum of Compromise dated 21.12.2020 extended limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act and Section 25(3) of the Contract Act[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC, the limitation period is not confined to three years from the original default or issuance of a Recovery Certificate[cite: 11]. Unbroken, successive acknowledgments of liability in audited balance sheets, OTS proposals, and formal compromise agreements renew limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 11]. Moreover, a written promise to pay a debt under a compromise constitutes a valid contract under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, giving rise to a fresh date of default upon subsequent breach; a debtor cannot benefit from its own default under a settlement[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A of the IBC applies Section 18 of the Limitation Act to IBC proceedings[cite: 11]. In light of Dena Bank, Bishal Jaiswal, and Vidyasagar Prasad, balance sheet entries prepared under Schedule III of the Companies Act constitute valid Section 18 acknowledgments[cite: 11]. When an application is withdrawn with liberty to revive upon settlement default, the relevant date of default is the breach of the compromise[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the debtor's balance sheets from 2014 to 2018, the written OTS offer of 30.01.2019, and the executed Memorandum of Compromise of 21.12.2020, finding clear, continuous, written admissions of debt[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the debt was repeatedly acknowledged and the compromise dated 21.12.2020 constituted a valid fresh promise, the restored Section 7 petition was within limitation, and failure to provide a certified order copy under NCLAT Rule 22(2) further mandated dismissal[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 78 / 2024 is dismissed[cite: 11]. All pending Interlocutory Applications, including IA No. 228/2024, are disposed of[cite: 11].
summary: Suspended Director Ravi Raman appealed against NCLT Chennai's order dated 12.12.2023 admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by JM Financial ARC against Corporate Debtor RR Info Park Pvt. Ltd., contending the claim was time-barred since the DRT Recovery Certificate was issued on 21.05.2013[cite: 11]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that continuous balance sheet entries from 2014 to 2018, written OTS proposals in 2019 and 2020, and a signed Memorandum of Compromise dated 21.12.2020 renewed limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act and created an enforceable promise under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act[cite: 11]. The restored petition following settlement default was well within limitation[cite: 11].

case_title: M/s Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited vs. M/s Shyam Baba Developers & Builders Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL) (Operational Creditor/Electricity Utility)[cite: 12]. Respondent No. 1 is M/s Shyam Baba Developers & Builders Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Auction Purchaser of Corporate Debtor's land and building in liquidation)[cite: 12]. Respondent No. 2 is Rohit Sehgal (Liquidator of Shree Shyam Pulp & Board Mills Ltd.)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pre-CIRP supply of electricity by UPCL to Corporate Debtor Shree Shyam Pulp & Board Mills Ltd. for its industrial manufacturing unit[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed electricity dues were Rs. 8,43,99,407/-, of which the Liquidator admitted Rs. 7,66,95,203/- in the list of stakeholders[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 27.03.2019[cite: 12]; liquidation ordered on 16.12.2020[cite: 12]; public announcement on 31.01.2020[cite: 12]; Liquidator admitted UPCL claim on 18.04.2022[cite: 12]; 7th e-auction held on 30.07.2021[cite: 12]; letter of possession issued on 03.09.2021[cite: 12]; Respondent No. 1 filed IA No. 4516/2022; NCLT allowed IA on 06.01.2023[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's Status Report evidencing distribution under Section 53 waterfall where admitted secured financial debt of Rs. 1589 Crores received Rs. 55.04 Crores and UPCL received nil distribution[cite: 12]; e-auction notice dated 17.06.2021 on 'as is where is' basis[cite: 12]; sale certificate and possession letter dated 03.09.2021 for Rs. 19.96 Crores[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed IA No. 4516/2022 in (IB)-386(PB)/2018 seeking directions to UPCL to energize/restore electricity connection without demanding past arrears[cite: 12]. NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench allowed the IA on 06.01.2023 directing UPCL to grant the connection, which UPCL challenged on appeal[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether an electricity distribution licensee can withhold or condition the grant or restoration of an electricity connection to a successful auction purchaser of a corporate debtor's assets in liquidation upon the payment of pre-CIRP electricity arrears, where the licensee submitted its claim in the liquidation process and the dues were dealt with under the Section 53 waterfall mechanism[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory electricity utility cannot condition or withhold the grant or energisation of an electricity connection to a successful auction purchaser acquiring assets of a corporate debtor in liquidation on the payment of outstanding pre-CIRP electricity arrears, when such arrears were lodged as an operational claim in the liquidation process and subjected to the statutory waterfall mechanism under Section 53 of the IBC[cite: 12]. Conditioning a fresh connection on pre-CIRP dues negates the clean slate doctrine and violates Section 238 of the IBC[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Electricity arrears payable by a corporate debtor constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21), making the utility an operational creditor under Section 5(20)[cite: 12]. By virtue of Section 238, the liquidation distribution mechanism under Section 53 overrides state electricity regulatory supply code regulations[cite: 12]. Precedents under SARFAESI auction sales (such as Srigdhaa Beverages and K.C. Ninan) are inapplicable to liquidation sales governed by the IBC and the Supreme Court rulings in Raman Ispat and Tata Power Western Odisha[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that UPCL's claim of Rs. 7.66 Crores was formally admitted by the Liquidator and distributed strictly under the Section 53 waterfall, resulting in nil dividend due to higher-priority secured claims[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The auction purchaser acquired clean title to the property; UPCL must grant the electricity connection without insisting on pre-CIRP arrears, justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 346 of 2023 is dismissed[cite: 12]. The order dated 06.01.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority directing UPCL to provide the electricity connection is affirmed[cite: 12].
summary: Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL) appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order directing it to energize an electricity connection for Shyam Baba Developers & Builders Pvt. Ltd., the successful auction purchaser of land and building of Corporate Debtor Shree Shyam Pulp & Board Mills Ltd. in liquidation[cite: 12]. UPCL demanded payment of Rs. 7.66 crores in pre-CIRP electricity arrears citing state supply regulations and 'as is where is' auction terms[cite: 12]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that once electricity arrears are submitted and adjudicated under the Section 53 liquidation waterfall mechanism, the utility cannot condition a connection on past dues, as doing so violates the clean slate doctrine and Section 238 of the IBC[cite: 12].

case_title: Indospirit Distribution Limited vs. Kristal Spirits India Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Indospirit Distribution Limited (Operational Creditor/Distributor); the Respondent is Kristal Spirits India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Purchaser)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply and distribution of alcoholic beverages and spirits by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor under commercial supply agreements and invoices[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed date of default is 01.11.2019[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The default occurred on 01.11.2019; the normal 3-year period of limitation was scheduled to expire on 01.11.2022[cite: 14]; the Supreme Court excluded the period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 in Suo Motu Writ Petition (C) No. 3 of 2020; the Section 9 petition was filed on 31.08.2023[cite: 14]. 5. case_title: Assistant Commissioner CGST & Central Excise, Kadi Division vs. Pradeep Kabra, RP of Cengres Tiles Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Assistant Commissioner CGST & Central Excise, Kadi Division (Statutory Operational Creditor); the Respondent is Pradeep Kabra (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Cengres Tiles Limited)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Assessment and statutory demand of central excise duty, central goods and services tax, penalties, and interest levied against the Corporate Debtor M/s Cengres Tiles Limited[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on statutory tax dues; Appellant filed an admitted claim of Rs. 11,76,90,942/-, against which the resolution plan provided an allocation of Rs. 1,00,000/-[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor; Committee of Creditors approved the resolution plan; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-1 approved the Resolution Plan on 13.09.2023; Appellant filed appeal challenging the approval[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statutory demand notices and assessment orders of CGST and Central Excise; admitted claim sheets confirming debt of Rs. 11,76,90,942/-; approved Resolution Plan providing Rs. 1,00,000/- to the tax department[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-1 approved the Resolution Plan of M/s Cengres Tiles Limited on 13.09.2023[cite: 15]. The Appellant appealed, arguing that under the Supreme Court's ruling in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Limited, its dues constituted a first charge and should be treated as secured debt rather than ordinary operational debt[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether statutory dues under Section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and Section 82 of the CGST Act, 2017 create a first charge elevating the tax department to the status of a secured operational creditor under the doctrine of State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Limited, or whether they remain operational debts subject to the priority scheme and Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a taxing statute creates a first charge on property but contains an express savings clause subordinating that charge to the provisions of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the statutory authority cannot claim the status of a secured creditor in CIRP, and its claim must be treated as an ordinary operational debt payable under Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and Section 82 of the CGST Act, 2017 use the qualifying phrase 'save as otherwise provided in... the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016', which is an express exception excluding the first charge from overriding the Code[cite: 15]. This distinguishes them from Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act considered in Rainbow Papers, which contained no such IBC carve-out[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of the Resolution Plan under Section 30(2)(b) to verify whether the amount allocated to the operational creditor was less than the amount payable under the liquidation waterfall of Section 53(1); the Appellant failed to demonstrate that the Rs. 1,00,000/- allocation was less than its liquidation value[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant's claim was properly classified as an operational debt, and the Resolution Plan conformed with Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, requiring dismissal of the appeal[cite: 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 844 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 15].
