case_title: Vikram Bajaj, Liquidator of Best Foods Limited vs. ASJ Finsolutions Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1612 of 2024 & I.A. No. 5885, 5886 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Vikram Bajaj, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Best Foods Limited (In Liquidation); the Respondent is ASJ Finsolutions Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Auction Bidder for Lot No. 5)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory e-auction sale of liquidation assets of Best Foods Ltd. conducted pursuant to notice and process document dated 25.10.2021 on 'As is Where is, Whatever There is and Without Recourse' basis for Lot 5 (land measuring 68K 17M at Village Nangal Khurd, Sonepat, Haryana)[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent was declared highest bidder on 15.11.2021 at Rs. 25,56,00,000/-; deposited 25% bid amount (EMD + part consideration) of Rs. 6,39,00,000/-; failed to pay the balance consideration of Rs. 19,17,00,000/- within the mandatory 90-day outer limit expiring on 14.02.2022[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 CIRP admitted on 02.02.2018; liquidation ordered on 01.03.2021; e-auction notice issued on 25.10.2021; auction held on 15.11.2021; Liquidator confirmed sale on 16.11.2021; 90-day outer payment window expired on 14.02.2022; NCLT dismissed extension application CA 85/2022 on 31.03.2023; NCLAT dismissed CA (AT) (Ins) 492/2023 on 21.04.2023; P&H High Court dismissed CWP 13489/2023 on 18.12.2023; Liquidator communicated forfeiture on 15.04.2024; NCLT allowed refund IA 1047/2024 on 02.07.2024[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Process document Clause 9 and Para 15 stipulating mandatory cancellation and forfeiture upon failure to pay balance within 90 days; Liquidator's confirmation email dated 16.11.2021; prior binding NCLT order dated 31.03.2023 and NCLAT order dated 21.04.2023 holding Respondent committed wilful default; subsequent re-auction on 14.06.2023 realizing Rs. 31.10 Crores[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After failing to obtain payment extensions, Respondent filed IA No. 1047 of 2024 under Section 60(5) for refund of Rs. 6.39 Crores[cite: 16]. NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed the application on 02.07.2024 applying the SARFAESI 'trinity test' and directing full refund, which the Liquidator appealed[cite: 16].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction to order the refund of earnest money deposit and part-sale consideration forfeited by a Liquidator under the e-auction process document and Schedule I of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations on equitable grounds or unjust enrichment[cite: 16]. 2. Whether the 'trinity test' formulated under SARFAESI Act jurisprudence applies to asset sales conducted under the IBC[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC read with Schedule I of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, the 90-day timeline for paying the balance sale consideration is statutory and mandatory; upon failure to pay within 90 days, cancellation of the sale and forfeiture of the earnest money deposit/part payment under the bid process document is lawful and complete[cite: 16]. The Adjudicating Authority cannot invoke general principles of equity, unjust enrichment, or the SARFAESI 'trinity test' to override express statutory terms or reopen concluded findings of wilful default[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 12 of Schedule I of the Liquidation Regulations mandates cancellation if payment is not received within 90 days[cite: 16]. The e-auction process document binds the bidder, and its forfeiture clauses must be strictly enforced[cite: 16]. Equitable tests under Rule 9(5) of the SARFAESI Rules cannot be imported into the IBC, which is a complete, time-bound code governed by the rule in Pratap Technocrats[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Finality of judicial records: the Tribunal's prior order dated 31.03.2023 and NCLAT's order dated 21.04.2023 had already conclusively held that the bidder committed wilful default with full prior knowledge of fractional land title issues, precluding collateral re-adjudication under a subsequent Section 60(5) application[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The forfeiture was valid under mandatory statutory regulations and contract terms; the Adjudicating Authority acted illegally in ordering a refund, requiring that the appeal be allowed and the refund order set aside[cite: 16].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1612 of 2024 is allowed[cite: 16]. The impugned order dated 02.07.2024 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench directing refund of the deposit is set aside[cite: 16]. Pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 16]. No order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: The Liquidator of Best Foods Limited appealed against NCLT Chandigarh's order dated 02.07.2024 directing the refund of Rs. 6.39 crores (25% bid deposit) to ASJ Finsolutions Pvt. Ltd. after the bidder failed to pay the balance purchase price of Rs. 19.17 crores within the mandatory 90-day limit for Lot 5 land[cite: 16]. The NCLT had granted the refund on equitable grounds using the SARFAESI 'trinity test' and noting that a subsequent re-auction fetched a higher price[cite: 16]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the refund order, ruling that the 90-day timeline under Schedule I of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations is statutory and mandatory, the Liquidator was bound to forfeit the deposit upon default, and equitable principles cannot override the Code[cite: 16].

case_title: Raj Kumar Sahni & Ors. vs. M/s Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Raj Kumar Sahni (Ex-Director and 50% shareholder of Corporate Debtor), Pramila Sahni, and Raj Kumar Sahni & Sons HUF; Respondent No. 1 is M/s Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Shareholder); Respondent No. 2 is Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 3 is Birendra Kumar Pasari (Common Director/Shareholder in both entities)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan and financial facilities advanced by Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd. to Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. between FY 2012-13 and 2018-19 to develop a real estate plotted colony project at Bahadurgarh, Haryana under letters cum agreement dated 24.09.2012 and 24.03.2013, including margin money for DTCP bank guarantees[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal financial debt of Rs. 14,55,36,849/- disbursed by Respondent No. 1; default occurred on 16.03.2020 upon non-payment following recall demand; debt exceeded the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Lakh; account declared NPA on 14.06.2020[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Term sheet discussed on 14.05.2012; margin money provided in 2012 and 2013; loan agreement acknowledged on 24.03.2013; DDJAY License No. 41/2018 obtained on 16.06.2018; recall demand notice issued on 16.03.2020; Section 7 petition filed on 19.10.2020; NCLT closed right to reply on 17.12.2020; Section 7 admitted on 22.02.2022; resolution plan approved by coordinate NCLAT bench on 24.01.2024[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheets of Corporate Debtor for FY 2012-13 to 2016-17 signed by Appellant Raj Kumar Sahni reflecting loan and finance costs in Note 9 and AS-18; Form 26AS records showing continuous TDS deduction and deposit on interest by Corporate Debtor; bank disbursement statements and ledger accounts[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP (IB) - 983(ND)/2020 under Section 7[cite: 18]. Corporate Debtor's right to file reply was closed on 17.12.2020 (upheld by NCLAT and Supreme Court)[cite: 18]. Appellants' Section 65 application IA 3626/2021 was dismissed, and NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV admitted Section 7 on 22.02.2022, against which this appeal was preferred[cite: 18].
legal_issues: 1. Whether funds disbursed by an entity holding shareholding under a project development arrangement constitute 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC when recorded as loans bearing interest with TDS deductions in the corporate debtor's audited balance sheets[cite: 18]. 2. Whether an appeal against Section 7 admission survives on merits after a resolution plan for the corporate debtor has already been approved by an appellate bench[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Monetary disbursements made for commercial project development that carry an interest component and are formally recorded as borrowings in the audited financial statements and tax filings (Form 26AS TDS) of a corporate debtor satisfy the statutory criteria of financial debt disbursed against the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 18]. Signed balance sheet entries operate as binding acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 18]. An appeal challenging a Section 7 admission order is rendered infructuous once a resolution plan for the corporate debtor has been approved by the appellate authority[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) defines financial debt broadly as debt along with interest disbursed against the time value of money; where financial statements reflect finance costs and TDS is deposited on interest, the transaction cannot be characterized as mere equity investment[cite: 18]. Under Section 7(5)(a), upon proof of debt and default exceeding the threshold, admission of CIRP is mandatory[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated signed audited balance sheets for FY 2012-13 to 2016-17 acknowledging loan liabilities and interest, supported by Form 26AS entries verifying statutory TDS payments, applying the evidentiary rule laid down in Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. v. Bishal Jaiswal[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Financial debt and default were conclusively established on the record, affirming the validity of the Section 7 admission order; furthermore, the subsequent approval of the resolution plan by a coordinate bench rendered the appeal infructuous[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 410 of 2022 is dismissed as infructuous and lacking in merit[cite: 18]. The admission order dated 22.02.2022 passed in CP (IB) - 983(ND)/2020 by NCLT New Delhi Bench-IV is affirmed[cite: 18]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 18].
summary: Shareholders and suspended director Raj Kumar Sahni appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 22.02.2022 admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Dilwara Leasing and Investment Ltd. against Corporate Debtor Vibrant Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. for default on loan facilities exceeding Rs. 14.55 crores[cite: 18]. The Appellants claimed the funds represented equity investment under a joint development term sheet rather than financial debt, alleging collusion under Section 65[cite: 18]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that signed audited balance sheets and Form 26AS TDS deposits established that the advances were interest-bearing financial debts under Section 5(8) with valid Section 18 limitation acknowledgments under Bishal Jaiswal[cite: 18]. Furthermore, the appeal was rendered infructuous as the corporate debtor's resolution plan had already been approved[cite: 18].

The e-auction process document binds the bidder, and its forfeiture clauses must be strictly enforced. Equitable tests under Rule 9(5) of the SARFAESI Rules cannot be imported into the IBC, which is a complete, time-bound code governed by the rule in Pratap Technocrats. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Finality of judicial records: the Tribunal's prior order dated 31.03.2023 and NCLAT's order dated 21.04.2023 had already conclusively held that the bidder committed wilful default with full prior knowledge of fractional land title issues, precluding collateral re-adjudication under a subsequent Section 60(5) application. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The forfeiture was valid under mandatory statutory regulations and contract terms; the Adjudicating Authority acted illegally in ordering a refund, requiring that the appeal be allowed and the refund order set aside.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1612 of 2024 is allowed. The impugned order dated 02.07.2024 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench directing refund of the deposit is set aside. Pending Interlocutory Applications are closed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Liquidator of Best Foods Limited appealed against NCLT Chandigarh's order dated 02.07.2024 directing the refund of Rs. 6.39 crores (25% bid deposit) to ASJ Finsolutions Pvt. Ltd. after the bidder failed to pay the balance purchase price of Rs. 19.17 crores within the mandatory 90-day limit for Lot 5 land. The NCLT had granted the refund on equitable grounds using the SARFAESI 'trinity test' and noting that a subsequent re-auction fetched a higher price. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the refund order, ruling that the 90-day timeline under Schedule I of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations is statutory and mandatory, the Liquidator was bound to forfeit the deposit upon default, and equitable principles cannot override the Code.

case_title: Avil Menezes, Liquidator of Sunil Hitech and Engineers Limited vs. Hinduja Leyland Finance Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Avil Menezes, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Sunil Hitech and Engineers Limited; the Respondent is Hinduja Leyland Finance Limited (Financial Creditor/Refinancer); prior lenders include Tata Capital Financial Services Limited (TCFSL) and UCO Bank Consortium (a 14-bank consortium led by UCO Bank)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed working capital facilities of Rs. 1,970 Crores from UCO Bank Consortium secured by hypothecation of all present and future assets (Consortium Agreement dated 05.12.2006, Hypothecation Deed dated 04.12.2006, and 8th Supplemental Deed dated 12.06.2016)[cite: 24]. CD had also availed asset financing from TCFSL against specific movable assets (approx. Rs. 20 Crores), which was fully repaid and closed on 24.03.2017[cite: 24]. Between 01.09.2016 and 30.11.2017, CD availed refinancing from Respondent aggregating Rs. 38,96,50,000/- on those movable assets, registering a charge with the RoC on 30.11.2017 without obtaining an NOC from UCO Bank Consortium[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt servicing occurred; Respondent filed a liquidation claim of Rs. 30,89,42,646/- on 26.11.2019 and sought to realize security interest over 291 movable assets under Section 52(1)(b) of the IBC[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced against Corporate Debtor on 10.09.2018; liquidation ordered under Section 33 on 25.06.2019; public announcement issued under Regulation 12; Respondent filed claim on 26.07.2019/26.11.2019; Respondent issued Section 52 realization notice on 28.11.2019; Liquidator sought asset details and consortium NOC on 18.12.2019; Liquidator rejected realization on 31.12.2019; Respondent filed IA No. 699 of 2021 on 22.02.2021; NCLT allowed IA on 19.12.2023[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Schedule 3 of the 8th Supplemental Deed dated 12.06.2016 establishing UCO Bank Consortium's first pari-passu hypothecation charge on all present and future movable assets; TCFSL closure letter dated 24.03.2017; loan documents from Respondent where equipment serial, engine, and chassis numbers were left blank, allowing identification of only 14 out of 291 assets; lack of NOC from UCO Bank Consortium[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed IA No. 699 of 2021 in CP (IB) 2295/NCLT/MB/2018 under Section 42 read with Section 60(5)[cite: 24]. NCLT Mumbai Bench-I on 19.12.2023 allowed the application, holding that refinanced assets fell outside the consortium's charge and UCO Bank Consortium had only a second charge because Respondent had registered its charge with the RoC[cite: 24]. The Liquidator appealed[cite: 24].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a refinancer of pre-existing movable assets holds a first exclusive charge entitling it to realize security interest under Section 52 of the IBC when the consortium lender holds a prior first pari-passu charge by hypothecation over all present and future movable assets and no NOC was obtained from the consortium[cite: 24]. 2. Whether registration of a subsequent charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 overrides a prior contractual first pari-passu charge governed by the doctrine of priority under Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 52 of the IBC read with Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, the right to realize a security interest outside the liquidation estate is restricted to a secured creditor who holds an exclusive first charge; a lender that refinances pre-existing movable assets without obtaining a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the existing first charge-holder holds only a subservient charge[cite: 24]. Under the doctrine of priority enshrined in Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (qui prior est tempore potior est jure), the prior charge prevails[cite: 24]. Registration of a subsequent charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 is merely a statutory mode of proof and cannot alter, improve, or supersede substantive charge priority[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted Schedule 3 Clauses 2 and 3 of the Working Capital Consortium Agreement, holding that an unreserved first pari-passu hypothecation on present and future movable assets attaches immediately upon discharge of earlier third-party financing[cite: 24]. The carve-out in Clauses 1 and 4 applies strictly to new fixed assets acquired through external term loans, not to refinancing of pre-existing movable assets[cite: 24]. Under Section 52(3) of the IBC read with Regulation 21, the creditor must substantiate its charge priority, which cannot be accomplished without the first charge-holder's NOC[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified whether the movable assets were new acquisitions or existing assets (which re-vested under UCO Bank's first charge upon TCFSL repayment on 24.03.2017), whether an NOC was obtained from the first charge-holder, and whether the creditor could identify the specific assets (only 14 of 291 were identifiable due to blank loan schedules)[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because UCO Bank Consortium held the first pari-passu charge over the movable assets and no NOC was obtained by Respondent, Respondent held only a subservient charge and could not realize the assets under Section 52; the assets form part of the liquidation estate, requiring the appeal to be allowed and the impugned order set aside[cite: 24].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 555 OF 2024 is allowed[cite: 24]. The Impugned Order dated 19.12.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in I.A. No. 699 of 2021 is set aside[cite: 24]. Pending Interlocutory Applications, if any, are closed[cite: 24]. No order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: Liquidator Avil Menezes appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 19.12.2023 in IA No. 699 of 2021, which permitted Hinduja Leyland Finance Ltd. to realize 291 movable assets under Section 52 of the IBC based on its RoC-registered refinancing charge of Rs. 38.96 crores[cite: 24]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the order, holding that upon repayment of TCFSL's loan, the first pari-passu hypothecation charge of the UCO Bank Consortium over all present and future movable assets attached[cite: 24]. Because Hinduja Leyland refinanced existing assets without obtaining an NOC from the UCO Bank Consortium, its charge was subservient[cite: 24]. Under Section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 52 of the IBC, registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act cannot supersede a prior first charge[cite: 24].

case_title: R.A.J. Krishna Construction Company Private Limited vs. Newera Solutions Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is R.A.J. Krishna Construction Company Private Limited (Operational Creditor/Contractor); the Respondent is Newera Solutions Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Assignee); third party is Home & Soul (H&S, Original Employer/Developer)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Turnkey project management and infrastructure construction awarded by H&S to the Appellant under work order dated 12.10.2018 (with addenda on 09.01.2019 and 14.12.2020) and MoU dated 07.12.2020, wherein the Corporate Debtor assumed project execution responsibility and Appellant raised Running Account Bills ('RA Bills') directly on the Corporate Debtor[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding operational default of Rs. 2.96 Crores (out of total RA Bills of Rs. 9.21 Crores, adjusting ad-hoc payments of Rs. 6.24 Crores) following project demobilization instructed on 01.10.2022[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: H&S issued arbitration invocation notice on 19.01.2023; Appellant replied to arbitration notice on 10.02.2023; Appellant issued Section 8 demand notice on 25.02.2023; Corporate Debtor issued reply raising dispute on 17.03.2023; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 205 (ND)/2023 was filed in 2023[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Work order dated 12.10.2018 containing arbitration clause 52; addenda dated 09.01.2019, 14.12.2020, and 14.03.2022; MoU dated 07.12.2020; unverified and unsigned RA Bills; arbitration notice dated 19.01.2023 raising claims of delay, poor workmanship, and damages; Appellant's reply dated 10.02.2023 referencing the original work order[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 205 (ND)/2023 under Section 9 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-II[cite: 25]. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petition on 26.10.2023 holding that the arbitration notice dated 19.01.2023 evidenced a valid pre-existing dispute regarding service quality under Section 8(2) and Section 5(6)(b)[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether an arbitration notice invoking arbitration over quality of works and contractual default, issued prior to the Section 8 demand notice in relation to the underlying work order, constitutes a valid 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) and Section 8(2) of the IBC so as to warrant rejection of a Section 9 application, even where the arbitration notice was issued by the original project employer rather than the corporate debtor[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An arbitration notice issued prior to a Section 8 demand notice regarding disputes arising out of the underlying contract and quality of works establishes a genuine, non-spurious pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(d) of the IBC, mandating dismissal of the operational creditor's insolvency petition[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted Section 5(6)(b) and Section 8(2)(a) of the IBC, clarifying that the statutory definition of 'dispute' includes an arbitration proceeding relating to the quality of goods or services qua the underlying work/transaction and does not strictly require that the dispute must have been initiated solely by the corporate debtor, provided the dispute directly pertains to the debt claimed[cite: 25]. Under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, arbitral proceedings commence on the date the request for arbitration is received[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied the 'Mobilox test' (Mobilox Innovations v. Kirusa Software), examining whether there was a plausible contention requiring further investigation that was not patently feeble, hypothetical, or spurious; the arbitral notice dated 19.01.2023 raising specific issues of project delay and defective performance prior to the demand notice met this evidentiary threshold[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because arbitral proceedings commenced on 19.01.2023 prior to the Section 8 notice dated 25.02.2023 relating to the identical underlying work order, a bona fide pre-existing dispute existed, justifying the Adjudicating Authority's rejection of the Section 9 petition and requiring dismissal of the appeal[cite: 25].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 83 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 25]. It will remain open to the Appellant to resort to other remedies that may be available to it under any other law[cite: 25]. No order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary: Appellant R.A.J. Krishna Construction Company Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 26.10.2023 dismissing its Section 9 IBC application against Newera Solutions Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 2.96 Crores arising from construction RA bills[cite: 25]. The Corporate Debtor resisted admission citing an arbitration notice dated 19.01.2023 issued by the project developer (Home & Soul) concerning project delay and poor workmanship under the original work order[cite: 25]. The NCLAT held that under Section 5(6)(b) and Section 8(2) of the IBC read with Mobilox principles, the arbitration notice predating the Section 8 demand notice constituted a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding quality of works, affirming the dismissal of the Section 9 petition[cite: 25].

case_title: Shantanu Jagdish Prakash vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Shantanu Jagdish Prakash (Personal Guarantor, Ex-Director, and Promoter of Corporate Debtor Educomp Solutions Limited); Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor/Lender); Respondent No. 2 is Kanti Mohan Rastogi (Resolution Professional)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities (term loans of Rs. 636.82 Crores, working capital of Rs. 543.80 Crores, and ECB of Rs. 434 Crores) availed by ESL from a consortium led by SBI, restructured under Master Restructuring Agreement (MRA) dated 25.03.2014 and secured by Personal Guarantee executed by Appellant in favour of Security Trustee (SBICAP Trustee Co. Ltd.) on 03.06.2015 for the benefit of lenders[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor's account was declared NPA on 31.03.2013; Corporate Debtor executed Revival Letter acknowledging debt on 30.11.2016; SBI issued Section 13(2) SARFAESI demand notice on 22.06.2018 requiring payment within 60 days (default on 21.08.2018); statutory Demand Notice dated 05.11.2020 demanded Rs. 532,99,88,089.76 as of 28.02.2021[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD account NPA on 31.03.2013; MRA executed on 25.03.2014; Personal Guarantee executed on 03.06.2015; Revival Letter signed on 30.11.2016; CIRP against CD admitted on 30.05.2017; SARFAESI Demand Notice issued on 22.06.2018 (60-day expiry on 21.08.2018); Demand Notice under Rule 7(1) issued on 05.11.2020; Section 95 petition CP(IB)-446(PB)/2021 filed on 01.04.2021; RP report under Section 99 submitted on 28.01.2022; NCLT admitted Section 95 on 31.05.2024[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Master Restructuring Agreement (MRA) dated 25.03.2014 (Clause O); Security Trustee Agreement (STA); Personal Guarantee Deed dated 03.06.2015 (Clauses 1.3.4, 1.3.6, 1.3.8, 28, 30, 34(d), 45); Revival Letter dated 30.11.2016; Section 13(2) demand notice dated 22.06.2018; Section 99 Report by the RP recommending admission[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed Section 95 petition CP No. (IB)-446(PB)/2021 against Shantanu Prakash[cite: 26]. NCLT New Delhi Bench-II admitted the petition on 31.05.2024 initiating PIRP[cite: 26]. Appellant challenged the admission on grounds of limitation, lack of privity of contract (since guarantee was with SBICAP), invalid invocation, and un-crystallised debt due to pending DRT proceedings[cite: 26].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a financial creditor has locus standi to initiate insolvency proceedings under Section 95 of the IBC against a personal guarantor where the guarantee was executed in favour of a Security Trustee for the benefit of consortium lenders[cite: 26]. 2. Whether the Section 95 petition was barred by limitation when the borrower account was declared NPA in 2013, but the debt was restructured in 2014, acknowledged via revival letter in 2016, and the guarantee invoked in 2018[cite: 26]. 3. Whether a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act constitutes a valid invocation of a personal guarantee[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 95(1) of the IBC, a financial creditor as the direct beneficiary of a personal guarantee held by a security trustee has independent locus standi to invoke the guarantee and initiate personal insolvency resolution process without joining or requiring action by the security trustee[cite: 26]. A demand notice issued under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act that expressly references the personal guarantee and demands discharge of borrower liabilities within 60 days constitutes a legally valid invocation[cite: 26]. The limitation period against a guarantor commences upon default following such formal demand, and successive acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act extend limitation[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 95(1) permits a creditor to apply 'either by himself or jointly with other creditors'[cite: 26]. In accordance with the rule in M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore, a beneficiary under a contract is entitled to enforce its covenants; hence the appointment of a security trustee under an MRA does not bar the creditor from exercising enforcement rights[cite: 26]. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, a signed revival letter resets the 3-year limitation clock, and following Syndicate Bank v. Channaveerappa Beleri, limitation against a guarantor begins upon expiry of the demand notice[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of the Personal Guarantee deed (Clauses 1.3.4, 1.3.8, 28) establishing joint and several enforcement rights for lenders, the Revival Letter dated 30.11.2016 extending limitation to 30.11.2019, and the SARFAESI notice dated 22.06.2018 triggering default on 21.08.2018, rendering the 01.04.2021 Section 95 filing timely[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The creditor had complete privity and locus as beneficiary, the guarantee was validly invoked, the claim was crystallized notwithstanding pending DRT counterclaims, and the petition was within limitation, justifying rejection of the appeal and affirmation of the PIRP admission[cite: 26].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1609 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 26]. The Impugned Order dated 31.05.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-II admitting the Section 95 petition is affirmed[cite: 26]. Pending Interlocutory Applications, if any, are closed[cite: 26]. No order as to costs[cite: 26].
summary: Appellant Shantanu Prakash, promoter and personal guarantor of Corporate Debtor Educomp Solutions Ltd., appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 31.05.2024 admitting SBI's Section 95 IBC petition for default of Rs. 532.99 Crores[cite: 26]. The Appellant contended that SBI lacked privity because the guarantee was executed in favour of SBICAP Trustee Co. Ltd., that the SARFAESI notice was not a valid guarantee invocation, and that the petition was time-barred[cite: 26]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that SBI as a beneficiary under the Security Trustee Agreement possessed full locus under Section 95(1), the Section 13(2) notice was a valid demand triggering default on 21.08.2018, and the application filed on 01.04.2021 was well within limitation[cite: 26].

case_title: Ulundurpet Expressways Pvt. Ltd. vs. Regional Director, Western Region
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ulundurpet Expressways Pvt. Ltd. (Company/Applicant); Respondent is Regional Director, Western Region, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Mumbai[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate capital reduction involving cancellation of 16,76,96,382 equity shares of Rs. 10 each fully paid-up (out of total paid-up share capital of Rs. 264,55,23,650/- divided into 26,45,52,365 equity shares), returning Rs. 11.33 per equity share (aggregating to Rs. 190,00,00,008/-) as determined by a registered valuer, to be converted and retained as an unsecured loan bearing 14% p.a. coupon repayable within 5 years out of future cash accruals[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No default in deposits or debt repayments; Appellant operates a four-lane highway on BOT (toll) model experiencing cash trap with accumulated initial losses, but generating steady operational cash flows and surplus revenue from toll rate revisions[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board approved capital reduction on 29.11.2022; shareholders unanimously approved the Special Resolution in EOGM on 29.11.2022; NCLT directed notices to creditors on 09.02.2023; CP No. 271/2022 filed before NCLT Mumbai; NCLT dismissed petition on 19.12.2023[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation report dated 29.11.2022 by registered valuer CA Harsh Chandrakant Ruparelia determining fair market value at Rs. 11.33 per share; unanimous (100%) shareholder approval in EOGM dated 29.11.2022; no-objection representations from secured and unsecured creditors; RD (Western Region) and ROC reports confirming no objections[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 271/2022 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-I under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 for confirmation of the capital reduction special resolution[cite: 28]. NCLT dismissed the petition on 19.12.2023, holding that capital reduction via conversion into interest-bearing unsecured loans to be repaid from future cash accruals is not permissible under Section 66(1)(b)(ii) as the capital was not currently 'in excess of the wants of the company'[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether a company limited by shares has the discretion under Section 66(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to reduce its share capital 'in any manner', including by converting reduced capital into interest-bearing unsecured shareholder loans repayable over time from future cash accruals, when the special resolution is passed unanimously by shareholders and no creditors or statutory authorities object[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 66(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, the reduction of share capital is a matter of domestic commercial concern for the company, which possesses the statutory discretion to reduce its share capital 'in any manner' as determined by a special resolution of its shareholders; the court or tribunal cannot substitute its business wisdom for that of the company once satisfied that the transaction is not unfair, no creditors are prejudiced, and statutory majorities are met[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The words 'reduce the share capital in any manner and in particular, may...' in Section 66(1) are illustrative and not exhaustive, conferring wide discretion upon the company[cite: 28]. Section 66(1)(b)(ii) does not restrict capital reduction to immediate cash payouts; a company may effectuate reduction by converting paid-up capital into deferred, interest-bearing unsecured loans repayable out of projected surplus cash flows[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied the principles from Reckitt Benckiser (India) Ltd. and Indian National Press: (i) ensuring the decision of the majority prevails, (ii) absence of unfairness or prejudice to minority shareholders, and (iii) verifying that all creditors have consented or their interests are protected; all three requirements were satisfied as shareholder approval was 100% and creditors/RD/ROC raised zero objections[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the statutory requirements of Section 66 were fully met, no creditors or regulatory authorities objected, and the scheme was equitable, the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing confirmation, warranting setting aside of the order and approval of the capital reduction[cite: 28].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 53 of 2024 is allowed[cite: 28]. The impugned order dated 19.12.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in CP No. 271/2022 is set aside, and the Special Resolution dated 29.11.2022 for reduction of share capital stands confirmed[cite: 28]. Pending applications are disposed of[cite: 28].
summary: Appellant Ulundurpet Expressways Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 19.12.2023 dismissing its petition under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking confirmation of a special resolution to reduce share capital by cancelling 16.76 crore equity shares (Rs. 190 Crores) and converting the consideration into unsecured shareholder loans at 14% interest repayable within 5 years[cite: 28]. NCLT had held that reduction repayable from future cash accruals was not in excess of wants under Section 66(1)(b)(ii)[cite: 28]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and confirmed the reduction, holding that Section 66 gives companies wide discretion to reduce capital 'in any manner', reduction is a matter of domestic corporate autonomy, and no creditors or regulators had objected[cite: 28].

case_title: Pawan Kumar vs. Central Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pawan Kumar (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Kaur Sain Spinners Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Central Bank of India (Consortium Lender); Respondent No. 2 is Punjab National Bank (Successor of lead bank Oriental Bank of Commerce / Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 3 is Nipan Bansal (Interim Resolution Professional)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium lending facilities extended to Corporate Debtor M/s Kaur Sain Spinners Ltd. by Oriental Bank of Commerce (lead bank) and Central Bank of India under Consortium Agreement dated 06.03.2017[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of credit facilities; account declared NPA by OBC on 31.08.2017 and Central Bank of India on 30.09.2017; total default amount claimed by PNB in Section 7 application was Rs. 246,30,21,036/-; DRT decree in favour of Central Bank of India stood at Rs. 49,44,65,248/-[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan agreement executed on 06.03.2017; NPA declared on 31.08.2017 and 30.09.2017; Central Bank filed OA No. 3000/2018; Central Bank filed Section 7 CP No. 351/Chd/Pb/2018 on 19.09.2018; PNB filed Section 7 CP(IB) No. 184/CHD/PB/2020 in 2020; DRT decree passed on 02.03.2020; SARFAESI possession notice issued on 11.05.2022; Punjab & Haryana High Court dismissed writ petitions on 24.05.2024; NCLT admitted PNB's Section 7 on 14.05.2024; Supreme Court disposed of SLP on 22.07.2024[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement dated 06.03.2017; NPA declaration notices; DRT decree dated 02.03.2020 for Rs. 49.44 Crores; cancelled recovery officer auction records of 05.11.2021/24.04.2023; Punjab and Haryana High Court common judgment dated 24.05.2024 in CWP Nos. 22367 of 2021 and 11117 of 2022 confirming auction cancellation and CIRP admission[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PNB filed CP(IB) No. 184/CHD/PB/2020 and Central Bank filed CP No. 351/Chd/Pb/2018 under Section 7[cite: 29]. NCLT Chandigarh Bench Court-I on 14.05.2024 admitted PNB's Section 7 application, initiated CIRP, and disposed of Central Bank's petition as infructuous[cite: 29]. Appellant appealed against the admission order alleging inter-se agreement violations and that Section 7 was a recovery measure during pending DRT/writ proceedings[cite: 29].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the initiation and pendency of debt recovery proceedings before the DRT or High Court writ petitions bar a financial creditor from invoking Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 29]. 2. Whether an inter-se consortium arrangement restricts a member bank or the lead bank from independently maintaining a Section 7 application upon establishment of debt and default[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of parallel recovery proceedings before the Debt Recovery Tribunal or under the SARFAESI Act, or writ proceedings challenging execution auctions, does not preclude a financial creditor from initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 of the IBC, as the Code provides an independent, overriding statutory remedy not confined to debt recovery[cite: 29]. Any inter-se consortium arrangement between lenders cannot bar a creditor from triggering Section 7 once debt and default exceeding the statutory threshold are established[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is required only to satisfy itself regarding the existence of a financial debt and the occurrence of default; once debt and default are established and the application is complete, admission is mandatory[cite: 29]. Section 7 proceedings are not barred by SARFAESI or DRT proceedings[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of undisputed financial debt exceeding statutory threshold, NPA classification dates, and failure of debtor to discharge the admitted liability of Rs. 246.30 Crores, alongside High Court findings affirming that parallel auction challenges were rendered infructuous by CIRP admission[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Financial debt and default were undisputed on the record, the lead bank validly prosecuted the Section 7 petition, and no grounds existed to interfere with the admission order, justifying dismissal with liberty to pursue OTS under Section 12A[cite: 29].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1095 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 29]. The order dated 14.05.2024 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench Court-I admitting Section 7 is affirmed[cite: 29]. If the OTS proposal submitted by the Appellant is accepted, Financial Creditors are at liberty to file an application under Section 12-A read with Regulation 30A within two weeks; failing which the IRP shall proceed with the CIRP in accordance with law[cite: 29]. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary: Suspended Director Pawan Kumar appealed against NCLT Chandigarh's order dated 14.05.2024 admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Punjab National Bank (lead bank) against Corporate Debtor M/s Kaur Sain Spinners Ltd. for default of Rs. 246.30 Crores[cite: 29]. The Appellant contended that parallel DRT auction proceedings and inter-se consortium agreements precluded Section 7 admission[cite: 29]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that parallel DRT proceedings and inter-se bank agreements do not bar a financial creditor from invoking Section 7, which is an independent statutory remedy[cite: 29]. Debt and default having been established, admission of CIRP was proper, subject to liberty to submit an OTS under Section 12A[cite: 29].

case_title: Embassy Commercial Projects (Whitefield) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Pankaj Srivastava, RP of Katerra India Private Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Embassy Commercial Projects (Whitefield) Pvt. Ltd. (Co-developer/Creditor); Respondent is Pankaj Srivastava (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Katerra India Private Limited); developer was Vikas Telecom Pvt. Ltd[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Turnkey engineering and build package contract awarded by developer Vikas Telecom Pvt. Ltd. to Corporate Debtor Katerra India Pvt. Ltd. for 'Parcel 3A & MLCP' at Embassy Tech Village, Bangalore, wherein Appellant was appointed co-developer; secured by Performance Bank Guarantees issued by Yes Bank on behalf of Corporate Debtor totaling Rs. 17.17 Crores[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor allegedly failed to perform, prompting Appellant to invoke bank guarantees for Rs. 17,17,53,862/- on 31.01.2023; Corporate Debtor issued legal notice on 13.07.2023 claiming Rs. 160,45,27,775/-; Appellant raised counter-claim of Rs. 78.16 Crores under the contract on 04.12.2023[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bank guarantees invoked on 31.01.2023; CD sent legal notice on 13.07.2023; CIRP initiated against CD on 08.09.2023; Appellant submitted Form-F claim for Rs. 78.16 Crores on 05.12.2023; RP issued demand-cum-arbitration notice for Rs. 160.45 Crores on 01.03.2024; RP rejected Appellant's claim on 11.03.2024; Appellant filed IA No. 545/2024 on 20.06.2024; NCLT dismissed IA on 20.11.2024[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Performance bank guarantee invocation letters; Corporate Debtor's demand-cum-arbitration notice dated 01.03.2024 asserting Rs. 160.46 Crores claim; RP email communication dated 11.03.2024 formally rejecting and refusing to admit Appellant's Rs. 78.16 Crores claim due to pending dispute and cross-claims; approved Resolution Plan[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 545/2024 in CP(IB) No. 74/BB/2023 under Section 60(5) seeking declarations that its claim of Rs. 78.16 Crores shall not be extinguished under the approved Resolution Plan and disclosure of its treatment[cite: 30]. NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the application on 20.11.2024 holding it barred under the clean slate doctrine laid down in Ghanshyam Mishra and Adani Power Limited[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) of the IBC can direct that an unadmitted, disputed counter-claim subject to ongoing arbitration proceedings shall not stand extinguished upon the approval of a Resolution Plan, in light of the 'clean slate' doctrine under Section 31(1) of the IBC[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved under Section 31(1) of the IBC, all claims and liabilities that are not part of the approved resolution plan stand extinguished under the 'clean slate' doctrine, and no party can invoke the residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to seek declarations protecting or preventing the extinguishment of unadmitted or disputed arbitral counter-claims against the corporate debtor or successful resolution applicant[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) of the IBC makes an approved resolution plan binding on all stakeholders and freezes claims so the successful applicant begins on a clean slate without surprise liabilities (Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons v. Edelweiss ARC)[cite: 30]. The residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) cannot be expanded to entertain civil or contractual arbitral claims already rejected by the RP, nor can it circumvent the finality of the resolution process (Adani Power v. Shapoorji Pallonji)[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the RP categorically communicated non-admission of Appellant's Form-F claim on 11.03.2024 due to cross-demands in pending arbitration, which communication was never challenged by the Appellant and attained finality; further, the resolution plan was already accepted, precluding injection of unadmitted liabilities[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The relief sought in IA No. 545/2024 directly conflicted with Section 31(1) and established clean slate jurisprudence, making the application non-maintainable and necessitating dismissal of the appeal[cite: 30].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 439 / 2024 is dismissed[cite: 30]. All connected pending Interlocutory Applications, if any, stand closed[cite: 30].
summary: Appellant Embassy Commercial Projects (Whitefield) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Bengaluru's dismissal of IA No. 545/2024 in the CIRP of Katerra India Pvt. Ltd[cite: 30]. The Appellant sought directions under Section 60(5) of the IBC declaring that its unadmitted counter-claim of Rs. 78.16 Crores, pending in arbitration, would not be extinguished upon approval of the Resolution Plan[cite: 30]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 31(1) and the Supreme Court rulings in Ghanshyam Mishra and Adani Power, all claims not included in an approved resolution plan stand completely extinguished to ensure the resolution applicant starts on a clean slate[cite: 30]. Residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) cannot be used to protect unadmitted claims[cite: 30].

case_title: Rahat Hussain vs. Divyesh Desai & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2373 of 2024 & I.A. No. 8905 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Rahat Hussain (Purchaser/Occupant of the shop); Respondent No. 1 is Divyesh Desai (Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor, Precision Fasteners Private Limited); other Respondents are ex-promoters/directors of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported sale of commercial shop premises by the Corporate Debtor (Precision Fasteners Pvt. Ltd.) through its Executive Director to the Appellant under an unregistered Agreement to Sell dated 07.09.2006 for a total consideration of Rs. 4,00,000/- executed on a Rs. 20 stamp paper[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Immovable asset title and possession dispute during liquidation; no loan default metrics involved, though consideration of Rs. 4,00,000/- was claimed to have been paid in 2006[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sale agreement executed on 07.09.2006; Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP in CP (IB) No. 1339/MB/2019; liquidation initiated; Liquidator filed MA 1423/2019; NCLT allowed MA 1423/2019 on 04.10.2024; NCLAT dismissed appeal on 07.01.2025[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unregistered Sale Agreement dated 07.09.2006 executed on a Rs. 20 stamp paper; company property records reflecting ownership in the name of the Corporate Debtor; statements of promoters/directors confirming the Executive Director had no board authorization to execute the sale agreement[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Liquidator filed MA 1423/2019 under Sections 43, 44, 66, and 67 of the IBC seeking recovery of possession of the shop. NCLT Mumbai Bench-I allowed the application on 04.10.2024, declaring the transaction fraudulent and invalid without conferring title and directing handover of possession, which order was appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 31].
legal_issues: Whether an unregistered Agreement to Sell executed on stamp paper confers valid title, ownership, or legally enforceable right over immovable property of a Corporate Debtor, or whether the Liquidator is entitled to take possession of the property under the IBC in terms of Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act, 1908 and Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 17(1A) and Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 read with Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, an unregistered agreement to sell does not transfer ownership, title, or create any legally enforceable property right in immovable property; consequently, immovable property standing in the records of the corporate debtor forms part of the liquidation estate and the liquidator is fully entitled to recover its custody and possession under the IBC[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Compulsory registration under Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act (inserted via Amendment Act 48 of 2001) mandates that documents containing contracts to transfer immovable property for consideration must be registered to protect possession; unregistered documents do not confer title nor enable the purchaser to resist repossession by the liquidator under the IBC[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court applied the legal standard laid down in Shakeel Ahmed v. Syed Akhlaq Hussain, verifying whether the transfer of title was supported by a registered conveyance deed; in the absence of registration, execution on a Rs. 20 stamp paper coupled with lack of board authorization established the invalidity of the transaction[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the agreement to sell was unregistered and the corporate debtor remained the recorded owner, the appellant acquired no title, justifying the liquidator's recovery of possession and dismissal of the appeal[cite: 31].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2373 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 31]. The order dated 04.10.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in MA 1423/2019 directing the Appellant to handover possession of the shop to the Liquidator is affirmed[cite: 31]. Pending Interlocutory Applications, including I.A. No. 8905 of 2024, are closed[cite: 31].
summary: Appellant Rahat Hussain appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 04.10.2024 allowing an application under Sections 43, 44, 66, and 67 of the IBC filed by Liquidator Divyesh Desai, directing the Appellant to handover possession of a commercial shop belonging to Corporate Debtor Precision Fasteners Pvt. Ltd[cite: 31]. The Appellant claimed ownership based on an unregistered Sale Agreement dated 07.09.2006 for Rs. 4,00,000/- executed on Rs. 20 stamp paper, arguing registration was unnecessary for government grants[cite: 31]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act, 1908 and Supreme Court precedent in Shakeel Ahmed v. Syed Akhlaq Hussain, an unregistered agreement to sell transfers no title, and the Liquidator rightly exercised custody over corporate debtor assets[cite: 31].

case_title: Drish Shoes Workers Union vs. Drish Shoes Ltd. Through Its Resolution Professional
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2281 of 2024 & I.A. No. 8501 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Drish Shoes Workers Union (representing industrial workmen); Respondent is Drish Shoes Ltd. through its Resolution Professional[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment and collective wage claims for industrial workmen of the Corporate Debtor, Drish Shoes Ltd., an industrial manufacturing unit that issued a pre-CIRP layoff notice[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following initiation of CIRP, the Workers Union submitted claims totaling Rs. 3,14,31,360/- for unpaid wages up to the insolvency commencement date; the RP verified and admitted Rs. 1,85,62,360/- (calculating dues only up to the date of layoff) and disallowed Rs. 1,28,69,000/- pertaining to the post-layoff period[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor issued a 45-day layoff notice on 31.07.2021, which continued indefinitely as operations never resumed; CIRP commenced on 12.05.2022; Workers Union filed claim for Rs. 3.14 Crores; RP admitted Rs. 1.85 Crores; NCLT directed re-examination in IA 2357/2023; RP reaffirmed calculation; Appellant filed IA No. 406/2024; NCLT dismissed IA on 01.07.2024[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Layoff notice dated 31.07.2021; claim submission forms by Workers Union; RP's verification reports calculating wages strictly up to 31.07.2021; lack of any adjudication or challenge before labour courts invalidating the layoff under Sections 25M or 25O of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Workers Union filed IA No. 406/2024 before NCLT questioning the RP's decision admitting only Rs. 1,85,62,360/- and seeking full wages up to CIRP commencement date. NCLT dismissed the IA on 01.07.2024, holding that validity of pre-CIRP layoff falls under labour law jurisdiction and Section 60(5) cannot be invoked for disputes arising dehors insolvency[cite: 33].
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional or the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) of the IBC has the jurisdiction to determine the legality of a pre-CIRP layoff under Sections 25M and 25O of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and whether workmen are entitled to compute wage claims for the layoff period up to the insolvency commencement date in the absence of a labour court determination[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional performs administrative and collative functions and lacks quasi-judicial adjudicatory jurisdiction to determine the legality of an industrial layoff or lockout effected prior to the corporate insolvency resolution process; similarly, the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) of the IBC cannot adjudicate disputes arising out of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 that occurred pre-CIRP dehors the insolvency proceedings, and claims for wages during such layoff periods must be established before competent labour authorities[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC is confined to questions of law or fact arising out of or in relation to the insolvency resolution process; challenges to pre-CIRP industrial actions under Sections 25M and 25O of the Industrial Disputes Act arise dehors insolvency and fall outside NCLT's domain[cite: 33]. Furthermore, Section 14(1) moratorium bars enforcement of claims against the debtor but does not create an embargo preventing workmen from seeking quantum determination of pre-CIRP dues before competent labour fora[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Era Labourer Union of Sidcul v. Apex Buildsys Ltd., the bench examined whether the closure/layoff was challenged before a competent labour authority; since no competent forum had set aside the layoff notice of 31.07.2021, the RP was bound to collate wages based on actual pre-layoff service[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP correctly restricted wage admissions to the pre-layoff period and the NCLT rightly declined to adjudicate industrial disputes, warranting dismissal of the appeal with liberty to seek remedies under labour law[cite: 33].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2281 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 33]. The order dated 01.07.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in IA No. 406/2024 is affirmed, with liberty reserved to the Appellant to pursue available legal remedies before competent labour fora[cite: 33]. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 33].
summary: Drish Shoes Workers Union appealed against NCLT's dismissal of IA No. 406/2024 challenging the Resolution Professional's admission of Rs. 1.85 Crores out of a claimed Rs. 3.14 Crores in workmen dues against Corporate Debtor Drish Shoes Ltd[cite: 33]. The Corporate Debtor had issued a layoff notice on 31.07.2021 prior to CIRP commencement on 12.05.2022, and the RP calculated wages only up to the layoff date[cite: 33]. The Appellant argued the layoff violated Sections 25M and 25O of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947[cite: 33]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the RP lacks adjudicatory powers and the NCLT has no jurisdiction under Section 60(5) over pre-CIRP labour disputes arising dehors insolvency[cite: 33].

case_title: Sanghi Textiles Private Limited vs. Sanghi Industries Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sanghi Textiles Private Limited (Shareholder/Petitioner); Respondents include Sanghi Industries Limited (Respondent No. 1 Company), Ravi Sanghi (R-2), Sudhir Sanghi (R-3), Siddharth Sanghi (R-4), Amit Sanghi (R-5), Swathi Sanghi (R-6), group companies SZF Pvt. Ltd., Balaji Zippers, Sanghi Poly Zips, Sanghi Synthetics, Alpha Zippers, Fanzy Zippers, SKK Zippers, Maruthi Fasteners, Sanghi Threads, Sanghi Filaments (R-7 to R-16), Sanghi Polyesters Ltd. in liquidation (R-17), and CIL Securities Ltd. (R-18)[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Petition filed for rectification of the register of members under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking correction and restoration of shareholding and rights in equity shares of Sanghi Industries Limited[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate ownership and member register rectification dispute; no loan or financial default metrics involved[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition CP/31/59/HDB/2018 filed before NCLT Hyderabad; NCLT dismissed the petition on 07.09.2023 for lack of jurisdiction; NCLAT decided connected appeals (Comp App 95 & 96 of 2023) on 01.12.2023 remanding the matters; Supreme Court dismissed appeals on 16.01.2024; NCLAT allowed the present appeal on 03.01.2025[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pleadings and records in CP/31/59/HDB/2018; share transmission and transfer documents; prior coordinate NCLAT judgment dated 01.12.2023 in Gireesh Kumar Sanghi v. Sanghi Industries Ltd.; Supreme Court order dated 16.01.2024 in Civil Appeal Nos. 536 & 537 of 2024 affirming the remand of identical disputes[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed CP/31/59/HDB/2018 on 07.09.2023 holding the Section 59 petition not maintainable due to complex disputed questions of fact and lack of summary jurisdiction. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT Chennai Bench challenging the dismissal[cite: 34].
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has rectificatory jurisdiction under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 to adjudicate complex and disputed questions of fact regarding title to shares, in view of the complete bar on civil court jurisdiction under Section 430 of the Act[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 59 read with Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013, the National Company Law Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to decide all applications for rectification of the register of members, even where the dispute involves contested facts and complex questions of title, because Section 430 creates a complete bar divesting civil courts of jurisdiction over matters that the Tribunal is empowered to determine[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013 completely ousts civil court jurisdiction over any matter the Tribunal or Appellate Tribunal is empowered to determine; harmonizing Section 59 with Section 430 (relying on Shashi Prakash Khemka v. NEPC Micon), the rectificatory powers of the NCLT cannot be narrowed or declined merely because facts are disputed or contested[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied the doctrine of judicial parity and binding precedent, following its own earlier ruling dated 01.12.2023 and the Supreme Court's order dated 16.01.2024 in connected appeals involving the same subject matter, which affirmed that the NCLT must adjudicate Section 59 proceedings on merits rather than dismissing for want of jurisdiction[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's dismissal of the Section 59 petition for want of jurisdiction was legally unsustainable; the impugned order was quashed and the matter remitted to NCLT Hyderabad to be decided afresh on merits[cite: 34].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 114 / 2023 is allowed[cite: 34]. The Impugned Order dated 07.09.2023 passed in CP/31/59/HDB/2018 is quashed, and the matter is remitted back to NCLT Hyderabad to decide the Company Petition afresh on its own merits in accordance with law[cite: 34]. All pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 34].
summary: Appellant Sanghi Textiles Private Limited appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 07.09.2023 dismissing its petition under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 (CP/31/59/HDB/2018) for rectification of the register of members of Sanghi Industries Limited as not maintainable[cite: 34]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench allowed the appeal and quashed the dismissal, holding that Section 430 of the Companies Act bars civil court jurisdiction and vests exclusive rectificatory power in the NCLT under Section 59 even when faced with complex disputed facts, as established in Shashi Prakash Khemka[cite: 34]. Maintaining parity with connected appeals affirmed by the Supreme Court, the matter was remitted to NCLT Hyderabad for adjudication on merits[cite: 34].

case_title: Amrit Rajani vs. Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Private Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 375 of 2023 & I.A. No. 1261, 1262 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Amrit Rajani (Erstwhile Director of Corporate Debtor Shri Balaji Entertainments Private Limited); Respondent No. 1 is Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Private Limited (Financial Creditor/Assignee of SVC Co-operative Bank Limited); Respondent No. 2 is Corporate Debtor Shri Balaji Entertainments Pvt. Ltd. through Liquidator Sandeep Goel; principal borrower was M/s Universal Textile Waterproof Company (India) (UTWC)[cite: 36]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term Loan of Rs. 2037.87 Lakhs and Overdraft of Rs. 423.29 Lakhs sanctioned by SVC Co-operative Bank on 18.06.2021/19.07.2018 to principal borrower UTWC, where Corporate Debtor acted as co-borrower and corporate guarantor under Deed of Guarantee dated 31.07.2018; SVC Bank assigned the loan to Respondent No. 1 on 27.02.2020[cite: 36]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayment occurred on 01.06.2019; account declared NPA on 02.12.2019; SVC Bank issued SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice demanding Rs. 29,89,96,940/-; total outstanding financial debt as of 30.04.2021 was Rs. 35,90,56,629/-[cite: 36]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: UTWC defaulted on 01.06.2019; NPA on 02.12.2019; assignment on 27.02.2020; Section 7 petition filed on 18.05.2021; CIRP admitted on 20.04.2022; public announcement on 22.04.2022; Form G issued on 22.06.2022 (EOI deadline 07.07.2022); zero EOIs received; 3rd CoC meeting held on 12.07.2022; 4th CoC meeting approved liquidation unanimously; NCLT ordered liquidation on 03.02.2023[cite: 36]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements and Corporate Guarantee Deed dated 31.07.2018 establishing co-borrower and guarantor status; Deed of Assignment dated 27.02.2020; SVC Bank ledger accounts and Supreme Court writ petition records confirming co-borrower status; Form G publication records showing zero EOIs; financial disclosures showing nil physical assets of Corporate Debtor and unexplained capital work of Rs. 1.34 Crores[cite: 36]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP (IB) No. 529/MB/2021 under Section 7, admitted on 20.04.2022[cite: 36]. Following failure to receive any EOI and disclosure of nil assets, the RP filed IA No. 2599 of 2022 under Section 33[cite: 36]. NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV allowed the application on 03.02.2023, ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor and appointing Sandeep Goel as Liquidator, which order the ex-director appealed[cite: 36].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor under Section 33(2) of the IBC upon an application by the RP following a unanimous (100%) resolution by the CoC, where the Corporate Debtor possessed no physical assets and zero Expressions of Interest were received during CIRP[cite: 36].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 33(2) of the IBC, where the Committee of Creditors resolves by a majority of not less than sixty-six percent of voting shares to liquidate the corporate debtor before confirmation of a resolution plan and intimates this to the Adjudicating Authority, the statute mandates that the Adjudicating Authority shall pass a liquidation order; the commercial wisdom of the CoC to liquidate a company possessing nil assets cannot be judicially second-guessed[cite: 36]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) uses the mandatory word 'shall', leaving no judicial discretion to the Adjudicating Authority to reject a liquidation application once the statutory voting threshold of 66% is satisfied by the CoC[cite: 36]. While the IBC prioritizes revival over liquidation, where a company has nil assets, no resolution applicants, and no possibility of revival, continuation of CIRP generates only deadweight administrative costs contrary to the objective of value maximization[cite: 36]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of the CIRP record demonstrating full statutory compliance: Form G published on 22.06.2022 yielded zero EOIs, the suspended management admitted the company possessed no physical assets, and the CoC resolved to liquidate with 100% voting majority[cite: 36]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC validly exercised its commercial wisdom to liquidate the assetless corporate debtor under Section 33(2), and the Section 7 debt was substantiated by bank records, warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 36].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 375 of 2023 is dismissed[cite: 36]. The impugned order dated 03.02.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV in IA No. 2599 of 2022 ordering liquidation of Shri Balaji Entertainments Private Limited is affirmed[cite: 36]. Pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 36]. No costs[cite: 36].
summary: Appellant Amrit Rajani, erstwhile director of Corporate Debtor Shri Balaji Entertainments Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 03.02.2023 in IA No. 2599 of 2022 ordering liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC[cite: 36]. The Corporate Debtor had guaranteed credit facilities of over Rs. 35.90 Crores extended by SVC Bank (assigned to Pegasus ARC) to principal borrower UTWC[cite: 36]. The Appellant alleged the CoC failed to explore revival and that loan documents were manipulated[cite: 36]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 33(2), once the CoC resolves by 100% vote to liquidate after Form G yielded zero EOIs and the debtor possessed no assets, the Adjudicating Authority has no option but to order liquidation[cite: 36].

case_title: J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Carnival Films Entertainment Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Assignee of Yes Bank Limited); the Respondent is Carnival Films Entertainment Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Borrower)[cite: 43]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities of Rs. 50 Crores advanced by Yes Bank Limited to the Corporate Debtor in 2017, which were restructured during the Covid-19 pandemic pursuant to RBI circulars via a binding letter dated 07.09.2020 converting accrued interest into a Funded Interest Term Loan (FITL) of Rs. 2,61,05,294.93[cite: 43]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on the repayment schedule under the FITL agreement beginning 31.10.2020; Yes Bank recorded the default with NeSL showing Rs. 2,55,35,784/- with default date 30.10.2020; subsequently, Yes Bank issued a loan recall notice dated 12.07.2021 recalling the entire facility with 7 days to pay, resulting in default on 19.07.2021; total outstanding claimed in Section 7 was Rs. 71,00,44,358.66 as on 30.11.2023[cite: 43]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Restructuring/FITL letter executed on 07.09.2020; first FITL repayment due on 31.10.2020; recall notice issued on 12.07.2021 giving 7 days; Corporate Debtor replied on 13.07.2021 admitting default; recall notice expired on 19.07.2021; assignment deed executed on 16.12.2022; Section 7 petition filed; NCLT passed query order on 22.05.2024; NCLT dismissed petition on 30.07.2024[cite: 43]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Binding restructuring letter dated 07.09.2020; recall letter dated 12.07.2021; Corporate Debtor's written reply dated 13.07.2021 admitting liability; Assignment Deed dated 16.12.2022; Form D Record of Default from NeSL bearing Unique Debt Identifier FITLMORTL11306867 showing authenticated default date as 30.10.2020[cite: 43]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 7 application CP (IB)/346(MB)2024 before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-IV; NCLT dismissed the application on 30.07.2024 holding that because the NeSL certificate recorded the default date as 30.10.2020 (falling between 25.03.2020 and 25.03.2021), the petition was barred by Section 10A of the IBC[cite: 43].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 IBC application is barred by Section 10A where an Information Utility (NeSL) certificate records an installment default date falling within the Section 10A period (30.10.2020), but the financial creditor formally recalled the entire loan facility post-Section 10A on 12.07.2021, choosing the date of default as 19.07.2021 upon expiry of the recall notice[cite: 43].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The date of default recorded in an Information Utility (NeSL) certificate is not sacrosanct or conclusive when the underlying contractual record and formal recall notices demonstrate a continuing and fresh default occurring outside the prohibited period under Section 10A of the IBC; where a creditor recalls the entire credit facility after the expiration of the Section 10A period, non-payment upon the expiry of the recall notice constitutes an independent and actionable date of default that is not hit by Section 10A[cite: 43]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A of the IBC prohibits initiation of CIRP for defaults occurring during the period from 25.03.2020 to 25.03.2021; it does not grant permanent immunity for ongoing non-payment where a creditor legitimately exercises its contractual right to recall the entire debt facility after 25.03.2021[cite: 43]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of the restructuring letter dated 07.09.2020, the formal recall notice dated 12.07.2021 granting 7 days to pay, the debtor's written admission dated 13.07.2021, and Part IV of Form 1, showing that the NeSL entry pertained to an interim installment default whereas the full facility default arose on 19.07.2021 (citing SIDBI v. Sambandh Finserve)[cite: 43]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The date of default of 19.07.2021 was validly pleaded and falls outside the Section 10A bar; NCLT erred in dismissing the petition solely on the basis of the NeSL entry, requiring the order to be set aside and the petition restored[cite: 43].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1831 of 2024 is allowed[cite: 43]. The impugned order dated 30.07.2024 is set aside, C.P. (IB)/346(MB)2024 is restored to its original number, and the matter is remanded back to the Tribunal to proceed in accordance with law[cite: 43]. Parties are directed to appear before the Tribunal on 16.01.2025[cite: 43].
summary: J.C. Flowers ARC appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 30.07.2024 dismissing its Section 7 IBC petition against Corporate Debtor Carnival Films Entertainment Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 71 Crores, which NCLT held barred by Section 10A because the NeSL certificate noted the default date as 30.10.2020[cite: 43]. The NCLAT set aside the dismissal and restored the petition, holding that the NeSL certificate date is not sacrosanct and related merely to an interest installment[cite: 43]. Because the lender formally recalled the entire loan facility on 12.07.2021 with 7 days to pay, the default crystallized on 19.07.2021, which falls outside the Section 10A period[cite: 43].

case_title: Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. vs. Presidia Araya Residents Welfare Association
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Real Estate Developer); the Respondent is Presidia Araya Residents Welfare Association (Financial Creditor in class representing 148 allottees)[cite: 44]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development and allotment of residential apartment units in real estate projects, specifically the 'Presidia Araya' project developed by the Corporate Debtor, involving payments of consideration and advances by homebuyers[cite: 44]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claims filed by 148 allottees establishing debt exceeding the statutory threshold limit of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4 of the IBC; specific claimed default amounts (principal and interest) and the precise date of default were disputed on merits and not decided in the maintainability order, being left for determination by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 44]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application registered as C.P. (IB) No. 327/Chd/Pb/2022 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench; Corporate Debtor raised preliminary objections on maintainability; NCLT passed order on 13.12.2024 upholding maintainability and listing the matter for 23.01.2025; NCLAT order passed on 20.01.2025[cite: 44]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joinder and authorization of 148 unit holders out of total 228 units in the project satisfying the statutory numerical threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1); Supreme Court settlement order in Civil Appeal No. 4467/2021 (Punit Beriwala v. Vipul Greens) setting aside an NCLT order upon settlement agreement dated 26.07.2021[cite: 44]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor raised preliminary objections to maintainability of Section 7 petition filed by the Association; NCLT Chandigarh Bench Court-I vide order dated 13.12.2024 held the petition maintainable with debt exceeding Rs. 1 Crore; Corporate Debtor appealed arguing NCLT impermissibly touched on merits during maintainability; NCLAT affirmed maintainability and remitted the questions of debt and default for fresh adjudication on merits[cite: 44].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed by a Residents Welfare Association on behalf of 148 allottees out of 228 units satisfies the statutory threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) and is maintainable without examining internal membership of the association[cite: 44]. 2. Whether an Adjudicating Authority may rely on an earlier NCLT decision that was subsequently set aside by the Supreme Court upon a settlement agreement[cite: 44].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 7 application initiated by an allottees' association representing the requisite statutory threshold of real estate allottees (at least 100 or 10% of total allottees) is legally maintainable, and the Adjudicating Authority is not required to investigate the internal membership of the association[cite: 44]. An order of an Adjudicating Authority that has been set aside by the Supreme Court—even if done upon a settlement—ceases to exist in law and cannot be relied upon as precedent[cite: 44]. Maintainability may be decided as a preliminary issue, while questions of debt and default must be adjudicated on merits[cite: 44]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpreting the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, where 148 units out of 228 total units join in the petition, the statutory numerical threshold is satisfied, and the vehicle of an Association filing on their behalf does not defeat maintainability[cite: 44]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Arithmetical verification of allottee numbers (148 out of 228 units) establishing compliance with the second proviso to Section 7(1), alongside examination of the Supreme Court's order in Punit Beriwala establishing that the cited precedent was set aside[cite: 44]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petition met all statutory maintainability requirements and maintainability was correctly decided in favour of the applicant; however, the nature of debt and default must be decided afresh on merits by the NCLT without relying on vacated precedents, justifying disposal/dismissal of the appeal[cite: 44].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 97 of 2025 is disposed of[cite: 44]. The finding that the Section 7 petition is maintainable is affirmed and stands closed in favour of the Applicant[cite: 44]. The Adjudicating Authority shall proceed to decide the Section 7 Application on merits afresh in accordance with law[cite: 44].
summary: Corporate Debtor Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. appealed against NCLT Chandigarh's order dated 13.12.2024 holding a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Presidia Araya Residents Welfare Association maintainable[cite: 44]. The Corporate Debtor contended that the Association lacked standing, its members were unverified, and NCLT improperly decided merits[cite: 44]. The NCLAT affirmed that the application filed on behalf of 148 out of 228 allottees satisfied the statutory threshold under Section 7(1) and was maintainable without inquiring into internal association membership[cite: 44]. Holding that a precedent set aside by the Supreme Court on settlement cannot be relied on, the NCLAT directed NCLT to determine debt and default on merits afresh[cite: 44].

case_title: Shikha Lal & Anr. vs. Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. Through Its RP Gaurav Katiyar
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1027 of 2024 & I.A. No. 3408 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shikha Lal and her father (Allottees/Homebuyers); Respondent is Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) through Resolution Professional Gaurav Katiyar (originally IRP Jitendra Arora)[cite: 45]. 2.
