COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of 4 BHK apartment D-1602 (size 2,225 sq. ft.) on the 16th floor in the project 'Casa Royale', Sector 1, Greater Noida West, under booking form and Builder Buyer's Agreement (BBA) dated 09.01.2019 for total consideration of Rs. 52,59,900/-, with construction to be completed within 12 months plus 3 months grace (by 09.04.2020)[cite: 45]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants deposited Rs. 26,22,955/- between 22.01.2019 and 22.03.2019; CD defaulted by stalling all construction; Appellants submitted a cancellation affidavit on 03.08.2019 requesting refund, but CD never refunded any amount nor cancelled the allotment documents[cite: 45]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BBA executed on 09.01.2019; cancellation affidavit submitted on 03.08.2019; UPRERA complaint filed on 05.09.2019 (stayed on 28.02.2020 due to CIRP); Section 7 CIRP admitted against CD on 08.11.2020; claim filed in Form CA on 25.02.2020; Appellants withdrew cancellation on 19.11.2020 and 20.12.2020; RP categorized Appellants under 'refund category' on 05.01.2021; NCLT dismissed IA 2791/2021 on 18.12.2023[cite: 45]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder Buyer's Agreement dated 09.01.2019; receipts of Rs. 26,22,955/-; cancellation affidavit dated 03.08.2019 stating allottee shall have no dues after taking refundable amount; withdrawal letter dated 19.11.2020 and email dated 20.12.2020; list of creditors published by RP on 24.03.2021; parity orders of NCLT in IA 1822/2021 and IA 2230/2021[cite: 45]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed IA No. 2791 of 2021 before NCLT New Delhi Court-III praying for direction to the RP to classify them under the 'Flat Buyers' category instead of 'refund category'[cite: 45]. NCLT dismissed the IA on 18.12.2023 holding that Appellants voluntarily surrendered the unit before CIRP and were only entitled to refund, which order was appealed to NCLAT[cite: 45].
legal_issues: Whether an allottee who submitted an affidavit seeking cancellation of an apartment allotment prior to CIRP, but was never refunded the deposited amount and whose agreement was never terminated by the corporate debtor, is entitled to withdraw the cancellation and be classified as a 'Flat Buyer / Allottee' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, or must remain relegated to the 'refund' category[cite: 45].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The submission of a unilateral cancellation request or surrender affidavit by a real estate allottee does not extinguish the underlying allotment contract or the allottee's status as a 'homebuyer/allottee' where actual refund of the deposited money was an express condition precedent for the cessation of rights and the corporate debtor failed to refund the consideration or cancel the contract; upon non-refund, the allottee is entitled to withdraw the surrender request and rank pari passu with other homebuyers in class for possession under a resolution plan[cite: 45]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8)(f) and its Explanation, allottees in a real estate project form a class of financial creditors entitled to delivery of units; a conditional surrender affidavit stating that rights cease 'after taking refundable amount' is an executory condition, and absent actual refund, the buyer-seller relationship and BBA remain subsisting[cite: 45]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Condition-precedent test: scrutinizing the language of the cancellation affidavit ('after taking refundable amount... I shall have no dues left') and examining whether the corporate debtor actually refunded the money or cancelled the documents prior to the allottees' written withdrawal dated 19.11.2020 and 20.12.2020[cite: 45]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The sine qua non for termination of the allotment was actual refund and document cancellation, neither of which occurred; therefore, the allottees' withdrawal of cancellation was valid, requiring their inclusion in the category of flat buyers and setting aside of the NCLT order[cite: 45].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1027 of 2024 is allowed[cite: 45]. The impugned order dated 18.12.2023 is set aside, and direction is issued to the Resolution Professional to include the name of the Appellants in the category of flat buyers[cite: 45]. Pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 45]. No costs[cite: 45].
summary: Homebuyers Shikha Lal and her father appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dismissing IA No. 2791 of 2021, which upheld the Resolution Professional's decision classifying them in the 'refund category' rather than as 'flat buyers' in the CIRP of Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd[cite: 45]. The Appellants had deposited Rs. 26.22 lakhs towards an apartment in 'Casa Royale' and submitted a cancellation affidavit in August 2019 due to stalled construction, but the developer never refunded their money, leading the Appellants to withdraw their cancellation in November 2020[cite: 45]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that actual refund was a condition precedent for extinguishing tenancy/buyer rights[cite: 45]. Since no refund or formal termination occurred, the buyer-seller relationship persisted, entitling the Appellants to be classified as flat buyers[cite: 45].

case_title: State Bank of India vs. IDBI Bank Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 321 of 2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 335 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are State Bank of India (in Comp. App. 321/2024) and IFCI Limited (in Comp. App. 335/2024), both Secured Financial Creditors; Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Bank Ltd. (Secured Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Deepika Bhugra Prasad (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Ess Dee Aluminium Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit and loan facilities extended to Corporate Debtor Ess Dee Aluminium Limited by a consortium of lenders including SBI, IFCI, and IDBI Bank, secured by charges and hypothecation over the movable and immovable properties of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred in debt repayment leading to admission into CIRP; IDBI Bank submitted a claim in Form-D for Rs. 1,46,12,18,998/-; following the sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern to Shakambhari Ispat & Power Limited, the Liquidator distributed sale proceeds based on charge priority and security interest rather than pro-rata admitted debt, allocating IDBI Bank only Rs. 1,26,10,109/- (treated as a 10% share), which IDBI Bank accepted under protest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on SBI's Section 7 petition on 14.02.2020; liquidation ordered on 08.10.2021; Stakeholders Consultation Committee (SCC) constituted on 07.12.2021; going concern sale to H-1 bidder finalized in 9th SCC on 30.08.2022; distribution methodology decided in 10th SCC on 26.09.2022; IDBI filed IA (IB) No. 1694/(KB)/2022 in 2022; NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed the IA on 20.12.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-D claim filed by IDBI Bank for Rs. 1,46,12,18,998/-; list of stakeholders dated 07.12.2021; minutes of the 9th and 10th SCC meetings; email dated 19.09.2022 from the Liquidator asserting that distribution followed NCLT Ahmedabad's ruling in Technology Development Board v. Anil Goel; written undertakings executed by secured creditors under Regulation 43 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations agreeing to refund excess distributions if ordered by courts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IDBI Bank filed IA (IB) No. 1694/(KB)/2022 in CP (IB) No. 1284/(KB)/2019 before NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-II challenging the Liquidator's distribution based on security interest and seeking pro-rata distribution under Section 53. By order dated 20.12.2023, the Adjudicating Authority allowed the application and directed the Liquidator to re-work the distribution among secured creditors on a pro-rata basis according to their admitted claims, which order was challenged in these appeals.
legal_issues: Whether under Section 53(1)(b)(ii) of the IBC, the sale proceeds of a Corporate Debtor in liquidation must be distributed among secured creditors who have relinquished their security interests under Section 52 on a pro-rata basis in proportion to their admitted financial claims, or whether distribution can be made on the basis of inter-se priority of charges and the valuation of their respective security interests.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 53(1)(b)(ii) of the IBC, when secured creditors relinquish their security interests to the liquidation estate pursuant to Section 52, they form a single, unified class ranking equally with workmen dues; the distribution of liquidation proceeds among such relinquishing secured creditors must be strictly on a pro-rata basis in proportion to their admitted claims, and neither inter-se contractual priority of charges nor individual valuation of security interests can be applied to alter the statutory waterfall. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 53(1)(b)(ii) uses the words 'between and among'—where 'between' integrates workmen and secured creditors to rank equally, and 'among' mandates absolute equality within the group of relinquishing secured creditors, meaning distribution strictly in proportion to their admitted claims without differentiating by the magnitude or priority of the relinquished security. The bench held that the Supreme Court's ruling in India Resurgence ARC v. Amit Metaliks remains binding law under Article 141 of the Constitution notwithstanding the reference in DBS Bank v. Ruchi Soya, and pre-IBC company law precedents under Sections 529 and 529A of the Companies Act, 1956 (such as ICICI Bank v. Sidco Leathers) are inapplicable to Section 53. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of the statutory scheme of Section 53(1) and the admitted claim lists; the Tribunal tested whether any statutory provision or SCC resolution permits deviation from pro-rata admitted claim distribution, holding that undertakings furnished under Regulation 43 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations cannot validate a distribution contrary to Section 53. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The distribution made by the Liquidator based on security interest was contrary to Section 53(1)(b)(ii) and the binding ratio of Amit Metaliks; the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in ordering a pro-rata redistribution based on admitted claims, justifying dismissal of both appeals.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 321 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 335 of 2024 are dismissed. The amount as per re-distribution in pursuance of the Impugned Order shall be made over to the Secured Creditors, including IDBI Bank Ltd., along with accrued interest as directed in the interim order dated 29.02.2024, subject to any final order passed by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal Diary No. 11060/2021. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Appellants State Bank of India and IFCI Limited challenged NCLT Kolkata's order dated 20.12.2023 in the liquidation of Ess Dee Aluminium Limited, which directed the Liquidator to redistribute liquidation sale proceeds among relinquishing secured creditors on a pro-rata basis according to their admitted claims, rather than based on security interest priority or valuation. The Appellants argued that inter-se charge priorities must be respected under Section 53. Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT held that under Section 53(1)(b)(ii) of the IBC and binding Supreme Court precedent in Amit Metaliks, secured creditors who relinquish their security interests rank equally as a single class and are entitled to distribution strictly in proportion to their admitted claims.

case_title: Mr. Amit Sangal Proprietor of M/s. Nitin Plastic vs. Mr. Kairav Anil Trivedi & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 916 of 2023, 792 of 2023 & 1034 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Amit Sangal, Proprietor of M/s. Nitin Plastic (Operational Creditor), Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Kairav Anil Trivedi (Interim Resolution Professional / Resolution Professional), Respondent No. 2 is Corporate Debtor (Prince MFG Industries Private Limited), and Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC) comprising Canara Bank, Axis Bank, and ICICI Bank.[cite: 2] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Operational Creditor initiated CIRP against the Corporate Debtor for unpaid dues arising from commercial supplies under Section 9 of the IBC.[cite: 2] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted financial debt of Financial Creditors stood at over Rs. 171.13 crores out of total claims of Rs. 286.95 crores; total liquidation value was assessed at Rs. 39.20 crores and fair value at Rs. 53.16 crores.[cite: 2] 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was admitted on 05.10.2021; the 1st CoC meeting was held on 10.11.2021 where confirmation of IRP as RP was dissented by CoC; MoU for contract manufacturing was executed on 10.11.2021 with retrospective effect from 05.10.2021; Resolution Plan was approved by CoC and by Adjudicating Authority on 15.05.2023.[cite: 2] 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Online e-voting results via Right2Vote dated 19.11.2021 showed dissent for IRP's appointment as RP; forensic audit report revealed fraud; IBBI suspended the RP for 6 months on 23.05.2023 for material irregularities and misrepresentation.[cite: 2] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority admitted the Section 9 petition on 05.10.2021, later approved the Resolution Plan on 15.05.2023 via IA 2977/2022, and dismissed the Appellant's objection (IA 3525/2022) and contempt petition, leading to the present appeals.[cite: 2]
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Interim Resolution Professional was lawfully confirmed and appointed as the Resolution Professional by the CoC.[cite: 2] 2. Whether the execution of the contract manufacturing MoU with a related party without CoC approval vitiated the CIRP and constituted a material irregularity.[cite: 2] 3. Whether an approved Resolution Plan tainted by material irregularities and misrepresentation by the RP can be sustained under Section 31 of the IBC.[cite: 2]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency professional cannot claim valid appointment as Resolution Professional without securing statutory approval by the required majority of the Committee of Creditors, and material procedural irregularities or misrepresentations vitiate the integrity of the CIRP.[cite: 2] 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22 and Section 27 mandate clear approval/confirmation of the IRP/RP by the CoC; executing material contracts like an MoU under Section 28 without prior CoC approval violates statutory mandates.[cite: 2] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented e-voting records (such as Right2Vote results) and disciplinary findings by the regulator (IBBI) override ex-post-facto justifications or collusive withdrawals of replacement applications by the CoC.[cite: 2] 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Material irregularities, concealment of facts, and statutory violations committed by the RP during CIRP render the subsequent approval of the Resolution Plan unsustainable, warranting setting aside of the approval order under Section 61(3)(ii).[cite: 2]
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 916 of 2023 and 792 of 2023 are allowed. The Impugned Order dated 15.05.2023 approving the Resolution Plan is set aside. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1034 of 2024 (Contempt Petition) is disposed of as infructuous. Parties are directed to appear before the Adjudicating Authority on 28.02.2025.[cite: 2]
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT order approving a Resolution Plan for Corporate Debtor Prince MFG Industries Private Limited. The NCLAT found that Respondent No. 1 (IRP/RP) was never lawfully confirmed by the CoC, manipulated meeting minutes, and executed an unauthorized contract manufacturing MoU with a related party in collusion with the suspended board. Noting that the IBBI had suspended the RP for misconduct and applying Supreme Court precedents on procedural safeguards and integrity, the NCLAT allowed the appeals, set aside the NCLT's approval of the Resolution Plan, and disposed of the related contempt petition.[cite: 2]

case_title: Malavika Hegde vs. IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Malavika Hegde, Shareholder and Director of Coffee Day Enterprises Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited (Financial Creditor / Debenture Trustee); Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional.[cite: 3] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In March 2019, the Corporate Debtor issued 2,000 unlisted, secured, redeemable non-convertible debentures aggregating to INR 200 crores on a private placement basis, governed by a Debenture Trust Deed dated 22.03.2019.[cite: 3] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The default was admitted to have occurred on 30.09.2019, with an outstanding claim of approximately Rs. 278.97 crores.[cite: 3] 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Debenture Trust Deed executed on 22.03.2019; default occurred on 30.09.2019; default notice issued on 28.07.2020; Section 7 application filed on 07.09.2023; NCLT admitted the petition on 08.08.2024.[cite: 3] 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Section 7 application was supported by an affidavit of Mr. Manohar Maddili, whose power of attorney dated 06.03.2019 was superseded by a subsequent power of attorney dated 22.02.2022 in favor of another officer, and lacked prior express authorization or majority debenture holder resolution as mandated by Clause 10.1(b) and Schedule II of the Debenture Trust Deed.[cite: 3] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Bengaluru Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 08.08.2024, prompting the present appeal by the director and shareholder.[cite: 3]
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Section 7 application was maintainable without complying with mandatory decision-making and majority consent requirements under the Debenture Trust Deed.[cite: 3] 2. Whether the deponent filing the affidavit in support of the Section 7 application possessed valid legal authority under the governing Power of Attorney.[cite: 3] 3. Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.[cite: 3]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Initiation of insolvency proceedings by a Debenture Trustee must strictly comply with the governance covenants of the Debenture Trust Deed requiring majority debenture holder consent, and the supporting affidavit must be verified by a legally competent and authorized attorney.[cite: 3] 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC read with notification rules requires strict adherence to institutional authorities; Article 137 of the Limitation Act dictates a 3-year limitation period from the date of default which cannot be arbitrarily stretched beyond statutory and extended COVID-19 grace periods without justification.[cite: 3] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a power of attorney is superseded by a subsequent board resolution and general power of attorney in favor of another person, an affidavit filed by the former attorney without express authorization is unauthorized and vitiates the petition.[cite: 3] 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Non-compliance with Debenture Trust Deed procedures, lack of valid authorization of the deponent, and filing the petition beyond the limitation period render the Section 7 application and the NCLT admission order legally unsustainable.[cite: 3]
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The Impugned Order dated 08.08.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is quashed, and the Section 7 application filed by Respondent No. 1 is rejected.[cite: 3]
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Bengaluru Bench order admitting Coffee Day Enterprises Limited into CIRP under Section 7 upon an application by IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited (Debenture Trustee). The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the application was initiated in flagrant violation of the mandatory decision-making clauses of the Debenture Trust Deed, was verified by an unauthorized person whose power of attorney stood superseded, and was barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act as it was filed on 07.09.2023 for a default occurring on 30.09.2019. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, quashed the admission order, and dismissed the Section 7 petition.[cite: 3]

case_title: Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP vs. Union of India & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 255 of 2024, 284 of 2024 & 285 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP, Kalpesh Mehta, and Udayan Sen (Auditors/Chartered Accountants), and Respondent No. 1 is the Union of India through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA).[cite: 4] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Investigation into the affairs of IL&FS and its subsidiary IFIN following financial defaults and payment crises.[cite: 4] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (fraud investigation and disgorgement proceedings under Sections 212 and 241-242 of the Companies Act).[cite: 4] 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SFIO investigation ordered under Section 212; 2nd SFIO Report submitted on 28.05.2019; prosecution launched and applications MA 2070/2019 (attachment) and MA 2071/2019 (impleadment) filed in 2019; convenience compilation filed on 07.02.2024; NCLT passed impugned order on 22.07.2024 rejecting Appellants' IAs.[cite: 4] 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: 2nd SFIO Report detailing systemic financial irregularities, corporate governance failures, and auditor complicity at IFIN.[cite: 4] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants challenged the admissibility of the SFIO Report and accompanying document compilation before the NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT dismissed their applications (CA 65, 117, 118 of 2024) on 22.07.2024, leading to the present appeals.[cite: 4]
legal_issues: 1. Whether the SFIO Investigation Report submitted under Section 212(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 is inadmissible as legal evidence in civil/tribunal proceedings under Section 212(15) read with Section 223(5).[cite: 4] 2. Whether the compilation of underlying documents tendered by the Union of India can be relied upon by the NCLT for adjudicating applications under Section 212(14A).[cite: 4]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The deeming fiction under Section 212(15) equating an SFIO investigation report to a police report under Section 173 CrPC is strictly limited to the framing of charges in criminal prosecutions and does not render the report inadmissible in civil or regulatory proceedings before the NCLT, particularly under Section 212(14A).[cite: 4] 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 223(5) excluding Section 212 reports from Section 223 only dispenses with formal authentication requirements for inspector reports and does not bar SFIO reports from being used as evidence.[cite: 4] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory provisions must be interpreted harmoniously so as not to render substantive powers like disgorgement applications under Section 212(14A) otiose or redundant.[cite: 4] 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SFIO Investigation Report and its underlying document compilation are fully admissible and competent to be relied upon by the NCLT in proceedings under Section 212(14A) of the Companies Act, 2013.[cite: 4]
operative_order: All the appeals (Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 255 of 2024, 284 of 2024, and 285 of 2024) are dismissed with parties bearing their own costs.[cite: 4]
summary: These appeals challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 22.07.2024 which rejected applications filed by auditors (Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP and others) challenging the admissibility of the 2nd SFIO Investigation Report and its document compilation in proceedings arising out of the IL&FS/IFIN fraud investigation. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that the deeming fiction under Section 212(15) of the Companies Act (equating SFIO reports to police reports under Section 173 CrPC) is confined to criminal prosecutions for framing charges and does not bar their use in civil and tribunal proceedings under Section 212(14A). Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeals, upholding the admissibility of the SFIO report and documents before the NCLT.[cite: 4]

case_title: State Bank of India & IFCI Limited vs. IDBI Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are State Bank of India and IFCI Limited; Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Bank Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Deepika Bhugra Prasad (Liquidator of Ess Dee Aluminium Limited).[cite: 6] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor Ess Dee Aluminium Limited admitted to CIRP on 14.02.2020; failed resolution led to liquidation order dated 08.10.2021; IDBI submitted a claim of Rs. 146.12 crores.[cite: 6] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Sale of Corporate Debtor as a going concern realized proceeds distributed by the Liquidator; IDBI's share calculated initially on a security interest/priority charge basis.[cite: 6] 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation ordered on 08.10.2021; SCC constituted on 07.12.2021; H-1 bidder declared on 30.08.2022; IA 1694/2022 filed by IDBI on distribution methodology; Adjudicating Authority allowed IA on 20.12.2023.[cite: 6] 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator distributed proceeds based on individual charges/security interests following NCLT Ahmedabad's view in Technology Development Board, which IDBI challenged via IA 1694/2022.[cite: 6] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed IDBI's application on 20.12.2023, directing re-distribution of liquidation proceeds pro-rata based on admitted claims under Section 53 of the IBC, leading to appeals by SBI and IFCI.[cite: 6]
legal_issues: Whether distribution of liquidation sale proceeds among secured financial creditors who relinquish their security interest under Section 52 should be done based on inter-se priority of charges (security interest) or pro-rata in proportion to their admitted claims under Section 53(1)(b)(ii) of the IBC.[cite: 6]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Secured financial creditors who relinquish their security interest rank equally under Section 53(1)(b)(ii) of the IBC, and liquidation proceeds must be distributed pro-rata in proportion to their admitted claims rather than on the basis of individual security interest or inter-se priority of charges.[cite: 6] 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The word 'among' in Section 53(1)(b)(ii) signifies equality within the group of relinquishing secured creditors, requiring equitable treatment proportional to admitted claims.[cite: 6] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Binding precedents of the Supreme Court in India Resurgence ARC Pvt. Ltd. v. Amit Metaliks Ltd. override conflicting NCLT rulings or prior company law principles regarding security value prioritization.[cite: 6] 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Liquidator erred in distributing proceeds according to individual security interest; distribution must strictly adhere to the waterfall mechanism under Section 53(1) on a pro-rata basis based on admitted claims.[cite: 6]
operative_order: Both appeals (Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 321 of 2024 and No. 335 of 2024) are dismissed. The Adjudicating Authority's order directing re-distribution is affirmed, subject to pro-rata distribution with interest as ordered on 29.02.2024 and subject to final orders of the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal Diary No. 11060 of 2021.[cite: 6]
summary: These appeals challenged the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated 20.12.2023 which directed the Liquidator of Ess Dee Aluminium Limited to re-work the distribution of liquidation sale proceeds among secured creditors. Appellants (SBI and IFCI) argued that distribution should follow inter-se security interest/priority of charge. The NCLAT Principal Bench, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Amit Metaliks, held that secured creditors who relinquish security rank equally under Section 53(1)(b)(ii) and must be distributed proceeds pro-rata based on their admitted claims. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's direction for proportional distribution.[cite: 6]

case_title: Pankaj Gambhir & Ors. vs. Abhishek Dutta (Official Liquidator)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are ex-directors and designated partners/partners of M/s Solutions Business Centre Pvt Ltd, and Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Abhishek Dutta, Official Liquidator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An insolvency petition under Section 9 of the IBC was filed against the Corporate Debtor in mid-2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 9 IBC application filed against the Corporate Debtor (exact default amount not specified in text). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application filed on 25.04.2018; Form No. 18 submitted to RoC on 03.11.2019; CIRP commenced on 14.03.2019; NCLT impugned orders passed on 17.05.2021 and 04.08.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form No. 18 submitted to the RoC where clause 15 regarding pending proceedings was answered in the negative by Mr. Ajay Vij, and an affidavit filed by Pankaj Gambhir stating leasehold units were vacated in December 2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Original Section 9 CP (IB) No. 475/ND/2018 was filed in 2018; NCLT New Delhi via orders dated 17.5.2021 and 4.8.2021 held appellants guilty of perjury, imposed a Rs. 2 lakh fine on each, directed RP to initiate perjury proceedings against Mr. Ajay Vij, and permitted the liquidator to file a complaint under Section 340 CrPC, leading to the present appeals.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the appellants committed perjury by answering negatively in Form 18 regarding pending proceedings during company-to-LLP conversion. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) has the jurisdiction to convict persons for offences under Section 68 of the IBC and impose fines. 3. Whether proceedings under Section 340 CrPC were lawfully initiated without recording findings of expediency in the interest of justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An incorrect declaration inadvertently made in Form 18 before the RoC regarding pending proceedings is immaterial to corporate conversion under the LLP Act and does not amount to perjury, nor does NCLT possess jurisdiction to convict persons under Section 68 IBC without trial by a Special Court under Section 236. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 58 of the LLP Act 2008 ensures pending proceedings continue against the LLP despite conversion, making Form 18 disclosures immaterial; Section 236 IBC mandates that offences be tried exclusively by Special Courts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Perjury requires a deliberate falsehood on a matter of substance where conviction is highly likely and expedient in the interests of justice, not immaterial inaccuracies or minor discrepancies between affidavits and counsel statements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding appellants guilty of perjury and convicting them under Section 68 IBC with fines, as NCLT lacks trial jurisdiction and no mandatory finding of expediency under Section 340 CrPC was recorded.
operative_order: The appeals are allowed. The conviction and fine imposed by the Adjudicating Authority vide impugned orders dated 17.05.2021 and 04.08.2021 are set aside. Pending applications are disposed of.
summary: These appeals challenged NCLT New Delhi orders holding ex-directors and partners of M/s Solutions Business Centre Pvt Ltd guilty of perjury, imposing a Rs. 2 lakh fine on each, and permitting a complaint under Section 340 CrPC. The NCLAT held that an incorrect negative declaration in RoC Form 18 regarding pending proceedings was immaterial to the company's conversion into an LLP under the LLP Act and did not constitute perjury. Moreover, the NCLAT ruled that NCLT lacks jurisdiction to convict individuals under Section 68 of the IBC, as trials are exclusively reserved for Special Courts under Section 236. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeals, setting aside the convictions, fines, and consequential orders.

case_title: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. & Anr. vs. Ravi Sethia
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. & Anr., and Respondent is Ravi Sethia, Resolution Professional of Morarjee Textiles Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Electricity connection granted by Appellant to Corporate Debtor for running its textile mill; unpaid electricity bill of Rs. 4,78,27,140 raised for January 2024[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid pre-CIRP electricity dues of Rs. 4,78,27,140[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 09.02.2024; electricity disconnected on 26.06.2024 and 28.08.2024; NCLT passed interim order on 03.09.2024 and final impugned order on 24.10.2024[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Notices issued under Section 56 of Electricity Act 2003; RP paid partial payment of Rs. 50 lakhs[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority allowed IA No. 4168 of 2024 filed by the RP directing restoration of electricity, leading to the present appeal[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether the electricity supply to a corporate debtor running a manufacturing facility can be disconnected during the moratorium period under Section 14(2) of the IBC for non-payment of pre-CIRP or current dues[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Electricity is classified as an essential supply under Section 14(2) read with Regulation 32 of CIRP Regulations, and its supply cannot be terminated or interrupted during the moratorium period[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(2) protects essential supplies, and distribution companies cannot discontinue supply during moratorium[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of proof that electricity is a direct input to the output produced, it remains an essential service under Section 14(2)[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority's direction under Section 14(2) restraining the electricity distribution company from disconnecting the connection necessary for running manufacturing facilities is upheld[cite: 8].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's direction not to discontinue electricity connection, with directions to the RP to endeavour to clear electricity dues[cite: 8].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Mumbai order directing MSEDCL to restore electricity supply to Morarjee Textiles Ltd. during CIRP[cite: 8]. The NCLAT held that electricity is an essential supply under Section 14(2) read with Regulation 32, and the power company cannot disconnect supply during moratorium[cite: 8]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal against the restoration direction while directing the RP to endeavour to clear dues[cite: 8].

case_title: Ankur Kumar vs. Sustainable Agro-Commercial Financial Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ankur Kumar (erstwhile Resolution Professional of Gangakhed Sugar & Energy Ltd.), and Respondent is Sustainable Agro-Commercial Financial Ltd.[cite: 9] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor executed a Deed of Guarantee dated 13.11.2014 for Rs. 2 crores securing loans extended to farmers[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim amount of Rs. 1,14,57,536[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 10.10.2019; last date for claims was 26.10.2019; guarantee invoked by Respondent on 18.09.2020; CoC approved Resolution Plan on 13.09.2021; claim in Form C submitted on 13.10.2021; NCLT passed order on 17.02.2023[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Guarantee was uninvoked as of the insolvency commencement date and was only invoked post-commencement on 18.09.2020[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority allowed IA 886/2022 filed by Respondent to accept its belated claim, which is challenged in this appeal by the RP[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether a claim based on a corporate guarantee that was uninvoked as of the insolvency commencement date and invoked post-commencement can be admitted in the CIRP of the corporate guarantor[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate guarantee that has not been invoked prior to the commencement of CIRP does not represent a matured claim or debt due as on the insolvency commencement date and cannot be admitted[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 13 of CIRP Regulations requires verification of claims existing as on the insolvency commencement date[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uninvoked guarantees cannot form the basis of a claim admissible in CIRP during moratorium[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the RP to accept a claim arising from a guarantee invoked after the commencement of CIRP[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The order dated 17.02.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in IA No. 886 of 2022 is set aside, and IA No. 886 of 2022 is rejected[cite: 9].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Mumbai order directing the Resolution Professional of Gangakhed Sugar & Energy Ltd. to accept a belated claim submitted by Sustainable Agro-Commercial Financial Ltd.[cite: 9] The NCLAT held that since the corporate guarantee was invoked on 18.09.2020, long after the CIRP commencement date of 10.10.2019, no matured debt or claim existed as on the commencement date[cite: 9]. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the NCLT order admitting the claim[cite: 9].

case_title: Krishan Kumar Jajoo vs. Piramal Enterprises Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Krishan Kumar Jajoo (Personal Guarantor), Respondent No. 1 is Piramal Enterprises Ltd. (Financial Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is Jayant Prakash (Resolution Professional)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan facility of Rs. 400 crores extended by Piramal Finance Limited to Hema Engineering Industries Limited (HEIL) under Facility Agreement dated 20.07.2017, secured by personal guarantee executed by Appellant[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 443,36,21,727[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Facility and guarantee executed on 20.07.2017; assignment on 22.03.2019; Section 95 application filed on 21.06.2021; RP appointed on 08.04.2022; NCLT passed impugned order on 11.06.2024[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statement of accounts and information utility records evidencing default and valid assignment of debt to Respondent No. 1[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority admitted Section 95 application via impugned order dated 11.06.2024, initiating Personal Insolvency Resolution Process (PIRP) against the Appellant[cite: 10].
legal_issues: 1. Whether financial creditors can initiate personal insolvency resolution process under Section 95 against a personal guarantor despite the existence of mortgages or liquidation proceedings against the principal borrower[cite: 10]. 2. Whether there is privity of contract between the personal guarantor and the assignee financial creditor[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The liability of a surety under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, and a creditor has the legal right to initiate personal insolvency proceedings against the guarantor independently or concurrently without needing to first exhaust remedies against the principal borrower's security[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 95 of the IBC allows creditors to initiate PIRP against personal guarantors upon default[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Valid assignment agreements and facility terms permitting assignment establish the assignee's standing as a financial creditor[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority's admission of the Section 95 application and initiation of PIRP against the personal guarantor is legally sound[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the impugned order dated 11.06.2024 is upheld[cite: 10].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT New Delhi order admitting an application under Section 95 of the IBC and initiating Personal Insolvency Resolution Process against personal guarantor Krishan Kumar Jajoo[cite: 10]. The NCLAT held that the lender's assignee had valid standing to initiate proceedings, that the guarantor's liability is co-extensive under Section 128 of the Contract Act, and that creditors are not required to exhaust primary mortgage security before proceeding against personal guarantors[cite: 10]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 10].

case_title: Bank of Baroda vs. Shree Rajasthan Syntex Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 888 of 2023, 890 of 2023 & 1492 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bank of Baroda (Financial Creditor), Respondent No. 1 is Shree Rajasthan Syntex Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and other respondents include SBI and IDBI Bank[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium financial facilities extended to Corporate Debtor; account classified as NPA in 2017; MSME registration obtained on 21.07.2020; OTS proposal of Rs. 30 crores given in 2022[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to NPA classification and Section 7 petition by Bank of Baroda for Rs. 13.61 crores exposure[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed by Bank of Baroda on 18.04.2022; Section 54C PPIRP application filed by Corporate Debtor on 25.07.2022; Adjudicating Authority admitted Section 54C and disposed of Section 7 on 19.04.2023; Base Resolution Plan approved on 22.08.2023[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SBI and IDBI holding 79.12% voting share approved PPIRP and Base Resolution Plan, while Bank of Baroda dissented[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank of Baroda challenged orders admitting PPIRP, disposing of Section 7, and approving the Resolution Plan[cite: 11].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the 14-day limit under Section 11A(3) for filing a pre-packaged insolvency application after a Section 7 petition is mandatory[cite: 11]. 2. Whether a dissenting financial creditor is entitled to differential payout under Section 30(2)(b) read with Section 53[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 11A(3) mandatorily requires the Adjudicating Authority to first dispose of a pending Section 7 application if a pre-packaged application under Section 54C is filed after 14 days; however, where a corporate debtor has been successfully resolved under PPIRP with majority approval and implementation, setting aside the entire process is not in the interest of justice[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) mandates that dissenting financial creditors must receive payouts not less than what they would receive under Section 53 liquidation[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: MSME status based on ITR records subsists unless revoked by competent authorities[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While Section 11A(3) is mandatory, setting aside an implemented PPIRP resolution plan is unwarranted; instead, dissenting financial creditors must be paid any differential amount due under Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 888 and 890 of 2023 are disposed of. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1492 of 2023 is partly allowed, directing payment of differential amounts to the dissenting appellant under Section 30(2)(b) within four weeks[cite: 11].
summary: These appeals challenged NCLT Jaipur orders admitting a pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PPIRP) for Shree Rajasthan Syntex Ltd., disposing of Bank of Baroda's Section 7 petition, and approving the Base Resolution Plan[cite: 11]. The NCLAT held that although Section 11A(3) mandates prioritizing Section 7 petitions when PPIRP applications are filed after 14 days, setting aside an implemented resolution plan for an MSME is uncalled for[cite: 11]. The NCLAT dismissed appeals against the PPIRP admission but partly allowed the appeal against the resolution plan, ordering payment of any differential dues to the dissenting bank under Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 11].

case_title: Punjab State Power Corporation Limited vs. Akums Lifesciences Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Punjab State Power Corporation Limited (PSPCL), and Respondent is Akums Lifesciences Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant / Corporate Debtor, formerly Parabolic Drugs Limited)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pre-CIRP electricity dues amounting to Rs. 3,87,96,889 claimed by PSPCL for the period prior to CIRP initiation[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding pre-CIRP electricity arrears of Rs. 3,87,96,889[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 23.08.2018; resolution plan approved on 12.01.2021; SRA paid Rs. 3.88 crores under protest on 19.03.2023 to restore electricity; NCLT passed impugned order on 05.07.2023[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: PSPCL failed to file its claim before the Resolution Professional during CIRP[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority allowed IA No. 164/2021 filed by the SRA, nullifying pre-CIRP electricity dues, leading to this appeal by PSPCL[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether an electricity distribution company can insist on the payment of pre-CIRP arrears as a condition for restoring electricity to a successful resolution applicant when no claim was filed during CIRP[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved under Section 31 of the IBC, all pre-existing claims and dues for which no claim is filed stand extinguished, and power distribution companies cannot condition the restoration of electricity on the payment of past pre-CIRP arrears[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC gives overriding effect over other laws, including the Electricity Act, 2003[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure of a statutory utility to file its claim during CIRP results in extinguishment of its pre-CIRP claims upon plan approval[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly nullified pre-CIRP electricity dues and ordered no insistence on past arrears[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. Connected pending applications are disposed of[cite: 12].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Chandigarh order nullifying pre-CIRP electricity dues of Parabolic Drugs Limited and ordering relief to Successful Resolution Applicant Akums Lifesciences Limited[cite: 12]. The NCLAT held that under Section 31 and Section 238 of the IBC, approval of a resolution plan extinguishes all unfiled pre-CIRP claims, and electricity distribution companies cannot demand past arrears as a precondition for restoring power[cite: 12]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 12].

case_title: ILD Owners Welfare Association vs. M/S. ALM Infotech City Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is ILD Owners Welfare Association; Respondent is M/s. ALM Infotech City Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent launched 'ILD Trade Centre' project; allottees executed Conveyance Deeds from 2015 onwards containing Clause 26 requiring payment of Rs. 100 per sq. ft. of super area towards Interest Free Maintenance Security (IFMS) for common area maintenance[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Demand notice of Rs. 2.95 crores sent by Appellant to Respondent on 06.10.2023 for unhanded IFMS maintenance corpus[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Occupancy certificate received on 19.11.2010; completion certificate on 03.06.2016; maintenance taken over by Appellant on 08.09.2022; Section 7 application filed in April 2024; NCLT rejected application on 30.07.2024[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Conveyance deeds reflecting IFMS collected towards maintenance of common areas, facilities, and amenities[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority rejected the Section 7 application on 30.07.2024, holding that IFMS is not a 'financial debt', leading to the present appeal[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether Interest Free Maintenance Security (IFMS) deposits collected from allottees under conveyance deeds for common area maintenance constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For a debt to qualify as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, there must be a disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money, carrying the commercial effect of a borrowing[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) and its explanation require a commercial effect of borrowing and disbursement for time value; routine security deposits or maintenance corpus payments do not satisfy this threshold[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examining the underlying contract (conveyance deed clauses) to determine the real nature of the transaction—whether it is a financial loan or an advance payment for operational maintenance services[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: IFMS deposits collected for maintenance services are not disbursed against the time value of money and do not qualify as financial debt; hence, a Section 7 application by an association seeking transfer of IFMS is not maintainable[cite: 17].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 17].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT New Delhi order rejecting a Section 7 application filed by the ILD Owners Welfare Association against M/s. ALM Infotech City Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT held that Interest Free Maintenance Security (IFMS) collected from unit holders under conveyance deeds for maintaining common areas does not involve disbursement against the time value of money and therefore does not constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 17].

case_title: Pramod Kumar Jain, Ex-Director of Aryan Ispat & Power Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mangesh Vitthal Kekre, IRP & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pramod Kumar Jain (Ex-Director of Corporate Debtor Aryan Ispat & Power Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Mangesh Vitthal Kekre (IRP); Respondent No. 2 is the Operational Creditor[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application for an amount of Rs. 6,13,48,161.98/-, comprising Rs. 4,97,22,461.16/- towards principal and Rs. 1,16,25,700.82/- towards interest[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The entire principal amount of Rs. 4,97,22,461.16/- was paid by the Corporate Debtor during the pendency of the proceedings before the Tribunal, leaving only the disputed interest component[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice sent on 05.07.2023; reply sent on 20.07.2023; principal paid and email sent on 31.01.2024; Adjudicating Authority admitted Section 9 application on 22.03.2024[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's ledger and email dated 31.01.2024 reflected a nil balance for principal dues, and interest was claimed unilaterally via invoice footnotes without a formal agreement[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Section 9 application solely for unpaid interest, leading to the present appeal by the Ex-Director[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable and can be admitted solely for an unpaid interest component when the entire principal operational debt has already been paid, particularly where the interest was unilaterally claimed via invoice footnotes without an express agreement between the parties[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC is not maintainable solely for the recovery of interest when the entire principal operational debt has been paid, as the spirit of the legislation is for the resolution of debt and not for recovery[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) restricts operational debt to claims arising from goods or services, and interest is recoverable only when expressly agreed upon by the parties; boilerplate interest clauses in invoice footnotes lacking a formal agreement or specified due dates are unenforceable[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the principal amount is accepted without murmur and shown as nil in the ledger, payments cannot be retrospectively adjusted towards unilateral interest claims without contractual backing[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting the Section 9 application solely for an unagreed interest component after the complete discharge of the principal debt[cite: 19].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated 22.03.2024 admitting the Section 9 application is set aside. No costs.[cite: 19]
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT order admitting a Section 9 application against Aryan Ispat & Power Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT noted that the Corporate Debtor had paid the entire principal amount of Rs. 4.97 crores, and the application was admitted solely for an unpaid interest component of Rs. 1.16 crores claimed unilaterally via invoice footnotes. Relying on precedents that the IBC is for debt resolution and not recovery, and that unagreed invoice interest clauses are unenforceable, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the admission order[cite: 19].

case_title: CA Ramchandra Dallaram Choudhary, Liquidator of Anil Limited vs. Adani Infrastructure & Developers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant is CA Ramchandra Dallaram Choudhary (Liquidator of Anil Limited); Respondent is Adani Infrastructure & Developers Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 20] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings of Anil Limited involving property and development rights disputes[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (refiling delay condonation application)[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 21.06.2024; appeal e-filed on 03.08.2024; defects notified by NCLT registry on 12.08.2024 to be cured by 19.08.2024; appeal refiled after 115 days delay[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clerical misplacement of original paper books, certified copies, and general affidavits by a Delhi-based filing clerk, coupled with translation delays[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 8709 of 2024 seeking condonation of 115 days delay in refiling the appeal[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether an inordinate refiling delay of 115 days caused by administrative oversight and alleged misplacement of documents by a filing clerk can be condoned in a time-bound IBC liquidation process without sufficient and reasonable cause[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the standard of scrutiny for refiling delays is less rigorous than for initial filing delays and the 7-day defect rectification rule under NCLAT Rules is directory, an applicant must still demonstrate a reasonable, justifiable, and sufficient cause for extensive delays, keeping in view the statutory mandate of timeliness under the IBC[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural rules must be interpreted to support the overarching objective of time-bound resolution and liquidation under the IBC[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Vague excuses regarding geographical distance between Ahmedabad and Delhi, technical email glitches without proof, and minor translation work cannot justify a nearly four-month refiling delay[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The explanation offered for the 115-day refiling delay is perfunctory and lacks bona fide diligence, warranting the dismissal of both the condonation application and the memo of appeal[cite: 20].
operative_order: IA No. 8709 of 2024 seeking condonation of 115 days delay in refiling is rejected. Consequently, the Memo of Appeal is also rejected[cite: 20].
summary: This order disposed of an application (IA No. 8709 of 2024) seeking condonation of a 115-day refiling delay in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 2316 of 2024, filed by the Liquidator of Anil Limited[cite: 20]. The NCLAT held that reasons such as geographical distance, minor translation tasks, and alleged misplacement of documents by a filing clerk did not constitute sufficient or justifiable cause for an inordinate delay of nearly four months, especially given the strict timeline requirements of IBC liquidation proceedings[cite: 20]. Accordingly, the NCLAT dismissed both the condonation application and the appeal[cite: 20].

case_title: Brand Steel & Power Pvt. Ltd. vs. Avishek Gupta (RP) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Brand Steel & Power Pvt. Ltd. (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant); Respondents include Avishek Gupta (Resolution Professional), Pinax Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant), and CoC members[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor Indian Pulp and Paper Private Limited on 22.07.2022; Form G published on 23.10.2022; appellant and SRA submitted expression of interest and resolution plans[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Resolution plan approval process for the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form G issued on 23.10.2022; initial plan submitted by appellant on 10.01.2023; CoC extended EOI and plan submission timelines in February 2023 without issuing a fresh Form G; SRA submitted plan; CoC approved SRA's plan on 11.08.2023 with 96.05% vote share; NCLT approved plan on 20.12.2024[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invitation for EOI Clause 6 permitted timeline extensions with CoC approval; final list of prospective resolution applicants published on 28.02.2023 included both the appellant and SRA[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan via IA No. 1490/KB/2023 and dismissed the appellant's challenge via IA No. 1407/KB/2023 on 20.12.2024, leading to the present appeals[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether extending the timeline for submission of Expression of Interest (EOI) and resolution plans without publishing a fresh Form G vitiates the CIRP and constitutes a material irregularity under Section 61(3)(ii) of the IBC[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Extending the timeline for submission of EOI and resolution plans with the approval of the Committee of Creditors, pursuant to enabling clauses in the original invitation for EOI, does not require the issuance of a fresh Form G, and an unsuccessful applicant who participated in the revised process cannot challenge it after voting[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 36A(4A) requires modification of EOI invitations to follow initial procedures, but mere extension of timelines authorized by initial terms does not amount to a modification requiring a fresh Form G[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Participants who take the benefit of extended timelines to revise and make their own plans compliant cannot turn around and challenge the process after voting concludes unfavorably[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No material irregularity was committed by the Resolution Professional or CoC, and the approval of the resolution plan by a thumping majority of 96.05% is valid and unassailable[cite: 21].
operative_order: Both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 194 and 195 of 2025) are dismissed[cite: 21].
summary: These appeals challenged the NCLT Kolkata Bench orders approving the resolution plan submitted by Pinax Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. for Indian Pulp and Paper Private Limited and rejecting the unsuccessful applicant's challenge[cite: 21]. The NCLAT held that extending timelines for EOI submission in accordance with the original invitation clauses and CoC approval did not mandate a fresh Form G, and the SRA was duly included in the final list of prospective resolution applicants[cite: 21]. Noting that the appellant actively participated in the revised process and challenged it only after voting, the NCLAT dismissed the appeals and upheld the plan approval[cite: 21].

case_title: Asean International Limited vs. Sanjeev Maheshwari, Liquidator of Varun Resources Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Asean International Limited (operational creditor/supplier); Respondent is Sanjeev Maheshwari (Liquidator of Varun Resources Limited)[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant supplied bunkers, fuel, fresh water, and oil to three vessels of the Corporate Debtor between 23-27 July 2017 under invoices totaling USD 173,182.97[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim of USD 173,183.17 plus subsequently claimed interest aggregating to USD 364,257.29[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor admitted to CIRP on 14.06.2017; liquidation ordered on 04.12.2018; public announcement issued on 06.12.2018 with deadline 02.01.2019; appellant filed belated claim on 23.03.2019, which was rejected on 30.03.2019; debit notes for interest issued on 25.06.2019; IA 1795 of 2023 filed on 27.03.2023; NCLT dismissed IA on 17.10.2023[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices dated 07.08.2017 contained no interest specification; interest debit notes raised two years later in June 2019; sub-contractors Gujarat Marines and Dushyant Patel filed Admiralty suits before the Bombay High Court[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed IA No. 1795 of 2023 on 17.10.2023, leading to the present appeal[cite: 22].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an operational creditor can claim interest on delayed payments when no interest was specified in the original invoices or claimed within the liquidation claim timeline. 2. Whether an application under Section 60(5) is maintainable to challenge a liquidator's claim rejection when the specific appellate remedy under Section 42 was bypassed. 3. Whether a liquidator can condition settlement payouts on the issuance of a No Objection Certificate (NOC) to avoid duplicate claims from sub-contractors[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor who fails to file a claim within the stipulated liquidation timeline or omits interest components cannot subsequently introduce belated interest claims via unilateral debit notes years later, nor can Section 60(5) be invoked to bypass the specific appellate remedy and 14-day limitation period prescribed under Section 42 of the IBC[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 42 mandates that appeals against a liquidator's claim rejection must be filed within 14 days, and failure to do so renders the decision final, precluding indirect challenges via Section 60(5)[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Invoices lacking express interest clauses and claims submitted without interest components crystallize upon rejection, barring subsequent unilateral additions[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator acted lawfully in rejecting belated interest claims and requiring an NOC to prevent double payments to sub-contractors who had instituted parallel Admiralty proceedings, and the appeal is devoid of merit[cite: 22].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 22].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Mumbai order dismissing IA No. 1795 of 2023 filed by Asean International Limited against the Liquidator of Varun Resources Limited[cite: 22]. The NCLAT held that the appellant failed to challenge the liquidator's 30.03.2019 claim rejection within the 14-day window under Section 42 of the IBC and could not revive the time-barred claim or introduce belated interest via Section 60(5)[cite: 22]. Furthermore, the NCLAT upheld the liquidator's demand for a No Objection Certificate to settle parallel Admiralty claims by sub-contractors and avoid duplicate payments[cite: 22]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 22].

case_title: Sandeep Jain vs. IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sandeep Jain (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Shree Vardhman Infraheights Private Limited); Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debenture Trust Deed dated 19.04.2016 executed for raising funds via non-convertible debentures; restated and amended trust deed executed on 04.11.2019 following a settlement agreement before the Delhi High Court; subsequent repayment schedule amendments on 23.11.2020 and 23.11.2021[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 263,00,46,668/- as on 30.09.2023, with default date occurring on 31.12.2021[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default on 31.12.2021; default notice issued on 27.09.2023; Section 7 application filed on 06.12.2023; NCLT admitted Section 7 application on 08.01.2025[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Restated trust deeds, default notices, financial statements acknowledging debt, and information utility records[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority admitted Section 7 application on 08.01.2025, leading to the present appeal by the suspended director[cite: 23].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the constitution of a Project Monitoring Committee (PMC) with majority financial creditor nominees under a settlement agreement constitutes financial creditor control over the project, thereby absolving the corporate debtor of default or barring Section 7 proceedings. 2. Whether admitted debt and default warrant mandatory admission of a Section 7 application[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The constitution of a Project Monitoring Committee (PMC) to monitor construction, sales, and collections under a settlement agreement does not absolve the corporate debtor and its obligors of their independent repayment obligations, nor does it bar the initiation of CIRP under Section 7 upon default[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once a financial creditor proves the existence of a financial debt and a default in repayment, the Adjudicating Authority is mandatorily required to admit a Section 7 application[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Explicit clauses in settlement agreements preserving repayment obligations override arguments of financial creditor co-promoter liability or project interference[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Debt and default being undisputed, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 application[cite: 23].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 23].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Principal Bench order dated 08.01.2025 admitting a Section 7 application filed by IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited against Shree Vardhman Infraheights Private Limited[cite: 23]. The NCLAT held that the appellant did not contest debt and default, and the establishment of a Project Monitoring Committee (PMC) under a prior settlement agreement was merely for project monitoring and did not alter or extinguish the corporate debtor's independent statutory repayment liability[cite: 23]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the admission of the corporate debtor into CIRP[cite: 23].

case_title: Navin Madhavji Mehta (Suspended Director) vs. Jaldhi Overseas Pte Ltd & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Navin Madhavji Mehta (Suspended Director of RR Metalmakers India Limited); Respondent No. 1 is Jaldhi Overseas Pte Ltd (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is the IRP; Respondent No. 3 is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Charter Party Agreement dated 15.03.2017 between Corporate Debtor and Operational Creditor for chartering vessel MV Aetolia to carry cargo from Port Redi to China; freight invoice of USD 653,312 raised on 18.04.2017; partial payment of USD 350,000 made on 04.08.2017; debit note for demurrage of USD 242,772.19 raised on 27.12.2017[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational debt claim of USD 523,141.45 (comprising freight balance and demurrage)[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised in 2017; Section 8 demand notice issued on 25.02.2020; reply sent on 09.03.2020; legal notice on 11.10.2022; re-served demand notice on 25.02.2020/30.12.2022; Section 9 petition filed in 2023; NCLT admitted petition on 22.04.2024[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence between parties showing ongoing disputes regarding third-party payments through Samruddha, BST, and Globe Chart, and lack of confirmation of demurrage[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority admitted Section 9 application on 22.04.2024, leading to the appeal by the suspended director[cite: 24].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a Section 9 application under the IBC is maintainable when there is a pre-existing dispute regarding operational debt and demurrage charges. 2. Whether letters requesting meetings or verification of accounts constitute an unequivocal acknowledgment of debt extending limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor raises a plausible, non-spurious pre-existing dispute regarding operational debt and unliquidated demurrage charges prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice, a Section 9 application under the IBC is not maintainable[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Section 9(5)(ii) of the IBC mandate the rejection of an application if a pre-existing dispute exists or if the debt is genuinely disputed[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tentative letters asking for reconciliation or stating that demurrage is unconfirmed do not amount to an admission of debt or liability[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that the corporate debtor admitted liability and in ignoring pre-existing disputes regarding freight payments and demurrage, warranting setting aside of the admission order[cite: 24].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated 22.04.2024 admitting the Section 9 application is set aside. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigours of CIRP[cite: 24].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Jaldhi Overseas Pte Ltd against RR Metalmakers India Limited[cite: 24]. The NCLAT held that the corporate debtor had raised valid, pre-existing disputes concerning freight payments through third parties and unconfirmed demurrage charges prior to the Section 8 demand notice, which were neither spurious nor illusory. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the CIRP admission order, and released the corporate debtor from insolvency[cite: 24].

case_title: Raman Gupta vs. Surendra Raj Garg, Resolution Professional of Metenere Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Raman Gupta (promoter/suspended director of Corporate Debtor Metenere Limited); Respondents include Surendra Raj Garg (Resolution Professional) and NARCL[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP against Corporate Debtor Metenere Limited commenced on 03.10.2020 on an application by State Bank of India[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Plan amount of Rs. 295,14,95,611 deposited by SRA[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 03.10.2020; CoC approved resolution plan of Orissa Metaliks Pvt. Ltd. with 98.94% vote share in the 35th meeting on 11.07.2024; Adjudicating Authority directed deposit of entire plan amount on 10.09.2024 and approved the plan on 04.10.2024[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan provisions protecting personal/corporate guarantees while requiring plan amounts to be kept aside in interest-bearing accounts for pending stakeholder claims[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan via order dated 04.10.2024 in IA No. 37 of 2024, leading to this appeal by the suspended director[cite: 25].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a resolution plan is conditional and invalid if it provides for setting aside plan proceeds in an interest-bearing account until adjudication of pending stakeholder applications. 2. Whether approval of a resolution plan discharges personal or corporate guarantors[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Approval of a resolution plan does not ipso facto discharge a personal or corporate guarantor under an independent contract, and a plan is not conditional merely because it directs plan proceeds to be held in interest-bearing accounts for distribution pending adjudication of claims by various stakeholders[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) compliance and commercial wisdom of the CoC govern plan approval, and maintaining deposits to protect stakeholder claims is valid[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Provisions preserving financial creditors' recourse against personal guarantees are legally permissible and binding[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in approving the resolution plan, as stakeholder interests were fully protected by depositing the entire plan amount in a fixed deposit[cite: 25].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 25].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Principal Bench order dated 04.10.2024 approving the resolution plan submitted by Orissa Metaliks Pvt. Ltd. for Metenere Limited[cite: 25]. The NCLAT held that setting aside the plan amount in an interest-bearing account to adjudicate pending claims of stakeholders ensures protection of all interests and does not render the plan conditional[cite: 25]. Furthermore, the NCLAT reiterated that approval of a resolution plan does not discharge personal guarantors under independent contracts[cite: 25]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 25].

case_title: Saturn Ventures & Advisors Pvt. Ltd. & Satish Gopinath vs. S. Gopalkrishnan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Saturn Ventures & Advisors Pvt. Ltd. (Intervenor/Appellant in 1st appeal) and Satish Gopinath (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Saturn Rings and Forgings Pvt. Ltd.); Respondents are S. Gopalkrishnan (RP) and Agrasen Engineering Industries Pvt. Ltd. (SRA)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bank of India filed a Section 7 application against Corporate Debtor Saturn Rings and Forgings Pvt. Ltd., admitted on 24.12.2021[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debt resolution of Saturn Rings and Forgings Pvt. Ltd[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 24.12.2021; RP filed IA 3478 of 2022 for plan approval and IA 787 of 2023 for fraudulent transactions; Intervenor filed IA 12 of 2023 claiming ownership of machinery; NCLT passed final order dismissing IA 12/2023 and approving the resolution plan[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audit revealed a fraudulent journal entry dated 31.03.2020 transferring plant and machinery worth Rs. 6.48 crores to the appellant post-filing of Section 7 petition, while the machinery was all along hypothecated to Bank of India and shown as a fixed asset with depreciation claimed by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed Saturn Ventures' application claiming machinery ownership and allowed the RP's application for avoidance of fraudulent transactions, leading to appeals by the intervenor and suspended director[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether a machinery claimed to be leased by a parent company (intervenor) belongs to the corporate debtor or constitutes a third-party asset exempt from the resolution plan, and whether a post-petition transfer of machinery via journal entry constitutes a fraudulent transaction under Sections 49 and 66 of the IBC[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor treats machinery as its own fixed asset, claims depreciation under income tax law, and hypothecates it to financial creditors while lacking any formal lease deed or rental payments, a post-petition transfer of the machinery via journal entry is fraudulent and void, and the asset forms part of the corporate debtor's estate for resolution[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 explanation excludes third-party assets held under valid contractual arrangements like bailment or trust, but unsubstantiated lease claims and fraudulent transfer entries cannot remove hypothecated assets from the liquidation estate[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Claiming depreciation under income tax law and hypothecating assets to banks as promoter contribution conclusively establish ownership by the corporate debtor rather than a lessee status[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly dismissed the intervenor's ownership claim and annulled the fraudulent transfer entry, upholding the inclusion of the machinery in the resolution plan[cite: 26].
operative_order: Both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 645 and 839 of 2024) are dismissed[cite: 26].
summary: These appeals challenged the NCLT Principal Bench order dismissing Saturn Ventures & Advisors Pvt. Ltd.'s application claiming ownership of a Wagner 630 machinery line and approving the resolution plan for Saturn Rings and Forgings Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 26] The NCLAT held that the machinery belonged to the Corporate Debtor, as evidenced by financial statements, income tax depreciation claims, and hypothecation agreements with Bank of India, and that a post-petition journal entry transferring the machinery to the parent company was fraudulent under Sections 49 and 66 of the IBC[cite: 26]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed both appeals[cite: 26].

case_title: Pradeep Agarwal & Ors. vs. Nutan Ispat And Power Private Limited & Connected Appeals
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 147 of 2020, 790 of 2021 & 299 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Pradeep Agarwal, Nutan Agarwal, and M/s Indo Lahari Bio Power Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is M/s Nutan Ispat and Power Private Limited (Corporate Debtor) / Bimal Khetan Group[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: MoU dated 31.07.2016 executed for transferring shareholding of Corporate Debtor to Khetan Group; appellants advanced Rs. 7,26,00,788/- for operational and financial liabilities pending takeover[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default of Rs. 7.26 crores[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoU signed on 31.07.2016; demand notices sent on 12.09.2018; Section 7 application filed on 24.10.2018 and dismissed on 02.12.2019; Memorandum of Settlement executed on 21.09.2019; arbitral award published on 15.11.2019; subsequent revival applications dismissed by NCLT in 2021 and 2022; parties entered into a mutual settlement agreement on 15.01.2025[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Dispute referred to arbitration resulting in an arbitral award on 15.11.2019, followed by a subsequent amicable settlement agreement dated 15.01.2025[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeals filed against NCLT orders dismissing the Section 7 petition and applications for reviving company petitions; during appellate proceedings, parties entered into a mutual settlement agreement on 15.01.2025[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application and related revival applications should be entertained or pursued when the underlying disputes have been referred to arbitration, culminated in an arbitral award, and subsequently resolved via a comprehensive mutual settlement agreement between the parties[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When parties to insolvency proceedings resolve their disputes amicably through a formal out-of-court settlement agreement during appellate proceedings, nothing survives for adjudication, and the appeals can be disposed of in terms of the settlement[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications cannot be maintained or revived once valid out-of-court settlements or arbitral awards extinguish or subsume the underlying claims[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Execution of a binding settlement agreement placed on record via interlocutory applications supersedes prior claims and litigation[cite: 27]. 4.
