DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In view of the mutual settlement agreement dated 15.01.2025 entered into between the parties, all three appeals stand disposed of as nothing survives for adjudication[cite: 27].
operative_order: All three appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 147 of 2020, 790 of 2021, and 299 of 2023) are disposed of in terms of the settlement agreement dated 15.01.2025, with no order as to costs[cite: 27].
summary: This judgment disposed of a set of three interconnected appeals (CA No. 147 of 2020, 790 of 2021, and 299 of 2023) challenging NCLT orders that dismissed a Section 7 application and subsequent revival applications involving Pradeep Agarwal and Nutan Ispat and Power Private Limited[cite: 27]. During the appellate hearings, the parties entered into a formal mutual settlement agreement dated 15.01.2025 and placed it on record via interlocutory applications[cite: 27]. Consequently, the NCLAT took the settlement on record and disposed of all three appeals accordingly[cite: 27].

case_title: Anuj Bajpai (Liquidator) & Inderdeep Construction Company vs. Anvesha Engineering & Projects Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Anuj Bajpai (Liquidator) and Inderdeep Construction Company (Successful Bidder); Respondent is Anvesha Engineering & Projects Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and Income Tax Department[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 9 application admitted on 25.01.2021; failure of resolution plans led to liquidation and sale as a going concern under Regulation 32(e) of Liquidation Regulations; e-auction conducted on 28.08.2023 won by Inderdeep Construction Company for Rs. 42.85 crores[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bid amount of Rs. 42.85 crores exceeding reserve price of Rs. 42.60 crores[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation ordered on 13.01.2023; unamended Regulation 32A(4) 90-day period expired on 19.04.2023; Regulation 32A(4) amended on 16.09.2022 removing the 90-day restriction and requiring sale in the first attempt; IA 950 of 2023 filed for condonation of delay; e-auction held on 28.08.2023; sale certificate issued on 25.09.2023; NCLT passed impugned order on 04.07.2024[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator complied with amended Regulation 32A(4) by conducting the going concern sale in the first attempt, distributing proceeds to stakeholders[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed IA No. 1479 of 2023 filed by the successful bidder for concessions/waivers and made adverse observations against the liquidator, leading to appeals by both the liquidator and the successful bidder[cite: 28].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the unamended 90-day time limit under Regulation 32A(4) applies to a going concern sale conducted after the rule amendment of 16.09.2022. 2. Whether a successful auction purchaser of a corporate debtor as a going concern in liquidation takes the company on a 'clean slate' free from past unpaid liabilities prior to distribution under Section 53[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An amendment to Regulation 32A(4) of the IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations on 16.09.2022 removing the 90-day time limit and requiring going concern sales to be conducted in the first attempt governs subsequent auctions, rendering delay condonation applications unnecessary; furthermore, successful purchasers of a corporate debtor as a going concern in liquidation acquire the company on a 'clean slate' free from past unpaid liabilities prior to Section 53 distribution[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Subordinate legislation amendments operating prospectively during ongoing liquidation proceedings govern procedural requirements like going concern sales[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Conducting a going concern sale in the first auction attempt following statutory amendments fulfills liquidation mandate without requiring condonation of technical delays[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the successful bidder's concession application and in making adverse remarks against the liquidator, warranting setting aside of the impugned order[cite: 28].
operative_order: Both appeals (CA No. 1698 and 1518 of 2024) are allowed, and the impugned order dated 04.07.2024 is set aside[cite: 28].
summary: These appeals challenged the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench common order dated 04.07.2024 which dismissed an application (IA No. 1479 of 2023) seeking reliefs and concessions filed by Successful Bidder Inderdeep Construction Company and made adverse remarks against Liquidator Anuj Bajpai[cite: 28]. The NCLAT held that the 16.09.2022 amendment to Regulation 32A(4) removed the 90-day restriction for going concern sales, and the liquidator had duly conducted the sale in the first attempt[cite: 28]. Reaffirming the 'clean slate' principle for going concern sales in liquidation, the NCLAT allowed both appeals and set aside the impugned order and adverse remarks[cite: 28].

case_title: Pradeep Kumar Agarwal & Ors. vs. Ghankun Steels Pvt Ltd & Connected Appeals
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 147 of 2020, 790 of 2021 & 299 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Pradeep Kumar Agarwal (HUF), Pradeep Agarwal, Nutan Agarwal, and Bamleashwari Nimesh Private Limited; Respondent is Ghankun Steels Private Limited (and connected entities across appeals)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor share transfer and financial advancement disputes governed by an MoU dated 31.07.2016 and subsequent settlement agreements[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed financial debt default[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application dismissed on 02.12.2019 (CA 147/2020); Memorandum of Settlement executed on 21.09.2019; arbitral award published on 15.11.2019; NCLT dismissed applications for revival of company petitions on 16.04.2021 (CA 790/2021) and 13.01.2022 (CA 299/2023); parties entered into a mutual settlement agreement on 15.01.2025[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Dispute referred to arbitration resulting in an award on 15.11.2019, followed by an amicable mutual settlement agreement executed on 15.01.2025[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Three connected appeals challenging NCLT orders dismissing Section 7 applications and revival petitions; parties filed interlocutory applications bringing on record a mutual settlement agreement dated 15.01.2025[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether appeals arising from the dismissal of Section 7 petitions and company petition revival applications should proceed to merits adjudication when the parties have executed a binding out-of-court mutual settlement agreement[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When disputing parties execute a formal mutual settlement agreement resolving all claims during appellate proceedings, the appeals are rendered infructuous and should be disposed of in terms of the settlement[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Insolvency proceedings cannot be maintained or revived where underlying monetary disputes are fully settled out of court[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acceptance of a settlement agreement by all parties obviates the need for judicial determination on merits[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: All connected appeals are disposed of pursuant to the mutual settlement agreement dated 15.01.2025[cite: 29].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 147 of 2020, 790 of 2021, and 299 of 2023 are disposed of in terms of the settlement agreement dated 15.01.2025, with no order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary: This judgment disposed of three connected appeals (CA No. 147 of 2020, 790 of 2021, and 299 of 2023) challenging NCLT orders relating to Section 7 petitions and company petition revival applications involving Pradeep Kumar Agarwal and related corporate entities[cite: 29]. Following the reservation of judgment, the parties entered into a formal mutual settlement agreement dated 15.01.2025, which was placed before the NCLAT via interlocutory applications[cite: 29]. The NCLAT took the settlement on record and disposed of all three appeals without adjudicating on merits[cite: 29].

case_title: Pioneer Packaging Industries Pvt. Ltd. vs. Abhisek Gupta (RP of Indian Pulp and Paper Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pioneer Packaging Industries Pvt. Ltd.; Respondents include Abhisek Gupta (Resolution Professional of Indian Pulp and Paper Pvt. Ltd.) and others[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Indian Pulp and Paper Pvt. Ltd[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (limitation and delay condonation in filing appeal against dismissal of application for consideration of EOI)[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 20.12.2024; uploaded on server on 24.12.2024; 30-day limitation period expired on 19.01.2025; appeal e-filed on 05.02.2025 with a delay of 17 days[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Delay of 17 days beyond the 30-day statutory period, exceeding the maximum 15-day condonable period under Section 61(2) proviso[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed IA No. 1450/KB/2023 on 20.12.2024; appellant filed appeal with a 17-day delay, leading to the present dismissal on limitation grounds[cite: 31].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the limitation period under Section 61(2) of the IBC begins from the date of the order or the date of uploading on the server. 2. Whether the NCLAT has jurisdiction to condone a delay exceeding the 15-day window provided in the proviso to Section 61(2)[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC is 30 days commencing from the date of the order, not from the date of uploading on the server, and the NCLAT lacks jurisdiction to condone any delay exceeding the 15-day condonable period under the proviso[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) proviso restricts the appellate tribunal's power to condone delays beyond 15 days after the initial 30-day period[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Computation of limitation from the date of pronouncement of the order leaves a delay of 17 days, which is beyond the 15-day maximum threshold[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the appeal was filed beyond the 45-day outer limit (30 days + 15 days), the tribunal has no jurisdiction to condone the delay, and the appeal is barred by limitation[cite: 31].
operative_order: The application for condonation of delay is dismissed, and consequently, the appeal is also dismissed as not duly constituted[cite: 31].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT order dated 20.12.2024 dismissing an application filed by Pioneer Packaging Industries Pvt. Ltd. seeking consideration of its Expression of Interest (EOI)[cite: 31]. The NCLAT held that limitation starts from the date of the order (not the server upload date), and since the appeal was filed with a 17-day delay, it exceeded the maximum 15-day condonable extension under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 31]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the delay application and the appeal as time-barred[cite: 31].

case_title: Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) vs. Harshad Hirji Thakkar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI); Respondent is Harshad Hirji Thakkar (Personal Guarantor)[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 95(1) application filed by SIDBI against personal guarantor Harshad Hirji Thakkar[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Personal insolvency application of SIDBI against the guarantor[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 95(1) application dismissed on 04.07.2024 as barred by time; recall application (IA 4399 of 2024) filed subsequently; dismissed on 09.10.2024; appeal filed with 43 days refiling delay[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Application seeking recall based on alternative interpretation of a Supreme Court order regarding limitation[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed the recall application on 09.10.2024, holding it to be a review petition which is not maintainable under NCLT powers, leading to the present appeal[cite: 32].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an Adjudicating Authority has the power to review its own orders under the guise of a recall application based on differing interpretations of law. 2. Whether an application under Section 95(1) dismissed as time-barred can be revived via a recall application[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority does not possess the power of review under the IBC, and issues arising from different interpretations of Supreme Court judgments cannot form the basis for a recall application[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLT lacks substantive review jurisdiction, restricting recall to narrow procedural grounds recognized by the 5-member bench precedent in Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disagreements over legal interpretations do not constitute a 'mistake apparent on the face of the record' correctable by recall[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the recall application as not maintainable, and the appeal lacks merit[cite: 32].
operative_order: IA No. 411 of 2025 (refiling delay) is condoned. The appeal is dismissed on merits[cite: 32].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 09.10.2024 which dismissed SIDBI's application seeking recall of an order dismissing its Section 95(1) personal insolvency petition as time-barred[cite: 32]. The NCLAT held that the NCLT has no power of review, and differing interpretations of Supreme Court rulings do not constitute grounds for recall[cite: 32]. Consequently, the NCLAT condoned the refiling delay but dismissed the appeal on merits[cite: 32].

case_title: Topline Comtech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Income Tax Officer, Ward No. 25(3), New Delhi & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Topline Comtech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.; Respondents are Income Tax Officer, Ward No. 25(3), New Delhi and Registrar of Companies[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company name struck off by ROC, NCT of Delhi & Haryana on 30.06.2017; Income Tax Department filed Section 252(1) read with Section 252(3) application for company restoration due to outstanding tax demand of Rs. 6,69,910/- for AY 2012-13[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Tax liability/outstanding demand of Rs. 6,69,910/- for AY 2012-13[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company struck off on 30.06.2017; demand notice issued on 30.11.2019; NCLT passed restoration order on 21.10.2024[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assessment order and demand notice for AY 2012-13 remaining unaddressed by the company during NCLT proceedings[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT allowed the Income Tax Department's restoration application via impugned order dated 21.10.2024 after noting the company failed to appear despite notice and paper publication, leading to this appeal[cite: 33].
legal_issues: Whether an order restoring a struck-off company under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, initiated by the Income Tax Department to recover outstanding tax demands, is sustainable when the company failed to appear or dispute the tax liability before the NCLT[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company's name may be validly restored to the Register of Companies under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, on the application of the Income Tax Department to facilitate tax recovery, particularly when the company fails to appear or dispute the underlying tax assessment and demand notice before the tribunal[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(1) and (3) empowers statutory authorities like the Income Tax Department to seek company restoration to protect revenue interests[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unchallenged assessment orders and demand notices create a valid premise for company restoration, and judicial presumption of correctness applies to official tribunal proceedings[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellants' failure to appear or contest the tax demands before the NCLT justifies the restoration order, and the appeal lacks merit[cite: 33].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and all pending applications are disposed of[cite: 33].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT order dated 21.10.2024 which allowed the Income Tax Department's application under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, to restore Topline Comtech Pvt. Ltd. to the Register of Companies for the recovery of outstanding tax demands of Rs. 6,69,910/- for AY 2012-13[cite: 33]. The NCLAT held that since the company failed to appear or dispute the tax demand before the NCLT despite notice and paper publication, the restoration order was fully justified[cite: 33]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 33].

case_title: Greenshift Initiatives Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sonu Gupta, Resolution Professional of Rolta Bi & Big Data Analytics Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Greenshift Initiatives Pvt. Ltd. (Assignee); Respondent is Sonu Gupta (Resolution Professional of Rolta Bi & Big Data Analytics Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP against Corporate Debtor Rolta Bi & Big Data Analytics Pvt. Ltd. commenced on 13.10.2023; public announcement made on 16.10.2023 with deadline 28.10.2023; Appellant entered into an Assignment Agreement on 06.11.2023 with Rolta Pvt. Ltd. (a related party) to acquire debt of Rs. 3,25,000/- for Rs. 3,48,742/-[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted claim amount of Rs. 3,48,742/-[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 13.10.2023; claim deadline on 28.10.2023; assignment executed on 06.11.2023 (post-CIRP commencement); NCLT rejected CoC seating application (IA 331/2024) on 13.01.2025[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assignment agreement executed post-CIRP commencement between a related party assignor and third-party assignee seeking CoC membership[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority rejected the appellant's application for a seat in the CoC with voting rights on 13.01.2025, leading to the present appeal[cite: 34].
legal_issues: Whether a third-party assignee who acquires a debt from a related party creditor of the corporate debtor subsequent to the commencement of CIRP is entitled to a seat in the Committee of Creditors (CoC) with voting rights under Section 21(2) of the IBC[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While third-party assignees of related-party debts in good faith are generally not disabled from participating in the CoC, an assignment executed post-CIRP commencement with the sole intention of bypassing related-party disqualifications, participating in the CoC, and sabotaging the process by diluting other creditors' voting shares treats the assignee akin to a related party barred under the first proviso to Section 21(2)[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: First proviso to Section 21(2) excludes related parties from CoC participation, and post-commencement debt assignments by related parties designed to circumvent this restriction are invalid for voting rights[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Timing of the assignment (post-CIRP commencement) and the identity of the assignor (related party) establish bad faith and intent to manipulate CoC voting[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly denied CoC membership and voting rights to the appellant assignee[cite: 34].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 34].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT order dated 13.01.2025 dismissing IA No. 331/2024 filed by Greenshift Initiatives Pvt. Ltd. seeking a seat and voting rights in the Committee of Creditors (CoC)[cite: 34]. The NCLAT held that although third-party assignees of related-party debts can generally participate in the CoC, an assignment executed on 06.11.2023—after the CIRP commencement date of 13.01.2023—with a related party assignor was done in bad faith to circumvent statutory disqualifications and dilute other creditors' voting shares[cite: 34]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the denial of CoC membership[cite: 34].

case_title: Jai Prakash Keswani & Harvinder Singh vs. MB Malls Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Jai Prakash Keswani (Promoter) and Harvinder Singh (Homebuyer); Respondents include MB Malls Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approval of resolution plan for Corporate Debtor MB Malls Pvt. Ltd[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor resolution plan approved by 100% vote share of CoC[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan on 20.09.2024; appeals filed by promoter and homebuyer in 2025 with condonation of 13 days delay[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan approved with 100% CoC voting share, providing unit handover within 9 months subject to receipt of Occupancy Certificate[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan and dismissed promoter objections via order dated 20.09.2024, leading to the present appeals[cite: 35].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a resolution plan is non-implementable, conditional, or contingent merely because unit handover is stipulated within 9 months subject to receipt of an Occupancy Certificate. 2. Whether a single dissenting homebuyer can challenge a resolution plan approved by a 100% CoC majority[cite: 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan providing for unit handover within a specified timeframe subject to receipt of an Occupancy Certificate is neither conditional nor contingent at the approval stage, and issues of implementation feasibility cannot be used to prematurely challenge plan approval; furthermore, a single homebuyer must sail or sink with the majority decision of homebuyers and cannot independently challenge a plan approved by a 100% CoC majority[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 and commercial wisdom preclude tribunals from second-guessing CoC commercial decisions on plan viability and feasibility[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: 100% CoC approval conclusively establishes plan viability and commercial acceptability[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in approving the resolution plan, and both appeals by the promoter and lone homebuyer lack merit[cite: 35].
operative_order: Delays in filing and refiling are condoned. All appeals (CA No. 92, 93, and 94 of 2025) are dismissed[cite: 35].
summary: These appeals challenged the NCLT order dated 20.09.2024 approving the resolution plan for MB Malls Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 35] The NCLAT held that objections regarding implementation feasibility (such as unit handover within 9 months subject to Occupancy Certificate) cannot be raised prematurely to challenge plan approval, and that the commercial wisdom of a 100% CoC majority is binding[cite: 35]. Furthermore, the NCLAT reaffirmed that a single dissenting homebuyer must sail or sink with the majority and cannot maintain an independent challenge[cite: 35]. Consequently, the NCLAT condoned delays but dismissed all appeals[cite: 35].

case_title: Employees Provident Fund Organization vs. H L Buildwell Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant/Appellant is Employees Provident Fund Organization (EPFO); Respondent is H L Buildwell Private Limited[cite: 36]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of H L Buildwell Private Limited[cite: 36]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (refiling delay condonation application)[cite: 36]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 17.08.2023; appeal filed on 27.09.2023; registry notified defects on 05.10.2023; initial refiling with 22 days delay on 03.11.2023; hard copy submitted on 15.12.2023; multiple subsequent defect notifications by registry spanning months; final refiling after an inordinate refiling delay of 205 days[cite: 36]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Repeated routine and clerical defect notifications (dim copies, illegible text, lack of attestation) and unproven allegations of file misplacement by the NCLAT registry[cite: 36]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: EPFO filed IA No. 3202 of 2024 seeking condonation of an inordinate refiling delay of 205 days[cite: 36].
legal_issues: Whether an inordinate refiling delay of 205 days caused by administrative delays within a government department, clerical errors, and unsubstantiated claims of registry file misplacement can be condoned in time-bound IBC proceedings without sufficient cause[cite: 36].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While sufficient causes for delay are condonable, an inordinate refiling delay of 205 days characterized by cavalier handling of routine clerical defects, repeated intimation of identical deficiencies by the registry, and unproven assertions of registry file misplacement does not constitute 'sufficient cause', and such laxity runs counter to the time-bound objectives of the IBC[cite: 36]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural rules requiring prompt defect rectification must be enforced to prevent delays in insolvency proceedings[cite: 36]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure to produce documentary evidence showing active follow-up or registry mishandling negates claims of sufficient cause[cite: 36]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The applicant failed to establish sufficient cause for the massive 205-day refiling delay, warranting dismissal of both the condonation application and the memo of appeal[cite: 36].
operative_order: IA No. 3202 of 2024 seeking condonation of 205 days delay in refiling is rejected. Consequently, the Memo of Appeal is also rejected[cite: 36].
summary: This order disposed of an application (IA No. 3202 of 2024) seeking condonation of an inordinate refiling delay of 205 days in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1700 of 2024, filed by the Employees Provident Fund Organization (EPFO)[cite: 36]. The NCLAT held that routine clerical errors, internal governmental delays in obtaining signatures, and unsubstantiated allegations that the NCLAT registry lost the physical file did not constitute sufficient or plausible cause for a massive 205-day delay, especially given the strict timeline mandates of the IBC[cite: 36]. Accordingly, the NCLAT rejected the condonation application and dismissed the appeal[cite: 36].

case_title: Union of India vs. Infrastructure Leasing and Financial Services Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Union of India / IL&FS; Respondents include various banks (Indian Bank, Canara Bank, PNB, ICICI Bank), GAIL India Ltd., NHAI, and State of Rajasthan[cite: 37]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution of IL&FS and its group companies under court monitoring following systemic financial crises[cite: 37]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial dues as of end January 2025 stood at Rs. 703 crores and outstanding annuities at Rs. 1115 crores[cite: 37]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interim orders passed on 15.10.2018; subsequent interlocutory applications heard and disposed of on 28.02.2025[cite: 37]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank guarantees extended pursuant to prior tribunal orders, project terminations with NHAI, and ongoing arbitral proceedings[cite: 37]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT Principal Bench considered numerous interlocutory applications on 28.02.2025, issuing directions regarding bank guarantee extensions, distributions, and adjournments[cite: 37].
legal_issues: Whether bank guarantees issued in favor of public authorities should be extended or kept alive during pending arbitral proceedings, and whether financial distributions can be processed amidst competing claims[cite: 37].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Bank guarantees directed to be maintained by interim tribunal orders must remain operative and be continued until the conclusion of underlying arbitral proceedings between the parties, and interim distribution requests require verification of correct financial figures[cite: 37]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Moratorium and interim protections under ongoing corporate resolution frameworks govern the continuation of performance and financial bank guarantees[cite: 37]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where contracts have terminated and matters are referred to arbitration, issues relating to contract performance and bank guarantees are best addressed within the arbitral forum[cite: 37]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Various interlocutory applications concerning bank guarantee renewals, commission claims, and distribution figures are disposed of with specific directions for continuation of guarantees pending arbitration and further hearings scheduled for April 2025[cite: 37].
operative_order: Various interlocutory applications are disposed of with directions keeping bank guarantees alive till arbitration conclusion and scheduling further hearings for 07.03.2025 and 04.04.2025[cite: 37].
summary: This order addressed a multitude of interlocutory applications filed in Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 346 & 347 of 2018 concerning the IL&FS resolution proceedings[cite: 37]. The NCLAT Principal Bench directed that bank guarantees linked to terminated projects with public authorities like NHAI and GAIL must remain in force until the conclusion of ongoing arbitral proceedings, while deferring financial distribution issues for further scrutiny[cite: 37].

case_title: STCI Finance Ltd. vs. IMP Powers Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is STCI Finance Ltd.; Respondents include IMP Powers Ltd. & Ors., the Liquidator, the Successful Bidder (SRA), State Bank of India, and other creditors[cite: 38]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation e-auction of the Corporate Debtor IMP Powers Ltd.; Appellant claims first pari passu charge with SBI over corporate assets[cite: 38]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted claim amount of the Appellant offered by the liquidator is Rs. 39,30,54,422/-[cite: 38]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority decided Appellant's IA on 22.04.2024; appeal disposed of on 06.08.2024 based on liquidator's affidavit offering payout; subsequent distribution objections raised by other secured creditors before NCLT on 20.08.2024; revival application (IA 6616 of 2024) filed subsequently[cite: 38]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's affidavit proposing to pay the appellant's admitted claim, followed by objections from other secured creditors regarding distribution proportions[cite: 38]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT initially disposed of Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1019 of 2024 on 06.08.2024; upon subsequent disputes over distribution before the NCLT, STCI Finance filed IA No. 6616 of 2024 seeking revival of the appeal[cite: 38].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal disposed of on the basis of a liquidator's statement offering payout can be revived when other secured creditors subsequently challenge the proposed distribution before the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 38].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an appeal is disposed of without entering into merits based on a liquidator's affidavit proposing full payout of an admitted claim, but subsequent proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority reveal active disputes among secured creditors regarding distribution, the disposed appeal is liable to be revived to ensure comprehensive adjudication[cite: 38]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Appellate tribunals possess inherent power to recall disposal orders and revive appeals when foundational assumptions or settlement premises fail[cite: 38]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Opening up of distribution disputes by co-creditors before the NCLT necessitates the restoration of the appellate challenge[cite: 38]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The previous disposal order dated 06.08.2024 is recalled, the appeal is revived, and the matter is clubbed with connected appeals for a complete hearing[cite: 38].
operative_order: IA No. 6616 of 2024 is allowed; the judgment and order dated 06.08.2024 is recalled, and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1019 of 2024 is revived and listed for hearing on 17.04.2025 along with Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1657 of 2024[cite: 38].
summary: This order addressed IA No. 6616 of 2024 filed by STCI Finance Ltd. seeking the revival of Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1019 of 2024, which had been disposed of on 06.08.2024 based on the liquidator's affidavit offering payout[cite: 38]. The NCLAT noted that subsequent to the disposal, other secured creditors raised substantial objections regarding the distribution mechanism before the NCLT, leaving the distribution issue open[cite: 38]. Consequently, the NCLAT recalled its earlier disposal order, revived the appeal, and directed it to be listed along with connected proceedings[cite: 38].

case_title: Owners Welfare Association of Universal Trade Tower vs. Universal Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Owners Welfare Association of Universal Trade Tower (UTT); Respondents are Universal Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and Atul Kansal (Resolution Professional)[cite: 39]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor Universal Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. admitted to CIRP on 03.07.2018 under Section 7; UTT is one of the projects of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 39]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate insolvency resolution process of Universal Buildwell Pvt. Ltd[cite: 39]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 03.07.2018; RP filed CA-500/2019 for identifying unit occupants; Association filed IA-3209/2021 seeking reverse CIRP and exclusion of UTT from CIRP; NCLT passed common order on 09.02.2023 dismissing/disposing of the applications[cite: 39]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan clause 8 noting that UTT project is fully sold to allottees and UTT is not an asset belonging to the Corporate Debtor in the project due to overselling and multiple duplicate sales[cite: 39]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority disposed of CA-500/2019 and IA-3209/2021 via order dated 09.02.2023, directing the RP to seek administrative assistance from the Deputy Commissioner, Gurugram, for verifying unit occupants without disturbing bona fide allottees, leading to the present appeal[cite: 39].
legal_issues: Whether a resolution professional can verify the chain of title and occupancy status of units in a completed commercial project (Universal Trade Tower) forming part of a corporate debtor under CIRP when multiple duplicate sales and overselling are alleged[cite: 39].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution professional is fully empowered and duty-bound to verify and ascertain the identity and occupancy capacity of unit holders in a project under CIRP to resolve issues of overselling and duplicate allotments, provided such verification is conducted in a civilised manner without causing inconvenience or disturbance to bona fide allottees[cite: 39]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) and CIRP duties require the resolution professional to compile accurate asset and occupancy statements even for projects excluded from resolution plans due to prior sales[cite: 39]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Administrative verification of unit occupants via local authorities is permissible to sort out multiple duplicate allotments without disturbing genuine owners[cite: 39]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in directing verification of unit occupants via administrative assistance while safeguarding bona fide allottees, and the appeal lacks merit[cite: 39].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, clarifying that the RP shall make enquiries strictly regarding the factual occupational capacity of unit holders in a civilised manner[cite: 39].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT New Delhi order dated 09.02.2023 passed in CA-500/2019 and IA-3209/2021 concerning the Universal Trade Tower (UTT) project of Corporate Debtor Universal Buildwell Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 39] The NCLAT held that the Resolution Professional is entitled to verify the occupancy and title chain of unit holders with administrative assistance from the Deputy Commissioner, Gurugram, to resolve issues of overselling and duplicate allotments, provided bona fide allottees are not disturbed[cite: 39]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal with clarifying directions[cite: 39].

case_title: Riju Ravindran vs. Pankaj Srivastava, RP of Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Riju Ravindran (Suspended Director & Promoter of Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd.); Respondents include Pankaj Srivastava (RP), Aditya Birla Finance Limited, GLAS Trust Company LLC, and BCCI[cite: 40]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 9 application filed by BCCI against Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd. admitted on 16.07.2024; subsequent settlement between appellant and BCCI leading to NCLAT setting aside CIRP on 02.08.2024, which was later stayed and set aside by the Supreme Court on 23.10.2024[cite: 40]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate insolvency resolution process of Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd[cite: 40]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 16.07.2024; CoC constituted on 21.08.2024; RP reconstituted CoC on 31.08.2024; NCLT heard IA 660/2024, 820/2024, and 837/2024 on 08.01.2025 and passed impugned order on 29.01.2025 setting aside CoC reconstitution without deciding IA 837/2024 (withdrawal application)[cite: 40]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supreme Court judgment dated 23.10.2024 setting aside NCLAT's earlier settlement order and directing deposit of Rs. 158 crores with CoC[cite: 40]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench passed order on 29.01.2025 on CoC re-constitution applications while leaving IA No. 837 of 2024 undecided, leading to the present appeal by the suspended director[cite: 40].
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should interfere with an NCLT order deciding CoC reconstitution when a withdrawal/settlement application (IA No. 837 of 2024) argued alongside remains reserved for orders[cite: 40].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an Adjudicating Authority hears multiple interconnected applications simultaneously but pronounces orders on only some while reserving or deferring others, the appropriate appellate remedy is to direct the Adjudicating Authority to expeditiously decide the pending application rather than interfering with the rendered orders[cite: 40]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) and NCLT procedural rules require time-bound disposal of all reserved applications[cite: 40]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Deferral of a Section 12A withdrawal application does not invalidate prior CoC reconstitution orders when higher court remands govern the insolvency process[cite: 40]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellant's grievance is fully addressed by directing the NCLT to dispose of the pending withdrawal application (IA No. 837 of 2024) within a strict timeframe[cite: 40].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with a direction to the Adjudicating Authority to decide pending application IA No. 837 of 2024 within one week[cite: 40].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT Bengaluru Bench order dated 29.01.2025 which disposed of applications regarding CoC reconstitution in the CIRP of Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd. (Byju's) without adjudicating a pending Section 12A withdrawal application (IA No. 837 of 2024)[cite: 40]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that rather than setting aside the CoC orders, the grievance should be remedied by directing the NCLT to expeditiously decide the pending withdrawal application[cite: 40]. Consequently, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal with a strict one-week timeline for the NCLT to rule on IA No. 837 of 2024[cite: 40].

case_title: G. Ravishankar vs. Hyderabad Pollution Controls Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ravi Shankar Gopalakrishnan; Respondents include M/s. Hyderabad Pollution Controls Ltd., S. Radhakrishnan, and Mrs. V. Thara[cite: 41]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition proceedings arising from CP/3/97/HDB/2022[cite: 41]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law dispute)[cite: 41]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned interim order passed on 07.02.2024; principal company petition decided on merits and disposed of on 03.12.2024; appeal filed against final order (e-filing No. 176/2025)[cite: 41]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Subsequent disposal of the underlying main company petition on 03.12.2024 rendering interlocutory appeal infructuous[cite: 41]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT Chennai Bench noted that the principal company petition had already been decided on merits on 03.12.2024, rendering the appeal against the interim order infructuous[cite: 41].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal arising from an interim order becomes infructuous when the main company petition is finally decided on merits during the pendency of the appeal[cite: 41].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging an interim order is rendered entirely infructuous and liable to be dismissed once the principal petition or suit is finally decided on merits during the pendency of the appeal[cite: 41]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interlocutory proceedings merge into or abate upon final adjudication of the substantive main petition[cite: 41]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Final disposal of the main company petition on 03.12.2024 establishes that the interlocutory challenge no longer survives[cite: 41]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal against the interim order has become infructuous and stands dismissed[cite: 41].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 25 of 2024 is dismissed as infructuous[cite: 41].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT interim order dated 07.02.2024 passed in CP/3/97/HDB/2022[cite: 41]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench noted that during the pendency of the appeal, the principal company petition itself was decided on merits and disposed of on 03.12.2024, and a separate appeal had been preferred against the final judgment[cite: 41]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the interim appeal as infructuous[cite: 41].

case_title: Aarif Ahsan Khan vs. Jayesh Sanghrajka (Resolution Professional)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Aarif Ahsan Khan; Respondent is Jayesh Sanghrajka (Resolution Professional)[cite: 42]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim submitted by homebuyer/claimant in the CIRP of the corporate debtor; partial rejection of claim by RP leading to IA No. 2772 of 2023[cite: 42]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Homebuyer claim verification and fund routing investigation through Ornate Developers[cite: 42]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 06.10.2023 dismissing IA No. 2772 of 2023 with directions to the RP to re-appreciate evidence regarding money routed through Ornate Developers and avoidance transactions; appeal heard on 14.02.2025[cite: 42]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Ongoing investigation by the RP into money routing and avoidance transactions concerning Ornate Developers[cite: 42]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority dismissed IA No. 2772 of 2023 on 06.10.2023 holding the application to be premature pending RP investigation; appellant sought to withdraw the appeal before NCLAT[cite: 42].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against the partial rejection of a claim can be withdrawn when the Adjudicating Authority directed the Resolution Professional to re-appreciate evidence and complete investigations regarding money routing and avoidance transactions[cite: 42].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant is permitted to withdraw an appeal as premature when the underlying claim verification is still undergoing active investigation by the resolution professional pursuant to specific directions of the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 42]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Claim adjudication under IBC allows remanding matters to the resolution professional for re-appreciation when avoidance transactions are under probe[cite: 42]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Premature appeals challenging incomplete claim verifications may be dismissed as withdrawn with liberty to await final adjudication by the RP[cite: 42]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In view of the appellant's statement seeking withdrawal while investigation is underway, the appeal is dismissed as withdrawn[cite: 42].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn, with observations that the RP shall admit valid claims upon completion of the investigation[cite: 42].
summary: This appeal challenged the NCLT order dated 06.10.2023 dismissing IA No. 2772 of 2023 filed by Aarif Ahsan Khan regarding the partial rejection of his claim[cite: 42]. The NCLAT noted that the Adjudicating Authority had directed the Resolution Professional to re-appreciate evidence concerning money routed through Ornate Developers and avoidance transactions, making the appeal premature[cite: 42]. Consequently, upon the appellant's request, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal as withdrawn with clarifying observations[cite: 42].

case_title: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India vs. Shriram General Insurance Company Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), and the Respondents are various Shriram group insurance and holding companies including Shriram General Insurance Company Ltd. and Shriram Life Insurance Company Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The respondent insurance companies proposed schemes of amalgamation with their respective holding/non-insurance companies under the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a company amalgamation dispute rather than a monetary default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Schemes of amalgamation were processed through first and second motion petitions before respective NCLT benches during 2023-2024, leading to impugned orders approving the amalgamations. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Production of NCLT tribunal orders, scheme documents, and regulatory no-objections from Regional Directors, Official Liquidators, and CCI, alongside IRDAI's objections based on the Insurance Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IRDAI filed four company appeals before NCLAT challenging NCLT orders approving amalgamations without prior approval under Section 35(1) of the Insurance Act, 1938.
legal_issues: Whether prior approval under Section 35(1) of the Insurance Act, 1938 is mandatory when an insurance company is amalgamated with a non-insurance holding company under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Amalgamation under the Insurance Act is restricted in applicability to the merger between two insurance companies, whereas the amalgamation of an insurance company with a non-insurance company is governed by the self-contained provisions of Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(1) of the Insurance Act does not create a bar or require prior approval from the Authority when an insurance company merges with a non-insurance entity, as the statute only contemplates amalgamation between insurers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of corporate restructuring records and statutory compliance under the Companies Act established that share configurations and voting rights remained protected without violating Section 6A of the Insurance Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In the absence of any statutory inconsistency or explicit bar in the Insurance Act, amalgamations between insurance and non-insurance companies under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act are valid without prior IRDAI approval under Section 35(1).
operative_order: The four Company Appeals (TA (AT) No. 04/2024 and others) lack merits and are dismissed. The Schemes of Amalgamation affirmed by the Impugned Judgments are confirmed, and all connected interlocutory applications stand closed.
summary: The Appellant, Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), challenged NCLT orders approving the amalgamation of insurance companies with their non-insurance holding companies without prior approval under Section 35(1) of the Insurance Act, 1938. The NCLAT held that Section 35(1) applies only to amalgamations between two insurance companies and does not bar the amalgamation of an insurance company with a non-insurance entity under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013. Finding no violation of Section 6A of the Insurance Act or inconsistency between the statutes, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals and confirmed the schemes of amalgamation.

case_title: Steel Authority of India Ltd. & Anr. vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No.1 is Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL), Appellant No.2 is Paradip Port Trust, and Respondents are the Competition Commission of India (CCI) along with various stevedoring entities operating at Paradip Port. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SAIL imported essential raw materials (coal and limestone) and engaged stevedoring contractors at Paradip Port through open tender processes, experiencing alleged cartelization among stevedores between 2012 and 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a competition law dispute regarding alleged bid rigging and cartelization. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information was filed under Section 19(1)(a) following a Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) Office Memorandum dated August 27, 2020, and CCI closed the information under Section 26(2) on July 7, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tender documents, management committee resolutions under the Paradip Port CFH Scheme 1994, and CVC inquiry observations indicating alleged cartelization among port stevedores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI formed a prima facie opinion that allegations were bald and uncorroborated, closing the information under Section 26(2) without ordering DG investigation, leading to the present appeal under Section 53B.
legal_issues: Whether the CCI was justified in closing the information under Section 26(2) of the Competition Act, 2002 without directing an investigation by the Director General, and whether the information constituted a statutory reference under Section 21.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An information filed under Section 19 of the Competition Act must contain concrete particulars, evidence, and details regarding the nature and operation of a cartel, and cannot be equated with a statutory reference under Section 21. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 26(2) empowers the CCI to close an information at the prima facie stage if allegations are bald and unsupported by material documents, without requiring a pre-decisional hearing for the informant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Vague allegations and common business linkages between bidders, without specific evidence of collusive bidding, price manipulation, or cartel operation, are insufficient to establish a prima facie case for investigation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the information lacked necessary particulars and evidence of anti-competitive conduct, the CCI committed no error in closing the case under Section 26(2).
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 11 of 2021 is dismissed with no order as to costs. All connected interlocutory applications stand closed.
summary: Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL) and Paradip Port Trust appealed against a Competition Commission of India (CCI) order dated July 7, 2021, which closed their information regarding alleged cartelization among stevedores at Paradip Port under Section 26(2) of the Competition Act, 2002. SAIL argued that the information was filed on CVC advice and should have been treated as a reference warranting investigation. The NCLAT held that information under Section 19 cannot be equated with a statutory reference under Section 21, and that bald allegations without supporting evidence of cartel operation do not warrant a DG investigation. The appeal was accordingly dismissed.

case_title: Axis Nirman and Industries Ltd. & Anr. vs. M/S Hotel Birsa Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Axis Nirman and Industries Ltd. and Axis Overseas Ltd., while Respondents include M/s Hotel Birsa Pvt. Ltd., Adbhut Vincom Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No.2 holding 49% shares), and promoter directors Smt. Salini Soy and late Prem Rajesh Soy. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Hotel Birsa faced severe financial distress and NPA status with HUDCO, prompting promoters to invite investments from appellants through share allotments funded by Rs. 2.10 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Term loan liabilities of approximately Rs. 11 crore owed to HUDCO. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Extraordinary General Meeting (EOGM) was allegedly held on February 18, 2010, increasing authorized share capital, followed by share allotments on March 19 and April 14, 2010. NCLT Kolkata passed its order on April 7, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Conflicting EOGM notices, certificate of posting receipts without proof of actual delivery, minutes of meetings, and absence of renunciation rights in rights issue offers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adbhut Vincom filed CP No. 370 of 2010 alleging oppression and mismanagement; NCLT allowed the petition, cancelled 210,000 shares allotted to appellants, and ordered a refund of Rs. 2.10 crores without interest, leading to remand by the Supreme Court and this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the increase in authorized share capital, amendment of Articles/Memorandum of Association, and subsequent share allotments complied with the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956, and whether they constituted oppression and mismanagement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An increase in authorized share capital and subsequent share allotments without prior amendment of the Articles of Association, lack of proper notice service, and failure to provide renunciation rights under Section 81 of the Companies Act, 1956 constitute oppression and mismanagement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 94(1) mandates an enabling provision in the Articles of Association and a special resolution under Section 31 to alter share capital and Memorandum of Association. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A certificate of posting receipt alone, when vehemently denied by a minority shareholder, is insufficient proof of notice service without corroborative evidence or proof of delivery. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the share capital increase and allotments violated mandatory statutory procedures and unfairly diluted the minority shareholder's stake, the NCLT rightly annulled the allotments and ordered a refund without interest.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 175 of 2017 is dismissed, directing Respondent No.1 to refund Rs. 2.10 crores to the appellants within 60 days without interest. All interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT Kolkata bench order dated April 7, 2017, which had cancelled 210,000 equity shares allotted to them in Hotel Birsa Pvt. Ltd. and ordered a refund of Rs. 2.10 crores. The NCLAT found multiple statutory violations, including increasing authorized share capital without amending the Articles of Association, issuing conflicting EOGM notices, failing to properly serve notice to the 49% shareholder Adbhut Vincom, and omitting renunciation rights under Section 81 of the Companies Act, 1956. The Appellate Tribunal concluded that these actions amounted to oppression and mismanagement, dismissed the appeal, and upheld the cancellation of shares and refund order without interest.

case_title: Alphabet Inc. & Ors. vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Alphabet Inc. and Google entities ("Google"), while Respondents include the Competition Commission of India (CCI) and Alliance of Digital India Foundation (ADIF). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Google operated the Android mobile operating system and Google Play Store, requiring app developers to mandatorily use Google Play's Billing System (GPBS) for paid apps and in-app purchases while charging service fees ranging from 15% to 30%. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is an antitrust/competition law matter. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information cases were registered during 2020-2021, DG submitted investigation reports on March 16, 2022, and CCI passed its final order on October 25, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Developer distribution agreements, payment policies, financial data submissions on revenue streams, and comparative integration methods for Google Pay versus rival UPI apps. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI found Google dominant in licensable mobile OS and Android app store markets, held it guilty of violating various provisions of Section 4, and imposed a penalty of Rs. 936.44 crores based on total turnover, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether Google abused its dominant position in the Android app store market by mandating GPBS, restricting payment processors, leveraging its position, and whether the penalty imposed by CCI on total turnover rather than relevant turnover was sustainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Abuse of dominance under Section 4 of the Competition Act requires effect-based analysis, and monetary penalties under Section 27(b) must be calculated based on relevant product-specific turnover rather than the entire turnover of the enterprise. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Mandatory imposition of proprietary billing systems as a pre-condition for app store access constitutes an unfair condition under Section 4(2)(a)(i) and unlawful leveraging under Section 4(2)(e). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: While mandatory GPBS and leveraging market dominance were established with anti-competitive effects, allegations concerning discriminatory pricing, market access denial to payment processors, and technical limitation under Sections 4(2)(a)(ii), 4(2)(b)(ii), and 4(2)(c) lacked sufficient evidence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: CCI's findings of violations under Section 4(2)(a)(i) and 4(2)(e) are upheld, but penalty calculation must be restricted to relevant turnover streams related to Google Play.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 04 of 2023 is partly allowed. Violations of Section 4(2)(a)(i) and 4(2)(e) and specific remedial directions are upheld, while other findings and directions are set aside. The penalty is modified and reduced to INR 2,16,69,12,773 (USD 2,98,89,312.39) based on relevant turnover.
summary: Google appealed against a CCI order dated October 25, 2022, which found Google dominant in Android mobile OS and app store markets, ruled that it abused its position through mandatory use of Google Play's Billing System (GPBS) and other practices, and imposed a penalty of Rs. 936.44 crores. The NCLAT upheld CCI's findings regarding violations of Section 4(2)(a)(i) (unfair conditions) and Section 4(2)(e) (leveraging dominance), but set aside findings under Sections 4(2)(a)(ii), 4(2)(b)(ii), and 4(2)(c). Citing the Supreme Court's Excel Crop Care precedent, the Appellate Tribunal held that penalties must be based on relevant turnover rather than total turnover, modifying and reducing the penalty to INR 2,16,69,12,773.

case_title: Debabrata Ray Choudhuri vs. The State Trading Corporation of India Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is a senior advocate (operational creditor), and the Respondent is The State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. (corporate debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The corporate debtor engaged the appellant to handle various legal proceedings and arbitrations from 2006 onwards, resulting in unpaid professional fee claims. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim of default amounting to Rs. 6,26,90,985/-, comprising a principal sum of Rs. 3,93,55,110/- and interest of Rs. 2,33,35,875/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Revised demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued on July 26, 2019, and the Section 9 application was filed before the NCLT on December 16, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices, fee schedules, emails acknowledging bill processing delays, TDS certificates, and corporate debtor's replies disputing bill accuracy and adherence to fee schedules. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Section 9 application on the ground of pre-existing disputes, leading to the current appeal under Section 61 of the IBC.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-existing dispute existed between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor regarding professional fee invoices prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected if a genuine and substantial pre-existing dispute regarding the invoices or fee calculations existed prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) requires the corporate debtor to bring to the notice of the operational creditor the existence of a dispute or record of pending proceedings upon receiving a demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the corporate debtor raises plausible objections contesting the arbitrary billing structure and lack of requisite documentation before the demand notice, the dispute cannot be branded as illusory or spurious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the corporate debtor successfully demonstrated the existence of a bona fide pre-existing dispute regarding the professional fee claims, the dismissal of the Section 9 application by the Adjudicating Authority is legally sound.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1985 of 2024 is dismissed.
summary: Debabrata Ray Choudhuri, a senior advocate, filed an appeal against an NCLT order dismissing his Section 9 application under the IBC for recovery of unpaid professional fees from The State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. The NCLAT held that the corporate debtor had successfully raised genuine and substantial pre-existing disputes regarding invoice calculations and adherence to approved fee schedules prior to the Section 8 demand notice. Finding no infirmity in the Adjudicating Authority's reliance on precedents like Mobilox Innovations and Sabarmati Gas, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. vs. Kuldeep Verma, Liquidator of KS Oils Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. (secured financial creditor), and Respondents include Kuldeep Verma (Liquidator of KS Oils Ltd.) and other secured creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor KS Oils Ltd. underwent liquidation, during which Phoenix ARC claimed security interest over the Haldia manufacturing unit assets (12.84 acres) and chose not to relinquish it. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Phoenix ARC's admitted claim stood at Rs. 793,45,16,428/-, while the Haldia property reserve price was fixed at Rs. 57,10,54,500/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation commenced on March 16, 2021 (with NCLT directions on January 6, 2023), and the liquidator informed the appellant on July 14, 2023 that the Haldia unit had become part of the liquidation estate. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-D claims, correspondence regarding possession handover on January 21, 2023, stakeholder consultation committee (SCC) minutes, and auction sale notices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Phoenix ARC filed MA No. 3 of 2023 before NCLT Indore, objecting to the liquidator's decision to include the Haldia unit in the liquidation estate and challenging sale notices. NCLT rejected the MA on February 16, 2024, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the secured creditor failed to comply with Regulation 21A(2) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, resulting in the secured asset automatically becoming part of the liquidation estate.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Regulation 21A(2) of the Liquidation Process Regulations, a secured creditor realizing its security interest must pay the specified liquidation costs and dues within 90 days from the liquidation commencement date, failing which the asset becomes part of the liquidation estate under Regulation 21A(3). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The obligation to make payments under Regulation 21A(2)(a) is mandatory and time-linked, and the secured creditor cannot evade compliance by shifting blame to the liquidator for not estimating expenses. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a secured creditor takes no steps under Regulation 37 to realize its security and fails to make mandatory payments within the 90-day window following asset handover, the asset merges into the liquidation estate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since Phoenix ARC failed to comply with the statutory payment timelines under Regulation 21A(2), the liquidator and NCLT rightly treated the Haldia unit as part of the liquidation estate.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 592 of 2024 is dismissed, subject to allowing IA No. 1166 of 2025 permitting the successful bidder Halder Venture Ltd. to deposit the balance auction amount with 12% interest within 30 days.
summary: Phoenix ARC appealed against an NCLT Indore order rejecting its application objecting to the liquidator's inclusion of the Haldia secured asset in the liquidation estate of KS Oils Ltd. The NCLAT held that because Phoenix ARC failed to make mandatory payments within 90 days as required by Regulation 21A(2) of the Liquidation Process Regulations and took no steps under Regulation 37, the asset automatically became part of the liquidation estate under Regulation 21A(3). The appeal was dismissed, and an intervention application by successful bidder Halder Venture Ltd. was allowed to complete the purchase.

case_title: M/s. Bhagyodayam Company represented by its Administrator, Adv. Jinan K.R. vs. Shri. William James & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Bhagyodayam Company represented by its court-appointed Administrator (Adv. Jinan K.R.), and Respondents are various individuals against whom recovery of diverted company funds was sought. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allegations of oppression, mismanagement, and illegal diversion of company funds and assets by former directors and respondents. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Various sums of money ordered to be recovered following auditor reports on misappropriated funds. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chennai appointed an administrator on August 28, 2018 / October 31, 2018 under Section 241/242. Execution petitions and subsequent miscellaneous applications were filed during 2021-2022, culminating in the impugned order dated December 2, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auditor reports, administrator demand notices, and records of fund diversion to subsidiary entities and individuals. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kochi Bench dismissed miscellaneous applications filed by the administrator seeking to draw formal civil decrees for money recovery, leading to 18 company appeals before NCLAT Chennai.
legal_issues: Whether NCLT has the power to draw a formal civil 'decree' under Order XX Rule 6A CPC based on an administrator's report, and how orders passed under Section 241/242 of the Companies Act are to be enforced under Section 424(3).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Tribunals constituted under the Companies Act do not function as civil courts and cannot formulate formal 'decrees' under Order XX Rule 6A CPC, but their orders are fully enforceable as decrees under Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(3) is a legislation by reference, giving tribunal orders the force and enforceability of civil court decrees without transforming tribunal adjudication into civil suits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A tribunal should not dismiss recovery applications on hyper-technical grounds merely because a party prayed for a 'decree'; courts have the inherent power to modulate relief and treat such prayers as requests for enforceable orders. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in dismissing the applications outright; the prayers seeking decrees should be modulated to seek executable orders enforceable under Section 424(3).
operative_order: The 18 Company Appeals are disposed of. The impugned orders are modified, and the prayers seeking decrees in the respective applications are read as requests for executable orders enforceable under Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013.
summary: An administrator appointed for M/s. Bhagyodayam Company filed multiple miscellaneous applications seeking civil decrees to recover misappropriated funds from respondents based on audit reports. The NCLT Kochi Bench dismissed the applications holding that NCLT cannot draw civil decrees. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that while NCLT cannot issue formal decrees under the CPC, its orders are enforceable as decrees under Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. The tribunal should have modulated the relief rather than dismissing the applications on hyper-technical grounds. The appeals were disposed of with directions allowing the administrator to seek executable orders.

case_title: IL&FS Financial Services Limited vs. Adhunik Meghalaya Steels Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is IL&FS Financial Services Limited (financial creditor), and the Respondent is Adhunik Meghalaya Steels Private Limited (corporate debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A loan agreement was executed on February 27, 2015 for Rs. 30 crores (disbursed amount Rs. 24.44 crores), secured by a share pledge agreement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account declared NPA on March 1, 2018; Section 7 application filed on January 15, 2024 for a claim amount of Rs. 55.45 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default occurred on March 1, 2018. The corporate debtor's balance sheet for FY 2019-20 was signed on August 12, 2020 and uploaded on the MCA portal on February 14, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan facility documents, default and recall notices issued in 2018, and corporate debtor balance sheets reflecting secured borrowings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Guwahati Bench dismissed the Section 7 application by order dated May 16, 2024 as being barred by limitation, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the limitation period for filing a Section 7 application is extended by balance sheet acknowledgements, and whether limitation commences from the date of signing the balance sheet or the date of uploading it on the MCA portal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of liability in a balance sheet under Section 18 of the Limitation Act extends the limitation period, and the relevant date for computing limitation is the date on which the balance sheet is signed by the authorized signatory, not the date of its uploading on the MCA portal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 specifies that a fresh period of limitation is computed from the time the acknowledgement in writing was 'so signed'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Even when taking the date of signing of the FY 2019-20 balance sheet (August 12, 2020) and factoring in the Supreme Court's suo motu COVID-19 limitation extension orders (attracting paragraph 5.III with a 90-day grace period ending May 30, 2022), a petition filed in January 2024 remains severely time-barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the petition was filed long after the expiry of the extended limitation period, the Adjudicating Authority correctly dismissed the Section 7 application as time-barred.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1379 of 2024 is dismissed, and the impugned order is upheld.
summary: IL&FS Financial Services appealed against an NCLT Guwahati Bench order dismissing its Section 7 application against Adhunik Meghalaya Steels as time-barred. The NCLAT held that limitation commences from the date the corporate debtor's balance sheet is signed, not when it is uploaded on the MCA portal. Factoring in the date of signing (August 12, 2020) and applying the Supreme Court's COVID-19 suo motu limitation extensions, the Appellate Tribunal concluded that the petition filed in January 2024 was well beyond the limitation period. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited & Anr. vs. Divyesh Desai (RP of GPT Steel Industries Ltd.) & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1103 of 2024 & No. 1084 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Divyesh Desai (Resolution Professional) and Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited (ARCIL, lead financial creditor), while Respondents include Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC) and the successful resolution applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GIDC granted a 99-year lease of industrial land (Plot No. 301 and adjacent plots) to corporate debtor GPT Steel Industries Ltd., on which the debtor operated its factory. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: GIDC claimed Rs. 3,96,92,490/-, out of which Rs. 1,54,35,313/- was admitted by the RP. GIDC subsequently issued a show cause notice and a lease termination order on April 7, 2022 for dues totaling Rs. 1,22,86,283/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on May 2, 2019. The resolution plan was approved by CoC on February 18, 2020. GIDC terminated the lease on April 7, 2022 during moratorium. NCLT passed orders on April 8, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease deeds, allotment letters, GIDC termination notices, claim admission records, and CoC resolution plan approval documents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed IA No. 461 of 2022 to set aside the lease termination, and IA No. 159 of 2020 for plan approval. NCLT Ahmedabad disposed of IA 461 by telling the RP to approach the GIDC appellate authority and remitted the resolution plan back to CoC in IA 159, leading to these two appeals.
legal_issues: Whether a lessor (GIDC) can terminate a land lease and initiate eviction proceedings against a corporate debtor during the moratorium period under Section 14 of the IBC, and whether NCLT can remand a resolution plan without finding violations of Section 30(2).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The termination of a lease and initiation of eviction proceedings by a lessor against a corporate debtor during an active moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC are illegal and hit by statutory freeze, and NCLT cannot remand a resolution plan back to the CoC without recording a finding of non-compliance with Section 30(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 preserves the status quo of corporate debtor assets (including leasehold rights) and prevents lessors from dispossessing the debtor during insolvency resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where leasehold rights form part of the corporate debtor's assets and are factored into a CoC-approved resolution plan, unilateral lease termination during moratorium is void. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in refusing to set aside the GIDC's illegal lease termination and in remitting the resolution plan without identifying Section 30(2) violations.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1103 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1084 of 2024 are allowed. The NCLT order dated April 8, 2024 in IA 461 of 2022 is modified to quash GIDC's lease termination and show cause notice, and the order remitting the resolution plan in IA 159 of 2020 is set aside, reviving IA 159 before the Adjudicating Authority for expedited disposal.
summary: ARCIL and the Resolution Professional appealed against NCLT Ahmedabad orders dated April 8, 2024, which had directed the RP to approach GIDC's appellate authority regarding a lease termination notice issued during moratorium and remitted the resolution plan back to the CoC. The NCLAT held that GIDC's lease termination and eviction notice issued during active moratorium were directly hit by Section 14 of the IBC and were void. Furthermore, the NCLAT ruled that NCLT cannot remand a resolution plan back to the CoC without identifying specific violations of Section 30(2). Both appeals were allowed, the lease termination was quashed, and the plan approval application was revived for early consideration.

case_title: Mr. Pranav Kanoria, Suspended Director of Bagalkot Cement & Industries Ltd. vs. Vyshali Energy Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pranav Kanoria (suspended director of corporate debtor Bagalkot Cement & Industries Ltd.), Respondent No. 1 is Vyshali Energy Pvt. Ltd. (operational creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is the interim resolution professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The operational creditor entered into an energy purchase agreement dated April 10, 2017 to supply renewable energy to the corporate debtor, raising tax invoices from March 2017 to February 2021 totaling Rs. 1,23,31,500/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed in the Section 9 petition was Rs. 1,42,16,355/- (Rs. 1,23,31,500/- principal plus Rs. 18,84,855/- interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 was served on March 2, 2022; the corporate debtor replied raising a pre-existing dispute on March 16, 2022, citing a letter dated April 21, 2021. The Section 9 application was admitted on September 11, 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Energy purchase agreement, invoices, demand notice, replies, emails, and corporate debtor's letter dated April 21, 2021 raising disputes regarding excess charges and arbitrary discontinuation of power supply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Section 9 application on September 11, 2023, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-existing dispute existed prior to the filing of the Section 9 application, and whether the operational creditor's failure to deny receipt of the dispute letter in its pleadings amounts to an admission under procedural principles.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a corporate debtor raises a plausible pre-existing dispute regarding operational dues prior to the filing of a Section 9 application, and the operational creditor fails to specifically deny the receipt or delivery of the dispute communication in its pleadings, the existence of a pre-existing dispute must be acknowledged, rendering the Section 9 petition unmaintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Section 9 of the IBC mandate the rejection of an insolvency application if a notice of dispute has been validly raised and exists prior to initiation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted assertions in pleadings regarding a dispute letter dated April 21, 2021 establish that the dispute is genuine, plausible, and not an afterthought. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since a pre-existing dispute was duly raised and unrefuted in pleadings, the admission of the Section 9 application is illegal and must be set aside.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1232 of 2023 is allowed, and the NCLT order dated September 11, 2023 admitting the Section 9 application is set aside. The Registrar is directed to return the deposited amount of Rs. 1,23,31,500/- along with accrued interest to the appellant within 15 days.
summary: Pranav Kanoria, suspended director of Bagalkot Cement & Industries Ltd., appealed against an NCLT order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Vyshali Energy Pvt. Ltd. The appellant contended that a pre-existing dispute was raised via a letter dated April 21, 2021 concerning excess charges and power supply discontinuation, which was never denied by the operational creditor in its pleadings.
