The NCLAT held that since the delivery and receipt of the dispute letter went unrefuted, a valid pre-existing dispute existed prior to the application. The appeal was allowed, the NCLT admission order was set aside, and the deposited funds were ordered to be returned to the appellant.

case_title: Manu Rishi Guptha vs. ICICI Securities Limited & Anr. (and connected appeals)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Manu Rishi Guptha (minority shareholder holding 0.002% shares), and Respondents include ICICI Securities Limited and ICICI Bank Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A scheme of arrangement involving the delisting of ICICI Securities Limited and its merger/amalgamation with ICICI Bank Limited through share swap was proposed and approved by shareholders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a corporate scheme and arrangement dispute. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT benches passed orders approving the scheme and dismissing shareholder objections on August 21, 2024, October 8, 2024, and October 9, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint valuation reports, fairness opinions by SEBI registered merchant bankers, SEBI relaxations under Regulation 42, and shareholder voting results (93.82% equity and 71.89% public shareholders approving the scheme). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed multiple company appeals before NCLAT challenging NCLT orders that sanctioned the scheme and dismissed his objections.
legal_issues: Whether a minority shareholder holding miniscule shareholding below the 10% threshold under Section 230(4) can maintain an appeal against a sanctioned scheme of arrangement, and whether the scheme suffers from unfair valuation, lack of reverse book building, or regulatory non-compliance.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Shareholders holding less than 10% of the shareholding threshold under Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 lack standing to object to a scheme of arrangement or maintain an appeal as 'aggrieved persons' under Section 421, and valuation conducted by independent experts using recognized methods cannot be interfered with. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 37 of the SEBI Delisting Regulations provides a valid alternate mode of delisting via a scheme of arrangement with built-in safeguards, overriding speculative claims favoring reverse book building. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Courts will not substitute their judgment for professional expert valuation unless glaring illegality or fraud is shown, and administrative warnings without findings of voting coercion do not invalidate shareholder democracy. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the appellant failed to meet the statutory 10% threshold to object and could not demonstrate any illegality in the approved scheme, the appeals are devoid of merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 328, 395, 393, and 332 of 2024 are dismissed. Pending applications are disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: Manu Rishi Guptha, a minority shareholder holding 0.002% shares in ICICI Securities, filed four appeals challenging NCLT orders that approved the scheme of arrangement for delisting ICICI Securities and amalgamating it with ICICI Bank. The NCLAT held that the appellant did not meet the mandatory 10% threshold under Section 230(4) of the Companies Act to object to the scheme and could not maintain the appeals. Furthermore, the tribunal ruled that the joint valuation by independent experts complied with SEBI Regulation 37, that reverse book building was not mandatory under the alternate delisting route, and that over 93% of shareholders had democratically approved the arrangement. All appeals were dismissed.

case_title: H.P. Arun Kumar & Ors. vs. Addanki Haresh, Resolution Professional of M/s. Right Engineers and Equipments Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are H.P. Arun Kumar, C.M. Nagaraj, and Usha (erstwhile directors and related parties of corporate debtor M/s. Right Engineers and Equipment India Private Limited), and Respondent is Addanki Haresh (Resolution Professional / Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The corporate debtor availed financial assistance of Rs. 14.80 crores from Sir M. Vishveshwaraya Co-operative Bank Limited under a loan agreement dated October 17, 2016, creating hypothecation and mortgage securities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on loan repayments, leading to admission of CIRP under Section 7 on October 29, 2019, with total claims amounting to Rs. 15,00,09,200/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Committee of Creditors (CoC) met on November 9, 2020 reviewing draft forensic audit reports; final forensic audit report was issued on November 20, 2020 (supplemented on November 3, 2021). NCLT Bengaluru passed the impugned order on February 2, 2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic audit reports identifying preferential transactions amounting to Rs. 24,29,874/-, Rs. 25,53,233/-, and Rs. 11,50,000/- made to the appellants. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed IA No. 482 of 2020 under Section 43 of the IBC. NCLT Bengaluru allowed the application on February 2, 2022, declaring the transactions preferential and directing restoration of funds, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether identified transactions amounting to Rs. 49.83 lakhs (subsequently enhanced to include Rs. 11.50 lakhs) qualify as preferential transactions under Section 43 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Transfers of funds by a corporate debtor to related parties and directors on account of antecedent liabilities that put them in a more beneficial position than under Section 53 distribution constitute preferential transactions under Section 43 of the IBC, unless proven to have been made in the ordinary course of business. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 43(1) and (2) capture antecedent debt transfers conferring preferential benefits, and once a forensic audit report establishes such transfers, the burden shifts under Section 101 of the Evidence Act to the respondents to prove ordinary course exceptions under Section 43(3). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unrebutted forensic audit reports and absence of supporting documentary evidence from the directors to substantiate ordinary course of business defenses validate the classification of transactions as preferential. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the appellants failed to discharge their evidentiary burden to prove ordinary course of business exceptions against the forensic audit findings, the Adjudicating Authority rightly declared the transactions preferential and ordered fund restoration.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 184/2022 is dismissed, and all connected interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: H.P. Arun Kumar and other suspended directors of Right Engineers and Equipments Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order dated February 2, 2022, which allowed IA No. 482 of 2020 filed by the Resolution Professional and declared certain fund transfers amounting to over Rs. 60 lakhs as preferential transactions under Section 43 of the IBC. The NCLAT held that the forensic audit reports clearly established preferential transfers to related parties and that the appellants failed to discharge their evidentiary burden under Section 101 of the Evidence Act to prove that these transactions occurred in the ordinary course of business. The appeal was accordingly dismissed.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. M/S Santoshi Hyvolt Electricals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is State Bank of India (financial creditor), Respondent No. 1 is Santoshi Hyvolt Electricals Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA), and Respondent No. 2 is Ms. Ritu Rastogi (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 9 application against corporate debtor Eon Electric Limited was admitted on October 13, 2020. The CoC approved a resolution plan submitted by SRA on September 15, 2022 with 99.26% vote share, and the RP filed IA No. 1629 of 2022 for plan approval on October 1, 2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Performance bank guarantees worth Rs. 15.84 crores were invoked by EESL between February and September 2023, increasing CIRP costs to over Rs. 23 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved the plan on September 15, 2022. Following bank guarantee invocations, CoC held meetings in July and November 2023 seeking to remit the plan back. SBI filed IA No. 26 of 2024 on December 1, 2023. NCLT Chandigarh dismissed IA 26 on November 19, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC meeting minutes, invocation letters of bank guarantees by EESL, and resolution plan provisions regarding performance guarantees. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed IA No. 26 of 2024 seeking to remit the resolution plan back to CoC for review/fresh Form G. NCLT Chandigarh dismissed the application as not maintainable, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors (CoC) can request to remit back a resolution plan to itself after it has already been approved and submitted to the Adjudicating Authority for approval under Section 31.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan approved by the committee of creditors is submitted to the Adjudicating Authority for approval, it is binding and irrevocable inter se the CoC and the successful resolution applicant, and neither the CoC nor the Adjudicating Authority can entertain requests to remit it back for modification or withdrawal based on subsequent events. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 18 (Explanation) of the CIRP Regulations restricts CoC meetings convened after plan submission from deciding on matters affecting the submitted resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Subsequent events such as invocation of bank guarantees known to be possible at the time of plan approval do not render an approved and binding resolution plan un-implementable so as to permit CoC remittal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since a CoC-approved and submitted resolution plan cannot be remitted back at the behest of financial creditors, the NCLT rightly rejected the application seeking remittal as not maintainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 62 of 2025 is dismissed, with observations that rejection of IA No. 26 of 2024 shall not preclude the appellant from raising statutory arguments under Section 31(1) proviso and Section 30(2) when the plan approval application is considered.
summary: State Bank of India appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing its IA No. 26 of 2024, which sought to remit an already approved resolution plan back to the CoC following the invocation of bank guarantees by EESL. Citing Supreme Court precedents in Ebix Singapore and Murari Lal Jalan, the NCLAT held that once a CoC-approved resolution plan is submitted to the Adjudicating Authority, it is binding and irrevocable, and the CoC has no jurisdiction to seek its remittal. The appeal was dismissed, though SBI was granted liberty to raise objections regarding statutory compliance and effective implementation under Section 31(1) when the main plan approval application is heard.

case_title: Rakesh Arora & Anr. / Rockman Advertising & Marketing (India) Ltd. vs. Acute Daily Media Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1606 of 2024 & No. 1608 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Rakesh Arora & Anr. (intervenors) and Rockman Advertising & Marketing (India) Ltd. (majority shareholder of corporate debtor Sharp Eye Advertising Pvt. Ltd.), and Respondents are Acute Daily Media Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (financial creditors) and promoters. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial creditors filed a Section 7 application against corporate debtor Sharp Eye Advertising Pvt. Ltd., which was admitted by NCLT on May 17, 2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a fraudulent initiation and penalty dispute under Section 65 of the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 admitted on May 17, 2022. IA No. 3602 of 2022 was filed under Section 65. NCLT passed the impugned order allowing IA 3602, recalling the admission order, and issuing show cause notices on June 12, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Decade-long oppression and mismanagement litigation between shareholders since 2013, collusive filings, and records establishing fraudulent initiation of CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT allowed IA No. 3602 of 2022, held that CIRP was initiated fraudulently, recalled the admission order, and issued show cause notices for penalty under Section 65(1). Appellants appealed seeking mandatory imposition of Rs. 1 crore penalties on financial creditors and promoters, leading to this judgment.
legal_issues: Whether Section 65 of the IBC permits imposing penalties on promoters or persons other than the applicant who initiates the insolvency process, and whether NCLT Rules Rule 59 applies to Section 65 penalty proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 65 of the IBC is a penal provision that must be strictly construed and can only be invoked to penalize the specific financial creditor, operational creditor, or corporate applicant who formally initiates the insolvency resolution process, and cannot be stretched to cover promoters through alleged vicarious liability or collusion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The definition of 'initiation date' under Section 5(11) confines initiation to financial, operational, or corporate applicants, and Rule 59 of NCLT Rules relates strictly to penalties under the Companies Act, 2013. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Penal statutes require strict construction; literal reading does not permit extending penalties beyond the direct initiator of insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since Section 65 penalties cannot be vicariously imposed on promoters and the Adjudicating Authority correctly opted to issue show cause notices before deciding on penalties, the appeals seeking automatic imposition of penalties are misconceived.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1606 of 2024 and No. 1608 of 2024 are dismissed, with observations that the Adjudicating Authority may proceed to pass appropriate orders regarding penalties on the financial creditors in continuation of the order dated June 12, 2024.
summary: Shareholders and intervenors appealed against an NCLT order dated June 12, 2024, which recalled a fraudulently initiated Section 7 CIRP admission order against Sharp Eye Advertising Pvt. Ltd. and issued show cause notices for penalties under Section 65 of the IBC. The appellants argued that penalties of Rs. 1 crore should have been immediately imposed not only on the financial creditors but also on the corporate debtor's promoters. The NCLAT held that Section 65 is a penal provision that must be strictly construed and applies only to the direct initiator of insolvency proceedings (financial/operational/corporate applicant), precluding vicarious penalization of promoters. The appeals were dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's procedure of issuing show cause notices.

case_title: M/s Riddhi Siddhi Gluco Biols Limited vs. Sunit Jagdishchandra Shah (Resolution Professional of Shree Rajeshwaranand Paper Mills Limited)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Riddhi Siddhi Gluco Biols Limited (operational creditor), and the Respondent is Sunit Jagdishchandra Shah (Resolution Professional of Shree Rajeshwaranand Paper Mills Limited, the corporate debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor's CIRP was initiated on December 7, 2022, after which Form-G was published inviting expressions of interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The appellant's admitted claim was Rs. 69,08,949/-, and total operational creditor claims stood at Rs. 18,34,60,969/- against a corporate debtor liquidation value where operational creditors were allocated nil. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CoC approved the resolution plan submitted by Mercury Terra Firma on January 29, 2024, with 97.36% voting share, and NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-II approved it on November 27, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC meeting minutes, valuation summaries showing fair and liquidation values, Form-G re-publication records, and resolution plan financial provisions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Riddhi Siddhi Gluco Biols Limited appealed against the NCLT order approving the resolution plan, alleging timeline violations, non-disclosure of valuation reports, and inadequate allocation for operational creditors.
legal_issues: Whether the resolution plan approval violated CIRP timelines beyond 330 days, whether non-disclosure of detailed valuation reports to operational creditors vitiated the process, and whether operational creditors received less than their liquidation value entitlement under Section 30(2)(b).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan cannot be challenged on timeline extensions or valuation report disclosures when extensions are backed by CoC commercial wisdom near completion and operational creditors receive more than their nil liquidation value entitlement, backed by a 97.36% CoC voting majority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) entitles operational creditors to receive not less than the amount payable in liquidation under Section 53, which is nil where liquidation value is exhausted by higher priority dues. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Operational creditors with no voting rights suffer no legal prejudice from receiving summary fair and liquidation values rather than full valuation reports, especially when CoC records valid confidentiality reasons under Regulation 35(2). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since all statutory mandates were fulfilled and the commercial wisdom of the CoC was soundly exercised, the plan approval is legally unassailable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 187 of 2025 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: M/s Riddhi Siddhi Gluco Biols Limited appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order approving the resolution plan for Shree Rajeshwaranand Paper Mills Limited. The appellant raised procedural challenges, including CIRP completion beyond 330 days, failure to publish Form-G on the IBBI website, non-sharing of detailed valuation reports, and inadequate payout to operational creditors. The NCLAT held that CoC-backed timeline extensions near completion are permissible, summary valuation values satisfy requirements for non-voting creditors, and the Rs. 60 lakhs allocated to operational creditors exceeded their nil liquidation value entitlement. Upholding the commercial wisdom of the CoC (97.36% vote share), the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mr. A.M. Ganesh vs. CA Mahalingam Suresh Kumar (Liquidator of M/s. Ganga Foundations Pvt. Ltd.)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. A.M. Ganesh (successful bidder), and the Respondent is CA Mahalingam Suresh Kumar (Liquidator of M/s. Ganga Foundations Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor Ganga Foundations Pvt. Ltd. went into liquidation, and during the 5th e-auction published on December 11, 2023, the appellant was declared the successful bidder for purchasing the corporate debtor as a going concern for Rs. 43,74,00,000/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The appellant deposited EMD of Rs. 4,37,40,000/- and 25% balance of Rs. 6,56,10,000/- (total Rs. 10,93,50,000/-), but defaulted in paying the remaining 75% balance sale consideration (Rs. 32,80,50,000/-) by the stipulated deadline of December 27, 2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT confirmed the sale on September 27, 2024, granting 30 to 90 days for balance payment. The appellant defaulted by December 27, 2024, and the liquidator issued a forfeiture letter on December 31, 2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-auction bidding process documents, letter of intent, payment receipts, default letters, and forfeiture notices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the appellant's applications seeking payment extension (IA 2488/2024) and challenging the forfeiture of Rs. 10,93,50,000/- (IA 84/2025), leading to these two company appeals.
legal_issues: Whether a successful e-auction bidder who defaults in paying the balance sale consideration within the stipulated 90-day period is entitled to an extension under 2024 IBBI Liquidation Amendments, and whether the liquidator can forfeit amounts paid beyond the earnest money deposit.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful auction bidder who defaults in paying the balance sale consideration within the maximum stipulated 90-day period under liquidation rules is bound by the forfeiture terms of the bidding document, and subsequent subordinate legislation amendments cannot be applied retrospectively to concluded auctions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: IBBI Liquidation Process Amendment Regulations, 2024 (effective February 12, 2024) empowering liquidators to extend balance payment beyond 90 days are prospective and do not apply to prior concluded auction notices. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Participants in e-auctions voluntarily submit to published bidding process documents and cannot subsequently challenge forfeiture clauses or payment schedules as arbitrary. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the appellant failed to remit balance consideration by the deadline and statutory amendments lack retrospective application, the liquidator's cancellation of sale and forfeiture of deposited amounts are fully justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 168 & 169 of 2025 are dismissed, and all pending interlocutory applications stand closed.
summary: Mr. A.M. Ganesh, a successful e-auction bidder for Ganga Foundations Pvt. Ltd. as a going concern, defaulted on paying the 75% balance sale consideration by December 27, 2024. The liquidator cancelled the sale and forfeited the Rs. 10.93 crores already paid pursuant to the bidding document terms. The appellant challenged this before NCLT and NCLAT, invoking the 2024 IBBI Liquidation Process Amendment Regulations for payment extensions. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the 2024 amendment is prospective and inapplicable to prior concluded auctions, and that bidders are strictly bound by the timelines and forfeiture clauses of the bidding document. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Satinder Singh Bhasin vs. Col. Gautam Mullick & Ors.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 1509 & 1557 of 2025 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1594 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Satinder Singh Bhasin (erstwhile director of Bhasin Infotech and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. - BIIPL), applicants in IA 1509 are majority shareholders holding approx. 69% shares, and respondents include financial creditors and the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consolidated CIRP against Grand Venezia Commercial Towers Pvt. Ltd. and Bhasin Infotech and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. was admitted by NCLT on December 4, 2023 under Section 7. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is an interlocutory clarification application regarding management control during an appellate stay. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT admitted Section 7 on December 4, 2023. NCLAT passed an interim order on December 7, 2023 staying further steps in the CIRP. Applications for clarification were adjudicated on March 7, 2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT admission order, NCLAT interim stay order, shareholder holding records, and Allahabad High Court writ petition filings concerning UPSIDC demands. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Majority shareholders (IA 1509) and appellants (IA 1557) filed interlocutory applications seeking clarification regarding management control of the corporate debtor and the authority of suspended directors to pursue a writ petition while an appellate stay of CIRP steps was operative.
legal_issues: Whether an appellate order staying 'further steps' in a CIRP suspends the legal fiction under IBC Sections 13 to 20 vesting management control in the IRP, thereby restoring control to the suspended board of directors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate stay of 'further steps' or admission in a CIRP pauses the progression of the resolution process but does not quash the admission order or restore management control to the suspended board of directors, as management and asset custody continue to vest in the IRP by statutory legal fiction under Sections 13 to 20 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 17 mandates that management vests in the IRP from the date of appointment upon admission, and a mere stay of further steps does not create a status quo ante or eliminate statutory prohibitions against erstwhile management running company operations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Permitting suspended directors to regain operational control during a stay of CIRP steps would create managerial vacuum risks and asset dissipation hazards contrary to insolvency objectives. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since a stay of CIRP steps does not quash the admission order or restore management to erstwhile directors, control remains with the IRP, though the RP must co-prosecute ongoing protective writ proceedings.
operative_order: I.A. No. 1509 & 1557 of 2025 are disposed of, clarifying that management control remains vested in the IRP under the IBC statutory framework, and directing the RP to join as a co-petitioner in the pending Allahabad High Court writ petition.
summary: Majority shareholders and erstwhile directors filed clarification applications in a pending appeal against the admission of CIRP against Bhasin Infotech and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (BIIPL), where NCLAT had earlier stayed 'further steps' in the CIRP. The applicants sought clarification on whether management control reverted to the suspended board of directors during the stay. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that staying further steps does not quash the admission order or lift the statutory legal fiction under IBC Sections 13-20; consequently, management and asset custody remain vested in the IRP. However, the RP was directed to join as a co-petitioner in a pending Allahabad High Court writ petition against UPSIDC to protect corporate debtor assets. Both clarification applications were disposed of accordingly.

case_title: Authum Investment and Infrastructure Limited vs. Ashdan Properties Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Authum Investment and Infrastructure Limited (Resolution Applicant), Respondent No. 1 is Ashdan Properties Private Limited (Resolution Applicant), Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional, and Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of corporate debtor AA Estate Private Limited commenced on December 6, 2022. Following extensions, the last date for submitting resolution plans was fixed as February 14, 2024 at 5:00 PM. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a resolution plan submission deadline and commercial wisdom dispute. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The deadline to submit plans was February 14, 2024. Respondent No. 1 submitted its plan on February 15, 2024 (one day late). CoC rejected the late plan on February 16/17, 2024, and conducted a challenge process on April 29, 2024 where Authum was declared H-1. NCLT allowed Ashdan's application on July 29, 2024, leading to this appeal. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP) timelines, email submissions, CoC meeting minutes recording rejection of late plans, and challenge process records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Ashdan Properties filed IA 1143/2024 before NCLT Mumbai seeking condonation of a one-day delay and consideration of its plan. NCLT allowed the IA and directed CoC consideration, which Authum challenged in this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can interfere with the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in refusing to consider a resolution plan submitted after the expiry of the mandatory timeline specified under Regulation 36B and Regulation 39(1B) of the CIRP Regulations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Regulation 39(1B) of the CIRP Regulations, the Committee of Creditors is statutorily prohibited from considering any resolution plan received after the deadline specified under Regulation 36B, and the Adjudicating Authority cannot substitute its view for the commercial wisdom of the CoC in refusing to entertain delayed submissions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 36B(6) and Regulation 39(1B) establish binding timelines for plan submissions, protecting the integrity of competitive bidding processes such as challenge mechanisms. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a prospective resolution applicant fails to submit its plan within extended deadlines and the CoC consciously resolves in its commercial wisdom to reject the belated submission, adjudicatory interference is unwarranted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the CoC validly exercised its commercial wisdom to reject a resolution plan submitted after the expiry of the deadline, the NCLT erred in directing its consideration.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1566 of 2024 is allowed, and the NCLT order dated July 29, 2024 is set aside. IA 1143/2024 filed by Ashdan Properties is rejected. The period from August 8, 2024 till date during which the interim order operated is excluded from CIRP.
summary: Authum Investment and Infrastructure Limited, a resolution applicant and H-1 bidder in a challenge process, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing the CoC to consider a resolution plan submitted by Ashdan Properties Private Limited one day after the final deadline. The NCLAT held that Regulation 39(1B) of the CIRP Regulations expressly prohibits the CoC from considering resolution plans received after the specified deadline under Regulation 36B. Furthermore, the CoC had consciously exercised its commercial wisdom to reject the belated plan before proceeding with a competitive challenge process. The appeal was allowed, the NCLT order directing consideration was set aside, and Ashdan's application was rejected.

case_title: Venus Buildtech India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Senbo Engineering Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Venus Buildtech India Pvt. Ltd. (operational creditor), and Respondent is Senbo Engineering Ltd. (corporate debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor was awarded work by Delhi Metro Rail Corporation and subcontracted certain work to the appellant. Appellant completed work and claimed Rs. 77,10,967/-. Upon non-payment, a civil suit was filed and decreed in appellant's favor on September 12, 2017 by the Additional District Judge, Patiala House Court, Delhi. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed via civil court decree, with execution proceedings initiated. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Civil suit decreed on September 12, 2017. Section 9 application filed on February 17, 2021. NCLT dismissed the application on August 4, 2023. 5. FACTual EVIDENCE: Subcontract work orders, unpaid invoices, civil court judgment and decree dated September 12, 2017, and execution petition records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the appellant's Section 9 application on August 4, 2023, relying on a Tripura High Court judgment to hold that a decree holder is a separate class of creditor under Section 3(10) and cannot maintain a Section 9 operational debt petition. This appeal challenged that dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor whose claim has been adjudicated and reduced to a civil court decree ceases to be an 'operational creditor' and is barred from maintaining an application under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mere adjudication of an operational debt and the passing of a civil court decree do not alter the underlying character of the transaction, and a decree holder whose debt arose from the provision of goods or services remains an operational creditor entitled to file an application under Section 9 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) defines operational debt broadly in respect of provision of goods or services, and a judicial decree merely crystallizes an existing operational claim without transforming its legal category. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examining the original transaction underlying a claim demonstrates that debt falling due for goods or services supplied retains its status as an operational debt notwithstanding subsequent judicial decrees. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that decree holders cannot qualify as operational creditors under Section 9 based on their decree status.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1317 of 2023 is allowed, and the NCLT order dated August 4, 2023 is set aside. Section 9 application is revived before the Adjudicating Authority to be heard and decided afresh in accordance with law.
summary: Venus Buildtech India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order dismissing its Section 9 application on the ground that an operational creditor holding a civil court recovery decree ceases to be an operational creditor and cannot maintain an insolvency petition. Citing earlier NCLAT precedents such as *Mukul Agarwal*, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that obtaining a civil court decree for unpaid goods or services does not divest a creditor of its statutory status as an operational creditor. The appeal was allowed, the dismissal order was set aside, and the Section 9 application was revived for fresh adjudication on merits.

case_title: Mr. Himanshu Srivastava, Liquidator of Fuji Lio Trading Private Limited vs. Ms. Garima Dua & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Himanshu Srivastava (Liquidator of Fuji Lio Trading Private Limited), and Respondents are Ms. Garima Dua and Ms. Sonal Verma (Directors of the corporate person)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Fuji Lio Trading Pvt. Ltd., incorporated on 11.11.2011 to promote business activities and technical collaborations for Futee Origin Corporation, resolved to close down operations due to slow business growth[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a voluntary liquidation proceeding where the corporate person has not committed any default[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Board resolved to initiate voluntary liquidation on 23.09.2019, followed by an EGM resolution on 22.10.2019 appointing the liquidator[cite: 23]. NCLT dismissed the dissolution application on 10.04.2024[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board resolutions, EGM resolutions, creditors' approvals, audit reports containing handwritten UDIN, and solvency declaration affidavits showing use of correction fluid/whitener[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT dismissed the Section 59 voluntary liquidation application with costs of Rs. 5,000/- on grounds of lack of due diligence regarding defective affidavits and handwritten UDINs, prompting the liquidator to appeal[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing a Section 59 voluntary liquidation application with costs on hyper-technical clerical defects in director solvency affidavits without granting an opportunity to cure the defects.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for voluntary liquidation under Section 59 of the IBC should not be dismissed outright with costs due to inadvertent clerical discrepancies or the use of correction fluid in directors' solvency declarations where the underlying substantive requirements of the statute are satisfied and parties are willing to file fresh cured affidavits[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59(3)(a) requires a declaration of solvency verified by affidavit, but minor procedural defects in documentation do not preclude the tribunal from granting an opportunity to rectify filings in compliance with natural justice[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Inadvertent signing of swapped declaration forms followed by correction fluid adjustments does not establish mala fide intent or deliberate tampering when directors affirm willingness to tender fresh affidavits[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority breached principles of natural justice by rejecting the petition without affording the liquidator or directors a chance to explain or remedy minor procedural defects[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 288/2024 is allowed, and the order dated 10.04.2024 is quashed[cite: 23]. Respondents are directed to file fresh declaration affidavits within three weeks, and NCLT Chennai is directed to reconsider the Section 59 application afresh on merits[cite: 23].
summary: The Liquidator of Fuji Lio Trading Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dismissing a Section 59 voluntary liquidation petition with costs due to clerical errors, specifically a handwritten UDIN on the audit report and correction fluid used on directors' solvency affidavits[cite: 23]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the defects were inadvertent, devoid of mala fide intent, and that the Adjudicating Authority violated principles of natural justice by failing to afford an opportunity to cure the defects[cite: 23]. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal, quashed the dismissal order, and permitted the directors to submit fresh affidavits for reconsideration of the dissolution petition[cite: 23].

case_title: Shri Krishan & Anr. vs. H.S. Oberoi Buildtech Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are homebuyers/allottees in the 'Earth Iconic' project, and Respondents include H.S. Oberoi Buildtech Private Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA) and the Resolution Professionals of Celestial Estate Pvt. Ltd. (CEPL) and Earth Infrastructure Ltd. (EIL)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants booked an apartment in the 'Earth Iconic' project developed by EIL on land owned by CEPL, receiving an allotment letter on 31.06.2012 and paying Rs. 15,15,450/- against total consideration of Rs. 22,82,918/-[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the developer in completing the real estate project, culminating in CIRP against EIL and CEPL[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against CEPL commenced on 11.03.2019, claims were invited up to 10.04.2019, CoC accepted the plan on 16.11.2019, and NCLT approved the plan on 15.03.2021[cite: 24]. Appellants submitted claims to SRA on 10.12.2023 and filed IA 112/2024 before NCLT, which was dismissed on 24.10.2024[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Allotment letters, payment receipts, approved resolution plan clauses (Clauses 6.5 and 6.13(iv)(c) providing for late claims up to 12 months with additional charges), and email communications[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissed IA No. 112 of 2024 refusing to entertain appellants' claim filed more than 2.5 years after plan approval, leading to this appeal[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can direct a Successful Resolution Applicant to admit claims of homebuyers submitted over two years and nine months after the approval of the resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan receives approval from the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31 of the IBC, all existing claims stand frozen, and claims not forming part of the approved plan are extinguished, precluding the subsequent admission of belated claims[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In accordance with the clean-slate doctrine under Section 31, no surprise or undecided claims can be foisted on a successful resolution applicant after plan approval, preserving CIRP certainty and finality[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Homebuyers who file claims with an inordinate delay (over 1700 days after the claims deadline and beyond the 12-month grace window under the plan) cannot demand claim inclusion based on books/CRM entries[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the resolution plan had attained finality and was under active implementation, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the belated claims[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 128 of 2025 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: Homebuyers in the 'Earth Iconic' project appealed an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting their application to direct the Successful Resolution Applicant, H.S. Oberoi Buildtech, to admit their claims[cite: 24]. The claims were submitted on December 10, 2023, nearly three years after the resolution plan was approved by the NCLT on March 15, 2021[cite: 24]. Relying on the Supreme Court's landmark rulings in Ghanshyam Mishra and RPS Infrastructure, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that upon plan approval under Section 31, all claims outside the plan stand extinguished under the clean-slate doctrine[cite: 24]. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, holding that admitting late claims would disrupt implementation and render the CIRP endless[cite: 24].

case_title: Nirmal Jain vs. Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Nirmal Jain (real estate allottee/financial creditor), and Respondent is Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd. represented by its Resolution Professional[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant initially purchased a studio apartment (Unit 1606) with an assured return under a BBA dated 22.11.2016, later transferred by the CD to commercial shop unit No. F-445A via a fresh BBA and Article of Agreement dated 02.01.2018[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total consideration paid was Rs. 54,62,000/-, and claim filed in Form CA totaled Rs. 59,21,650/- (Rs. 55,12,000/- principal plus Rs. 4,09,650/- interest)[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Following dishonor of assured return cheques, appellant filed Section 7 on CP (IB) 1725/PB/2018, which was withdrawn on 05.03.2019 pursuant to a written settlement agreement[cite: 25]. Subsequent CIRP was initiated on 22.08.2019[cite: 25]. RP reduced the claim on 25.06.2022, and NCLT dismissed IA 4809/2022 on 21.11.2023[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BBAs, Articles of Agreement acknowledging receipt of Rs. 54,62,000/-, two receipts dated 02.01.2018, formal settlement agreement dated 05.03.2019, and NCLT withdrawal orders[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP admitted only Rs. 24,87,100/- and classified appellant as 'collateral' because the cash receipt of Rs. 29,74,900/- was absent from debtor accounts and the unit was double-allotted[cite: 25]. NCLT dismissed appellant's challenge, prompting this appeal[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional and Adjudicating Authority were justified in disallowing a portion of the financial creditor's claim on the ground that a cash receipt was not reflected in the corporate debtor's books, despite explicit acknowledgment in signed agreements and settlement deeds.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional cannot reject or curtail a financial debt claim substantiated by formal bilateral agreements and court-recorded settlement accords merely because an admitted cash receipt is omitted from the internal accounts maintained by the corporate debtor[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Claim verification under Section 60(5) of the IBC requires examination of composite legal documentation; the corporate debtor's failure to maintain proper accounting entries cannot defeat undisputed contractual acknowledgments[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where execution of Builder Buyer Agreements, Articles of Agreement, and a court-recognized settlement agreement containing explicit admissions of the entire received sum is undisputed, unprinted cash receipts cannot be discarded as unauthenticated[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP and the NCLT committed patent error in disregarding admitted contractual documents, warranting setting aside the claim reduction[cite: 25].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 225 of 2024 is allowed, and the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 21.11.2023 is set aside[cite: 25].
summary: Nirmal Jain appealed against an NCLT order upholding the Resolution Professional's decision to drastically reduce her admitted claim from Rs. 54,62,000/- to Rs. 24,87,100/- and reclassifying her as a collateral creditor[cite: 25]. The RP had disallowed Rs. 29,74,900/- on the ground that the cash payment was not reflected in the corporate debtor's books[cite: 25]. The NCLAT Principal Bench observed that the corporate debtor had explicitly acknowledged receipt of the entire Rs. 54,62,000/- in the Builder Buyer Agreement, the Articles of Agreement, and a formal 2019 settlement agreement recorded before the tribunal[cite: 25]. Holding that a debtor's failure to maintain proper accounts cannot prejudice an allottee whose payments were contractually admitted, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned order[cite: 25].

case_title: Priti Batra & Anr. vs. H.S. Oberoi Buildtech Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Priti Batra and Dhiraj Batra (homebuyers/allottees in the 'Earth Iconic' project), and Respondents are H.S. Oberoi Buildtech Private Limited (SRA) along with the Resolution Professionals of CEPL and EIL[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking and allotment of a residential unit in the 'Earth Iconic' project developed by EIL on land owned by CEPL, with partial payments deposited by the appellants[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in handover of the real estate unit due to the corporate insolvency of the developer and land-owning company[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claims submission deadline expired on 10.04.2019, CoC approved the resolution plan on 16.11.2019, and the Adjudicating Authority confirmed the plan on 15.03.2021[cite: 26]. Appellants filed their claim with the SRA in December 2023, and NCLT dismissed their application (IA 77 of 2024) on 24.10.2024[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Project allotment documents, payment records, approved resolution plan terms, and belated claim correspondence[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III rejected the appellants' IA No. 77 of 2024 seeking admission of their claims post-plan approval, leading to this statutory appeal under Section 61[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether a homebuyer can seek admission of a claim before the Successful Resolution Applicant more than two and a half years after the approval of the resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved by the Adjudicating Authority, all claims not part of the plan are legally extinguished, and no belated claim can be entertained against the Successful Resolution Applicant[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC accords finality to approved resolution plans, operating on the clean-slate principle to protect the revival of the corporate debtor from endless liabilities[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Undue delay of over 1700 days from the public claim notice and failure to avail the 12-month grace window under the resolution plan bars any equitable relief[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the application for claim admission since belated claims cannot be imposed on an approved and implemented resolution plan[cite: 26].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 129 of 2025 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 26].
summary: Appellants Priti Batra and Dhiraj Batra challenged an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting their application to compel the Successful Resolution Applicant (H.S. Oberoi Buildtech) to admit their claims in the 'Earth Iconic' project[cite: 26]. The claims were submitted more than two years and nine months after the resolution plan was sanctioned by the NCLT on March 15, 2021[cite: 26]. Applying the clean-slate doctrine established in Ghanshyam Mishra and RPS Infrastructure, the NCLAT held that all unsubmitted claims stand extinguished upon plan approval under Section 31 of the IBC[cite: 26]. Finding no error in the NCLT's refusal to reopen the resolution process, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 26].

case_title: Ketan C. Bagadia vs. Radhakrishnan Dharmarajan (Liquidator of Nexus Electro Steel Ltd.) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ketan C. Bagadia (Ex-Managing Director/Promoter of Nexus Electro Steel Ltd.), Respondent No. 1 is the Liquidator, and Respondent No. 2 is M/s. Chinar Steel Segment Centre Pvt. Ltd. (Auction Purchaser)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor Nexus Electro Steel Ltd. was ordered into liquidation on 09.09.2022. After three failed going-concern auctions, the liquidator issued an auction notice on 20.05.2023, successfully auctioning the debtor on 11.06.2023[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation following failure of CIRP; sale certificate was issued on 17.07.2023 and proceeds distributed[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Auction notice issued on 20.05.2023, auction conducted on 11.06.2023, sale certificate issued on 17.07.2023[cite: 27]. NCLT Chennai dismissed appellant's IA 1123/2023 on 11.03.2024, and this appeal was refiled after a 224-day delay on 23.12.2024[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auction sale notices, SCC minutes approving reserve prices, sale certificate dated 17.07.2023, and liquidator's progress reports showing full distribution of proceeds[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 1123 of 2023 seeking to annul the auction notice and condone delay in proposing a Section 230 compromise scheme[cite: 27]. NCLT dismissed the IA as infructuous due to finalized sale and distribution, prompting this appeal[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether an auction sale conducted during liquidation can be set aside and delay condoned for submitting a Section 230 compromise scheme after the sale certificate has been issued and proceeds distributed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A completed liquidation auction sale cannot be nullified to consider a belated compromise scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act once the auction has concluded, the sale certificate has been issued, and sale proceeds have been distributed to stakeholders[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 2B of the Liquidation Process Regulations mandates time-bound submission of compromise schemes; an ex-director cannot impede liquidation by tendering belated schemes after third-party rights have crystallized[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Dilatory conduct by the promoter in questioning auction proceedings coupled with unanimous SCC rejection of belated compromise proposals precludes appellate interference[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because third-party title crystallized upon issuance of the sale certificate and proceeds distribution was complete, the challenge to the auction was properly dismissed[cite: 27].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 36 / 2025 is dismissed, and all pending interlocutory applications stand closed[cite: 27].
summary: Ketan C. Bagadia, former Managing Director of Nexus Electro Steel Ltd., appealed an NCLT Chennai order dismissing his application to declare an auction notice void and condone delay in submitting a Section 230 compromise scheme[cite: 27]. The liquidator had conducted the auction on June 11, 2023, issued the sale certificate to Chinar Steel Segment Centre on July 17, 2023, and distributed the proceeds[cite: 27]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the appellant was guilty of inordinate delay and that a finalized auction sale where rights have crystallized in favor of a bona fide purchaser cannot be disturbed for a belated compromise scheme[cite: 27]. The appeal was accordingly dismissed[cite: 27].

case_title: J.K. Paper Fibre Resources vs. Sunit Jagdishchandra Shah (Resolution Professional of Shree Rajeshwaranand Paper Mills Limited)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is J.K. Paper Fibre Resources (operational creditor), and Respondent is Sunit Jagdishchandra Shah (Resolution Professional of Shree Rajeshwaranand Paper Mills Limited)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational debts arising from the supply of goods to corporate debtor Shree Rajeshwaranand Paper Mills Limited, which was admitted to CIRP on 07.12.2022[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The RP admitted appellant's claim of Rs. 7,40,60,531/- out of Rs. 7,61,15,758/- claimed, against a total operational debt pool of Rs. 18,34,60,969/-[cite: 28]. The approved plan offered Rs. 60 lakhs to operational creditors against a nil liquidation entitlement[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 07.12.2022. CoC approved Mercury Terra Firma's plan on 29.01.2024 with a 97.36% vote share, and NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-II approved it on 27.11.2024[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC minutes (specifically 17th and 23rd meetings), fair and liquidation valuation records, Form-G re-publication details, and resolution plan payout terms[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant appealed under Section 61 against the plan approval, citing CIRP breach of 330 days, failure to publish Form-G on the IBBI website, non-sharing of full valuation reports, and inequitable distribution under Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether the approval of a resolution plan by the NCLT is vitiated by CIRP extensions beyond 330 days, non-sharing of detailed valuation reports with operational creditors, or payment of Rs. 60 lakhs against admitted operational debts of Rs. 18.34 crores.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of demonstrable contraventions of Section 30(2), the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors approved by statutory majority is paramount and immune from judicial review regarding business decisions and financial payouts[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) requires payment to operational creditors of not less than their liquidation value under Section 53, which is fully satisfied when operational creditors receive positive payouts against a nil liquidation value[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Operational creditors who participate in CoC meetings without voting rights suffer no prejudice from receiving bare fair and liquidation values instead of detailed valuation reports where CoC records valid confidentiality grounds under Regulation 35(2)[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Extensions beyond 330 days granted by the Adjudicating Authority when the CoC was at an advanced stage of plan consideration are valid under the Essar Steel doctrine, warranting dismissal of the appeal[cite: 28].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 76 of 2025 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 28].
summary: Operational creditor J.K. Paper Fibre Resources challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-II order approving the resolution plan submitted by Mercury Terra Firma for Shree Rajeshwaranand Paper Mills Limited[cite: 28]. The appellant alleged procedural flaws, including CIRP extension beyond 330 days, omission of Form-G on the IBBI website, non-furnishing of full valuation reports, and an unfair payout of Rs. 60 lakhs against Rs. 18.34 crores in operational debt[cite: 28]. The NCLAT held that CIRP extensions nearing completion are permissible under Essar Steel, non-voting operational creditors cannot claim prejudice over valuation report confidentiality, and the payment exceeded their statutory minimum nil liquidation entitlement[cite: 28]. Reaffirming the commercial wisdom of the 97.36% CoC majority, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 28].

case_title: Manish Mukim vs. Ms. Rakhi & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Manish Mukim (suspended director of corporate debtor Chandrima Fashion Fabrics Private Limited), Respondent No. 1 is Ms. Rakhi (Proprietor of Srinivasa Cloth Mills, operational creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is Sanjay Khandelwal (IRP)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of fabric materials by the operational creditor to the corporate debtor under invoices raised between April 2019 and October 2019, followed by a formal Settlement Deed dated 31.01.2020 agreeing to a settled sum of Rs. 1,14,84,292/-[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed in the Section 9 application filed on 17.11.2020 was Rs. 1,14,54,363/-[cite: 29]. Barring one instalment of Rs. 10 lakhs due on 28.02.2020, eleven subsequent instalments fell due between 31.03.2020 and 31.12.2020[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised April-October 2019[cite: 29]; first Section 8 demand notice issued 25.11.2019[cite: 29]; Settlement Deed executed 31.01.2020[cite: 29]; second Section 8 demand notice issued 19.06.2020[cite: 29]; Section 9 petition filed 17.11.2020[cite: 29]; NCLT Kolkata admitted the petition on 24.04.2023[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Fabric supply invoices, Settlement Deed dated 31.01.2020 setting an instalment payment schedule, Section 8 demand notices, and receipts evidencing subsequent full settlement payment of Rs. 64,53,250/- to the operational creditor by July 2024[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 9 application on 24.04.2023[cite: 29]. Suspended director appealed, and the NCLAT stayed CIRP on 16.06.2023[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable when the majority of default instalments under a settlement deed occurred during the prohibited period under Section 10A of the IBC, causing the remaining legally actionable default to fall below the mandatory threshold of Rs. 1 crore under Section 4[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any default occurring during the suspension period under Section 10A of the IBC is completely barred from forming the basis of an insolvency petition, and if the remaining debt falling outside the Section 10A window fails to satisfy the statutory pecuniary threshold under Section 4, the application is non-maintainable[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A creates a complete statutory freeze for any default arising on or after 25.03.2020 for the notified period, and defaults occurring therein cannot be aggregated to meet the threshold under Section 4[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the agreed payment schedule demonstrated that only one instalment of Rs. 10 lakhs fell due prior to 25.03.2020, with all subsequent defaults falling squarely within the Section 10A prohibited window[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Excluding the Section 10A-protected defaults, the legally cognizable operational default was below Rs. 1 crore, rendering the Section 9 application invalid[cite: 29].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 617 of 2023 is allowed; the NCLT order dated 24.04.2023 admitting CIRP is set aside, and the corporate debtor is released from CIRP[cite: 29]. A cost of Rs. 1,00,000/- is imposed on the Operational Creditor for pursuing a vexatious application[cite: 29].
summary: Manish Mukim, suspended director of Chandrima Fashion Fabrics, appealed an NCLT Kolkata order admitting a Section 9 CIRP petition filed by operational creditor Srinivasa Cloth Mills based on breach of a settlement deed[cite: 29]. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that, under Section 10A of the IBC, defaults occurring between March 25, 2020, and the end of the notified suspension period cannot be counted toward insolvency initiation[cite: 29]. As only one Rs. 10 lakh instalment fell due prior to March 25, 2020, the actionable default failed to meet the Rs. 1 crore threshold under Section 4[cite: 29]. Noting that the operational creditor had also received the full settlement amount during appellate proceedings, the NCLAT set aside the admission order, terminated the CIRP, and imposed Rs. 1 lakh costs on the creditor[cite: 29].

case_title: Merico Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. / Nagri Farm Tea Co. Ltd. vs. Ram Ratan Modi (RP of Duncans Industries Ltd.) & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2189 of 2024 & No. 2291 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Merico Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd., Sammelan Tea & Beverages Pvt. Ltd., and Nagri Farm Tea Co. Ltd. (third-party entities in possession of tea gardens), and Respondents are Ram Ratan Modi (RP of Duncans Industries Ltd.) and Uniglobal Papers Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA)[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Duncans Industries Ltd., which ran tea gardens leased by the State of West Bengal[cite: 30]. SRA submitted a resolution plan approved by 99.20% vote share of the CoC and sanctioned by NCLT Kolkata on 18.10.2024[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a resolution plan approval and leasehold asset boundary dispute[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 05.03.2020[cite: 30]; NCLAT decided asset title of tea gardens on 02.08.2024[cite: 30]; NCLT Kolkata approved the SRA's resolution plan on 18.10.2024[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Government tea garden leases, MoUs executed with appellants, previous NCLAT judgment dated 02.08.2024 holding only three tea gardens as subsisting corporate debtor assets, and approved resolution plan clause 9.2.1[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata approved the resolution plan in IA (IB) No. 237/(KB)/2022 and granted SRA liberty to pursue or make renewal applications before the lessor State Government for expired tea estate leases, which appellants challenged[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction while approving a resolution plan by granting the SRA liberty to pursue lease renewal applications before the State Government for tea gardens whose leases had expired prior to CIRP[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The approval of a resolution plan permitting a successful resolution applicant to step into the corporate debtor's shoes and pursue statutory lease renewals with the lessor does not exceed tribunal jurisdiction or prejudice third parties, provided the adjudication expresses no opinion on the merits of renewal, which remains strictly within the lessor government's domain[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 approval conveys to the resolution applicant only existing rights and pending claims/applications of the corporate debtor without creating new substantive property titles beyond what the debtor held[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where previous appellate rulings have conclusively demarcated which properties constitute corporate debtor assets and which do not, a mere administrative liberty to apply for lease renewal cannot infringe upon possessory claims of non-stakeholder entities[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's order did not decide the grant or rejection of renewals, leaving it entirely to the discretion of the State of West Bengal[cite: 30].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2189 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2291 of 2024 are dismissed with the clarification that the Adjudicating Authority expressed no opinion on the merits of lease renewals[cite: 30].
summary: Entities operating tea estates formerly leased to Duncans Industries Ltd. appealed an NCLT Kolkata order approving the resolution plan submitted by Uniglobal Papers Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 30]. The appellants objected to plan provisions granting the Successful Resolution Applicant liberty to pursue lease renewals with the State of West Bengal for tea gardens whose lease periods had expired[cite: 30]. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that upon plan approval, the resolution applicant steps into the shoes of the corporate debtor to pursue pending or fresh renewal applications[cite: 30]. Clarifying that the NCLT's directions did not adjudicate the merits of lease renewal, which remains solely within the prerogative of the State Government, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals[cite: 30].

case_title: Darwin Platform Infrastructure Limited vs. Union Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Darwin Platform Infrastructure Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA), and Respondents are Union Bank of India, State Bank of India, consortium lenders, and the RP of Lavasa Corporation Limited[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Lavasa Corporation Limited commenced on 30.08.2018[cite: 31]. SRA's resolution plan was approved by CoC on 13.12.2021 and sanctioned by NCLT on 21.07.2023, requiring Rs. 100 crore upfront payment within 90 days of the effective date (25.07.2023) and submission of a Rs. 25 crore PBG[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: SRA failed to infuse the upfront payment of Rs. 100 crore and required CIRP costs within 90 days or at any point over 409 days following the effective date[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Effective date achieved 25.07.2023[cite: 31]; upfront payment was due by 23.10.2023[cite: 31]; lenders decided to invoke PBG on 06.04.2024[cite: 31]; PBG invoked on 08.04.2024[cite: 31]; NCLT passed the impugned order on 06.09.2024[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved resolution plan terms, Monitoring Committee minutes (notably the 7th meeting dated 19.03.2024), Joint Lenders Meeting records, PBG invocation letters, and lack of deposit records[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SRA filed IA 1956/2024 challenging PBG invocation, while UBI filed IA 2520/2024 seeking CIRP re-initiation[cite: 31]. NCLT Mumbai rejected SRA's IA and allowed UBI's IA, reviving CIRP[cite: 31]. SRA appealed[cite: 31].
legal_issues: Whether the lenders were justified in invoking and forfeiting the Performance Bank Guarantee under CIRP Regulation 36B(4A) and whether the Adjudicating Authority rightly re-initiated CIRP when the SRA failed to make mandatory upfront payments beyond agreed implementation schedules[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adherence to implementation timelines is an essential pillar of the IBC, and an SRA that fails to infuse mandatory upfront funds within the scheduled period is liable to have its Performance Bank Guarantee forfeited under Regulation 36B(4A), empowering the tribunal to revive the resolution process[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Regulation 36B(4A) of the CIRP Regulations, performance security stands forfeited if the resolution applicant fails to implement or contributes to the failure of implementation of the approved plan[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pendency of collateral litigation or appeals without an express stay does not justify an SRA's complete failure to infuse funds for over a year[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Darwin Platform failed to demonstrate bona fide intent or infuse upfront capital after over 400 days, the PBG encashment and revival of CIRP were lawful[cite: 31].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 2012-2013 of 2024 are dismissed, upholding the NCLT order encashing the PBG and re-initiating CIRP[cite: 31].
summary: Darwin Platform Infrastructure Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant for Lavasa Corporation, challenged an NCLT Mumbai order that upheld the forfeiture of its Rs. 25 crore Performance Bank Guarantee and re-initiated CIRP due to non-implementation[cite: 31]. The appellant failed to pay the required Rs. 100 crore upfront infusion within 90 days, citing pending appeals as justification[cite: 31]. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that in the absence of a judicial stay, ongoing litigation cannot excuse total non-compliance with plan timelines[cite: 31]. Over 409 days having elapsed without any capital infusion, the Appellate Tribunal affirmed that under Regulation 36B(4A), the lenders were fully entitled to forfeit the PBG and restore CIRP[cite: 31].

case_title: ATA Freight Line (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Registrar of Companies, Mumbai & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is ATA Freight Line (India) Pvt. Ltd. (creditor of struck-off company), Respondent No. 1 is Registrar of Companies (RoC) Mumbai, and Respondent No. 2 is Sun Clearing and Forwarding Services Pvt. Ltd. (the struck-off debtor company)[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant was an operational creditor of Respondent No. 2, which owed a principal sum of Rs. 43,49,134/- with interest[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of debt of Rs. 43,49,134/- leading creditor to seek revival of debtor company to recover dues[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RoC struck off Respondent No. 2's name; Appellant filed CP No. 372/2021 under Section 252(3); NCLT allowed petition with clerical error on 22.03.2022; NCLT dismissed modification application IA 106/2022 on 11.10.2022[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC report stating no objection to restoring Respondent No. 2 in the interest of creditors, and averments in CP 372/2021 specifically praying for restoration of Respondent No. 2[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai mistakenly restored the petitioner's own name instead of the struck-off company's name on 22.03.2022, and subsequently refused to rectify the error by dismissing IA 106/2022[cite: 32]. This appeal was filed challenging the refusal to rectify[cite: 32].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in dismissing a modification application filed under Section 252(3) to correct a clerical error where the tribunal inadvertently ordered the restoration of the creditor applicant's name instead of the struck-off debtor company's name[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority must correct accidental clerical or drafting errors in its orders where the pleadings, creditor standing, and regulatory reports unequivocally establish that restoration was sought for the struck-off debtor company rather than the creditor applicant[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 expressly allows a creditor to seek restoration of a struck-off company to enable recovery of outstanding debts[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pleadings in the company petition and the RoC's explicit no-objection report clearly demonstrated that the relief claimed was the revival of the debtor entity[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT took a hyper-technical approach in denying the rectification of its own inadvertent mistake, warranting modification of the order[cite: 32].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 39 of 2023 is allowed, and the NCLT order dated 11.10.2022 is modified to the extent that Respondent No. 2, M/s Sun Clearing and Forwarding Services Pvt. Ltd., is restored to the Register of Companies maintained by RoC Mumbai[cite: 32].
summary: ATA Freight Line, a creditor of struck-off entity Sun Clearing and Forwarding Services Pvt. Ltd., filed a petition under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act to restore the debtor company to recover its dues of Rs. 43.49 lakhs[cite: 32]. The RoC issued a no-objection, but the NCLT Mumbai mistakenly entered the petitioner's name instead of the debtor's name in the operative restoration order, and later refused to rectify this error[cite: 32]. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that the record clearly showed the creditor was seeking the revival of the debtor company and that the NCLT erred in failing to correct its clerical error[cite: 32]. The appeal was allowed, and the restoration of the debtor company was ordered[cite: 32].

case_title: Tata Capital Ltd. vs. Arjun Agarwal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Tata Capital Ltd. (transferee of Tata Capital Financial Services Ltd., financial creditor), and Respondent is Arjun Agarwal (Personal Guarantor to Corporate Debtor)[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan and credit facilities extended by the financial creditor covered by personal guarantees executed by the respondent[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the personal guarantor in satisfying invocation of the personal guarantee[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial creditor filed an application under Section 95(1) against the personal guarantor; NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the petition on 08.01.2025[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, personal guarantee deeds, demand notices, and NCLT Kolkata dismissal order holding Section 95 non-maintainable without a pending corporate debtor CIRP[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed the Section 95 petition on the sole ground that no CIRP or liquidation proceeding was pending against the principal corporate debtor, which the financial creditor appealed[cite: 33].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 95 of the IBC against a personal guarantor is maintainable before the NCLT when no insolvency resolution process or liquidation is pending against the principal corporate debtor[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 95(1) of the IBC by a financial creditor against a personal guarantor is maintainable before the NCLT irrespective of whether any corporate insolvency resolution process or liquidation proceeding is pending against the principal corporate debtor[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As settled in State Bank of India vs. Mahendra Kumar Jajodia (affirmed by the Supreme Court) and Anita Goyal vs. Vistara ITCL, the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority to entertain Section 95 petitions against personal guarantors is independent of ongoing corporate debtor proceedings[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prior NCLT orders declaring Section 95 non-maintainable in the absence of a pending CIRP run counter to binding appellate precedents and are per incuriam[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in rejecting the Section 95 petition at the threshold on maintainability, requiring its revival for adjudication on merits[cite: 33].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 345 of 2025 is allowed; the NCLT order dated 08.01.2025 is set aside, and the Section 95 application is revived before the Adjudicating Authority for consideration on merits[cite: 33].
summary: Tata Capital Ltd. appealed an NCLT Kolkata order that dismissed its Section 95 application against personal guarantor Arjun Agarwal on the ground that no CIRP was pending against the corporate debtor[cite: 33]. Following the precedent in *Anita Goyal vs. Vistara ITCL* and the Supreme Court-affirmed decision in *SBI vs. Mahendra Kumar Jajodia*, the NCLAT Principal Bench held that an insolvency petition against a personal guarantor under Section 95 is maintainable before the NCLT even in the absence of pending CIRP or liquidation proceedings against the principal debtor[cite: 33]. The appeal was allowed, the dismissal order was set aside, and the application was revived for determination on merits[cite: 33].

case_title: The Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner, Employees' Provident Fund Organisation vs. Shri Amier Hamsa Ali Abbas Rawther (Liquidator of M/s. Floram Shoes (India) Pvt. Ltd.)
appeal_number: Contempt App. 2/2025 in Comp. App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 35/2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is The Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (EPFO), and Respondent is Shri Amier Hamsa Ali Abbas Rawther (Liquidator of M/s. Floram Shoes (India) Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: EPFO submitted claims in the liquidation proceedings of corporate debtor Floram Shoes (India) Pvt. Ltd., which were subject to redetermination following earlier appellate directions[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory provident fund dues claimed against the corporate debtor[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLAT rendered judgment in CA (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 35/2024 on 19.11.2024 directing the liquidator to reconsider appellant's claims within three weeks of receiving supporting documents[cite: 35]. The liquidator concluded proceedings and reserved final orders, after which appellant initiated contempt proceedings[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLAT judgment dated 19.11.2024, claim documents submitted before the liquidator, and records showing the liquidator concluded hearings and reserved orders[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant initiated contempt proceedings alleging non-compliance and procedural impropriety by the liquidator regarding the directions in paragraph 4 of the order dated 19.11.2024[cite: 35].
legal_issues: Whether a contempt application under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable against a liquidator for alleged procedural lapses when the liquidator has concluded the remand proceedings and reserved orders subject to substantive appellate remedy[cite: 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Contempt proceedings cannot be used as a substitute for judicial review or appeal to challenge procedural shortcomings or decisions of a liquidator who has acted upon remand directions and concluded proceedings[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not cover situations where the underlying order has been substantively acted upon and consequential decisions remain subject to independent statutory appeal[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Showing that the liquidator concluded the claim re-examination and reserved final orders negates willful disobedience of remand instructions[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because grievances regarding the liquidator's determinations must be agitated in substantive appellate proceedings rather than contempt, the contempt petition is non-maintainable[cite: 35].
operative_order: Contempt Application No. 2/2025 is dismissed, leaving all substantive contentions open for the appellant to argue before an appropriate appellate forum[cite: 35].
summary: The Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner (EPFO) filed a contempt application against the Liquidator of Floram Shoes (India) Pvt. Ltd., alleging willful disobedience of NCLAT directions dated November 19, 2024, which had directed the liquidator to reconsider EPFO's claim[cite: 35]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench observed that the liquidator had already conducted the proceedings and reserved final orders[cite: 35]. Holding that any procedural lapses or grievances regarding the liquidator's determination must be challenged through substantive appellate remedies rather than disguised under Section 425 contempt proceedings, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the contempt application[cite: 35].

case_title: Kamal Kumar Harlalka vs. Sudha Sarma (Liquidator) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kamal Kumar Harlalka (suspended director of the corporate debtor), and Respondent No. 1 is CS Sudha Sarma (Liquidator)[cite: 36]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor underwent liquidation, and during the process the company was sold as a going concern to a successful auction purchaser[cite: 36]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a post-liquidation sale proceeding regarding locus to pursue pending civil litigation[cite: 36]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed orders on 18.12.2023 regarding liquidation and sale; NCLT Guwahati dismissed IA No. 117/GB/2024 on 20.12.2024[cite: 36]. This appeal was filed with an 11-day delay, which was condoned[cite: 36]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Title Suit No. 334 of 2021 filed by the corporate debtor against a financial creditor in Civil Court, liquidation estate records, going-concern auction sale documents, and distribution reports[cite: 36]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The suspended director filed IA 117/GB/2024 before NCLT Guwahati seeking leave to pursue Title Suit No. 334/2021; NCLT dismissed the application for lack of locus standi, which was appealed[cite: 36].
