legal_issues: Whether a suspended director of a corporate debtor that has been sold as a going concern during liquidation possesses locus standi to pursue and defend a pending title suit on behalf of the corporate debtor[cite: 36].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate debtor is sold as a going concern during liquidation, all rights, assets, and litigations belonging to the debtor transfer to the purchaser/liquidator, divesting the suspended director of any locus standi to pursue litigation on the corporate debtor's behalf[cite: 36]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 33 and Section 35 of the IBC, the statutory authority to institute, defend, or continue legal proceedings on behalf of the corporate debtor vests exclusively in the liquidator (or the going-concern acquirer) to the exclusion of suspended management[cite: 36]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Establishing that the liquidation estate has been fully auctioned and proceeds distributed precludes ex-directors from reviving separate possessory or litigation rights over debtor assets[cite: 36]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the suspended director's leave application, as granting such leave would undermine the going-concern sale[cite: 36].
operative_order: Comp. App (AT) (Ins) No. 287 of 2025 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 36].
summary: Kamal Kumar Harlalka, suspended director of a corporate debtor, appealed an NCLT Guwahati order refusing him leave to pursue Title Suit No. 334 of 2021 against a financial creditor in civil court[cite: 36]. The Adjudicating Authority had noted that the corporate debtor had already been sold as a going concern and its liquidation estate distributed[cite: 36]. The NCLAT Principal Bench affirmed that under Section 33 of the IBC, the statutory right to represent and pursue litigation on behalf of a corporate debtor vests exclusively in the liquidator and the successful going-concern purchaser[cite: 36]. Finding that the ex-director lacked locus standi, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 36].

case_title: M/s. Mantri Developers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ace Enviro Tech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: IA Nos. 1293 & 1295/2024 in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 129/2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant is M/s. Mantri Developers Pvt. Ltd. (49.99% shareholder of corporate debtor Tarun Realtors Pvt. Ltd.), and Respondents include Ace Enviro Tech Pvt. Ltd. (operational creditor) and financial creditors[cite: 37]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 9 application admitted against Tarun Realtors Pvt. Ltd. on 20.07.2023[cite: 37]. An appeal was initially filed by suspended director S. Baaskaran, who subsequently resigned on 12.08.2024[cite: 37]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt leading to CIRP admission on 20.07.2023[cite: 37]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Admission order passed on 20.07.2023[cite: 37]; NCLAT dismissed the appeal on 14.10.2024 upon director's resignation[cite: 37]; Supreme Court directed CIRP continuation on 22.11.2024[cite: 37]; Karnataka High Court remanded recall consideration on 10.12.2024[cite: 37]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resignation letter of suspended director S. Baaskaran dated 12.08.2024, shareholding records showing Mantri Developers holding 49.99%, and High Court/Supreme Court writ and SLP orders[cite: 37]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following dismissal of the appeal on 14.10.2024 due to the sole appellant's resignation, the shareholder filed recall applications IA Nos. 1293 & 1295/2024 seeking substitution and revival of the appeal[cite: 37].
legal_issues: Whether a shareholder can maintain an application under Section 151 CPC to recall an order dismissing an appeal and substitute itself in place of a suspended director who resigned during appellate proceedings[cite: 37].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A shareholder cannot substitute itself in place of a resigned suspended director to maintain or revive an appeal challenging CIRP admission, nor can an appellate tribunal exercise general recall powers under Section 151 CPC outside strictly defined procedural fraud exceptions[cite: 37]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The power of recall is not an inherent general power of the NCLAT and is confined strictly to the narrow parameters laid down by the Five-Judge Bench in *Union Bank of India vs. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramaniam*[cite: 37]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The status of a shareholder is legally distinct from that of a suspended director; when an appeal initiated by a director becomes non-maintainable upon resignation, a single non-majority shareholder cannot step into the director's shoes to sustain the challenge[cite: 37]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The recall application was misconceived as the tribunal lacked jurisdiction to substitute the shareholder or reopen the dismissed appeal[cite: 37].
operative_order: IA Nos. 1293 and 1295 of 2024 are dismissed, and the dismissal order dated 14.10.2024 is confirmed[cite: 37].
summary: Mantri Developers, a 49.99% shareholder of Tarun Realtors Pvt. Ltd., filed applications to recall an NCLAT order dated October 14, 2024, which had dismissed the company appeal against CIRP admission because the suspended director representing the appeal had resigned[cite: 37]. The applicant sought to be substituted in place of the director to keep the challenge alive[cite: 37]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that tribunal recall powers under *Union Bank of India vs. Dinkar Venkatasubramaniam* are strictly limited and cannot be invoked under Section 151 CPC[cite: 37]. Furthermore, a shareholder holds a statutorily distinct status and cannot be substituted for a resigned director to maintain an insolvency appeal[cite: 37]. The recall applications were accordingly dismissed[cite: 37].

case_title: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority vs. Sandeep Gupta, Shalini Gupta & Anoop Kumar Mittal (SRA) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA, operational creditor), and Respondents are the Successful Resolution Applicant consortium (Sandeep Gupta & Ors.) and the Resolution Professional[cite: 38]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of leasehold land to the corporate debtor; GNIDA submitted claims in CIRP for over Rs. 21 crores, of which Rs. 18,24,96,973/- was admitted[cite: 38]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in lease dues and premium; the resolution plan proposed Rs. 6,79,07,777/- to GNIDA as full and final satisfaction[cite: 38]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved on 24.08.2023; GNIDA's appeal against plan approval dismissed as time-barred on 21.02.2024; SRA filed IA 2233/2024 to compel compliance, disposed of on 03.10.2024, prompting this appeal[cite: 38]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease agreements, admitted claim records, CoC-approved resolution plan, escrow deposit receipts of Rs. 6.79 crores, and previous dismissal orders on limitation[cite: 38]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT directed GNIDA to accept the escrow deposit in IA 2233/2024 on 03.10.2024 since plan approval had attained finality[cite: 38]. GNIDA appealed claiming status as a secured creditor under the *Prabhjit Singh Soni* precedent[cite: 38].
legal_issues: Whether a statutory authority can challenge its financial payout under an approved resolution plan after its appeal against the plan approval order has been dismissed and attained finality[cite: 38].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once an order approving a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC attains finality after an unsuccessful appeal, a creditor cannot indirectly challenge the quantum or classification of its payout in collateral execution proceedings[cite: 38]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 binds all creditors and authorities to the approved resolution plan, and questions of entitlement or secured status cannot be reopened once plan approval is final[cite: 38]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Finality of the approval order dated 24.08.2023 bars re-adjudication of debt classification or entitlement under subsequent case law[cite: 38]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly directed GNIDA to accept the deposited amount, as the approved resolution plan was binding and immutable[cite: 38].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 320 of 2025 is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 38].
summary: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) appealed an NCLT order directing it to accept Rs. 6.79 crores deposited by the Successful Resolution Applicant in full satisfaction of its claim[cite: 38]. GNIDA argued that pursuant to the Supreme Court's ruling in *Prabhjit Singh Soni*, it was entitled to be treated as a secured operational creditor and receive a higher payout[cite: 38]. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that because GNIDA's previous appeal against the resolution plan approval order had been dismissed as time-barred, the plan approval had attained absolute finality under Section 31 of the IBC[cite: 38]. A creditor cannot re-litigate its payout in collateral implementation proceedings, and the appeal was accordingly dismissed[cite: 38].
